Australian army whistleblower released on parole after more than two years in jail
- Published
A whistleblower jailed for leaking military secrets about Australia's involvement in Afghanistan has been released on parole after serving 27 months.
In 2024, David McBride was sentenced to five years and eight months after pleading guilty to stealing top secret defence documents and giving it to the media.
His actions later led to a landmark inquiry that found evidence that Australian forces had unlawfully killed 39 Afghans during the war.
On Thursday, a spokesperson for the Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said McBride's "parole was considered and granted". The ex-military lawyer, who is being treated for lung cancer, will serve the rest of his sentence in the community under supervision.
Shortly after the decision, advocacy group The Information Rights Project released a statement on McBride's behalf, according to national broadcaster ABC.
He thanked his family "who never gave up on me and whose fighting spirit, love and humour inspired me every day" and praised "all my amazing supporters from around both Australia and the world who sent me such inspirational messages".
McBride also revealed that he had been diagnosed with treatable lung cancer and would be having surgery to remove part of his lung.
His lawyer Edwina Lloyd described the decision to grant his parole as "the right one", in a statement according to the ABC.
She said McBride's life has been "defined by service to Australia", both as a legal officer for the Australian Defence Forces (ADF) and having served time for his crimes.
During his court case, prosecutors argued that McBride's actions had been motivated by "personal vindication", and that the way he gathered, stored and then leaked the documents endangered Australia's national security and foreign policy.
But McBride's lawyers asked for leniency, saying he shared the information with "honourable" intentions and out of a sense of personal duty.
In sentencing McBride, the judge said while he was of "good character", sharing military secrets was a "gross breach of trust" and he had shown "no contrition" for his actions.
The material he leaked to the ABC underpinned a series of reports in 2017 called The Afghan Files which provided unprecedented insight into Australia's elite special forces in Afghanistan, including allegations of war crimes.
In 2020, the Brereton Report found "credible evidence" that elite soldiers have unlawfully killed 39 people.
A special watchdog - the Office of the Special Investigator - was set up to look into the actions of 19 ADF members. Of its 53 cases, 39 have been finalised and two former Special Air Service (SAS) soldiers have been charged.
Ben Roberts-Smith, Australia's most decorated living soldier, is facing five counts of the war crime of murder after he was charged earlier this year, while Oliver Schulz faces one count of the same charge.

They own 2 excavators in Gaza and can't keep up with demand as families dig for remains
Old machinery, shortages of parts, fuel and oil, make retrieving remains from rubble slow, painstaking work
In the heart of Gaza City, several members of the Al-Drimli family dig for the remains of their friend and neighbour in the rubble of their former home, using only shovels, buckets, a wheelbarrow and their hands.
It's the middle of the day on Monday and the sun's rays are strong. The men work in silence, their heads covered by orange towels or the hoods of sweatshirts. The sounds of shovels clanging in rubble and the buzz of an electric saw fill the air.
The men fill the dusty wheelbarrow with rubble and wheel it to a nearby pile — it barely puts a dent in the mounds of broken cinder block and metal rebar remaining from the six-storey residential building that was hit by an airstrike in November 2023.
The Al-Drimli family had already recovered the remains of their loved ones at the site and is now looking for a neighbour who was sheltering with them when a strike destroyed the building.
The Gaza Health Ministry estimates that there are between 8,000 and 10,000 bodies still under the rubble almost three years after the start of the war between Israel and Hamas.
"We work with our hands because the cost of equipment today is very expensive and unavailable," Ayman Al-Drimli told CBC News freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife.
Officials and heavy equipment operators in Gaza say there are currently only about a dozen barely functioning excavators in the strip. They say the machines, which were frequently targeted by strikes during the war, are difficult to maintain under current conditions, which include a lack of parts for repair as well as oil and fuel shortages.
Excavators in high demand
Samir Sabra and his son, Uday Sabra, run two excavators in the Gaza Strip. He says the oil alone needed to run one excavator costs at least 2,500 shekels (about $1,175 Cdn) — not a price he can easily afford.
"We can't run the equipment like this," he told CBC on Monday. "There is no maintenance, no equipment and no spare parts."
Later that day, his son was at a different site just off the main road in Gaza City digging for remains with members of the Palestinian Civil Defence, a volunteer organization of first responders who visit strike sites to search for survivors and recover bodies.
"People call us every day," Uday said, noting he and his father can't keep up with the demand for their services. "There isn't enough equipment for the work because there are so many martyrs under the rubble."
He says he's been working at this site for a week and isn't done yet.
"The amount of damage and destruction in this country, one machine or two machines won't do anything."
Equipment targeted during war
Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for the Palestinian Civil Defence, says there still aren't many excavators available in the strip because they were targeted by strikes during the war.
"There was a policy and strategy of the Israeli army to destroy this equipment," he said.
The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) did not respond to questions from CBC News about strikes targeting heavy machinery in the strip.
Basal says Civil Defence hires out only one excavator at a time to avoid making the situation worse.
“We are working with the International Committee for the Red Cross on this group of victims under the rubble with one digger who works three days and stops for one day for maintenance,” he said at the site in Gaza City where Uday Sabra was working.
Basal says that despite last October's ceasefire agreement, which included a point on allowing more heavy machinery and equipment to clear rubble and roads, there hasn’t been a change on the ground.
"If we remain in this situation in Gaza," he said, "we are talking about long years of … removing the bodies from under the rubble."
Border restrictions
Humanitarian aid groups have stated that Israeli restrictions on fuel, oil and spare parts are hampering efforts to maintain machinery like hospital generators, ambulances, water pumps and water trucks.
The United Nations notes that restrictions on the entry of heavy equipment have slowed the process of reaching and recovering remains, and Civil Defence recently urged the international community to act to get machinery into the strip to help do this.

In a statement to CBC News, the IDF said it fulfils its obligations under international law, noting that the policy for the entry of heavy equipment into the strip is "determined based on security considerations" and "in accordance with directions from the political echelon."
The statement also said "fuel tankers enter Gaza every day via international organizations."
Back at the site in Gaza City, Uday continued to dig, slowly but surely making a dent in the mounds of rubble.
He says he will keep coming back until he can recover the remains and give the dead some peace.

Ex-Cambridge professor who faced plagiarism claims, weeks of public scrutiny, found dead
Jason Arday, who was university's youngest Black professor, resigned earlier this month
A British sociologist who resigned last week from the University of Cambridge following weeks of public accusations of plagiarism and media scrutiny was found dead Friday.
Jason Arday, who became Cambridge's youngest Black professor in 2023 at age 37, resigned after coming under intense media pressure over allegations of plagiarism in his academic work and questions surrounding claims about his athletic and fundraising accomplishments.
The Times and Telegraph newspapers, along with the BBC and Sky News, reported that Arday, 41, was found "unresponsive" inside a home in Battersea, south London, on Friday afternoon.
In a statement issued by his publisher, Simon & Schuster U.K., Arday's family said they were "in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."
"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone," the family said, adding that for three years Arday was "subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse … by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him."
The Metropolitan Police said only that a 41-year-old man was pronounced dead in Battersea, without naming the man, in accordance with its policy.
"At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," the police statement said.
Cambridge vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice, who earlier announced that the university would investigate the circumstances surrounding Arday's employment, said she was "desperately saddened" by the news.
"Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," she said.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Arday's death was "a tragedy on so many levels."
"It's not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It's a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this," Burnham told reporters.
London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Arday had been "the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn't have faced."
Former Conservative home secretary James Cleverly, who is Black, wrote on X that academic institutions "have serious questions to answer."
"They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a Black wunderkind to show off; they pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit," he said.
'Profound toll'
In resigning as professor of sociology of education, Arday wrote in a statement that "the relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
He said his stepping down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me." He has denied plagiarism, but admitted to some mistakes when working on his doctorate.
Supporters, including more than two dozen academics and politicians, had described the plagiarism allegations as a "smear campaign" designed to undermine Arday and other Black people who hold "positions of influence."
Arday's appointment at Cambridge highlighted his personal story of overcoming dyslexia, developmental delays and autism that he said left him non-verbal until the age of 11 and illiterate until his late teens.
Cambridge opens investigation into accusations
Questions about Arday's qualifications were raised publicly last month by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the university after his criticism of diversity, equity and inclusion programs sparked widespread protests.
On July 24, the Times published an analysis of Arday's 2015 PhD thesis highlighting what it said were multiple examples of passages that were "identical or near-identical" to an earlier paper written by another researcher.
British media also raised questions about Arday's claims that he had raised 5.5 million pounds ($10.3 million) for charity through feats such as running 30 marathons in 35 days and 600 miles in six days.
Dozens of Cambridge academics had signed a letter calling for an independent inquiry into how Arday was appointed. Cambridge initially stood by Arday, saying that the plagiarism allegations had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University, which awarded Arday's doctorate.
The university then changed its stance and said it opened an investigation "following new information about Professor Arday's qualifications and honorary appointments."
Prentice said this week that Cambridge would review its hiring processes. She stressed that "our staff of color are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community."
"This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge," she said Thursday.

The Trump administration is recruiting private security firms to conduct federal government-authorized operations, including cyber attacks, against overseas-based criminal organizations that commit hacks on US persons, organizations, or government entities.
In a National Security Presidential Memorandum issued Thursday, US President Donald Trump directed the National Coordination Center (NCC), which operates under the Homeland Security Task Force, to develop a program for conducting specific cyber operations that combat foreign transnational criminal organizations (TCOs). The Departments of Justice and Homeland Security will provide oversight. The lynchpin of that program is bringing in private sector companies to participate.
Devil will be in the still-undefined details
A fact sheet that accompanied Thursday’s memo listed ransomware, sextortion schemes, phishing campaigns, financial fraud, and impersonation scams as activities eligible for private-sector security firms to target. The memo said such firms could “conduct Cyber Surveillance Operations and Cyber Effects Operations” against “cyber-enabled” TCOs. Such groups are defined as “any foreign group that conducts cyber-enabled crime against the United States Government, a United States person, or United States interests, and that is not an institutional part of a foreign government or wholly operated under a foreign government’s direction.”
The new program is the first time the federal government will authorize private companies to conduct offensive cyber operations against overseas hackers. The memo appears to permit companies participating in the program to use spyware or launch offensive attacks intended to destroy TCO data or systems. The memo doesn’t rule out certain types of offensive attacks, such as those that use encryption to lock targets out of their networks or performing DDoSes. Up until now, the government has prohibited the private sector from taking such actions without court-authorized approval.

Somewhere along the county road between Independence and Manchester, I lost Rob Sand.
This had been a distinct possibility when I agreed to join the 44-year-old Democratic candidate for governor on a segment of a weeklong bike ride across Iowa. Unlike Sand, I am not a biker—merely a leisurely walker and, like any good Millennial woman, an occasional Pilates-doer. Which is why, on a long, low-grade hill dotted with Queen Anne’s lace, my quads began to burn, my pace slowed, and the subject of my story disappeared into a rainbow river of helmets. A minute later, the sag wagon overtook me. Soon so did a 9-year-old boy.
Thankfully, my humiliation was short-lived. These days in Iowa, one can never truly be without Rob Sand. Even as I panted alone at the back of the peloton, I could hear people chattering about the man who would be governor. “Was that who I think it was?” they said. And, “Oh, I just love him!” At one point, a fit-looking cyclist who turned out to be the former NFL wide receiver Tim Dwight pulled up beside me to lament Iowa’s unfulfilled economic potential. “This is why,” he said, “we need Rob.”
Sand, the state auditor, is ubiquitous in Iowa. On any given day, one might encounter him in a TV ad, promising jail time for corrupt politicians; on Instagram, talking through a mouthful of Casey’s breakfast pizza; and at a town hall singing “America the Beautiful” with a bipartisan crowd of gray hairs. Sand is something rarely found in nature: a successful Iowa Democrat. Which is perhaps why his presence generates such mania. Biking with him across the state felt a little like showing up to a middle-school slumber party with Taylor Swift—or riding shotgun in the popemobile. Despite Sand’s bike helmet and lack of signage, hundreds of people recognized him and begged for selfies. “I nearly killed Iowa’s next governor!” yelled a man in Winthrop who bumped into Sand’s bike. People often used both his first and last name, running them together into a single word. “I lent my bike pump to Robsand!” another man declared in Independence.
Sand’s party has struggled to gain purchase in Iowa since the dawn of the Trump era, and a Democrat hasn’t been elected governor since 2006. The funny thing is, Sand is not a particularly proud Democrat. He tends to refer to the party as “the lesser of two evils” and made a face when I asked whether he enjoyed being in it. “I can’t imagine saying I like being in any political party,” he told me. “I love being a dad.” Before addressing a crowd in Des Moines County last year, Sand’s staff asked for party insignia to be removed from the walls to make the space more inclusive.
The auditor obviously wants to steer clear of the national party’s noxious fumes. But whereas his progressive contemporaries distance themselves by railing against the establishment, Sand’s campaign approach has been different: Quietly, and with an easygoing optimism that Fred Rogers would envy, Sand questions the concept of partisanship itself. “Our political system is broken, and it’s broken mostly because it’s run by two private clubs” that make voters “feel trapped” into making a binary choice, he told a crowd last month in Newton. “The good news is that Iowa is a place where we have typically said we are going to make politics work for ordinary people.”
National Democrats like what they see—even if they find it tough to describe. Sand “is doing the opposite of what almost every other politician is doing,” the strategist and former Pete Buttigieg adviser Lis Smith told me. He isn’t a loud progressive, but he also doesn’t sound like a corporate moderate, Adam Carlson, a pollster, agreed. “Sand is doing a third thing.”
In November, Sand will be up against a potentially strong GOP candidate. But his most daunting adversary will be the math: Registered Republicans outnumber Democrats by almost 200,000 in Iowa. Which means that Sand plans to spend the next 11 weeks telling Iowans that he can be trusted, in spite of the D behind his name. Will enough of them believe it?
Sand had been annoyed the last time I wrote about him. I’d included all of the relevant background details in my story: that he grew up in Decorah, a town near the Minnesota border, which explains his long vowels (Sand pronounces it “Dee-corah”); that he went to Brown University and worked a few modeling jobs in Europe before attending law school and working for seven years as a prosecutor. I’d explained that, like any good red-state Democrat, Sand loves to hunt and spends Sunday morning in church—and that his wife’s brothers called him “Baby Jesus” for his tendency toward self-righteousness.
But Sand was concerned about something else: that I had not fully captured his frustration with America’s two-party political system. “I was hoping you’d get more into election reform,” he texted me—a sentence that, I am confident, no one has ever said before or since. At the time, I did not imagine that many readers were pining to hear a state auditor’s thoughts on the decline of bipartisanship. But here we are, three summers later, and Sand is still talking about the same ideas: moving to an open-primary system and implementing “approval voting,” which would allow Iowans to support more than one candidate. More remarkable, voters are listening.
Sand is a Democrat because “Jesus is for the little guy, and the Democratic Party, at its best, is for the little guy.” But his more inclusive vision wouldn’t require party affiliation. The scramble to replace Graham Platner in Maine, for example, wouldn’t have happened under Sand’s system, he said. Or, “if a really old candidate, hypothetically, had a bad debate experience, and everyone was like, Um, maybe this person is too old to do this, it wouldn’t be a crisis.” The reforms would reward civility, Sand added, and prevent one-party domination of a state.
Republicans have had total control over Iowa for a decade. In that time, they’ve dramatically cut income taxes, redirected hundreds of millions of public dollars toward private schools, and restricted abortion after six weeks. Right now, the state is facing a $1 billion budget shortfall and the second-highest cancer rate in the country.
But Sand does not harp on Republicans. Actually, a Sand political event doesn’t really feel like one: Each town hall begins with a round of applause for the Republicans, independents, and Democrats (for good measure) who showed up, then transitions into a group rendition of “America the Beautiful.” Sand speaks for a while about his policy priorities (corruption, public education, affordability) before opening the floor to questions, some friendly and others confrontational. The event I attended in Newton concluded with a resounding cheer for—you guessed it!—a return to divided government in Iowa.
An observer might fairly describe all of this as just a tad cringe. But one person’s cringe is another’s stirring call for unity. “There’s a movement afoot for change, and he comes along at a good time,” Steve Mullen, a retired teacher, told me in Newton.
It helps that Sand does not behave like most Democrats. He is not, for example, easily drawn into culture-war debates or bandwagon slogans. Early in his campaign when a radio host asked him whether biological males should be allowed to play in women’s sports, Sand answered succinctly, “No.” In January, after federal officers killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis, Sand did not join in the calls to abolish ICE. “He’s taken some of the cultural issues that dog Democrats in red states off the table,” Adam Jentleson, the founder of the center-left think tank Searchlight, told me.
The progressive left, as you might imagine, is not wild about Sand. Some were disgusted, for example, that the Democrat did not release a statement denouncing ICE after Good’s and Pretti’s deaths. Others see Sand’s comments on trans athletes as a betrayal of the LGBTQ community. Still, most seem to find the state auditor tolerable. “He’s a happy warrior for nonpartisan technocratic efficiency and anti-corruption,” Adam Green, the co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, told me. Sand might slap that on a billboard.
Iowa’s state auditor can seem a little naive. Even if he becomes governor, Sand would almost certainly be working with a Republican state legislature that won’t be eager to hand him any wins. But Sand says he isn’t worried. “There’s still a lot of people of good faith in that caucus,” Sand told me at a deli in Manchester after we’d finished our bike ride. State GOP lawmakers know that they’ll need to have something to show for their public service when they “reach the pearly gates.” Had Sand met a politician recently? I thought. When I voiced my doubts out loud, Sand looked stricken. “I am really hopeful,” he said.
Meanwhile, Republicans are busy trying to convince Iowa voters that the auditor is more extreme than his kumbaya suggests. “It’s like The Truman Show,” Zach Lahn, Sand’s GOP opponent, says in one campaign video. “He’s not a moderate.” In another, Lahn pledges to take back Iowa’s public-school curriculum “from the Marxists who hijacked it.”
Lahn, a former Republican operative, seemed to come out of nowhere in June when he defeated incumbent Representative Randy Feenstra for the GOP nomination. More specifically, Lahn came from Kansas. Although he was born and raised in Iowa, he has lived in Wichita, where he founded a private school, for much of the past decade. The Des Moines Register reported that Lahn splits his time between Iowa and his second home in Kansas, where some of his children live, although Lahn reassured Iowans that if he is elected governor, he will be in the state “as much as humanly possible.” (Lahn did not respond to my requests for comment.)
But Lahn’s outsider status might help him. He has no elected-office experience and is not yet a known quantity in Iowa, which means that he does not wear the albatross of incumbency. So far, he’s campaigned on protecting small farms from corporate agriculture, an unusual Republican position in the state. For this, as well as his pledge to ban mRNA vaccines and improve the state’s water quality, Lahn has also received the MAHA stamp of approval. Several conservative Iowans along the bike route told me that they wouldn’t have voted for Feenstra, but they were considering Lahn’s “new ideas.”
Lately, Republicans have accused Sand of doing too much stumping and not enough of his day job; they’ve also drawn attention to the significant campaign donations from his wife and her wealthy family. But Lahn’s main project ahead of November will be to remind Iowans that Sand, regardless of his rhetoric, is running as a Democrat. At Sand’s Newton town hall, a Lahn supporter named Carrie Atkinson asked the auditor to declare the number of weeks at which he would support a ban on abortion. Sand answered that he thought Roe v. Wade was a reasonable decision. “He didn’t answer my question!” Atkinson told me later. At another event, a local Republican activist named Gary Loeffler asked Sand to justify his support for abortion as a Christian. There are “many verses in the Bible that say life begins at breath,” Sand said, an answer that enraged some religious conservatives.
Republicans believe, or say they believe, that Sand, a wealthy guy with an Ivy League education, is far more liberal than he lets on. Loeffler offered a disturbing visual: Like an infested cob of sweet corn, Sand might look normal on the outside, but inside, he’s “full of worms.”
Luckily, I was able to test Loeffler’s hypothesis—by traveling to Sand’s hometown and peering into the proverbial husk. In Decorah, along the Upper Iowa River, I attended Nordic Fest, a celebration of Scandinavian heritage that included Viking battle reenactments, Nordic dancers, and a parade featuring Sand in the back of a convertible. It felt a little like visiting Bedford Falls with George Bailey. “This is Rob Sand; he’s a good friend of my eldest son!” the announcer said as the auditor drove by. Sand’s aunt, who ran the lefse stand, trotted into the street to give him a package of fresh Norwegian flatbread. Sand’s father asked me in Norwegian if I spoke the language of my ancestors. (I do not.)
After the parade, Sand offered a wry tour of his hometown. Walking down the main drag, he pointed out the old teen center. “Can you guess how many times we went?” Near a statue of a long-snouted woodland creature, he explained: “Trolls are out in the world and can be dangerous.” Quickly, we were overwhelmed by friends and well-wishers. Among them was Andy Rasmussen, Sand’s best friend from high school. Sand was always smart and ambitious, Rasmussen, who does autobody work in Decorah, told me later. He liked to skateboard and bowhunt. He didn’t drink, but he’d give friends rides to parties. “The running joke was that someday Rob’s gonna be president,” Rasmussen said. But what were Sand’s politics back then? I wanted to know. Is he a Trojan horse of socialist corn worms? Rasmussen basically shrugged. “He will generally talk to and listen to anybody that’s out there.”
Others who knew Sand during college and law school similarly described a man committed to listening. At Brown in the early 2000s, Sand frequently criticized the Bush administration in his column in the school paper. Still, he recruited Stephen Beale, a conservative columnist at the paper, to start a new class on conservative thought, featuring readings from Edmund Burke, Barry Goldwater, and Pat Buchanan. Sand is still “being his authentic self,” Beale, who now works as a freelance writer, told me. “He really does care about hearing the other side.”
I thought about Sand’s cheering section at the Nordic Fest parade. “Light ’em up, Rob!” one man had shouted. But Sand had waved him off. “No, no, no,” he’d said.
The next two months may not be so friendly. So far, Sand has outraised Lahn, but Republicans are pouring millions into the state, partly thanks to a high-profile Senate bid from Democrat Josh Turek and three surprisingly competitive House races. Expect ads from both parties to be vicious—and pervasive. On Thursday, screaming activists for Turning Point Action chased Sand around the Iowa State Fair.
Right now, Sand looks reasonably well positioned for victory. The Cook Political Report has changed its analysis of the race from “lean Republican” to “toss up,” and new polling shows Sand leading Lahn by five points. If he succeeds, Democrats might finally be able to say out loud what many have believed for years: that Iowa still defies partisan categorization.
Many Iowans are only now starting to pay attention. Before I lost Sand on the bike ride, a middle-aged man named Ethan Vaas had rolled up next to us. “Are you who I think you are?” he asked Sand, sounding more suspicious than excited. The two chatted for a moment, but Vaas soon pedaled away, looking unimpressed. An hour later, though, he was back, this time to talk with Sand about his job and his kids. Vaas wasn’t sure how he’d vote this year, he told me later. He typically “leans right.” But there was something different about Sand.

 Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

The Supreme Court on Thursday (August 13, 2026) criticised the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), the country’s food regulator, for not introducing front-of-pack warning labels on packaged food products indicating sugar, salt and saturated fat levels.
A Bench headed by Justice J.B. Pardiwala asked the FSSAI whether it did not want children to grow up healthy.
The hearing was based on a petition filed by the Kerala-based NGO, 3S and Our Health Society, seeking directions from the Centre to introduce front-of-pack warning labels.
“Are you taking the court for a toss?” Justice Pardiwala asked Additional Solicitor General Brijender Chahar on learning that nothing much had moved in the FSSAI on the issue of labelling.
“We are doing this in public interest. Keep it in mind. We are not doing it for ourselves. Why are you not abiding by our order? We know the pressure on you. Will you do it on your own or should we pass an order?” Justice Pardiwala asked the government side.
Mr. Chahar said one-third of enterprises were based on traditional food, exposing items like ‘namkeen’ to be categorised as unhealthy.
“You should be concerned about the health of young children. They are addicted,” Justice Pardiwala said.
An FSSAI affidavit had earlier said the front-of-pack labelling was in format with global practices and provided consumers with simplified information on nutritional content.

Bengaluru: The students and alumni of the National Law School of India University (NLSIU) here have opposed CJI Surya Kant and Bar Council of India Chairman Manan Kumar Mishra attending the upcoming convocation of the varsity. In a statement dated August 15, the students and alumni condemned the now-withdrawn BCI order to halt the enrolment of students of NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, and expressed their solidarity with the students at NALSAR, who they said have shown exemplary courage and moral conviction in speaking truth to power.
"We are aware that the BCI has closed all proceedings against NALSAR. However, the fact that such unconstitutional and illegal "proceedings" can be initiated by a statutory body against students and faculty members of a public university in the first place does not alter the nature or the larger impact of such actions or dilute the responsibility of the Chairman and the BCI," the statement signed by 165 graduating students of the Class of 2026, 409 current students and 128 alumni said.
Students question convocation invite
They claimed that even after the recall of the ban on enrolment and the inquiry order, the BCI has acknowledged the "arbitrary" and "illegal nature" of its actions. According to them, a university convocation is a monumental event in a student's academic life, meant to celebrate years of hard work and perseverance.
NLSIU students back NALSAR peers, demand BCI apology
In a country where access to higher education is severely restricted by barriers of class, caste and gender, and poorly designed and conducted entrance examinations, a convocation marks an important achievement for families. "In this context, inviting persons in high office to confer degrees to students towards whom they have publicly expressed their disdain and condescension is offensive, humiliating, and a mockery of students and their struggles," it said.
Students demand BCI apology
"We stand in unconditional solidarity with our fellow students at NALSAR who have shown exemplary courage and moral conviction in speaking truth to power." They have demanded that the Bar Council of India unconditionally apologise to the student and faculty community at NALSAR for attempting to infringe their fundamental right to free speech and expression.
It said BCI's actions create a "chilling effect" on free speech not only for the students and faculty members at NALSAR but for students and citizens across the country by sending them a clear signal that an "act of dissent" will be met with severe personal and professional consequences.
Opposition to convocation attendance
NLSIU students oppose CJI, BCI chief at convocation
"(We) express our strong disapproval of Manan Kumar Mishra attending the convocation of NLSIU without taking responsibility for his conduct and stand in solidarity with NALSAR in their request to reconsider the choice of the Chief Justice of India as Chief Guest for their convocation and express our strong disapproval of the CJI attending the convocation of NLSIU for the same reasons," it stated.
Also Watch:
CJI backs right to protest
"It's a dialogue between students and me," Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said on August 14 as he sharply pulled up the Bar Council of India for its order that the 2026 graduates of Hyderabad's NALSAR University of Law not be enrolled as advocates following their objections to his proposed campus visit.
Students have a right to protest, the CJI-led bench said a day after the BCI directed all state bar councils not to enrol any 2026 graduate of the university until further orders. The order was reversed within hours after an uproar on social media.

Tehran – Iran on Saturday demanded that Qatar release three of Tehran’s pilots whose aircraft went down early in the Middle East war, though the Gulf state denied it was detaining them.
Iran had previously reported one pilot killed and others missing after a sortie to Qatar in March, but news of their alleged capture was not publicized at the time.
“Three Iranian pilots were captured alive by Qatari forces after their Su-24 fighter jets crashed during the war,” Gen. Mohammad Bagherzadeh of the Iranian armed forces said according to the Fars news agency.

For centuries, the rock was seen as a warning. When it began to emerge from the Danube, beneath Gellért Hill in Budapest, it meant the river had fallen so low that floating mills could no longer operate, crops were probably failing, and hunger would almost certainly follow. That is why, in the Hungarian capital, where over time the boulder became little more than a legend, it was named Ínség-szikla – the Rock of Starvation.
Today, amid record-low water levels on the Danube, the rock has not only emerged from the water, but surfaced almost in its entirety, along with the sandy riverbed on which it rests, astonishing geologists and government scientists sent to examine it. And, much as the rock was said to warn, Hungary is now facing an unprecedented energy crisis that has forced the country to shut down all but one of its Danube-cooled nuclear reactors for the first time in 44 years.
The Guardian travelled for more than 100 miles (160km) along the banks of the Danube, the EU’s longest river, which sustains the 10 countries it crosses, visiting villages and towns where residents are struggling to secure drinking water and farmers are fighting to keep their crops alive.
Pócsmegyer
Last week, the Hungarian prime minister, Péter Magyar, warned that the economic damage caused by this year’s drought was expected to surpass that of the historic dry spell that devastated Hungary’s farmland in 2022.
While the full extent of the losses is still difficult to assess, István Somogyi, a 56-year-old farmer from Pócsmegyer, a village on the Danube, in Pest County, has already done his calculations.
“I’ve lost nearly 50% of my harvest this year and it could go up to 70%,” he said. “It’s gone. Everything has dried up. Since I started farming this land after the end of communist rule, I’ve never seen a catastrophe like this.”
Somogyi said the unprecedented crisis did not come out of nowhere, and that the heatwaves and droughts of previous years had already offered a warning. Scientists say that human-caused climate breakdown is making every heatwave in the world more intense and more likely to happen.
“You could see this coming,” he said. “The harvest was already poor last year. But we were lucky because the Danube stayed high. Despite the intense heat, there was still enough water in the soil. This time, there is no hope of saving our crops.”
On the near-deserted roads running alongside the river, families with children sought relief in the Danube’s shallow waters, while, not far away, military water tankers were siphoning water from rural wells, hauling vital supplies to the storage pools that feed the local grid.
Szentendre
Across the river from Pócsmegyer, on the opposite bank of the Danube, lies Szentendre, a town known for its community of artists. During the most intense days of the heatwave, some evening performances have been held by candlelight in an effort to reduce electricity consumption.
Here, in recent weeks, vast, desert-like islands have emerged. The exposed riverbed is cracked like a mosaic of hard, dry clay, baked by suffocating heat that has pushed temperatures in Budapest close to 42C, with overnight temperatures hitting a high of 28C. Europe is warming faster than any other continent, with intense summer heat and prolonged drought being amplified by the deepening human-caused climate crisis. Extreme conditions continue to fuel wildfires and strain water supplies.
In some stretches of the Danube near Szentendre, it is now possible to walk through it with the water barely reaching above your ankles.
“Swimming and navigation are banned here,” said László Balázs, 44, head of the local river rescue service. “But people escaping the heat still enter the water, unaware it can suddenly drop into deep pools where they risk drowning.”
At the end of June, Budapest police (BRFK) said three people had gone missing in the Danube over a single weekend. Water police later recovered one body near Iváncsa, while searches continued downstream for the other two missing swimmers.
The drought and resulting disruption to energy supplies have also left some Hungarian towns struggling with shortages of drinking water. In a room inside Szentendre’s tourist information office, thousands of bottles of water are stored ready to be distributed, particularly to elderly and vulnerable residents.
“About 4,000 to 5,000 households were left without water,” said József Gulyás, 62, Szentendre’s deputy mayor. “We distributed 25 tonnes of water and received about 100 emergency calls a day. We had never experienced anything so serious. Elderly women would hug the officers delivering water and burst into tears.”
Budapest
Driving from north to south, towards the Hungarian capital, Budapest, where the level of the Danube under normal conditions reaches an average height of 2 to 3 metres, and can rise as high as 8 metres, intense summer heat and continuing drought conditions caused the river to fall to a record low of just 14-19 cm on 4 August.
The water levels have fallen so dramatically that, as the Danube has retreated, it has revealed a succession of relics long hidden beneath its waters, including the remains of a woolly mammoth, a bridge destroyed after the second world war in Budapest, a Nazi warship and an unexploded British bomb.
The water is so low in the capital that on 28 July, at about 4.30pm, Gábor Kürti, president of the Magyar Kerékpárosklub (Hungarian cyclists’ club) and owner of a cargo bike company, left his office in central Budapest, jumped on his bicycle and, in an unprecedented feat, rode for 30km along the exposed bed of the Danube, with his journey quickly going viral on social media.
“I wanted to show that if you can cycle along the bed of the Danube for 30km, it means that, because of this climate emergency, we have literally hit rock bottom,” he told the Guardian.
Riding his KTM X-Strada 20 gravel bike, Kürti set off from the mouth of the Szilas stream (Szilas-patak) and made his way across fine gravel, large pebbles, hard-packed sand and mud, eventually reaching the ferry terminal at Vác about three hours later.
“For many people it was an extraordinary adventure. For me, it was heartbreaking,” he said. “Cycling through parts of the river where, as a child, I used to swim or go kayaking, and which I could now cross on a bicycle, filled me with an indescribable sadness. It was like looking at the scene of a terrible accident. Throughout that journey, the scale of the catastrophe was unfolding before my eyes.”
Nagytétény
Kürti took the Guardian into what, until only a few months ago, was the striking floodplain forest in Nagytétény named Kis-Háros-sziget, a protected area home to climbing plants, wild vines and several families of European beavers.
The river is reached by walking across ground that would normally lie several metres beneath the water. Here, one branch of the Danube has receded so dramatically that it came to an abrupt halt, blocked by an exposed riverbed left behind by the drought.
Its dry, clay-like surface looks like an image from a future shaped by the escalating human-caused climate crisis. Yet this is happening now. Passersby walk across what was once the river, their feet sinking into patches of mud. Kayakers struggle to make their way through the remaining shallow channels; many eventually give up, lift their kayaks on to their shoulders and walk home.
Hungarian authorities have been pumping water into large areas of the country’s nature reserves such as the one in Nagytétény, to keep marshlands from drying out as the drought intensifies.
Paks
Continuing south, the road finally reaches Paks, home to Hungary’s nuclear power plant, its towers rising above the horizon. Here, municipal workers have been working weekends to keep more than 700 threatened trees alive and water the town’s flowerbeds.
“I’ve been doing this job for 18 years,” said Szilvia Farkas, 39, who is employed by Dunakom Zrt in Paks, owned entirely by the municipality, to plant and water trees and plants. “I have never seen so much vegetation dry out in all my years doing this job, and I have never worked as hard as I have this year to try to keep it alive.”
Dunakom Zrt uses its own drilled well for water extraction. In addition, the company is able to extract water from a decantation basin. The public is not permitted to use tap water for irrigation at the moment; instead, residents collect greywater and use it to water their gardens.
In the country’s more marginalised and deprived areas, the water crisis has compounded longstanding problems for thousands of people who were already living in difficult conditions before the drought, struggling with inadequate access to running water and sewage systems.
Géza Orsós Renáta, 43, who lives with her four children in a small farmhouse on the outskirts of Paks, has never had access to running water. Orsós, who also works for Dunakom Zrt, helping to water public green spaces drying out in the heat, has long relied on water from a neighbour.
“Even in winter, we have to pump water and heat it in large bowls so we can wash,” she said. “Now a friend brings us water once a week. But it is becoming unbearable.”
Driving back from Paks, tall, swollen clouds occasionally gather on the horizon in the clear skies above Budapest, appearing to promise the return of rain, only to fade by evening, dashing the hopes of an entire country.
For now, people can do little but cling to the hope that the Rock of Starvation will disappear once more beneath the currents of the Danube, returning to the depths of the river and becoming little more than a legend again.
But Somogyi, who grew up hearing the story of the boulder passed down through generations, and who is now witnessing the consequences of the warning it was said to foretell, knows it will not.
“The drought will return next year,” he said. “That is the trend. And there isn’t much that we can do.”

People are betting on wildfires on Polymarket. What could go wrong?
Lawmakers are warning that predictions markets could make a bad wildfire season worse.
The 2026 wildfire season on the West Coast is shaping up to be an especially bad one: In Oregon, more than 2 million acres have already burned, breaking a record set just a few years ago, in 2024. In neighboring Washington state, suburbs around the city of Spokane recently burned in an increasingly common example of fires reaching urban and suburban areas (as my colleague Caitlin Dewey covered recently). And the consequences are spreading far beyond where the fires are burning, with hazardous smoke from the Pacific Northwest drifting as far away as New England.
Much of this is a story about climate change, as increasingly dry, hot summers provide ample fuel for fires. But the crisis is also being made worse by the Trump administration: Staff cuts to the US Forest Service have left the agency stretched thin and unable to respond as effectively to fires, while a planned reorganization is also set to shutter Forest Service labs researching and tracking wildfires. EPA research into wildfires and wildfire smoke has also been slashed.
All of this — plus a Trump administration shift away from letting some fires burn themselves out, which has further increased the workload on wildland firefighters — has also resulted in a more dangerous fire season for firefighters; Reuters reported this week that firefighters are “being overrun by wildfires at the highest rate in two decades” — with months still to go until the end of the season.
Go a little deeper
As if the above weren’t enough to worry about, lawmakers are also raising a brand-new fire season concern: prediction markets. Specifically, the possibility that bettors could turn to arson in order to manipulate prediction markets — and earn themselves some money.
Polymarket, on its international platform, has offered users the chance to bet on everything from when and where a fire might spread to when it could be contained or extinguished, which resulted in more than $1 million in bets on major fires in California last year. High Country News reported in June that a new prediction market, called Wyldfyre, had launched specifically for betting on wildfires.
Legislators like Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-OR) have pointed out that, unlike most other natural disasters, fires are easily started or spread by humans, creating a real risk that people could attempt to manipulate markets.
“Offering bets on destructive wildfires threatens to minimize communities’ suffering all so the rich and powerful can profit,” Merkley and eight other Democratic senators wrote in a letter to the head of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission last week. “There’s also the heightened risk—according to state and local fire officials—that individuals could be tempted to commit arson in order to make sure their bets are successful. By offering contracts on fires, prediction market sites run the risk of encouraging people to influence fires that have already started, creating additional concerns around public safety and insider trading.
One link for later
➨ Build (your attention span) back better. Beset as we are by short-form video and tweets, it can often feel like our attention spans are slipping unavoidably away. The good news, it turns out, is that decline doesn’t have to be permanent — there are ways to rebuild attention, including by simply letting your brain rest more.

France has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador to Central African Republic over allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns.
The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony.
The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach.
The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said.
The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.”
The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings.
Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011.
According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month.
He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence.
Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra.
French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries.
The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” between France and CAR when he visited Bangui in March.

VisionQuest
Marvel’s streaming TV portfolio has kind of been all over the place: a handful of hits, a few misses, and a bunch of middling offerings. Anthropic is watermarking text generated by Claude to comply with EU law
Other AI companies are also required to watermark content.
Anthropic has revealed how it's watermarking text generated by Claude AI to comply with the European Union's new AI transparency rules. The company said its text watermarking will not have easy-to-see visuals, will not be distinguishable to the people who read it and will not be adding hidden characters to the text. Instead, Anthropic's method involves leaving a pattern in the text that can only be decoded by someone who has the key for it.
The company explained that large language models pick one word at a time when generating text by choosing from a list of potential appropriate words to use. They pick words randomly, as long as they make sense for the context of what they're generating. With watermarking on, Claude will use a key to decide on what word to choose instead of using an arbitrary random number generator to pick the next word.
In its example, Anthropic used the digits of pi as a key. Say, the key starts with the digit 2 from the pi sequence 3.1415926535. The next word generated is the sixth in the list of choices, then the fifth, the third and then the fifth again. This method is an adaptation of Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text approach to watermarking, which the team described in a paper published in Nature. Watermarking doesn't affect the quality of Claude's output or slow it down, the company said, and it will not require extra tokens or make generations more expensive.
Of course, AI-generated prose typically has tells. Models are fond of using certain sentence constructions like "this isn't [X], it's [Y]," for instance. But those tells are only enough to let you know that an AI was involved in writing that text, not the model used. Anthropic will release an API that has "keys" to decode Claude's watermarking and will be able to say whether the its AI generated the block of text being checked.
Anthropic admits that its text watermarking method does have limitations. It can't tell whether Claude actually wrote the text or just edited it, which means if you ask the AI to edit something for you, it will be watermarked too. As the company explains, it can only tell that Claude was likely involved with the text at some point. Even translations will be watermarked. If Claude has only proofread and lightly edited the text, or if the text is too short, the watermark may not be enough to be detectable. Take note that lightly editing Claude-generated text probably won't remove its watermark. If you want to be sure, you will need to rewrite it completely.
There have been some concerns on how watermarking would affect code, since it may not be copyrightable without significant human input. If one could prove that an entire codebase was AI-generated, they could copy and then iterate on it. Anthropic said, though, that code has "generally less watermarking than some other forms of text" because it typically requires exact output. If there are no choices to be made in the text generation, then watermarking can't be applied.
Anthropic will also watermark images by adding a cryptographically signed note in its metadata that says it was generated by Claude. In its announcement, the company said it was applying watermarks to all of Claude's output at launch because it doesn't have sure ways to implement the changes by region. The changes will affect output across all Claude products that use models released after August 2. Anthropic will also add watermarking capability to older Claude models over the coming months.

Babies and toddlers are sweltering in some daycares. Should there be mandatory AC?
Parents, educators, advocates calling for maximum indoor temperature laws
On the hottest days last summer, Lyndsay MacKay would arrive at her 16-month-old son's daycare to find him in a diaper, his skin sticky and his hair plastered to his head.
He would collapse in her arms. Some nights, he'd fall asleep at the dinner table.
She said she knew the educators were doing what they could: ice cubes in the water tables, offering popsicles, darkening the rooms and placing cool cloths on the infants and toddlers.
"But at the end of the day, they're still hot, they're sweaty, they're exhausted," said the Toronto mother and early childhood education professor at Humber Polytechnic.
"From a health and safety and from a development perspective, the children are not — the children are almost just surviving the day."
MacKay is among the growing number of parents, educators, health and legal advocates across Canada lobbying for maximum indoor temperature at daycares, likely 26 C, akin to standards adopted for long-term care facilities in Ontario.
What to watch for
Like seniors, infants, toddlers and preschool-aged children are at a higher risk of developing heat exhaustion and its more severe form, heatstroke.
In part, it's because they have a higher metabolism than adults, creating more heat in their bodies. And, since their sweat glands are less efficient, it's harder to cool down. Plus, babies and young toddlers can't tell caregivers they're overheated.
Even preschoolers likely can't recognize what's happening, said Dr. Kirstin Weerdenburg, a pediatrician in the emergency department at Halifax's IWK Health Centre.
"They don't have a way to explain how they're feeling, so it's [about] knowing their behaviours and all those other physical signs and symptoms," she said.
"If someone's not paying attention to that, they might get, you know, looked over until you get to the more extremes."
In young children, Weerdenburg said, symptoms can look like fatigue, flushed skin, irritability — even having trouble walking, which is a sign of dizziness.
But heat illness presents on a spectrum, so if kids are acting out of character on a hot day, she said it's worth paying attention.
Kids can often be treated at home with fluids and a cool room. But extreme cases of dehydration can make babies or young children too tired to drink, so they require IV fluids, the pediatrician said.
In the most severe cases, organs like the liver and kidney can shut down as the body redirects blood to the skin to help cool it. The heart speeds up, causing an arrhythmia, as it tries to pump more blood faster.
Keeping watch in the heat
Watching for signs of heatstroke is stressful for educators, said Amy O'Neil, executive director of Toronto's Treetop Children's Centre, noting they're not health-care professionals and don't have the training to make a diagnosis.
It's why she introduced air-conditioning at her child-care centre in 2019, and why she thinks the provincial and federal governments should also consider high temperatures in daycares to be unacceptable.
It's not a "comfort issue" but a matter of safety, said O'Neil, who is also board chair of Toronto Community for Better Child Care, an advocacy group of parents and educators for well-funded, publicly available child care.
"It's really hard to understand why the legislation — and in Ontario, it's the Child Care and Early Years Act — is so clear about maintaining minimum indoor temperatures in the winter, yet it's completely silent on maximum indoor temperatures during extreme heat."
It cost upwards of $40,000, between $5,000 and $7,000 for each unit, to install eight air conditioners in June 2019, O'Neil said, paid for from the centre's reserve fund.
"It's a lot of money for a non-profit community-based child-care centre to swallow."
Ontario Premier Doug Ford did say last summer that he would "look at" maximum indoor temperatures in daycare.
"I can't answer if we're putting 'em into standards," he told The Trillium in August 2025 in response to a question about temperature regulations. "We did that with the long-term care, now they all have air conditioning, and so we'll look at it with the kids as well."
It doesn't appear there has been any movement on the issue.
In response to an email to Ford's office asking about an update this week, the education minister's office instead provided a statement.
"Licensed child-care operators are responsible for providing a safe environment for the children in their care, including taking appropriate steps to protect them during periods of extreme heat," said part of the statement from Minister Paul Calandra's office.
What the regulations say
Other provinces have similarly vague regulations. None have instituted maximum indoor temperatures, though some regions require a heat source in the winter.
In B.C., regulations under the Community Care and Assisted Living Act require only that licensed daycares "provide a healthy and safe environment and maintain emergency response procedures," according to a statement from the province's Ministry of Health.
While the regulations do "not establish a specific indoor temperature limit," the statement notes that provincial health authorities have guidelines recommending the 26 C threshold, though these are not enshrined in law.
In Nova Scotia, a campaign recently launched by the parent advocacy group For Our Kids to regulate temperatures in schools, where many daycares operate year-round. Though the province's Early Learning and Child Care Regulations includes detailed guidelines about other essentials — providing developmentally appropriate toys, utensils and a safe place and opportunity for sleep — there is nothing about maintaining safe temperatures.
A spokesperson for Nova Scotia's education department said design guidelines for newer child care centres supported by the province include modern heating, ventilation and AC systems, which were also eligible expenses under minor and major infrastructure projects funded by the department.
However, "older buildings rely more on opening windows during cooler morning hours, placing a CSA-approved [Canadian Standards Association] fan in classrooms, and encouraging everyone to drink extra water," the statement continued.
It's unclear, too, how many daycares across Canada have air-conditioning.
Getting that data and monitoring exactly how hot daycare classrooms are getting is critical, according to Jacqueline Wilson of the Canadian Environmental Law Association. CELA has been calling both for maximum indoor temperature legislation and funding for retrofitting, noting that Ontario was able to do that for the long-term care industry in 2021.
While there's significant research showing that a maximum temperature of 26 C is appropriate for older adults, children's bodies may require an even lower threshold, Wilson said.
In its 2025 report on daycare temperatures, CELA suggests the exact temperature should be revisited every two years as more evidence becomes available and summers get hotter. Indeed, Environment and Climate Change released a forecast earlier this year suggesting that 2026 to 2030 is expected to be the warmest five-year period ever recorded.
More wildfires, too
Wildfires are increasing alongside summer temperatures, something Kate Lawes contended with when at her daycare, Tree of Life Nature Play School in Victoria.
She jokingly recalls how her public health authority used to issue "slip, slap, slop" heat advisory notices. Now, they focus on extreme temperatures, wildfires and air quality.
On the warmest days, she used to plan outings by the ocean or the forest — where the temperature would often be five to 10 degrees cooler. But the wildfires and accompanying air quality warnings make that impossible, the daycare manager said, as does opening the windows to allow cooler air inside in the early morning.
"We err on the side of caution," she said. "Their lungs are still growing and developing."
She closed her school during the heat dome in 2021 that killed 619 people in B.C. and led to a maximum heat bylaw enacted in New Westminster, B.C., this summer for tenancy buildings.
It also prompted her daycare to buy a heat pump, an electric device that provides cooling in summer and heat in winter, which wasn't covered by the province's emergency preparedness fund.
Now the children and staff feel comfortable, she said, and it's lifted the stress that kids might become sick from the heat.
In Toronto, MacKay is thankful her son's daycare now has air-conditioning.
"He has energy," she said. "He's bright. He's not a wet noodle — he is a live wire."

Are some soldiers colluding with Nigeria's criminal gangs? A recent arrest prompts questions
- Published
A Nigerian soldier has been arrested over allegations he supplied military uniforms to "terrorist" and "criminal" groups, the army says.
Private Mohammed Yusuf was caught on Saturday evening at a bus stop in the north-eastern city of Maiduguri, military spokesperson Mohammed Goni said the following day.
The soldier, who was previously stationed at a factory for army equipment, was allegedly attempting to flee across the border into neighbouring Cameroon.
He deserted his unit earlier this month, Goni said, before relocating to Maiduguri, where he went into hiding with the help of an "associate".
Yusuf has not publicly commented on the case against him, but the arrest has reignited speculation that collusion could be the reason behind rampant insecurity in the country.
A variety of armed groups - including militant Islamists, separatists and gangs who kidnap civilians for ransom - have been causing problems for the authorities, and some of them deceptively wear military uniforms.
Now, in a nation that for over a decade has been blighted by armed attacks on civilians, people are wondering whether these assaults are failing to subside because criminal elements and security personnel are working together.
It is not unreasonable to believe some of these groups are being assisted by military personnel, Bashir Galma, a security analyst and retired army major, told the BBC.
"I know there have been instances where plans are made for an attack on a location and the information finds its way to either [militant Islamist group] Boko Haram or another criminal gang," he said, suggesting an insider tip-off.
At least 3,000 kidnappings and 3,580 killings by armed groups took place between January 2024 and April 2025 alone, data from Nigeria's National Human Rights Commission records
The alarming surge in mass abductions has been attributed to gunmen known locally as bandits, as well as insurgent attacks from Boko Haram and its offshoot, Iswap.
Attacks on schools have also been making the headlines, although this has been a problem for years. Between April 2014 and May 2026, there were 26 major school attacks with at least 2,416 students abducted, the International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) says.
Ransom payments are estimated to run into millions of dollars annually, according to official data.
In April 2025, the governor of Nigeria's embattled Borno state, Babagana Zulum, alleged that informants and collaborators for Boko Haram insurgents were operating within the country's armed forces, political class and local communities.
"What we need to do is to strengthen our intelligence and to deal with them ruthlessly," he said during a security meeting.
Months later, a special court-martial sentenced three Nigerian soldiers to life imprisonment for their involvement in a major arms and ammunition racketeering scheme. The army said they were guilty of theft, unlawful dealing in ammunition, and "aiding the enemy".
Security analyst Galma told the BBC he believes poor pay breeds such corruption within soldiers. There is also the "issue of ideology" - some personnel might hold a secret allegiance to other groups, he said.
A current serving soldier, who spoke to the BBC on the condition of anonymity, admitted that there have been instances of soldiers "caught dealing with the other side" but said such matters are often "hushed and dealt with internally".
One man, freed after his family paid a 57m naira ($42,000; £31,000) ransom, described a disturbing scene upon his release.
"They dropped us off in one location and there were security personnel who they shook hands and laughed with," he told the BBC, asking not to be named.
He believes the security forces he saw may have received a portion of the ransom, though he has no proof that this was the case.
Farmer Yahuza Isa, who was kidnapped in Zamfara state, expressed the frustration shared by many victims.
"I myself know where these criminals are," he said. "So why not deal with them completely?"
Another survivor, who endured a 30-day ordeal in late 2024, said he suspected collusion "at a much higher level".
He described hearing a helicopter landing very close to the hidden camp where he was held blindfolded.
"The first time I heard it I was expecting that the Nigerian Air Force... had come to rescue us," he said. "But we could hear the helicopter leaving afterwards."
He heard it several more times, leading him to believe the gangs had some form of high-level logistical cooperation.
Security expert Abdullahi Abdullahi said he believed armed groups are not just getting help from security forces, but from civilian informants.
"And that is why the issue is continuing after all these years," he said.
The persistent security challenges point to a failing system, but the arrest of Yusuf shows the military is – at the very least – acknowledging that the problem exists within its own ranks.
Whether that acknowledgment will translate into meaningful action remains to be seen.
Yusuf remains in custody, and investigations are continuing to determine the full extent of his alleged operation and whether others were involved.
The military's director of media operations, Maj Gen Markus Kangye, did not respond to a BBC request for comment.

Archdiocese of Quebec to pay out $31.5M to sexual abuse victims after judge approves settlement
Lawsuit covers people who say they were sexually abused by staff dating back to 1940
A Quebec Superior Court judge has approved a historic $31.5-million settlement in a class-action lawsuit against the Archdiocese of Quebec.
The deal ends years of legal action for claimants who said they were sexually assaulted by members of the Archdiocese since 1940.
Quebec Superior Court Justice Danye Daigle approved the settlement earlier this week, led by representative plaintiffs Gaétan Bégin and Pierre Bolduc.
Both men have said they were sexually assaulted by parish priests starting in the 1950s and 1960s when they were aged 14 and 12 respectively.
Daigle heard emotional testimony from victims during a public hearing in July, to determine whether the out-of-court agreement and the requested fees, were in the best interests of the class members.
After the hearing, Bégin described it as a historic day. Now 86, Bégin said the boy whose life was was robbed, is still with him every day.
But he said the worst isn't so much what happened to him, but the suffering he says he unwittingly inflicted on his family.
"The collateral damage is indescribable," Bégin said.
Around 200 people have already joined the class action.
The Dufresne Wee law firm says other victims have 90 days to to submit a claim outlining the alleged abuse and its impact on their lives.
Lawyer Justin Wee has said the $31.5 million settlement is one of the biggest against a diocese in Quebec.
The compensation fund will be financed by the Archdiocese of Quebec, the Séminaire de Québec, Collège François-de-Laval — formerly known as the Petit Séminaire de Québec — and the Mutual Insurance of Quebec Fabriques.
In addition to the $31.5-million compensation fund, the defendants have agreed to cover the costs associated with administering the claims process, including adjudicators’ fees and expenses such as obtaining medical records and expert opinions when necessary.
The amount each person receives will be determined by two retired judges appointed to assess the claims. Victims will also receive a written apology form the Archdiocese of Quebec.
In an online statement, Diocesan officials welcomed the news, saying they hope this next phase of reparation will help victims "continue their journey toward peace and healing. "
If you’re in immediate danger or fear for your safety or that of others around you, please call 911. For support in your area, you can look for crisis lines and local services via the Ending Sexual Violence Association of Canada database.

Morocco arrests 111 migrants headed to Spain's Ceuta as sides step up crackdown
Moroccan police used tear gas to disperse groups gathered at border, Spanish media reports
Moroccan police arrested at least 111 people on Saturday as they tried to enter Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta, amid tightened security on both sides of the border after social media posts called for another mass migrant crossing.
The attempted crossing came two weeks after more than 72,000 migrants surged into Ceuta, sparking tensions within the European Union and fuelling anti-immigration rhetoric among far-right parties worldwide. At least 96 people died in the attempt to reach European soil.
A source in Morocco's Interior Ministry told Reuters those detained included 109 migrants from sub-Saharan Africa and two Moroccan citizens arrested in or around Fnideq, the Moroccan city opposite Ceuta.
According to Spanish news agency EFE, Moroccan police used tear gas to disperse groups of migrants gathered on hills about three kilometres from the border. Reuters later saw hundreds of police officers, some in riot gear and others in plain clothes, returning from the hills outside Fnideq.
EFE and Spanish state broadcaster TVE said Morocco's Interior Ministry ordered their journalists to leave Fnideq immediately, without providing an explanation.
In Ceuta, Spanish soldiers guarded supermarkets while police heavily patrolled the enclave's main streets. The city was calmer than in the days after the deadly crossing attempt on July 30.
Madrid has since installed a maritime barrier and deployed more than 500 additional police from mainland Spain, raising the total in Ceuta to more than 1,600. The Interior Ministry said the reinforcements would remain for as long as needed.
"We'll continue to deploy whatever personnel are necessary to restore normality as soon as possible and prevent events like those of July 30 from happening again," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Thursday.
About 5,000 migrants remained in Ceuta, the minister said. Reuters saw hundreds sheltering from scorching heat under makeshift bamboo shelters on the urban beach of El Trampolin.
Grande-Marlaska said migrants who entered irregularly would not be allowed to stay in the enclave, travel to mainland Spain or obtain legal status, except in rare cases involving extreme vulnerability. Those without a right to remain would be returned to Morocco, he said.
Earlier this week, Rabat said it was monitoring "the circulation of social media posts and messages of unknown origin" calling for a mass crossing on Aug. 15, warning it would prosecute organizers and participants.
A Reuters witness saw reinforced security near the border, including police vans with wire shields and road checkpoints. Local media reported similar measures near Spain's other North African enclave, Melilla.
Authorities prevented several groups from boarding trains and buses to northern Morocco in cities such as Casablanca, Fez and Kenitra.
However, witnesses told Reuters that some migrants from sub-Saharan Africa were bypassing security checkpoints by taking mountain routes towards Fnideq.
One witness said the schools in Fnideq had been turned into accommodation for security forces deployed near the border.
'Don't cross now, my brothers'
Many of the young people who entered Ceuta on July 30 were fishing, swimming or washing at Tarajal beach on Friday.
Driss Sadik, a 22-year-old from Fez who said he swam for five hours to reach Ceuta, urged others not to follow his example.
"The important thing I would advise people trying to cross: Don't cross now, my brothers. You're only going to suffer," he told Reuters.
The warning was echoed by Adil Jamil, 17.
"Those who enter aren't going to benefit from anything. There will just be more and more of us, and they won't find a solution for all," he said.
Jamil said that the mass border crossings were "planned by the people" who pick a date, gather in Fnideq and cross together to find strength in numbers.
"If I had stayed with my parents, I would've died slowly. But if I risk my life, arrive and build my future ... it will be better," he said.
