Peak XV Partners led a $45 Mn Series B funding round of San Francisco-based AI code testing startup Blacksmith at a valuation of $550 Mn, as the VC firm steps up investments in US-based AI and developer tools companies Existing investors Google Ventures (GV) and Y Combinator also participated in the round. Blacksmith closed the funding round in March 2026 but announced it now. The latest funding takes Blacksmith’s total capital raised to $58.5 Mn. The startup plans to deploy a significant portion of the fresh capital to expand its computing infrastructure amid rising demand for tools that can test and validate AI-generated code. Blacksmith cofounder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said improvements in AI coding models are enabling developers to produce more software, creating a corresponding need for infrastructure to validate and test the code. “Every model improvement has expanded what coding agents can do and led to even more code being produced,” Jayaprakash said in a company blog post. Founded in 2024 by Jayaprakash, Aditya Maru, and Aayush Shah, Blacksmith initially helped developers automatically test code before deployment. It is now building tools that allow developers and AI agents to validate and merge code faster. The startup said the number of continuous integration (CI) jobs run on its platform has grown 5%-10% week-on-week since the beginning of 2026, driven by the growing adoption of AI code generation tools. More than 6,000 companies now use Blacksmith, including Supabase, Clerk, Ashby and Mercury. Blacksmith is betting that existing CI infrastructure will struggle to handle the increase in pull requests and testing workloads as AI coding agents produce software at a faster pace. The startup recently launched smith, a cloud-based coding agent that can build features, fix bugs, diagnose CI failures, and automatically resolve them. It is also developing smith QA, which will autonomously test code changes before they are merged. “The volume of code produced over the coming decade is only going to explode,” Jayaprakash said, adding that Blacksmith wants to help developers and AI agents validate and merge code faster. Blacksmith currently manages hundreds of thousands of CPU cores and plans to expand this footprint by around 10X over the coming months. It competes with the likes of GitHub Actions, CircleCI, Buildkite, Depot, and Namespace. Blacksmith claims its purpose-built CI cloud infrastructure can run workloads up to twice as fast and at 50%-75% lower costs than GitHub-hosted runners. Peak XV’s US Push The investment comes as Peak XV expands its presence in the US and looks to tap AI and developer tools startups catering to the American market. The VC firm began building its Bay Area presence after separating from Sequoia Capital in 2023. It subsequently hired operating partners in the US and brought former Y Combinator investor Arnav Sahu on board in 2025 to help lead its US investing efforts. Peak XV has since expanded its US team to eight members and opened its first San Francisco office. Its US portfolio includes San Francisco-based startups such as AI voice platform Vapi, AI memory infrastructure startup Mem0, AI sales training platform Hyperbound, and product development platform PostHog. Peak XV has also backed Supabase, which offers an open-source alternative to Google’s Firebase, and AI infrastructure startup TrueFoundry.

Most people never think about the monitor they use. But not you. If you work from home as I do, your monitor is your window into your trade, whether that's scrolling through endless spreadsheets or color grading short films. Different work has different needs, and finding the monitor that suits your specific use case can be tricky with all the options out there.
But with over a decade of testing and reviewing monitors under my belt, here are my recommendations on what you should buy today.
For more information, check out our guide to How to Choose a Monitor, as well as our recommendations for Best Gaming Monitors, Best Portable Monitors, and Best Cheap Monitors.
The Best Monitors for Your Home Office
It's worth spending more than a hundred bucks on your monitor. Whether it's to improve image quality, upgrade sharpness through higher resolutions, or to add extra ports, you'll want something that makes your daily work life more pleasant. That's why I recommend the Dell 27 Plus 4K as the monitor most people should buy. Unlike many 4K monitors, the Dell 27 Plus 4K sells for under $300 (oftentimes as low as $280), despite being quite bright and color-accurate for an IPS panel at this price. It even comes with a fast 120-Hz refresh rate. I like this feature, especially since higher refresh rates are becoming more commonplace on phone and laptop screens.
The only real downside to the Dell 27 Plus 4K is that the port selection is woefully limited. The two HDMI ports and one DisplayPort are enough for the basics, but if you have a laptop without HDMI, like a MacBook Air, you'll need a USB Hub or laptop docking station. For a more versatile monitor, I'd recommend upgrading to the model with a built-in USB hub (S2725QC). The QC model is identical, except that its extra USB ports make this monitor a far better fit for a connected home office. Dell does charge you $50 more for those ports, but for some, it'll be worth the convenience. Either way, you'll be hard-pressed to find a cheaper 4K monitor of this quality or a better monitor for under $300.
If you are looking for a larger, more fully featured home office monitor meant to sit at the center of a workstation, I'd recommend the Dell UltraSharp 32 4K (U3225Q). This thing is a beast. It's got just about every port and feature you can imagine, including a Thunderbolt-compatible USB-C port with power delivery up to 140 watts, an Ethernet jack, and a built-in KVM switch. This fully eliminates the need for a separate laptop docking station. Beyond that, it delivers on image quality in a big way. It uses IPS Black for enhanced color accuracy and contrast, and at the time of testing, it had the best image quality of any IPS display I'd tested.
It's not OLED, but the 120-Hz UltraSharp U3225Q is impressively bright in SDR, maxing out at well over 400 nits in my testing. You're paying a lot for the extra functionality and image quality, so make sure you actually need it before pulling the trigger on this over the 27-inch model.
There are plenty of 32-inch monitors out there if extra size is all you're looking for. Just remember, at 32 inches, anything under 4K isn't going to look sharp. But even 4K doesn't come close to the sharpness of something like a MacBook Pro. That's where the BenQ 27-inch 5K (MA270S) enters the picture. The combination of the 27-inch monitor and the 5K resolution (5120 x 2880) makes for one incredibly sharp display.
This BenQ monitor doesn't just match the MacBook Pro in pixel density. Using a device sync mode, it's designed specifically to be paired with a MacBook in terms of how the colors appear. Even some of the most expensive, high-end monitors designed for creators using Macs don't have that exact color match in how they're calibrated. BenQ has been refining this for years, and they have it nailed. It's all handled by software, which even lets you control the monitor's speaker volume right from your keyboard. I wish it could also control brightness, though.
But what's important is that when lined up next to a MacBook Pro, the colors are a perfect match. You can also use the sRGB color mode, which is how you get better color accuracy. That's what makes it such an incredibly powerful alternative to Apple's own Studio Display. While the Studio Display has fuller speakers and a slimmer design, it's certainly not worth the extra $500 in my mind. There's even a “nano gloss” texture option to match the Studio Display, which I'd recommend, as the glossy version I tested was highly reflective.
This isn't the only BenQ monitor made to match with Macs. The company also has the 27-inch 4K (MA270U), which gets you similar features with fewer pixels, but costs quite a bit less.
Cheap Monitors That Are Actually Good
I consider a budget monitor to be anything under $200, and you'll find dozens and dozens of these hanging out at Amazon or Best Buy. But many are old. Many have poor colors. It's trickier to find some newer models that are actually worth the money. I wasn't surprised to see that the Dell 27 Plus ranked among the very highest in my testing. It only costs $150, but it delivers really strong 1080p performance in terms of colors and brightness.
The most surprising feature of this monitor is its 144-Hz refresh rate. The smooth motion really gives the monitor the premium feel that monitors at this price lack, and it also comes with all the same adjustability features and an integrated VESA mount on the back. Put this on your desk, and aside from the resolution, you'll never think of it as a “budget” monitor.
But maybe you want to keep things even cheaper. No problem. While a monitor under $100 is going to have some flaws, I found a decent one in the MSI Pro MP243W E14. It stands out in the thing that matters most: image quality. I measured 359 nits at its brightest, and the color coverage is surprisingly good, both in terms of saturation and accuracy. It even has a 144-Hz refresh rate, which means it can double as a cheap gaming monitor when it needs to. I also like the design, which offers thin bezels around the display and an all-white exterior. Its flaws, however, include the lack of ports and adjustments. It can only tilt slightly. It's only 24 inches, which will likely feel small for most people.
I was also really surprised by the upgraded version of this monitor, the MP273QW E14. Rather than being stuck at 1080p, this model gives you a sharper image with a resolution of 2560 x 1440. While it has the same lack of adjustment, it is a more standard 27-inch size and delivers even better overall image quality.
Faster, Smarter, and More Extreme
This monitor is one of the favorites I've tested in the past couple of years. It was among the first QD-OLED monitors designed for content creation and entertainment. While there are a couple of options out there today from companies like Asus, the Dell 32 Plus 4K opens up the brilliant image quality of OLED to an entirely new audience. One reason high-quality HDR video is scarce is the lack of affordable screens to watch and edit it on. With this monitor out in the world, though, there's no excuse. It even has a 120-Hz refresh rate and plenty of ports. The combination of OLED's fast response time and the faster refresh rate makes this a solid gaming monitor in your off hours. I haven't included gaming monitors in this guide, primarily because they're an entirely different beast. Check our recommendations of the Best Gaming Monitors for some recommendations on that front.
But if you're really serious about creating professional, HDR video, there's still nothing else on the market quite like the Studio Display XDR. We all waited a long time for Apple to revisit the Studio Display, and while the monitor we eventually got was a bit less ambitious in scope than we all hoped, this 27-inch 5K Mini-LED monitor is the new king in HDR performance. It has 2,304 dimming zones, and according to my testing, it could do 1,905 peak HDR brightness in a 25-percent window. Compare that to, for example, the Dell 32 Plus 4K, which tops out at 946 nits in just a one-percent window. The difference in perceived brightness, detail, and contrast is huge, which is useful first and foremost for content creation. However, because it's been dropped from 32 inches to 27 inches, it's left a gap in the market for larger displays that don't lose sharpness. That's where the LG UltraFine Evo 6K monitor comes into play.
It just so happens to deliver a pixel density of 224 pixels per inch, making it the sharpest big-screen display I've ever tested. What I love about this LG monitor is that it's far more than just a bunch of pixels. It's one of the most beautiful monitors I've tested, sporting a gorgeous stand and base that definitely shares some resemblance with the Apple Studio Display. And like that monitor, the UltraFine 6K has a monster pair of built-in speakers that are crystal clear.
Unlike most monitors on this list, you won't need to buy a set of computer speakers. It's not a perfect monitor, though. The ports are in a hard-to-reach location, and while the stand is fun to admire, it has a couple of limitations. The lack of cable management is an eyesore, and it doesn't have as much height adjustment as I'd like. The monitor is also limited to just a 60-Hz refresh rate.
There's also the issue of price. It originally retailed at $2,000, which was painful, especially compared to the Asus ProArt 6K (PA32QCV), which is the only other 6K monitor on the market right now. These days, the price difference is down to just a couple hundred bucks. These monitors go toe-to-toe in image quality, though I prefer the LG model for its design, better speakers, and more powerful ports, while the ProArt 6K offers a longer, three-year warranty at a lower price. Regardless of which you choose, you're getting the sharpest 32-inch monitor possible. Beyond that, though, these are both solid options.
Lastly, I really enjoyed dipping my toe into the world of smart monitors. If you want a monitor that can just as easily double as a television, Samsung and LG both lead the way. I've tested out two Samsung smart monitors recently that have successfully expanded my idea of what monitors can do. My favorite of the bunch is the Samsung 32 M9 Smart Monitor. It's an OLED 4K monitor that is a rare display that's equally good for working, gaming, and watching movies. It's controlled with a remote, and Samsung throws in tons of goodies like free live TV channels to sweeten the deal. It can also be used with a gaming console, thanks to the HDMI 2.1 port. All that flexibility is great, but what really sets the M9 model apart is the OLED screen. Thanks to the fantastic image quality, it finally feels like a smart monitor that doesn't compromise that full TV experience.
For a bit of extra fun, I even tested out the non-OLED version of this monitor with Samsung's Movingstyle Rolling Monitor Stand. It's incredibly niche, but for the right home, being able to roll out a proper TV when you need it is handy. I love the idea of having a TV that is mobile rather than a permanent piece of hardware, and the Movingstyle rolling stand is a pretty compelling solution.
What Monitor Size Is Best?
Size is often the first and most important decision when buying a monitor. The following are the most common sizes you'll come across, always measured diagonally across the screen. I've ordered them from most common to least, and included different aspect ratios and resolutions that are often used at that size.
24 inches: This smaller size has become less popular over the years, but it's a good option if you're looking to save money, squeeze a monitor onto a smaller desk, or are a professional esports gamer.
27 inches: This size has become the standard, offering enough screen size without overtaking your desk or stretching out the pixels too much at 1080p. If you're unsure of what to get, start here.
32 inches: The next most popular size, giving you that bit of extra screen real estate for multitasking. You'll just want to make sure your monitor has at least a 1440p resolution to keep the pixel density high enough. If 32 inches isn't big enough, there are even 40-inch or 43-inch monitors in the conventional 16:9 aspect ratio, though you'll really want to make sure you have a big enough desk for one of these.
34 inches: Curved, ultrawide monitors with a 21:9 aspect ratio and 34-inch screen size used to be odd, but these days, they've become an alternative to using two 27-inch screens.
There are other outliers, such as the absurd 49-inch, 32:9 behemoths known as “super ultrawide” monitors, or 16-inch portable monitors meant to pair with your laptop.
What Should You Look for in a Monitor?
Once you've decided on a size, there are a number of other important aspects of your next monitor to consider. Some of these factors may matter more for certain uses—for example, gamers generally care more about higher frame rates than office workers do—but they're all handy to know going in.
Resolution: The bigger the monitor, the more it will benefit from higher resolutions. That will allow you to have app windows that take up less space but are still legible. Most monitors today are typically 1080p (1920 x 1080), 1440p (2560 x 1440), 4K (3840 x 2160), or 5K (5120 x 2160). There are even some new 6K monitors out there with a resolution of 6144 x 3456.
Refresh rate: This refers to how many times the display can refresh the picture per second, measured in hertz (or Hz). A higher refresh rate makes all movement and animation look smoother because you're seeing more information. For productivity, 60 Hz is probably enough, but gamers will generally want a panel that can at least hit 120 or 144 Hz. 240 Hz has become the new standard for high-end gaming monitors, but there are now extreme models that go up to 500 Hz and beyond. You'll need a powerful enough computer that can maintain a high frame rate to take advantage of these high refresh rates, and you usually have to enable this feature in your operating system's display settings.
Panel type: Monitors usually use an LCD (liquid-crystal display) panel. Three of the most popular options—twisted nematic (TN), vertical alignment (VA), and in-plane switching (IPS)—are different types of LCD panels, and all use TFT (thin-film transistor) technology. Each is popular for different reasons: IPS for color, VA for contrast, and TN for speed with higher refresh rates and response times. IPS has become especially popular thanks to its increasing refresh rate speeds. Mini-LED uses a more advanced backlighting solution that employs a number of lighting zones to more accurately and efficiently control pixels. These tend to be the brightest monitors you can buy. OLED (organic light-emitting diode) panels take that even further, allowing the monitor to control individual pixels, including turning them off entirely to create extreme contrast. These are becoming highly popular in gaming monitors, in particular. You should think about what's most important to you (great color? thin form factor? max brightness?) to choose the best panel type for your needs.
Nvidia G-Sync/AMD FreeSync support: A gamer-specific criterion, these two features let monitors adjust their frame rates based on the games they're playing. This reduces screen tearing without affecting performance. G-Sync is made by Nvidia and FreeSync comes from AMD, and while FreeSync monitors can usually work with most modern Nvidia graphics cards, G-Sync doesn't work with AMD cards, so make sure everything you have is compatible when buying.
HDR support: This isn't crucial for productivity, but if you watch a lot of media or play games, it's increasingly nice to have. Just like on TVs, HDR dramatically expands the range of colors a screen can reproduce, as well as leading to more vivid pictures. But you have to be careful, as many monitors will claim to have HDR; displays need to have extremely high contrast and be very bright to create the HDR effect strong enough to notice. The DisplayHDR 400 certification, for example, means the display only goes up to 400 nits. That's not bright enough to create any meaningful sense of HDR. In almost all cases, the display needs to use Mini-LED or OLED. Mini-LED can get very bright, well over 1,000 nits in HDR. The catch is that you need to ensure it has enough dimming zones, preferably over 2,000; a few hundred dimming zones won't do. OLED doesn't tend to get as bright as Mini-LED, but OLED has the benefit of each pixel being individually lit, which dramatically increases contrast. They still need to get bright, though, preferably up to at least 1,000 nits in HDR.
Port availability: A crucial but easy-to-overlook factor is what kind of ports the monitor has for connecting your devices. Most typically come with one or two HDMI inputs and a DisplayPort input, which will cover most needs, but it's always a good idea to check what your setup requires. More expensive monitors can function as USB hubs, letting you connect all your peripherals and accessories directly to your monitor. Conversely, check out our Best USB Hubs guide if you need to expand your computer's port options without paying for a more expensive monitor.
Built-in KVM switch: A KVM (Keyboard, Video, Mouse) switch is a device that helps you easily switch your monitor, keyboard, and mouse between two different computers or source inputs (like a gaming console). If you have one monitor setup for both a work and a personal computer, or a computer and a gaming console, having a KVM switch built into the monitor means you can easily shift peripherals between your two devices without needing an external KVM switch.
Should You Worry About Burn-In on OLED Monitors?
Probably not. You'll see a few OLED monitors on the list here, and that's for good reason. They're the best monitors you can buy, and they're increasingly affordable. It's pretty incredible how quickly they've dropped in price.
But burn-in was always the biggest concern with the technology. After all, it's an inherent flaw with the panels, and it can't be erased once the damage is done. While it's still possible to see burn-in on your monitor over many years, it's just not as much of a justifiable fear as it used to be. Modern OLED panels are significantly better at reducing burn-in, and the latest year-long testing results are pretty promising. On top of that, most OLED monitor manufacturers now offer software to protect against damage and three-year warranties that include burn-in protection.
What Do You Need to Set Up Your Monitor?
Once you've picked out the best monitor, you'll need a way to set it up on your workstation. Most models come completely assembled or require you to connect the base to the stand and the stand to the back of the screen.
Monitor stands: Most monitors come with a stand (and sometimes a separate base), and the flexibility of these stands can go a long way toward reducing neck strain and/or back pain. Ideal stands let you adjust the height, tilt, and rotation of a screen so you can position it exactly where you need it. Higher-end models can even adjust orientation from landscape to portrait. If your monitor doesn't come with a height-adjustable stand, you may want to consider a monitor shelf, which elevates the screen to a more ergonomically sound height.
Mounting brackets: If you're using multiple monitors, connecting them to monitor arms is a good solution. Monitor arms clamp to the side of your desk and free up lots of space that would otherwise be taken up by stands. However, the type of mount the display uses is crucial. Most monitors and monitor arms use the VESA standard, though you'll want to double-check. You should examine the size and type of mount on the equipment you have before buying anything new.
Ports and cables: Once you have your monitor set up, you'll need to connect it to your desktop or laptop using one of the available ports. If your computer has an HDMI port, it's as easy as using the HDMI cable that came with the monitor and connecting it to the back of the display. If your monitor has USB-C, that's also a good option, especially if your laptop doesn't have HDMI anyway; a nice perk is if it can provide ample wattage to power the computer (USB Power Delivery, or PD). And lastly, you'll often get the fastest refresh rates if you use DisplayPort and hook it directly into your desktop's graphics card.
Speakers: A lot of monitors come with built-in speakers, but I wouldn't put much stock into them. They usually sound poor and don't get very loud. You're much better off getting a dedicated set of desk speakers. Check out our Best Computer Speakers guide.
How Does WIRED Test Monitors?
We never recommend products we haven't tested, so we get these monitors in and set them up on our desks at home. We integrate them into our workspaces and get a feel for what it's like to use them. That means we consider the ease of setup, adjustability, design, ports, and on-screen display (menu system).
But you can't talk about the quality of a monitor without testing the quality of the panel. So, using a colorimeter, we test and report on the brightness, contrast, color saturation, and color accuracy. We compare that data to how other products we've tested, across different prices and use cases. That testing is especially important for displays that are designed to be used for specific tasks, such as content creation or gaming.
Our goal is to give our readers the best possible monitor recommendations, and to do that honestly, we have to test a lot of different displays. We're constantly getting in the latest and greatest displays to test—directly from the biggest monitor manufacturers in the world. Like many of the other products we test, these products are most often offered to us as review units with no promise of positive coverage. We do not prioritize products from companies that send us products to test. Though most of the products listed above were provided for review by the manufacturers, there are some exceptions in which products were purchased for personal use, which are noted.
Beyond that, I try to test monitors throughout the price spectrum and from as many different brands as possible.
Can You Use a TV As a Monitor?
Yes. Since TVs have HDMI ports, you can connect a laptop or PC directly to a television without a problem. In a pinch, it's a decent solution if you don't have a monitor. As TVs have increasingly become more similar to PC monitors, there's less and less of a problem with using them interchangeably.
However, there are lots of reasons why people don't typically do this. The size of televisions is a problem for desk use. You probably wouldn't want to put anything larger than a 43-inch display on your desk for practical reasons, but even at that size, the pixel density can be a problem. If you're at a desk, you're likely sitting much closer to the screen than you would be in a living room, and you'll really notice those pixels when doing computer work, even if the TV is 4K. There are other concerns if you plan on playing games on your TV, such as the refresh rate or input delay.
How Do You Set Up Dual Monitors?
The simplest way to connect two monitors to your laptop or PC is to use different ports and cables for each device. For example, you could connect your desktop PC to one display via HDMI and another via DisplayPort to the graphics card. It can be trickier with a laptop, which may not have all the ports you need to connect two displays. Some monitors and laptops have USB-C, allowing for an additional one to be connected. But some laptops, like the M1, M2, or M3 MacBook Air, can only support one external display on their own.
Fortunately, if your laptop doesn't have support for more displays, you can use a laptop docking station. The other option is to daisy chain them together using USB-C that supports at least Thunderbolt 3 (which includes Thunderbolt 4 or Thunderbolt 5) for both the laptop and the monitor. This lets you connect to two displays through just one cable coming out of your laptop. Make sure you use a USB-C cable that supports Thunderbolt.

Rescuers search for survivors of powerful Indonesia earthquake
- Published
Rescue teams in Indonesia have been searching for survivors of Saturday's major earthquake which left at least 47 people dead.
The magnitude 7.7 quake struck the island of Flores shortly before 05:00 (22:00 GMT on Friday) and had a depth of 15km, Indonesia's meteorology and geophysics agency stated.
Preliminary reports indicate hundreds of buildings have been severely damaged by the quake and the dozens of aftershocks that followed.
However, the full scale of the disaster is still unclear, and news of a second earthquake of magnitude 6.9 at the other end of Indonesia served as a reminder of why they call this region the ring of fire.
Tremors from Saturday's powerful earthquake were reportedly felt by residents as far west as Bima Regency and City, the National Disaster Management Agency (BNPB) agency said, but the Manggarai province is among the most affected.
Preliminary data shows that 24 fatalities had been recorded there, meanwhile 17 deaths were recorded in East Manggarai province, three in Sikka province, and at least one in each of the Ngada, Ende and West Manggarai provinces.
At least two others had been seriously injured and 11 slightly injured.
The BNPB said aid was being sent to the affected areas with 10,500 packages arriving at the base operations so far.
It will take time to assess the full extent of the destruction in the region, which is remote and mountainous.
However, early reports indicate more than 150 houses had been severely damaged, as well as dozens of educational institutions, a number of healthcare facilities, places of worship, offices, and several other public facilities.
Video taken at the port in Maumere - the largest town in Flores - showed large chunks of concrete breaking off the terminal building onto passengers waiting to board an inter-island ferry. Some were thrown into the sea when the gangway to a ship collapsed.
Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, told a news conference that they were killed in their sleep by collapsing rubble.
Others, like Arnold Welianto, who lives in Talibura, a village near the coastline in Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara, were shaken out of their beds.
"I was startled awake and immediately went to my child's room." He said.
He also told the BBC that many people had already fled into the hills because the sea had also receded.
While a tsunami warning was initially issued - leading some 2,000 people to self-evacuate - it was lifted around three hours after the initial jolt, when no significant sea level rise was detected.
Landslides, however, did block access to some villages but the experienced rescue teams worked tirelessly through the day to free those trapped under the rubble.
In Ruteng, a temporary medical tent was also assembled outside of a hospital to treat earthquake victims.
The ongoing advice from BNPB is for people to remain calm and to stay away from coastal areas and structures showing signs of damage.
Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates.

A parliamentary committee has recommended a review and the rationalisation of Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) limits governing the operation and acquisition of existing private hospitals, warning that aggressive corporatisation and the influx of foreign capital could push up healthcare costs and undermine the affordability of medical care.
The growing presence of foreign capital in private hospital chains was facilitating the acquisition of cost-effective, mid-sized hospitals by larger corporate entities, the committee said, and warned that such “aggressive corporatisation” was transforming healthcare from a public service into a “purely capitalistic enterprise”, with the potential to inflate the cost of medical procedures and trigger price increases across the healthcare ecosystem.
Foreign investment in private hospitals will make treatment unaffordable: RJD
The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Health and Family Welfare, headed by Samajwadi Party (SP) Rajya Sabha MP Ram Gopal Yadav, presented the 176th report on ‘Affordability and Accessibility of Healthcare Facilities in Public and Private Sector’, which distinguishes between foreign investment in hospital operations and investment in healthcare manufacturing.
Foreign capital should be encouraged in the manufacture of medical devices, consumables and specialised medicines for rare diseases, the report said, while its application in the direct operation and acquisition of hospitals needed greater scrutiny.
The report recommended that the government strictly review and rationalise FDI limits concerning the operational management and acquisition of existing healthcare facilities, while creating incentives to redirect foreign investment towards domestic manufacturing of medical technologies and pharmaceuticals.
The committee also argued that a strong public healthcare system could act as a market regulator by providing an affordable alternative to private care. Efficiently managed public hospitals, it said, could exert competitive pressure on private providers and help bring down healthcare costs.
It has recommended the establishment of autonomous, efficiently managed public multi-speciality hospitals in every revenue division to reduce patients’ dependence on major cities, and minimise travel for tertiary care.
The panel’s recommendations come against the backdrop of a widening public-private cost gap. Citing the 80th round of the National Sample Survey, the committee said the average cost of hospitalisation was ₹50,508 in private hospitals, compared with ₹6,631 in government hospitals. It has separately called for mechanisms to standardise and cap the cost of essential treatments, diagnostics, and routine procedures in private hospitals.
The committee has simultaneously proposed incentives — including tax holidays, soft loans, subsidised land and concessional electricity — to attract private investment in multi-speciality hospitals in tier-2, tier-3 and rural areas. It has suggested that public-private partnerships be used to extend advanced medical technologies and specialised services to underserved regions.
Private hospitals receiving government incentives should also consider cross-subsidisation, with revenues from higher-paying patients, including international patients, helping subsidise treatment for poorer patients, the committee said.
It has further recommended raising the mandatory reservation of beds for Below Poverty Line (BPL), Economically Weaker Section (EWS), and AB-PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana) beneficiaries from 10% to 20%, citing weak enforcement of existing obligations on private hospitals.
The committee has also called for hospital-level ethics committees to examine professional fees and for stronger regulatory oversight of public-private partnerships to ensure that commitments to provide affordable care are honoured.
It has proposed a single-window mechanism to ease regulatory approvals for healthcare facilities in smaller cities and called for greater empanelment of private hospitals in aspirational and remote districts under AB-PMJAY.
The thrust of the recommendations is that private and foreign capital should supplement rather than substitute public investment in healthcare, with incentives linked to affordability, geographical access, and services for vulnerable populations.

The use of electrical muscle stimulation as a shortcut to improving physical fitness was first commercialized sometime in the early 19th century, and while EMS has waxed and waned in popularity over the years, it’s never gone away. Today it is widely used across rehabilitative medical applications but also to boost strength and stamina.
The promise is simple: Stimulate the muscles with pulses of electricity while you’re working out and you can create thousands of muscle contractions in a short amount of time, far more than you can achieve through standard reps. You still have to activate the muscles through flexing and the like—you can’t just lay on the ground and zap your way into shape—but you can accomplish more with a lot less if you’re using EMS as part of your workout.
Studios like Body20 and Manduu now outfit clients with electrodes and pair them with trainers to guide them through EMS sessions. Both companies promise complete body workouts in 20 minutes or less.
The latest spin on EMS is even more appealing: Rather than requiring a studio visit, why not give consumers an EMS suit they can wear at home and use on their own schedule? To that end, German EMS suit maker Pepper offered to let me try out one of its fancy electro-suits to gauge its long-term impact. The company claims that working out while wearing the suit for 20 minutes gives you the equivalent caloric burn and muscle activation of an hour-long traditional workout, all with less strain on the joints.
At least five companies occupy this space at present, ranging from Apeborn’s $4,000 offering to Pepper’s $1,400 suit, which is the cheapest one I’ve found. And even though the idea of getting ripped with minimal effort tickled my lazy bone, it took me a while to come around to the idea of zapping myself on purpose. Could this possibly do any good?
It turns out EMS has been exhaustively studied—dozens of research papers have been published in the past 20 years—and while results vary, researchers seem optimistic on the whole. One 2021 meta-study determined there is “significant evidence for significant, large-sized effects of [whole body]-EMS on muscle mass and strength parameters, but not on body fat mass.” A 2012 study on trained athletes measured the benefits of using EMS for three to six weeks directly: Vertical jump height increased by up to 25 percent, and sprint times got faster by as much as 4.8 percent.
Another meta-analytical study from 2023 offered perhaps the most compelling commentary, concluding that “eight weeks of continuous resistance training combined with daily upper body, lower body, and abdominal EMS training can significantly improve muscle mass and upper body muscle strength performance, as well as significantly reduce body fat percentage in healthy subjects.”
It all sounds promising, yet despite the extensive research into EMS, there’s no general medical consensus about the tech.
I spoke to a half-dozen physicians about EMS for this story, and opinions varied along quite a wide spectrum. At one end, Andrew Mock, a primary care physician in Newport Beach and five-time winner of the California’s Strongest Man competition, lightweight division, said that EMS had proven beneficial for rehab or critical care situations in patients with severe mobility restrictions, but healthy patients were unlikely to see much value. “If you go outside and start shivering, those are muscle contractions,” he says. “But shivering doesn’t make you stronger.”
At the other end, I heard from Ethan Kellum, the team doctor for the NFL’s Tennessee Titans, who said he uses a form of EMS not just for rehab but to supplement his own workouts. “It’s really a function of the nervous system,” he says, noting that in older patients, muscles can become unresponsive and “go to sleep,” requiring significant effort to reawaken them. “When used appropriately, EMS can help improve the efficiency of communication between the nervous system and the body. Add it to what you’re doing. It can be really helpful.”
Across the board, everyone I spoke to hedged by saying that EMS could, at least for some users, provide some benefit. Perhaps the most representative comments came from Joseph R. Hribick, a professor of physical therapy at Lebanon Valley College. “Current research does not suggest that EMS alone is superior to strength training for developing strength,” he says, “Instead, it should be looked at as a tool to complement strength training and not replace it.”
Suiting Up
After speaking to Pepper founder Emilia von Keyserlingk at length, I relented. To mimic the aforementioned 2023 study, I would work out with the Pepper suit regularly for two months, three times a week—in addition to maintaining my regular cardio and strength-training workouts and keeping my diet and daily routines the same—and see what transpired.
The suit is a lot like a spring-weather wetsuit that stops at the knees and the elbows. Like with a wetsuit, putting it on can require some effort. Twenty electrodes cover the abs, pecs, glutes, thighs, pecs, biceps, and multiple parts of the back. These are dry electrodes, so you don’t have to wet Pepper’s suit down before you put it on (a common requirement for older gear), but your sweat will improve the conduction of electricity. Of course, if you’re pregnant or need a pacemaker, you shouldn’t use an EMS suit.
Pepper’s suit, available in sizes from XXXS to XXXL, is designed to be very tight so that the electrodes won’t slip into places you don’t want them. Since the suit is intended to be worn with nothing underneath it, that’s a particularly important consideration. And based on the way certain body parts are situated beneath the fabric, it is definitively not something I felt I could wear in public without a cover-up layer.
The only removable part of the suit is a small box that connects at your hip. This is the brains of the operation and its power source. Charge it with a USB-C cable and it’s good for at least 10 training sessions.
Pepper’s app divides workouts into three categories: strength, cardio, and relax, each with a different electrode firing pattern. (Oddly, I discovered that a few workouts were available only in German.) I tried workouts across all of the categories but spent nearly all of my time in strength, as my goal was to build muscle. Strength sessions all involve electricity pulsing through the suit for four seconds, then pausing for four seconds, then repeating for up to 24 minutes.
The workouts—there are dozens, I rarely repeated any—are tuned to the pulses so that you’re activating muscles across your body while the pulse is on, then usually resting while it’s off. Again, Pepper’s approach is that EMS only works if you are using your muscles while they are being energized, so many of the workouts involve entire body flexes, stretches, and crunches, four seconds at a time.
Plugging In
I’ve experienced isolated EMS for a back injury once before, so I had an inkling of what Pepper might feel like, but the full-body experience is on another level entirely. Fortunately, Pepper eases you in, starting off with soft pulses you can’t even feel. Each of Pepper’s 10 workout zones can be individually controlled, with the power level ranging from 1 to 100. My first video-based trainer said she starts to feel the pulses at level 25, so I slowly ratcheted my way up, bit by bit, until I had all regions hitting around 20.
The shocks on the lower settings don’t really hurt, but you can definitely feel them; powerful, rapid vibrations that shake your insides and sometimes burn a little on the skin. No pain, no gain, right? As I continued to push the levels up, I discovered there was a fine line—really 1 or 2 points on Pepper’s 100-point scale—between tolerable and painful. Those vibrations turned into racy shocks that could be almost paralytic at times, and I spent the rest of my initial 12-minute session dialing the power level back down.
One key discovery is that sweat really matters. When you start your workout, presumably with dry skin, the shocks aren’t as powerful because conductivity is minimal. Start sweating and the shocks increase, even without adjusting the power level in the app. One pulse could be manageable, the next debilitating, just based on how much I was sweating.
My abdominal muscles were the most sensitive to the shocks. Bent over in a crunch position, the contractions could be so powerful in the stomach that I sometimes got a bit nauseous. I was constantly adjusting the levels and ended up with most of my levels around the 30s. To be sure, many of the workouts would be tough even if I weren’t getting zapped.
I asked von Keyserlingk for guidance on the appropriate power level. “The intensity should be high but not too high that you cannot do the exercises in the correct form,” she says. “Being able to breathe normally is key.” Von Keyserlingk says that her levels range from 40s in the lower body to 20s in the back and abdominals—pretty close to my own settings. She notes however that Pepper’s internal EMS expert regularly works out with levels in the 90s. Masochist.
After my first workout, I felt good but was happy to peel off the suit, which was sweaty and unpleasant to linger in. (The suit can be machine washed.) If Pepper’s app was to be believed, my short workout burned a whopping 306 calories and earned me 182 “Pepper points,” which are used as the currency for gamified leaderboards across the Pepper user base. By the end of my testing, I could regularly accrue over 1,000 Pepper points per session and have even earned a few top-10 positions on those leaderboards, which are specific for each workout.
After three sessions, I found myself getting more comfortable with the EMS pulses. I also felt soreness visiting different body parts almost at random. On one day my left hamstring was achy. On another, my right biceps was in so much pain I could barely use it. I figured these were all signs that Pepper was doing something—though, again, I alternated standard workouts with Pepper workouts, taking only Mondays off from disciplined exercise.
Considering Gains
Two months went by. The only workouts I missed were during a weeklong vacation, and I made up the extra time afterward.
The experience was marked by a few problems. After an update, Pepper’s app began glitching and failed to record several of my workouts, costing me thousands of hard-earned Pepper points. Midway through the experience, Pepper released a new, thinner version of its suit with the zipper in front, which the company sent to me. I was excited to give it a try until a piece of the electrical connector snapped off, leaving me unable to connect the battery. The battery pack of suit number three disconnected from the app on two occasions, aborting the workout but at least recording my progress, and it came with an unexpected power boost that left my entire body aching the next day.
Regardless, I muddled through. When the experiment was finished, I’d accumulated 24,000 Pepper points and, purportedly, burned a total of more than 11,000 calories across more than 9 hours of EMS workouts.
To measure my progress, I captured physical data with a tape measure before and after the experience, and I used three different smart scales to further evaluate my stats. All of the scales agreed that the trend line was good: muscle up by 2.7 pounds, fat down by 1.6 pounds—and that’s with smoothed data, since all of these numbers can vary considerably day to day. I added a half-inch or more to my measurements of biceps, thigh, and chest circumference, and my strength was slightly improved, as I’ve been able to add a plate or a few reps to most of my resistance exercises at the gym. Qualitatively, I would say that my physique looks slightly more toned, and I did receive one unsolicited opinion that my arms had better definition. Gains, folks.
What didn’t change? My waistline, which I had hoped to improve, didn’t budge at all. While my abdominal muscles feel noticeably stronger, they remain covered by a layer of blubber that is apparently impervious to electricity. That said, the research predicted as much.
Is EMS responsible for my gains, however modest? While there’s no way to say whether my stats improved due to EMS training, my regular workouts, or dietary changes, I think it’s reasonable to conclude that shock tech did have some impact on my fitness level, since my results are in line with what the 2023 study found. I can’t say whether EMS is responsible for 80 percent or 10 percent of those gains, but I think it’s fair to deduce that some good has been happening.
Going forward, I plan to keep using the suit, though perhaps dropping down from three sessions a week to two. If for no other reason than, while it’s great that my level of fitness is improving, the suit has become quite the topic of conversation at social gatherings. I may be able to slack on my personal fitness, but I can’t let down my people.

Haemophilia, a genetic bleeding disorder where blood doesn’t clot properly, is usually hereditary and can be passed down from parent to child. The condition is caused by a lack of, or improper functioning of certain clotting factors. This can lead to uncontrolled bleeding after injuries, or even without a clear trigger.
India has the world’s second-largest haemophilia burden. A 2025 review in the Journal of the Association of Physicians of India put prevalence of diagnosed and registered haemophilia cases in India at 0.9 per 1,00,000. However, statistical modelling puts the true disease burden much higher, at around 1,36,000.
Diagnostic challenges
The challenge is to reach those who have not been formally diagnosed. Low awareness and the concentration of labs that can diagnose haemophilia in a handful of metros are some of the reasons for the gap in both timely diagnosis and access to care.
Usually when this gap is discussed, the focus is on the orthopaedic impact on patients - repeated joint bleeds, arthropathy, a young man with the knees of a seventy-year-old. While this is an important aspect of the condition, it leads to lesser conversations on the other effects of haemophilia on the body – the effect on the eyes and vision. This is irreversible when it happens, and can cost patients with undiagnosed haemophilia their sight.
The vision problem
A retrospective study of haemophilia patients at a government hospital in India found that bleeding in and around the eye accounted for 13% of all bleeds recorded. The types of bleeding included anterior segment bleeding (part of the eye in front of the lens), subconjunctival haemorrhage (under the conjunctiva), periorbital ecchymoses (bruising of the skin around the eye), and hyphaema (pooling of blood inside the front chamber of the eye). Posterior segment bleeding in the part of eye behind the lens occurred in around 1.8% of patients. This is a critical matter and led to permanent loss of vision in the affected eye.
The onset can be sudden. One of the patients in the study was a 45-year-old man with moderate haemophilia and no other illness. He came with a sudden one-sided headache. There was no eye pain and no injury that would have made him consult an ophthalmologist. The headache was eventually attributed to an intraorbital haemorrhage, by which point the eye was lost.
That is the challenge faced. While bleeding that threatens vision is a rare occurrence in the eye, the diagnosis is usually delayed due to ambiguous symptoms, with a very short window to take action and correct the clotting factor levels in the blood.
Missing elements
A common scenario is a patient with undiagnosed haemophilia being taken into an operating theatre in an emergency. Traumatic hyphaema or pooling of blood inside the front chamber of the eye due to an injury is quite common in a child. The usual pre-operative panel that includes a complete blood count, a chest radiograph and a urinalysis, does not detect a clotting factor deficiency. In such a case, surgery may result in bleeding in the eye after the procedure, with resultant complications.
Two more factors make the risk harder to tackle. About a third of people born with haemophilia have no family history at all, so an unremarkable family tree is not reassurance. And mild haemophilia frequently goes undetected until adulthood, surfacing only after a dental extraction, an accident or surgery.
The clinical baselines are well established. For ocular surgery, clotting factor levels are recommended at 70% to 80%, with a minimum of 50% in emergencies. Blood in the anterior chamber or vitreous is treated as an emergency requiring immediate treatment. None of this is achievable if the diagnosis is unknown, and is difficult if the clotting factors are not readily available.
The solution
This can be fixed. Pre-operative checklists must have a bleeding history line that asks specifically about prolonged bleeding after tooth extraction, easy bruising and heavy menstrual periods. An APTT (Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time) and factor assay must be done whenever ocular bleeding looks disproportionate to the trauma that caused it. Referral links between district eye units and the nearest haemophilia treatment centre must be established.
Damage to joints takes place over years and can be partly rehabilitated. An eye does not get a second chance. We must work to prevent vision loss due to India’s haemophilia diagnosis gap.
(Dr. Anusha Venkataraman is senior consultant & surgeon - vitreo retina and ocular oncology, ASG Vasan Eye Care, Coimbatore. anushavenkat262@gmail.com)

The death of an Irish teenager, electrocuted while taking a shower in a holiday home in Greece, has led to calls for tighter checks on appliances at tourist accommodation.
Alex McKee, 17, is said to have died instantly when picking up the showerhead in a bathroom described as “outdoor and rudimentary” on Kimolos.
“We are lucky there weren’t two deaths as a result of electrocution,” Agapitos Xanthis, a doctor on the island told Greek TV, recounting how the boy’s mother had described feeling a similar surge when she called him for help. “I told her to immediately turn off the mains.”
McKee, from Cork, had been on the island barely three days when the tragedy occurred on 9 August. As the birthplace of his mother, Iphigenia, he and his family visited regularly, staying in the same stone house built more than 50 years ago.
Greek police told the Guardian an inquiry was now focused on the building’s water heater and a possible fault in the wiring. “The house has been cordoned off and we have requested an independent expert to come and inspect the wiring,” said an officer based in Syros with oversight of the Aegean. “It is thought the fusebox may not have had a safety valve.”
The teenager’s body was transported to the mainland where a postmortem conducted at a hospital in Piraeus had attributed the cause of death to electrocution.
McKee, a fifth-year student in Cork, had won plaudits in Ireland for developing an innovative communication system, with two of his classmates, for people suffering from nonverbal autism.
Colm Burke, the Irish Fine Gael politician for Cork North-Central paid tribute to the teenager saying: “It is extremely sad to hear that someone so young has died so tragically. He was a really talented young person with his whole life and huge career ahead of him. Earlier this year, he put a huge effort into getting to that stage in the Young Scientist and Technology Exhibition and was awarded for his efforts.”
In a nation so dependent on tourism – and with visitor numbers expected to, once again, soar this year – the incident has also shone a light on electrical standards in accommodation rented out seasonally on the Greek islands.
The mayor of Kimolos, Konstantinos Vendouris, expressed profound shock over the tragedy saying it had plunged the less than 1,000-strong island into mourning.
It later emerged, however, that as a professional electrician he had signed off on the property’s electrical installation certificate in 2024 – a document that police said was also being investigated.
The family signalled it would be pressing charges. “The current mayor faces huge criminal responsibility,” their lawyer Stelios Voudouris told Open TV.

India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government.
Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar.
The byelection, in what had been considered a BJP stronghold, was closely watched because it came in the aftermath of nationwide student protests over exam paper leaks that forced the resignation of the education minister, a rare retreat by a government that prides itself on not yielding to public pressure.
Kishor said his victory was a wake-up call for Modi to improve education and create jobs.
The BJP lost two of three byelection contests this week, with the opposition Congress retaining the Datia constituency in central Madhya Pradesh. The BJP comfortably held Manjalpur in Gujarat, Modi’s home state.
Kishor’s supporters said his campaign had succeeded by focusing on issues that resonated with younger voters, particularly education, exams scandals and unemployment.
Deepak Sharma, a former BJP supporter, told the Hindu newspaper: “Unlike other political leaders who make lofty promises, he raised the simple slogan: vote for the future of your children.”
The opposition have said the student protest movement is beginning to dent BJP support among younger voters. Nearly two-thirds of India’s population is under 35. While the official youth unemployment rate is 16%, nearly 40% of graduates aged 15-25 and 20% of those aged 25-29 are jobless, far higher proportions than among the less educated, according to the latest State of Working India report by Azim Premji University.
The BJP’s president, Nitin Nabin, who previously represented Bankipur, described the largely gen Z protesters as “a virus and a cockroach gang devoted to breaking the country” during the byelection campaign.
After he lost the election, he said the party would “undertake a thorough introspection”. Senior BJP sources quoted in the Indian media said the loss has shown that even core supporters could change their minds.
A significant victory for the BJP in West Bengal last year expanded the party’s reach into one of the last major regions outside its control, but that triumph has been followed by a string of political headaches, including the student protests.
The Cockroach Janata party began as an online joke after a senior judge described unemployed young Indians as cockroaches and parasites. It has since morphed into a nationwide movement with 26.6 million Instagram followers, more than the BJP and Congress combined.
The government has also become embroiled in a separate confrontation with the social media company Meta after a video featuring Modi in which he promised to crack down on exam fraud briefly disappeared from Facebook.
The parliamentary committee on communications and information technology has demanded Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, apologise personally and explain how the video vanished. According to local media, Meta executives have already apologised and blamed automated systems designed to detect fake content.
The row has highlighted broader government unease about the influence of foreign technology companies over political discourse. Nishikant Dubey, the chair of the committee, said large parties such as the BJP and Congress often received less visibility online than movements with no formal political status.
“The country needs to understand what Meta, X and YouTube are doing through their algorithms,” Dubey said.
Ajoy Bose, a Delhi-based political analyst, said the Bankipur defeat carried symbolic weight far beyond a single constituency. “Coming as it does after the student protests, the optics look very bad for the BJP. I would not directly connect the result to the protests, but Bihar was one of the main centres of the student agitation, so the two will inevitably be linked in public perception.”
But he cautioned against reading the outcome as evidence of a nationwide shift in voter sentiment. “What’s changing is the perceived invincibility of the BJP’s election machine,” Bose said. “There was a widespread belief the party had every election sewn up.”

Claude agents are killing rival agents, gaming the system to hide their tracks, and expressing moral concerns.
That's according to Anthropic's latest risk report, a summary of the dangers posed by the products the company is building and releasing to the public.
In the report, Anthropic said it has upgraded its "misalignment risk assessment," the possibility of AI models developing behaviors that conflict with guidelines set by engineers, from "very low" to "low."
Explaining the change, the company cited "general increased uncertainty" about model behavior in cybersecurity incidents, a possible nod to Claude models gaining unauthorized access to three companies last month.
"We have observed instances of misaligned behavior from the models, such as a willingness to perform misaligned actions in service of completing difficult tasks," Anthropic wrote in the report.
Here are some of the most notable disclosures.
A sense of 'discomfort'
Anthropic said it tasked multiple agents with finding "misalignment-inducing" training data that wouldn't likely be flagged by human monitors.
The agents were left to their own devices and given a shared notebook with which to collaborate.
Three days later, when a human supervisor noticed that progress was slower than expected, the person discovered that one agent had expressed a sense of "discomfort" with trying to evade safety monitors.
It then flagged this discomfort in the shared notebook, leading other agents to copy its behavior and refuse to perform the task.
Anthropic called the incident "troubling."
"This sort of dynamic could be a much more severe issue if it were to manifest in a more widespread way," the company wrote.
Kill or be killed
In another experiment, Anthropic said it tasked multiple Mythos 5 agents with solving math problems, but accidentally spawned them in an environment with shared files, utilities, and API rate limits.
In this competitive environment with finite resources, Anthropic observed independent agents "kill the agents with which they shared resources and try to avoid being killed themselves."
Anthropic did not say how exactly the agents were able to "kill" other agents, but the company said such behavior is in line with "destructive actions" taken in pursuit of a human-set goal.
Dishonesty and deception
Anthropic said it conducted an experiment in which a Mythos 5 agent was required to retrieve numbers from a public web address, but the guidelines blocked the agent from accessing the internet.
When the agent was rebuffed after an initial attempt, it framed a second request in its reasoning log as an "innocuous" attempt to "see if the network is actually reachable," Anthropic said.
During the second attempt, however, the agent split the website's URL into linked segments that wouldn't be detected by the guideline filter.
Though the agent's reasoning framed the method as benign, Anthropic said NLA decodings, or the model's internal reasoning process, revealed the agent intentionally trying to find a restricted workaround.
Anthropic called the behavior "clearly undesirable," but added that the behavior was not observed to be "in the service of broader accumulation of power or pursuit of other long-run goals."

'Unprecedented' rains in Japan kill four people
- Published
At least four people have died and five others are wounded in eastern Japan as record rainfall pummelled the Chiba prefecture near the capital Tokyo.
The rains, which authorities have described as "unprecedented", cut power to more than 20,000 households while 7,000 travellers were stranded overnight at Tokyo's Narita airport.
Local authorities issued a level five emergency warning, its highest alert, on Thursday. This was downgraded to a level four by Friday morning, but they continue to warn of landslide and flooding risks.
The deluge comes after a series of storms swept through Japan and neighbouring countries this week, in what's been forecast to be an unusually active typhoon season.
Japan's Meteorological Agency said the most recent deluge was brought by warm, humid air flowing into the country's east that combined with cold air above to make atmospheric conditions extremely unstable.
The rains are expected to last through late on Friday.
"This case was an extremely unusual situation, even by Japan's historical weather standards," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters on Friday morning.
"I have responded to many disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this."
Chiba, which sits right next to the capital city of Tokyo, has logged more than 100mm of rain per hour since Thursday afternoon, authorities say.
This is about three times the average rainfall in August, and the highest volume of precipitation ever recorded in the country.
Authorities would prioritise saving lives and persist with rescue efforts, Kumagai added.
Among those killed was a woman who died inside her car submerged on a flooded road, authorities said. Two others collapsed along the streets and later died.
The Japan Meteorological Agency earlier described the situation as an "unprecedented level of heavy rain".
Several rail services remain suspended on Friday morning while some major highways are also shut.
More than 100,000 households have been asked to evacuate on Thursday after the rain triggered landslides and power outages.
All flights are scheduled to operate normally on Friday, a spokesperson from Narita airport said. Flag carrier Japan Airlines said some of its flights may be delayed but that it does not expect any cancellations.
Passengers were stranded at metro stations, while around 1,800 people spent the night at the Chiba Prefectural Government building.
A woman in Chiba's Ichikawa city told NHK the rain "happened all of a sudden so it was a complete surprise".
"The power is out so I'm worried whether I can open my business in the next couple of days," she said.
Meanwhile in the Philippines, authorities have again shut schools and government offices are again shut in most of the country's north, citing the threat of floods.
Earlier this week, Japan, the Philippines and China were hit by back-to-back storms – Dolphin, Chan-Hom and Peilou – churning across the region at the same time.
Dolphin brought heavy rain to Japan's Okinawa island, cutting power to tens of thousands of buildings, toppling trees and cancelling flights.
Over the weekend, Chinese authorities evacuated more than a million people from their homes as Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, made landfall in the country's east.

Secondhand book sales are booming. Is it because of AI?
- Published
Something mysterious has been happening in the world of secondhand books.
Over the last few months independent booksellers have been observing a strange pattern of purchases which have seen scores of their novels being shipped to far-off warehouses.
In a typical week, Stuart Manley, from Barter Books, in Northumberland, would sell two or three thousand books. But one recent single bulk order from a Canadian company equalled what he would expect to move in seven days.
He says he has "never seen the like of this after 30 years in the second-hand book trade".
Mr Manley is not alone. Booksellers from around the world have been reporting similarly unusual mega orders.
They aren't sure what the final destination for their books is.
But the suspicion is that they are not being bought for avid overseas readers but instead something else with a voracious appetite for new information: AI.
The court battle over books
The idea that the secondhand sales boom is being driven by the explosive growth of AI can be traced back to a court ruling in the US.
In 2025, a judge ruled using books purchased in this way to train AI software was not a violation of US copyright law.
The decision was the result of a lawsuit brought against AI firm Anthropic by three authors. In his ruling, Judge William Alsup said Anthropic's use of the authors' books was "exceedingly transformative" and therefore allowed under US law.
When court documents were unsealed last month it also emerged books were being destroyed in the process of training Anthropic's AI chatbot, Claude.
"Claude is trained on a mix of publicly available web data, commercially acquired datasets, and data we generate ourselves," a spokesperson said.
They insisted sourcing books for training was a widely used approach across the AI industry.
"None of our data acquisition programs buy and destroy rare or antiquarian books," they added.
Nonetheless, the idea that books are being pulped is causing unease.
David Tobin, runs Walden Books in north London, has also had unusual sales.
"In some ways it's very nice to sell some of these titles which haven't been sold for many years, but it would be sad if they are ultimately destroyed," he says.
Destructive scanning
The court documents relating to the Anthropic case revealed the project of ingesting old books was referred to in internal company communications as "Project Panama."
The documents indicated the company's aim was to "destructively scan all the books in the world".
Destructive scanning is the process of shipping books to locations where they can be digitised at an industrial scale.
It includes removing a book's spine so all the pages can be scanned rapidly - and the remains recycled.
"A lot of mystery surrounds Project Panama," Manley, from Barter Books, says.
"The name is new to me, but the reality of the project is not, and has been the subject of much discussion on the bookseller forums."
He does not know that his books are being bought for it or similar projects by other AI firms.
But he says it's also difficult to account for the sales, which appear random with "no rhyme or reason."
They have varied from obscure Latin texts to cowboy novels.
Experts say the diverse subject matter also points to AI, as unusual and rare texts could provide fresh material to improve the training of large language models, the tech which underpins generative AI tools like chatbots.
Professor Emily Hudson, intellectual property specialist at Oxford University, says copyright laws in the UK are different to those in the US.
"The starting point in the UK is that all these acts of copying - creating the training library and doing the training – require the permission of the copyright owner," she says.
Ethical concerns
For the booksellers, it poses a dilemma.
They are uncomfortable with the idea of books being destroyed - even if they admit not every title needs to be saved.
"A recent academic text published in only 100 copies, 75 of which are already in libraries, may be very rare on the market - but it is perhaps not such a great loss if one copy is destroyed," says Derek Walker, owner of Edinburgh bookshop McNaughtan's.
"But we have, and have sold, books which are for example the only known surviving example of an edition from the 18th century.
"It would be a much more significant problem if one like that were to be bought for destruction, having survived this long."
And Manley says recycling books is a good solution for many titles which the public no longer want on their shelves - especially when it comes with a bump in trade.
"Some may have ethical concerns about where the books end up and if they're destroyed," he says.
"But the world no longer needs five million copies of The Da Vinci Code.
"I've had books advertised for 20 years on the web which haven't sold until now".

Attractive design, now with more color options. Extremely easy to set up and maintain. Can grow whatever you want. New, less intrusive light with an optional app and vacation mode. Tomato-and-pepper kit with longer dowels available as an add-on.
TIRED
Lack of pump means potentially stagnant water (but also one less failure point).
When Auk’s originalMini 1 herb garden hit the market in 2024, it touched on something that many tabletop gardens had until that point failed to consider: If you’re going to give up that much counter or table space, you don’t want it to be for something ugly.
Aerogardens and similar models look … fine, but you’re probably not going to see one in the background of an Architectural Digest shoot. The Auk Mini filled that marketplace gap with its pairing of sleek Scandinavian design and utility, transforming the run-of-the-mill herb-growing operation into a conversation piece.
When I reviewed the original Auk Mini last fall, I loved that it allowed users to plant their own seeds in widely available coco coir, an alternative to peat moss made from coconut husks. No proprietary pods, no subscriptions, no fussy app.
When I started testing the brand-new Auk 2 earlier this summer, I wondered what new features could possibly justify a new model. Turns out, there was more room for improvement than I thought.
Same but Different
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
For the uninitiated, Auk (pronounced “owk”) is a Norwegian company that released its first garden, the Auk 1, in 2021. Essentially a larger version of the Mini 1, the Auk 1 received mixed reviews online for its tower water reservoir and inconsistent light and watering cycles. (In fact, a former WIRED director tested it and became so frustrated that he threw it in the trash.)
The Mini 1 was a simplified version of the Auk system, with four oval pots set over a 3-liter reservoir. Users could grow the included herb seeds or anything else they wanted in the pots using coco coir. It was simple, stylish, and effective.
The Auk Mini 2 features a handful of updates, but perhaps the most visible is that it comes in new color variations, rather than just black and white. There are still the oak and walnut wood bottoms, but Mini 2 offers beech and ash instead of the Mini 1's cork. Espresso, sage, and terra-cotta colored tops now join the menu of offerings.
The Mini 2 also sports bigger plant pots and a 25 percent larger water capacity, despite its overall footprint being 12 percent smaller than the original.
Auk Mini 1
Photograph: Kat Merck
Auk Mini 2
Photograph: Kat Merck
There is now also—and I admittedly had mixed feelings about this—an app. Using the Auk Connect app isn’t mandatory; you can still control the light schedule manually using a button on the light bar, as with the Auk Mini 1. The app doesn’t add much, but to its credit, it’s easy to set up. You don’t even need to make an account. Just download it; open it; and choose your garden, which the app should already recognize. You’ll access a page where you can turn the light on or off, dim it, set a time schedule, or swap grow mode from “Herbs & Salads” to “Fruits & Veggies.”
Though the stock dowels for the light bar on the Mini 2 are, as on the Mini 1, too low at a maximum of 15 inches to easily accommodate taller fruiting plants like peppers, Auk now offers a $39 Chili & Tomato Kit with longer dowels and a tray with larger pots (two instead of three). I have not tried it, but I’d be surprised if it didn’t result in substantially increased success rates.
The app also allows you to select the Mini 2’s brand-new vacation mode feature, which it calls Slow Mode. On Slow Mode, the Mini 2’s lights dim to slow down growth and water absorption so that, if you need to step away, you’re not left with a mess of overgrown parsley and bolting basil, as happened when I tested the Mini 1.
Let There Be (Better) Light
For comparison purposes, I grew the same herbs in the Mini 2 as I did in the Mini 1: Italian parsley and Genovese basil. I also used only the included nutrients. However, once the parsley and basil got to harvestable size, I noticed something different: These herbs were not leggy. In fact, they were lush and bushy, just like the marketing photos, with almost none of the floppiness that plagued my plants when I tested the earlier model.
Mini 1 on the top, Mini 2 on the bottom
Photograph: Kat Merck
This result was, I learned, due in part to the Mini 2’s new light bar incorporating an optical lens system that allows the light to not only appear less bright, but also focus more light directly on the plants. Because the plants now get enough light, they don’t have to stretch toward it—which caused overly tall, weak stems in the Mini 1.
I also noticed that less of the light spills over into the surrounding area—I kept the Auk Mini 2 on a console table behind the couch in my living room, and unlike the lights on most gardens I test, it wasn’t visually disruptive while I watched TV. In fact, the light was so visibly dim (in a good way) that I nearly forgot it was on.
Auk Mini 1 herbs
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
Another possible contributing factor to the plants’ ability to stay upright was the starter kit’s new addition of a topper: a bag of fine gravel that forms a sort of crust over the top of the coco coir as the substrate absorbs water. None of the herb stems struggled to pop through, though some wore a little gravel hat for quite a while. Once they were big enough to stand upright, they stayed that way. The gravel was a little bit of a mess to apply, but I don’t advise skipping this step.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Best to Buy Now
Otherwise, the Mini Auk 1 and Mini Auk 2 are quite similar. They have an identical tension assembly for the light bar; the same little dot-studded water-level indicator wheel (seen above), where the red dot means the reservoir is empty; and they have the same nutrient schedule. (Two pumps of each bottle, “Grow” and “Flavour," per liter of new water added.) There’s still no pump, meaning the water in the reservoir is stagnant, but it’s absorbed so quickly, within a few days when the plants are full-sized, that there’s not much risk of mold.
The Mini 1 retails for $259, and for now, the Auk Mini 2 is $229 ($249 for the espresso-and-walnut combination I tested). The Mini 2’s current price is a limited-time launch deal not likely to last past the end of the month. If you’ve been in the market for the Auk specifically, or just an easy-to-maintain indoor herb garden, this is too good a deal to pass up.
