I used Claude Cowork to organize my downloaded courses and build a local offline course player with progress tracking, autoplay, subtitles, a Pomodoro timer, mobile access, and custom study plans. It runs on Mac or Windows and keeps everything on your device.
There are plenty of course streaming platforms out there. All of those come with a learning management system where the courses are organized by default and let you keep track of your progress. Some even motivate you to finish the courses on time, while others spam your email inbox because you left on the second day of starting a course.
But I sometimes prefer learning courses offline. I download the entire catalog, whether it’s a YouTube video playlist or courses from third-party websites (if allowed).
Then, I put my phone in silent mode, turn on the Pomodoro timer for 45 minutes to finish as many as possible. This is the most productive way, and the one I recommend to everyone. However, it can get increasingly complex if you have multiple courses and thousands of videos that you need to organize.
Moreover, if you are playing them offline, it’s hard to track your progress, which can quickly create a frustrating experience.
For years, I had no choice except to carefully write a separate note of where my videos are located and how many videos I have finished in each session. But that has changed once I built my own course player. Thanks to Claude, I have built a local course player that organizes all my courses into simple folders and keeps track of my progress. Moreover, since I built it myself, I can add a few features as I want on top of the existing setup.
For instance, I added a native Pomodoro timer, which allows me to focus for 45 min without any distractions, and added the ability to autoplay the next video, which websites lack by default. You need to manually play the next video.
And it doesn’t stop here. Since you are building it on your own using AI, you have complete control to add whatever features you like and can fix all your pain points that you are currently facing while you are learning something offline.
In this guide, you are going to learn how I use Claude Cowork to organize my messy download folders. You will also learn how I created a simple offline course tracker website that organizes files into folders and keeps track of my progress, and also how you can add additional features to it.

How to Build a Local Offline Course Player Using Claude Cowork
This can be done with other co-working agents from OpenAI, such as ChatGPT Work, Codex, and Google’s Antigravity, or using other AI models of your choice. The process is pretty much straightforward and very simple; these AI models will do everything for you and can keep staring at the screen until it’s done and finish your chores.
Before going to the steps, remember that to do this, you need a Claude subscription to access the Claude Cowork feature and a Mac or Windows laptop to create a local course. Now, let’s get started.
Step 1: First, open the Claude app on your Mac or Windows and switch to the Home tab
Step 2: Now switch to Cowork mode.
Step 3: Now select the location of the folder where all your courses are located. Tap on the Add a Folder option.
Step 4: Now enter this prompt and press Enter; this even works if your course files are in zip folders.
Prompt:
“I have a folder of video courses on my computer. Connect to it and help me organize it based on what is actually there. Do not assume any folder structure. First, survey the folder without changing anything. Report the total number of courses, videos, and total storage size. Identify all video formats, including MP4, MKV, WebM, MOV, AVI, and any videos stored inside ZIP or RAR archives. Explain whether the content is stored as a flat folder of videos, one folder per course, nested sub-courses, or a mixture. Identify extra files such as SRT or VTT subtitles, PDFs, slides, exercise files, and code. Look for real problems, including sub-courses buried inside unrelated courses, duplicate content, empty folders, inconsistent or messy names, and filenames that do not sort correctly, such as “Lesson 10” appearing before “Lesson 2.” Then tell me honestly whether the folder is already well organized. If it is, say so and stop. Do not reorganize it unnecessarily. Only propose changes that fix problems you actually found. If changes are needed, show me a detailed plan before touching anything. Specify exactly which folders will be moved, renamed, or set aside, and ask for my approval. If multiple approaches are reasonable, explain them and ask which one I prefer. Never delete anything. Before treating files as duplicates, prove they are identical by comparing filenames and sizes or by calculating checksums, and show me the evidence. Move anything unwanted into a reversible “_removed” folder. After approval, execute the plan and verify that nothing was lost. Reconcile the video count and total size before and after, then show me the final course catalog. Keep subtitles and resources alongside their related videos. Never re-encode, rename, or modify video files themselves. Only reorganize folders. If the folder is very large, work efficiently and avoid reading every file unless necessary”
Step 5: That said, Claude now organizes the course into neat folders, which means 50% of your work is already done.
Step 6: Now, enter this prompt. You can simply copy and paste the prompt on Claude Cowork chat.
Prompt:
I have a folder of video courses on my computer. Build me a local course player that runs on my own machine. First, inspect my folder and adapt to how my content is actually stored. It might contain loose video files, videos inside ZIP bundles, one folder per course, nested subfolders, or a mix. Support MP4, MKV, WebM, MOV, M4V, and AVI files. Tell me what you found before you start building. Create one self-contained Python 3 script using only the standard library, with no pip installations, and save it inside my courses folder. Also create a double-clickable launcher so I never need to use the Terminal. The script should run a local web server and automatically open the course player in my browser. Automatically build a catalog where each top-level folder is treated as a course, and each subfolder or ZIP file is treated as a lesson or section. Sort videos naturally so “Lesson 2” appears before “Lesson 10.” Skip folders starting with “_” or “.” and hide empty courses. If videos are inside ZIP files, stream them directly from the ZIP without extracting them. Support HTTP Range requests for both regular files and archived videos so seeking and mobile playback work correctly. If SRT or VTT subtitle files are stored beside a video, load them as captions. If PDFs, slides, exercise files, code, or other resources are stored inside a lesson, list them as downloadable resources. Skip subtitles and resources gracefully when none are available. The home page should show course cards with completion percentage, video count, lesson count, a Continue Watching row, and search across courses and lessons. The player should include the video and lesson playlist, automatically resume videos from where I stopped, provide mark-complete checkboxes, display per-course progress, and save everything to a local JSON file. When a video ends, show a three-second countdown with the next video’s title and then play it automatically. Let me cancel the countdown or skip the wait, and make auto-next toggleable. Add a configurable Pomodoro timer with a default 45-minute focus period. When the timer ends, pause the video, remind me to take a five-minute break, and play a chime. Include pause, resume, and reset controls. Add a floating, draggable, and resizable panel that can load another website so I can ask questions without switching tabs. Add a Focus Mode that makes the video fill the screen while keeping the floating panel visible above it. Add a roadmap planner where I can choose a course and enter a deadline in days. When I’m asked what to buy if you want to get into making electronic music, I often recommend Elektron’s budget-minded Model:Samples and Model:Cycles grooveboxes. They don’t grab headlines the way Teenage Engineering’s gear or the Telepathic Instruments Orchid do, and even compared to the company’s higher-end and more niche musical offerings like the Digitakt, Octatrack, or Tonverk, they’re often overlooked. But as my collection has grown to include fancier and far more expensive instruments, I still find myself coming back to the Model series.
Don’t overlook Elektron’s budget electronic music instruments
I keep coming back to the criminally slept-on Model:Samples and Model:Cycles.
Those looking to get their first groovebox are often drawn to more familiar brand names like Korg or Roland. And lots of people on Reddit will be quick to recommend the Novation Circuit Tracks (which I personally find confusing and mediocre-sounding). This is probably also partially due to the reputation Elektron gear has for being obtuse. If you’re an established music maker and aren’t deterred by a complicated workflow, you’re probably going to pick up a more powerful Elektron box, like the Digitone or Syntakt. That leaves the Models lineup in a weird no man’s land, and that’s a shame.
The primary difference between the two Models instruments is that the Model:Cycles uses FM synthesis and the Model:Samples, appropriately enough, plays samples. (It is not technically a sampler, however, since it can’t record samples, and instead they have to be loaded over USB.)
The Model:Cycles is built around a streamlined version of the engine found in the Digitone, one of my favorite-sounding synths of all time. This is a modern take on FM that can do the cold bells and icy pads you associate with iconic instruments like the DX7 (the iconic sound of the ’80s). But it also does modern glassy keys and aggressive turn-of-the-millennium EDM bass.
The two are more alike than not, though. They’re both six-track grooveboxes with six velocity-sensitive pads and plenty of knobs for hands-on controls, and they look almost identical. But most importantly, they feature Elektron’s legendary step sequencer without being nearly as intimidating as the company’s more expensive and notoriously complicated offerings.
The sequencer is built around what the company calls “trigs” and “locks.” Trigs are basically just events, typically triggering a note, and locks are just step-specific settings. It seems like a simple enough concept, but it makes these instruments far more capable than they might seem at first blush.
Six tracks isn’t a lot to work with. Once you’ve loaded up a kick, snare, and hi-hat, then you’ve only got three more tracks for bass, any melodic elements, and additional percussion. But sound locks allow you to change samples or presets on a per-step basis. That means, so long as they never play simultaneously, you can have your kick and snare share the same track, then you can put your hi-hats and other percussion on a second track, and leave the four other tracks for everything else. This is just the most obvious example of how locks expand the possibilities of what might seem rather limited on paper.
The sequencer can be treated like a simple step sequencer where you drop a four-on-the-floor kick and a snare on the backbeat. But it also grows with you as your skills improve, and you want to create more complex tracks. Trig conditions, for example, allow you to set rules that govern when certain steps are triggered, like only every third time through the loop, only when you press the fill button, or only if a previous trig condition is met. This means that you can create a huge amount of variety in a single 64-step pattern. And then you can chain several of those patterns together to create complex and evolving arrangements that just aren’t possible on most gear in this price range.
The Models boxes are also just incredibly fun. Where Elektron’s other gear demands a lot of menu diving, the Model:Samples and Model:Cycles are immediately approachable and built for live performance. It’s easy to trigger a drum fill with the push of a button, tweak a knob to open the filter on a bass, or briefly bathe a lead melody in delay.
Control-all might be the most fun feature, which, as you might have guessed, allows you to control all the tracks simultaneously. Bury your entire track in reverb as you start cranking up the distortion and lowering the pitch of all your samples to create a mangled, chaotic breakdown. And then immediately undo it all and drop the beat again by pressing the function and pattern buttons. The Model:Samples and Model:Cycles encourage jamming in a way that frankly a lot of electronic music gear just doesn’t, and it’s an absolute blast.
Now, they’re not without their flaws. The pads are pretty mediocre. Having to load samples via USB rather than recording them directly kinda sucks. And the lack of polyphony (each sequencer track can only play one note at a time) is a bit of a bummer. But at $349, it’s hard to complain. Plus they can be snagged used for as little as $200 on Reverb or Craigslist. Frankly, they’re some of the best bargains in music hardware and a great place to start your journey into producing electronic music.

Taiwan drone defences fall short against Beijing’s evolving technology, audit reveals
Taipei’s effort to build a modern counter-drone shield has suffered setbacks, including the collapse of an army procurement contract
Taiwan’s push to build a modern counter-drone shield has come under renewed scrutiny after an official audit uncovered technical shortcomings and a key procurement programme collapsed following repeated testing failures.
The developments have fuelled concerns that Taipei’s efforts to match Beijing’s rapidly evolving drone technology are being undermined by capability gaps, procurement failures and delays in building an integrated counter-drone network.
According to a recent report by Taiwan’s Audit Office, the military’s NT$3.55 billion (US$111 million) fixed-site counter-drone programme has significant shortcomings, despite being designed to protect airbases and other key military facilities.
The audit found the system, developed by the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology (NCSIST) – Taiwan’s top weapons developer – could not detect or jam the 5.1GHz frequency used by newer People’s Liberation Army drone models.
It also found the programme was running six to 12 months late because of construction delays and shortages of key components, and warned that the shortcomings could undermine the protection of military bases.
“The system’s detection and countermeasure functions remain incomplete and implementation has fallen behind schedule,” the report said, urging the defence ministry to improve the programme.

Athens cleans its all-marble Olympic stadium for the first time in over a century
Athens’ iconic Panathenaic Stadium is undergoing its first systematic cleaning in more than a century
ATHENS, Greece -- It has welcomed marathon runners, rock stars and the first modern Olympic athletes. Now it’s time for a monumental scrub.
Athens’ U-shaped Panathenaic Stadium — made entirely of white marble — is getting its first systematic cleaning in more than a century.
Rebuilt for the first modern Olympics in 1896, the site is the ceremonial send-off point for the Olympic flame, including for Los Angeles 2028.
The stadium is made of the same glittering marble used on the Acropolis, making the cleanup job delicate.
The work is revealing a monument changed by time, weather and millions of visitors. Cleaners in white and blue overalls move across the stadium’s 47 steep tiers with thin spray lances, using clean water at carefully controlled, low pressure. Machines vacuum up the runoff as they go.
“The goal of cleaning is not to make everything white. It’s to remove the dirt and the first layers of organic material that are deposited on the surface,” said Dimitris Selemis, a senior conservator at the site.
“The idea is to clean all the material that (contains) dirt from the surface, so we have a better understanding of the monument,” he said, noting that there is more weed growth and dirt in areas that receive less direct sunlight.
Crews are also using steam to remove blotches of chewing gum, which have turned black over time. Stadium officials say chewing gum, high heels and soft-drink stains are among the main culprits that stain the marble.
Now slowly being revealed, the original gleaming look of the venue earned it the widely used Greek nickname “Kallimarmaro,” or beautiful marble.
“We call it Kallimarmaro because it is made of the finest marble, the best that was ever produced ... We are very proud of it,” Isidoros Kouvelos, president of the Hellenic Olympic Committee, told The Associated Press in an interview.
“It needed to be cleaned of everything that has accumulated over all these years," he said. "This way the Panathenaic Stadium will show all its brilliance and will once again be the foremost monument of humanity for the Olympic Movement.”
Built into a natural ravine, the stadium’s site was used for ancient Greek athletic contests and later Roman spectacles before falling into centuries of disuse.
Since its 1896 revival, it has staged fashion shows, rock concerts, boxing matches and national celebrations — as well as lavish patriotic ceremonies ordered by a military dictatorship in the 1960s.
Today, it’s a popular draw for tourists. Apart from the cleanup, the Kallimarmaro is also getting a new track, upgraded lighting and fresh support facilities. The project is privately funded by a shipping company and overseen by the Hellenic Olympic Committee with guidance from Culture Ministry experts.
The work will continue through 2026 but is currently concentrated on the stadium’s “sling,” or curved end, in time for the next torch-passing ceremony on Sept. 10.
That will be for the Dakar Youth Olympics, scheduled for Oct. 31-Nov. 13 in Senegal, which will be the first Olympic competition ever hosted in Africa.
IOC President Kirsty Coventry, a swimming gold medal winner from Zimbabwe, is due to attend the Sept. 10 ceremony, Kouvelos said.

Adam Driver, Inde Navarette, Sadie Sink and Christopher Abbott are among new stars in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s live-action reboot of “X-Men,” contributing to the legacy of the casts who starred as the mutants before them.
Navarrette, Sink and Abbott — along with Samara Weaving, Kit Connor and Maya Boyd were the new cast members introduced by Marvel President Kevin Feige at the D23 convention Friday night in Anaheim, Calif., while Driver was introduced via video.
Directed by Thunderbolts* filmmaker Jake Schreier, the new X-Men film is pegged for a May 5, 2028, release. Some of the reveals weren’t surprises, including Sink’s Jean Grey, who was already introduced in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, while recent reports already indicated Weaving would be playing Emma Frost and Connor would be donning the visor as Scott Summers/Cyclops.
Given that reports surfaced that Navarrette — one of the stars of the summer horror blockbuster Obsession — had met with Marvel and expressed a desire to play Mystique, the only real surprises about her casting came with the announcement that she would be playing Rogue.
As such, the night’s biggest reveals came with the announcements that Boyd will be playing Storm, while Driver — who previously embodied Kylo Ren/Ben Solo for Disney’s Star Wars franchise— would take on the villainous role of Mr. Sinister. Feige said in a recent interview with the Happy Sad Confused podcast that he’s been asking Driver to join the MCU, but he has always turned them down.
Here’s a rundown of the actors starring in the MCU’s X-Men reboot and the stars who have played the roles before them.
Sadie Sink: Jean Grey
Prior to Sadie Sink playing the role of Jean Grey in Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Famke Janssen played the empath/telepath in X-Men (2000), X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), The Wolverine (2013) and X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014).
X-Men: The Last Stand also included a scene featuring a young Jean, played by Haley Ramm, while Sophie Turner played the young Jean in X-Men: Apocalypse (2016) and X-Men: Dark Phoenix (2019).
Kit Connor: Scott Summers/Cyclops
Heartstopper star Kit Connor’s version of Cyclops was preceded by James Marsden’s turn as the laser-eyed mutant in X-Men (2000), X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006) and X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014). Marsden is reprising the role in the upcoming MCU film Avengers: Doomsday.
Meanwhile, Tim Pocock appeared as Cyclops in X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009), while Tye Sheridan played him in X-Men: Apocalypse (2016) and X-Men: Dark Phoenix (2019) and appeared in an uncredited turn as the character in Deadpool 2 (2018).
Maya Boyd: Ororo Munroe/Storm
Prior to Maya Boyd, Halle Berry starred as Ororo Munroe/Storm in X-Men (2000), X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006) and X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014).
In addition, Alexandra Shipp played the mutant with the power to create severe weather disturbances in X-Men: Apocalypse (2016) and X-Men: Dark Phoenix (2019).
Samara Weaving: Emma Frost
Before Samara Weaving was hired to play Emma Frost in the new X-Men movie, the telepath who can turn her exterior into a diamond was played by Tahyna Tozzi in X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009) and January Jones in X-Men: First Class (2011).
Christopher Abbott: Charles Xavier/Professor X
Before Christopher Abbott was hired to play Charles Xavier/Professor X, the ultimate telepath was played by Patrick Stewart in X-Men (2000), X2: X-Men United (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men Origins: Wolverine (2009), The Wolverine (2013), X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014), Logan (2017) and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022). Stewart will also reprise Professor X in Avengers: Doomsday.
James McAvoy played the young version of Professor X in X-Men: First Class (2011), X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014), X-Men: Apocalypse (2016) and X-Men: Dark Phoenix (2019), and appeared in an uncredited cameo as the character in Deadpool 2. Laurence Belcher played Charles as a 12-year-old in X-Men: First Class.
Adam Driver: Nathaniel Essex/Mr. Sinister
Adam Driver’s turn as Nathaniel Essex/Mr. Sinister will mark the first time the character has appeared in a live-action X-Men film. The genius villain is telepathic and has several powers, including superhuman strength, telekinesis, energy projection, shapeshifting and teleportation.
The MCU’s new X-Men movie, which has not been officially titled, will be released in theaters on May 5, 2028.

A state court in Washington this week ordered Kalshi to stop offering sports gambling and a variety of other wagers on its prediction market. King County Superior Court Judge John McHale issued a preliminary injunction in response to a lawsuit filed against Kalshi by the state of Washington.
“The order requires Kalshi to stop offering, accepting, or facilitating wagers on sports, elections, politics, entertainment, culture, tech and science, or mentions in Washington,” said a press release yesterday from Washington Attorney General Nick Brown. “Kalshi must implement an IP address and residency-based geofence by August 19 and a multi-source geofencing solution by September 2. This does not include all the wagers offered on Kalshi, but it includes a substantial part of their business, which in recent years has been increasingly driven by sports wagers.”
Kalshi is not licensed by the state Gambling Commission and is not registered to conduct business in Washington, the court order said. McHale found that Kalshi ads claiming “that it offers ‘legal betting’ in Washington state are likely to mislead a reasonable consumer that such gambling activities are legal under state law.”
Under the court order, Kalshi could face penalties of up to $120,000 per day if it fails to complete the implementation of the ordered geofencing by September 2. “Kalshi will not prohibit users from exiting positions they already hold. The State reserves, and does not waive, the right to seek recovery for fees and losses incurred by Washington consumers on or after September 2, 2026,” the order said.

Female police officer facing probe over viral video of her dancing in uniform
Hong Kong police launch internal investigation and order officer to remove the video, which has gone viral on mainland Chinese social media

The video, which has gone viral in recent days, shows a short-haired female constable making hand gestures and moving to upbeat music. Her face is partly obscured by a filter featuring dog ears and a muzzle.

The Tamil Nadu Police have launched a multi-pronged strategy to eradicate substance abuse in the State. The launch of a new force, Anti Narcotics Task Force (ANTF), does not seem to be just another initiative in rhetoric but a concerted effort to end the prevalence of drugs, especially ganja, by taking on drug syndicates, smugglers, and others involved in the high-stakes illegal business.
Three months after the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) assumed power, it has taken the first big step towards fulfilling Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay’s election promise that he would end the drug culture in the State.
Since May 10 this year, 5,082 drug-related cases have been registered in the State and 7,214 suspects have been arrested on the charges of trafficking, possession, and distribution of drugs. More than 7,000 kg of ganja, 112 kg of other drugs, and 3.4 lakh tablets (prescribed drugs obtained without authorisation) were seized.
The special force has been formed in the wake of reports of youth, including college students, getting addicted to ganja and drugs such as methamphetamine or meth, a highly addictive synthetic stimulant, freely available in rave parties. The link between crime and drug addiction is also proven. It is in this context that the government constituted the ANTF, involving multiple stakeholders and law-enforcement agencies.
Though attempts were made in the past to dismantle inter-State drug syndicates and neutralise their supply chain and manpower, the unlawful activity continued to thrive with the suspects adopting newer means of transport and distribution. Even as the State police managed to curtail ganja cultivation in the tri-junction forest area of Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Karnataka, the flow of the drug continues from Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
After intensive search operations on train and road routes along inter-State borders, smugglers have stopped moving ganja in large quantities. Now, they engage small-time peddlers to smuggle less than 4 kg to 5 kg per consignment, mostly by train.
Flowing from neighbouring States
While the Narcotics Intelligence Bureau-Criminal Investigation Department (NIB-CID) and the local police have been working in coordination with Central agencies, such as the Narcotics Control Bureau, to contain the prevalence of drugs, the efforts did not yield the desired result. The police suspect that the inflow of ganja or marijuana or cannabis continues from neighbouring States, Andhra Pradesh in particular. Besides local consumption, ganja and other synthetic drugs are smuggled to Sri Lanka with the help of illegal boat operators for further transhipment to South-East Asian countries.
The high-capacity ANTF is a dedicated force. It was born out of a major overhaul of the State’s strategy to combat drug trafficking and substance abuse aimed at achieving a ‘Drug-Free Tamil Nadu’. The new architecture, sanctioned through a Government Order issued on August 8 this year, seeks to replace the existing enforcement framework with a dedicated, technology-driven, and intelligence-led system. The initiative combines specialised policing with financial investigations, cyber-surveillance, treatment and rehabilitation of drug addicts, youth engagement, and community participation.
It seeks to significantly expand the State’s dedicated anti-narcotics field force by strengthening it with technology. As many as 65 specialised ANTF police stations have been sanctioned; they will cover 37 police districts and eight city police commissionerates. Each of these stations will have one Inspector of Police, four Sub-Inspectors, and 20 police personnel. Together, they will provide 1,625 dedicated personnel for field-level narcotics enforcement across Tamil Nadu.
Not meant for routine policing
A key feature of the new arrangement is that ANTF personnel would not be deployed for routine policing to make sure that the force remains an exclusive deployment agency tasked to maintain sustained surveillance, intelligence-gathering, and investigation of organised drug trafficking networks.
Before the creation of the dedicated ANTF, narcotics enforcement was largely handled by 15 NIB-CID units that functioned under the Enforcement Bureau-CID. While these units played an important role in preventing and detecting narcotics offences, the government realised that the relatively limited manpower and infrastructure available with the 15 NIB-CID units had made it difficult to maintain continuous State-wide surveillance and penetrate sophisticated trafficking networks.
What was needed was a sufficiently strong centralised headquarters with specialised capabilities for State-wide intelligence analysis, cyber-analytics, darknet monitoring, and financial investigation. But none of this was present; the NIB-CID largely relied on local police for intensive combing operations. Further, personnel attached to the local police stations were required to deal with law-and-order duties, regular crime investigation, and other responsibilities. This often limited the sustained attention that could be devoted to organised narcotics networks. However, the ANTF intends to overcome these hurdles and address these gaps through a centralised command structure and specialised field units.
The ANTF headquarters will be headed by an Additional Director-General of Police and an Inspector-General of Police, assisted by two Superintendents of Police (SP-I for Operations and SP-II for Intelligence and Administration). The headquarters will have 10 specialised wings to integrate intelligence, investigation, technology, operations, legal support, and administration.
Among the key components is a dedicated cyber lab equipped to undertake digital forensics, mobile-data extraction, darknet monitoring, open-source intelligence, and cryptocurrency and blockchain analysis.
A centralised crime records bureau will profile drug offenders, track repeat offenders, map trafficking routes, and identify drug hotspots. A special operations and investigation unit will focus on high-value cases, synthetic drug laboratories, international connections, and complex darknet distribution networks. Field intelligence units will collect information on cultivation sources, inter-State transit corridors, and maritime and coastal smuggling routes.
Legal team to help in searches
The ANTF will also have a dedicated legal unit to provide guidance on search and seizure procedures, investigation, filing of chargesheets, and trial proceedings. A 24x7 control room and helpline will provide real-time operational coordination. The police have solicited information from members of the public on drug-related offenders through the designated toll-free number 10581, while a WhatsApp chatbot facility will be available on 9498410581.
“One of the most significant changes in the State’s anti-narcotics strategy will be a greater emphasis on financial investigation. Instead of limiting enforcement to the seizure of drugs and arrest of individuals involved in street-level distribution, the ANTF will identify the financial networks supporting organised trafficking,” says Director-General of Police and Head of the Police Force Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal.
Investigators would trace illicit financial flows, identify key players and alleged kingpins, and pursue the freezing and attachment of movable and immovable properties belonging to traffickers and their accomplices under applicable legal provisions. “The objective is to weaken the financial foundations of organised drug syndicates and make trafficking increasingly difficult and unprofitable,” Dr. Aggarwal said.
Realising that policing and seizures alone cannot eliminate substance abuse, the government has roped in other departments. The Health and Family Welfare Department will establish protocols for referring first-time and small-quantity drug users for medical treatment, counselling, and rehabilitation. The government also plans to strengthen de-addiction centres, relapse tracking, case-management systems, and drug-testing facilities at district hospitals. Periodic district-level surveys have been envisaged to assess drug-use patterns and demographics for more effective healthcare interventions.
The School Education and Higher Education Departments will integrate awareness of substance abuse into educational programmes and strengthen Anti-Drug Clubs and Student Police Cadets on school and college campuses. Student volunteers from the NSS and the NCC would be mobilised as ‘Anti-Drug Warriors’. Sports competitions would be conducted regularly across the State to encourage young people to participate in constructive activities and discourage drug abuse.
When the Chief Minister administered a pledge against drug abuse in Chennai recently, about 2,000 students took part. More than one crore people joined the event online by logging into the Drug Free Tamil Nadu application. The government has also involved the Rural Development and Municipal Administration Departments to help create village- and ward-level anti-drug committees to strengthen community vigilance. Local bodies that have achieved ‘Drug-Free Village’ or ‘Drug-Free Ward’ status will receive State-level recognition and incentives.
The Information and Public Relations Department, the publicity arm of the government, will coordinate sustained public awareness campaigns, social media outreach, and community engagement programmes. The aim is not only to increase awareness of the dangers of drugs but also to encourage public reporting and reduce the stigma associated with seeking treatment.
The new framework also provides for a structured system of monitoring and accountability. At the district level, weekly reviews would be chaired by the Collector, along with the District Superintendent of Police or the City Police Commissioner and the local body administrative heads. At the State level, fortnightly reviews would be chaired by the ADGP (ANTF) to assess field operations and tactical progress.
Apex review every month
An apex review will be held every month under the chairmanship of the Chief Secretary. It will focus on coordination among departments, implementation of policy measures, and the overall impact of the anti-narcotics programme. The Chief Minister will be apprised of the outcome of filed operations, seizures, and overall progress and impact of the ANTF on a fortnightly basis, according to police sources.
The government expects the ANTF to mark a shift from conventional drug seizures towards dismantling entire trafficking networks. By combining dedicated manpower with cyber-capabilities, intelligence-gathering, financial investigation, and inter-departmental action, Tamil Nadu aims to tackle both the supply of narcotics and the demand for drugs.
The broader objective is to neutralise organised trafficking networks, protect children and young people, improve access to treatment and rehabilitation, and strengthen community participation in preventing substance abuse — ultimately paving the way for a safer and healthier ‘Drug-Free Tamil Nadu’.

Chawinga sisters fire Malawi into Wafcon final
- Published
Malawi's Chawinga sisters were once again the stars of the show, sharing three goals as the Scorchers continued their fairy tale run at the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) by booking their place in the final with a 3-1 victory over Algeria in Rabat.
Belying their status as the lowest-ranked side playing in Morocco, the Southern Africans, who are making their Wafcon debut, were too strong for their opponents, adding Les Fennecs to their list of scalps having already defeated heavyweights Nigeria and Ghana earlier in the tournament.
But the scoreline failed to tell half the story of a frantic, end-to-end encounter which featured two first-half red cards awarded after the intervention of the video assistant referee (VAR) and a slew of presentable opportunities which were spurned by both sides.
Algeria defender Morgane Belkhiter had already seen red for denying Malawi skipper Tabitha Chawinga a goalscoring opportunity before the older of the two sisters broke the deadlock in the 33rd minute, executing an acrobatic overhead kick which cannoned off the crossbar and hit the turf before spinning wildly back over the goal line.
Temwa Chawinga extended the lead in the first minute of first-half added time before her team-mate Rose Kadzere was also dismissed before the break following another extended VAR check, this time for a studs-up lunge.
The second half was only marginally more sedate, with Ikram Adjabi initially giving Algeria hope before Tabitha Chawinga's second goal snuffed out any chance of a comeback.
The Scorchers will face Cameroon in Sunday's final (19:00 GMT), looking to become the fourth nation to lift the Wafcon trophy and complete what would be a remarkable underdog story.
Sisters live up to pre-tournament hype
Malawi's success at an expanded 16-team tournament in Morocco is proving that women's football in Africa has the potential to grow beyond the traditional big names.
Excluding the inaugural edition in 1998, they are the first debutant to reach the final.
But having already booked their place at next year's Fifa Women's World Cup in Brazil, courtesy of their run to the last four, the Scorchers are now on the verge of something very special - and anything looks possible with the Chawinga sisters firing on all cylinders in attack.
With Tabitha helping OL Lyonnes to another French title last season, and with Temwa winning a second golden boot and MVP award with NWSL side Kansas City Current, there was plenty of hype ahead of this campaign.
All of it now appears justified as the sisters have scored nine of their team's 12 goals - with five for Temwa and four for Tabitha - and appear to have a level of pace, power and positional awareness which opposition defences struggle to cope with.
Tabitha's opener in this match will be remembered for a long time.
When Asimenye Simwaka, who just two weeks ago was running in the 200m and 400m semi-finals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, headed a corner back into the middle of the penalty area, the elder Chawinga looked to pose little danger given she had her back to goal.
But the 30-year-old twisted to apply a clever left-footed overhead kick which beat Algeria goalkeeper Chloe N'Gazi but not the crossbar.
As N'Gazi also twisted to avoid being struck by the ricochet, she probably thought she would be able to collect the ball on the bounce, but the backspin meant it could only end up in the back of the net.
Belkhiter's red card, which had come midway through the first half, had looked harsh, even if replays clearly showed the defender catching Tabitha on the back of the heel.
The challenge came a long way from goal and Belkhiter's team-mate Roselene Khezami, who was challenging from Chawinga's other side, did get something on the ball as she lunged in at the same time.
Temwa Chawinga took advantage of the numerical advantage to round N'Gazi and stroke home to make it 2-0, but Kadzere's deserved red card shortly after opened the door to the North Africans.
The Malawi midfielder just about made contact with the top of the ball before going over the top and catching Marine Dafeur above the ankle.
The challenge, however, came inside the Algeria penalty area and was totally unnecessary.
Algeria's Melissa Bethi and Temwa Chawinga both missed glorious opportunities inside the opening minutes of the second period before Adjabi's strike on the hour.
Two Malawi defenders made a mess of dealing with Dafeur's deep free-kick, allowing the forward to fire back across goal on the volley to half the deficit.
Both sides looked to be running out of steam before Tabitha Chawinga settled the contest with her second goal, driving into the penalty area almost unchallenged to side-foot home from just outside the six yard box.
Ranked 153rd in the world, Malawi have taken Wafcon by storm.
One final hurdle remains in the form of Cameroon, after they saw off the hosts on penalties, but on this form the Chawinga sisters will feel anyone is beatable.

Sambhal school canopy collapse during Independence Day event kills boy, injures 2
An entrance canopy collapsed during an Independence Day function at a private school in Sambhal, killing an eight-year-old boy and injuring two students. The incident triggered an official inquiry as authorities inspected the campus and assured assistance to the victim's family.
A joyous Independence Day celebration at a private school in Uttar Pradesh's Sambhal district turned tragic on Saturday when the canopy at the school's main entrance collapsed, killing an eight-year-old boy and seriously injuring two students.
The accident occurred during an Independence Day programme at Al Hasnain Public School in Madala village under the Asmoli police station area. A CCTV recording of the incident has surfaced, showing the moment the structure gave way as children gathered around it to watch the celebrations.
According to officials, several local children had come to the school to watch the Independence Day function. Some of them climbed onto the entrance canopy while others stood below it. Unable to bear the weight, the structure suddenly collapsed, trapping children under the debris.
Local residents rushed to the spot after hearing screams and launched a rescue effort. The trapped children were pulled out from the rubble and taken to a nearby hospital.
The deceased was identified as Nizamuddin, an eight-year-old boy who had come to watch the programme. Doctors declared him dead on arrival. Two students of the school, Saif Ali and Shaidana, sustained serious injuries and were referred to a higher medical centre for treatment.
The incident prompted an immediate response from the district administration. District Magistrate Ankit Khandelwal, Superintendent of Police Krishna Kumar Bishnoi, along with other senior officials and members of the education department, reached the school and conducted an inspection.
Officials also met the school management and gathered details about the circumstances leading to the collapse. Later, they visited the deceased child's family and assured them of all possible assistance.
Speaking to reporters, SP Krishna Kumar Bishnoi said the Independence Day programme was underway when a group of children climbed onto the canopy. "One child who was not a student of the school was standing below the structure. The canopy collapsed after several children climbed on it, trapping three children under the debris. One child died while two others were injured," he said.
District Magistrate Ankit Khandelwal said preliminary findings suggested that the structure collapsed due to the additional load of children standing on top of it. He confirmed that the injured children were undergoing treatment and that an inquiry into the incident had been initiated.
Family members of the deceased said Nizamuddin had gone to the school carrying a flag to watch the Independence Day celebrations. They said the wall-like structure suddenly gave way, trapping him beneath the rubble.
Police said the victim's family has, for now, declined to pursue legal action. Authorities, however, are continuing their investigation into the circumstances of the collapse while assessing the safety of the school premises.

Flesh-eating bacteria sounds like the premise of a bad horror movie, but it’s a growing – and potentially fatal – threat to people in the U.S. and beyond.
Vibrio vulnificus, a type of flesh-eating bacteria that thrives in warm seawater, is once again threatening the safety of beachgoers and raw shellfish enthusiasts. To date, Louisiana has reported nine cases, with five fatalities, and Florida has reported 14 cases, with two fatalities. As of late June, Maryland has reported 72 cases.
I’m a professor at the Indiana University School of Medicine, where my laboratory studies microbiology and infectious disease. Here’s why health officials are so concerned about this deadly infection – and ways to avoid contracting it.
What does ‘flesh-eating’ mean?
There are several types of bacteria that can infect open wounds and cause a rare condition called necrotising fasciitis. These bacteria do not merely damage the surface of the skin – they release toxins that destroy the underlying tissue, including muscles, nerves and blood vessels. Once the bacteria reach the bloodstream, they gain ready access to additional tissues and organ systems. If left untreated, necrotising fasciitis can be fatal, sometimes within 48 hours.
The bacterial species group A Streptococcus, or group A strep, is the most common culprit behind necrotising fasciitis. But the U.S. Centers for Disease Control points to Vibrio vulnificus as an additional suspect. There are only 150 to 200 cases of Vibrio vulnificus infections in the United States each year, but the mortality rate is high, with 1 in 5 people succumbing to the infection. Cases have also increased in Europe.
How do you catch flesh-eating bacteria?
Vibrio vulnificus primarily lives in warm seawater but can also be found in brackish water – areas where the ocean mixes with freshwater. Most infections in the U.S. occur in the warmer months, between May and October. People who swim, fish or wade in these bodies of water can contract the bacteria through an open wound or sore.
Vibrio vulnificus can also get into seafood harvested from these waters, especially shellfish like oysters. Eating such foods raw or undercooked can lead to food poisoning, and handling them while having an open wound can provide an entry point for the bacteria to cause necrotising fasciitis. In the U.S., Vibrio vulnificus is a leading cause of seafood-associated fatalities.
Why are flesh-eating bacteria infections rising?
Vibrio vulnificus is found in warm coastal waters around the world, like those of the southern Gulf Coast states in the U.S. But rising ocean temperatures due to global warming are creating new habitats for this type of bacteria, which can now be found along the East Coast as far north as New York and Connecticut. A recent study noted that Vibrio vulnificus wound infections increased eightfold between 1988 and 2018 in the eastern U.S.
Vibrio vulnificus is also spreading into coastal areas of Northern Europe and the Baltic Sea as a consequence of climate change driving warming water temperatures.
Climate change is also fueling stronger hurricanes and storm surges, which have been associated with spikes in flesh-eating bacteria infection cases due to increasing contact with seawater or brackish water.
The number of people around the world who are most vulnerable to severe infection, including those with diabetes and those taking medications that suppress immunity, is on the rise.
What are symptoms of and treatments for necrotising fasciitis?
Early symptoms of an infected wound include fever, redness, intense pain or swelling at the site of injury. If you have these symptoms, seek medical attention without delay. Necrotising fasciitis can progress quickly, producing ulcers, blisters, skin discoloration and pus.
Treating flesh-eating bacteria is a race against time. Clinicians administer antibiotics directly into the bloodstream to kill the bacteria. In many cases, damaged tissue needs to be surgically removed to stop the rapid spread of the infection. This sometimes means amputating affected limbs.
Researchers are concerned that an increasing number of cases are becoming impossible to treat because Vibrio vulnificus has evolved resistance to certain antibiotics.
How do I protect myself?
The CDC offers several recommendations to help prevent infection.
People who have a fresh cut, including a new piercing or tattoo, are advised to stay out of water that could be home to Vibrio vulnificus. Otherwise, the wound should be completely covered with a waterproof bandage. The tiniest scrape or cut is enough for Vibrio vulnificus to get under your skin. One case was even traced to freshly shaven legs.
People with an open wound should also avoid handling raw seafood or fish. Wounds that occur while fishing, preparing seafood or swimming should be washed immediately and thoroughly with soap and water.
Anyone can contract necrotising fasciitis, but the elderly and people with weakened immune systems are most susceptible to severe disease. This includes people taking immunosuppressive medications or those who have pre-existing conditions such as liver disease, cancer, HIV or diabetes.
It is important to bear in mind that necrotising fasciitis presently remains very rare. But given its severity, it is beneficial to stay informed.
Cases of infection by Vibrio vulnificus are about as rare as shark attacks. While shark bites get more attention, the microscopic shark that is Vibrio vulnificans can also rob you of life or limb.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Sept. 25, 2023.

India is attempting to do something the world has never seen before. So claimed Niti Aayog, the government of India’s policy thinktank, earlier this year. It said that no major economy has tried to expand GDP nearly eightfold within a generation while simultaneously redirecting its energy and industrial systems to reach net zero within two generations. Hence its detailed report’s claim that there is “no historical precedent”.
There is something to this. China industrialised at vast scale, but not on a sustainable net zero path. Korea, Japan and Europe became wealthy by industrialising before decarbonising. Today, rich nations have already satisfied the basic demands of their people and created the infrastructure and high per-capita energy use that India is still trying to build. The world’s most populous country has to do this while also reducing emissions.
The climate emergency is all too real for New Delhi. In April, on a single day, all of the planet’s top 50 hottest cities were in India. Yet the country still relies heavily on coal, especially at moments of peak power needs. This sets up a dangerous feedback loop: heat drives cooling demand; cooling demand drives coal-burning; coal‑burning drives temperatures higher. India is trying to change course. Non-fossil fuel sources now account for more than half of installed electricity capacity.
The report assumes India reaches $30tn GDP by 2047, with rising urbanisation, industrialisation and living standards. India’s net zero path will be judged politically by who bears the costs and who captures the gains. But the thinktank reasons that as India grows fast, so energy and infrastructure demand and investment rise too, and, voilà, India continues to grow fast. This may be a virtuous cycle. But left unexplained is what source of demand gets the process going and sustains it.
That requires a political economy of investment. It means explaining who spends first, who guarantees demand, how businesses are induced to keep building when existing factories are not fully used, and how private profitability is maintained when consumption’s share of national income falls.
India’s solar success partly answers these questions. In a 2025 paper, the political economist Mathias Larsen argues that India’s advances in sunlight-powered electricity came because the state created a market, used public sector financial firepower and protected domestic producers. That is not a story of private finance spontaneously allocating capital. It is a story of state-made demand.
But solar is one sector. A whole-economy transition may not work the same way. What happens when domestic demand can’t soak up the state-created capacity? China answered that question through exports, but only because of a historically exceptional bargain. Washington opened the American market to China on favourable trading terms in 1979. Nothing reversed that access. China’s government was allowed to heavily intervene in the macro- and micro-economy to drive rapid industrialisation and growth inside the US-led trading global system.
India faces a far more hostile environment. It is industrialising in a world of fragile supply chains, climate trade barriers and Chinese export overcapacity. That makes the question of India’s domestic demand more important, not less. The mainstream view still assumes private investors will allocate capital efficiently once cash is mobilised. But that does not explain why firms would invest at the necessary scale unless the state spends first, guarantees markets and coordinates sectors. This, sadly, may be the truth that cannot speak its name.

A powerful 7.7-magnitude quake struck eastern Indonesia early on Saturday, the US Geological Survey said, triggering a tsunami warning and prompting hundreds to evacuate.
The quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region with a depth of 10km at 5:58am on Saturday, Indonesia time. The epicentre of the shallow quake was 68km (42 miles) north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province.
The initial quake was followed by two aftershocks, including one with a magnitude of 6.1.
No immediate casualties have been reported.
“Suddenly it started to shake and I panicked,” 31-year-old hospital customer service official, Lukas Lotar, told AFP.
“Patients also fled the hospital, the jolt was big. I saw some walls were cracked,” he said.
Indonesia’s meteorology, climatology and geophysics agency (BMKG) issued a tsunami warning and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks.
“Tsunami modelling results indicate that this earthquake has the potential to generate a tsunami in the provinces of East Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi, and West Nusa Tenggara,” BMKG earthquake and tsunami director Wijayanto said.
An alert was issued for waves ranging from 0.5 metres to three metres (1.6 to 9.8 feet).
Residents in the town of Maumere on Flores Island, were evacuating to higher ground, an AFP correspondent reported.
He said the sea in the area could be seen receding, a common phenomenon ahead of a possible tsunami.
Images broadcast on Indonesian television showed damaged buildings and hundreds of people in nearby Nagekeo regency evacuating.
Authorities have not reported any casualties, but said tsunami waves between 19 and 30 centimetres have been detected.
Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the “Ring of Fire”, an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin.
Separately, Australia’s tsunami warning centre said the undersea earthquake will have “no tsunami threat to the Australian mainland, islands or territories”.

A second passenger train derails in England in 2 days
A passenger train has derailed near London, marking the second such incident in two days
LONDON -- A passenger train derailed near London on Friday, British Transport Police said, the second derailment in two days after two people were seriously injured when another train came off the tracks on Thursday.
Police said officers, paramedics and firefighters were at the scene near Wickford train station in Essex, about 30 miles east of London (48 kilometers), after receiving reports that the rear carriages of a train derailed. The carriages were in an “upright position," police said, and no injuries were reported.
National Rail said officials were working to understand what happened, and major disruptions to train services were expected through Friday afternoon.
The incident came less than 24 hours after a train from London to Eastbourne went off the tracks outside the southern English town of Lewes. Three carriages overturned, seriously injuring two people and causing minor injuries for 18 others.
All passengers were evacuated within about three hours, the transport police said.
The cause of the derailment is under investigation.

Air India pilot's reported cannabis test: What it can and can't tell investigators
- Published
Reports that an Air India pilot tested positive for cannabis after a flight sound like the sort of finding that should make an aviation investigator sit up.
But the reported result has not been officially confirmed, and even a confirmed positive would not necessarily be the smoking gun it might appear to be.
On 4 August, an Air India Airbus A320 flying from Phuket to Delhi suddenly lost about 91m (300ft) of altitude, injuring 13 passengers and four crew members. The aircraft, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew, landed safely in Delhi. The incident is under investigation.
Both pilots underwent routine post-flight screening for psychoactive substances, India's aviation ministry said. It said the captain's initial test produced a result requiring "confirmatory testing", external and that both pilots had been removed from flying duties pending the inquiry.
Earlier this week, a number of media reports, citing sources, reported that the captain subsequently tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory laboratory test. Air India has not confirmed the result. The reports have triggered a storm over pilot drug testing and aviation safety in India.
There is, so far, no official finding linking the captain's alleged drug-test result to the sudden loss of altitude. Investigators are examining the incident more broadly, including technical, operational, medical and human factors, and it remains unclear what caused the aircraft to plunge.
The obvious question is whether cannabis had anything to do with it.
The less obvious one is harder: what does a positive cannabis test actually tell us about a pilot's state of mind several hours earlier?
Quite a lot is known about how cannabis affects performance of complex tasks. Much less is known about how to turn a positive test into a reliable timestamp for impairment.
Some of the most directly relevant evidence comes from a rather unusual source: pilots.
In a 1976 experiment, external, 10 pilots smoked a modest dose of marijuana and then flew a simulator. Their performance deteriorated, with errors in altitude, heading and radio navigation. The effects were evident for at least two hours and generally disappeared within four to six hours, the study found.
A decade later, researchers returned to the question of what happens after the obvious "high" has worn off., external
Ten experienced private pilots were tested on a flight simulator 24 hours after smoking cannabis. They showed significant deterioration in several measures, including elevator and aileron control, landing accuracy and vertical and lateral deviation on approach. Most strikingly, the pilots did not realise that their performance had deteriorated, the study found.
A 1991 follow-up, external produced a similar warning.
Nine active pilots flew a simulator after smoking a cigarette containing 20mg of THC, or tetrahydrocannabinol - the main psychoactive compound in cannabis and the chemical responsible for the "high" and many of the drug's effects on the brain and motor skills.
Performance was impaired when checked 15 minutes, four hours, eight hours and 24 hours later. Seven of the nine pilots showed some impairment at 24 hours, but only one was aware of the drug's effects, the study found.
These studies are small, old and were conducted with aircraft simulators rather than modern airliners. They cannot tell us what happened in the Air India cockpit. But experts believe they likely establish something useful: cannabis can interfere with the sort of fine motor control, attention and complex human-machine interaction that flying demands.
A review , externalby aviation-medicine specialist David Newman for Australia's Transport Safety Bureau reached a similar conclusion.
Cannabis affects behaviour, cognition and psychomotor performance in a dose-dependent way, and complex tasks such as flying are particularly sensitive. The review also found evidence of residual effects lasting up to 24 hours.
The science has become more complicated, however, as cannabis use has become more widespread and the potency of cannabis products has increased in many parts of the world.
A 2022 randomised clinical trial, external led by Thomas Marcotte at the University of California San Diego tested 191 regular cannabis users.
Those who smoked THC performed worse on a simulated driving task, but the researchers found that impairment could not be inferred from the THC content of the cannabis, the users' previous experience or their blood THC concentration.
The drug initially impaired performance, but after about four-and-a-half hours, those who had taken it were performing about as well as people who had not received the active drug.
That finding matters enormously for aviation testing.
A positive test can show that THC is present, but not necessarily when cannabis was consumed or whether the person was impaired at the time. The relationship varies with the dose, how it was consumed, frequency of use and individual biology, experts say.
This is one reason cannabis presents regulators with a problem that alcohol does not.
"Unlike with alcohol where there's a more robust relationship between alcohol concentrations in blood and impairment, the association is much more complex with THC. THC rapidly leaves the bloodstream after smoking, and there is limited to no correlation between blood THC concentrations and impairment," Marcotte told the BBC.
"In people who use at least occasionally, THC can be detectable in blood for days and sometimes weeks after last use, particularly in more frequent users. This is long after any acute impairment has subsided."
Studies show that impairment after smoking cannabis typically lasts three to five hours. When cannabis is ingested, such as in an edible, impairment lasts longer - typically six to eight hours, and sometimes more.
After edible use, the metabolite 11-OH-THC (11-hydroxy-THC) is often more closely associated with impaired cognitive function than THC itself, which may be present at lower concentrations, says Marcotte.
Not surprisingly, there is no equivalent universally accepted cannabis test that can say: this person is currently too impaired to fly.
Canada has responded by taking a deliberately blunt approach. After legalising recreational cannabis in 2018, Transport Canada introduced a rule, external prohibiting flight crews and flight controllers from consuming cannabis for at least 28 days before duty.
The regulator says the rule was intended to address the uncertainties surrounding cannabis impairment and detection; and airlines can impose stricter rules.
The American aviation experience offers another warning against reading too much into a positive test.
A 2026 US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) study , externalof pilots killed in US civil aviation accidents between 2018 and 2022 found that 52.8% had at least one drug detected, while 27.7% had two or more. THC was the main driver of the increase in illicit-drug detections. But the NTSB stressed that the study was about drug presence, not whether pilots were impaired.
Clearly, finding cannabis in someone's system does not, by itself, establish that it caused an incident or accident.
But there are cases where investigators have gone further. In a 2011 Canadian crash, a Cessna 208B pilot had 50.1 nanograms per millilitre (ng/ml) of THC in his blood. The Transportation Safety Board concluded, external that the amount of psychoactive cannabinoids was sufficient to impair cognitive processes and likely affected the pilot's planning and conduct of the flight.
The opposite has happened, too.
In a 2017 New Zealand helicopter crash, external, THC was detected in the pilot's blood after cannabis use two days earlier. A forensic toxicologist concluded that he was unlikely to have been under its influence at the time of the accident, and investigators found cannabis very unlikely to have contributed.
The lesson from these cases is not that a positive cannabis test means nothing. It is that its meaning depends on the concentration, timing, circumstances and other evidence available to investigators
In the Air India case, investigators will need to establish much more than the alleged fact that the captain's confirmatory test was positive.
They will need to know what sample was tested, whether it contained THC itself or a metabolite - a substance produced when the body breaks THC down - at what concentration, and what that can say about the timing of use.
Air India is to immediately test all its pilots for banned substances after the incident, expanding on existing rules that require at least 10% of pilots to undergo random screening.
Urine, blood and even saliva can show that someone was exposed to THC, but they cannot reliably establish when it was used or whether the person was impaired at a particular point several hours earlier, according to Marcotte. Saliva is more closely linked to recent use, but can still detect THC many hours - and potentially a day or two - after consumption, he says.
Experts believe the question is not simply: Was the pilot using marijuana?
It is threefold: Was cannabis consumed? Was the pilot impaired while flying? And did that impairment contribute to the aircraft's sudden loss of altitude?
The first may soon be answered. The other two are considerably harder.

In 1920, Danish physiologist August Krogh was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine “for his discovery of the capillary motor regulating mechanism.”
His work addressed a fundamental question: how does muscle receive enough oxygen when its demand rises sharply during exercise? Krogh showed how changes in the capillary circulation could help meet this increased demand by bringing blood closer to muscle fibres and increasing the surface available for oxygen exchange.
The work had important implications for medicine because understanding how oxygen reaches tissues is central to conditions in which blood supply is impaired, including cardiovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes and wounds that fail to heal. The principles of microcirculation and tissue oxygenation that Krogh helped establish are now relevant to understanding tissue injury, wound healing, exercise physiology and the effects of impaired blood flow.
From zoology to physiology
Schack August Steenberg Krogh was born on November 15, 1874, in Grenaa, Denmark. He entered the University of Copenhagen in 1893, initially studying medicine before turning to zoology.
At the university, he joined the laboratory of physiologist Christian Bohr and became interested in respiration and the exchange of gases in living organisms. He obtained his zoology degree in 1899 and continued working in Bohr’s laboratory.
Krogh combined experimental biology with quantitative measurements and developed instruments for studying physiological processes. His research included respiration, gas exchange and water and electrolyte regulation.
In 1916, he became professor of zoophysiology at the University of Copenhagen.
The oxygen supply problem
Krogh focused on how oxygen moves from blood to tissue.
Muscles can increase their oxygen consumption considerably during exercise. Oxygen carried in the blood must diffuse from capillaries through surrounding tissue before reaching individual cells. The distance between a cell and a perfused capillary therefore affects oxygen delivery.
Krogh investigated capillary distribution in muscle and compared resting and active tissues. He observed that more capillaries appeared to contain blood when muscles were active.
In papers published in The Journal of Physiology in 1919, he combined these observations with mathematical calculations of oxygen diffusion. He proposed that bringing additional capillaries into functional use during activity would increase the available exchange surface and shorten the distance oxygen had to travel through tissue.
This work formed the basis of what became known as the Krogh cylinder model, a conceptual model describing oxygen diffusion from a capillary into the surrounding tissue.
The Nobel-winning discovery
Krogh went further than describing differences in capillary perfusion. He proposed a capillary motor regulating mechanism, through which capillary diameter and blood content could change according to the functional needs of tissue.
The Nobel Committee recognised this work in 1920.
In his Nobel lecture, Krogh described how the number of blood-filled capillaries varied with the activity of tissue. He argued that additional capillaries were brought into use during muscular activity, helping increase the area available for oxygen exchange.
The discovery shifted attention towards the microcirculation — the network of small vessels responsible for delivering oxygen and nutrients to tissues and carrying away metabolic products.
What modern physiology says
Some elements of Krogh’s original explanation have since been revised.
Modern studies do not support the simple idea that skeletal-muscle capillaries are routinely switched between completely closed and open states. Nor are capillaries considered the principal site of active blood-flow regulation.
Much of that regulation occurs upstream, particularly in arterioles. Modern microscopy has also shown that many muscle capillaries are already perfused at rest.
Capillary recruitment is therefore understood more precisely as changes in the pattern and extent of capillary perfusion rather than simply the opening of previously closed vessels.
Krogh’s central insight, however, remains important: the organisation of the capillary network and the distance oxygen must travel through tissue are crucial determinants of oxygen delivery.
From capillaries to insulin
Krogh’s career later intersected with another major medical development -- insulin.
In 1922, he and his wife, physician Marie Krogh, travelled to North America. Marie had diabetes and encouraged him to investigate the newly developed insulin treatment.
During the trip, Krogh visited Toronto, where Frederick Banting, Charles Best and their colleagues had developed methods for producing insulin. Krogh subsequently obtained permission to produce insulin using the Toronto method in Scandinavia.
Back in Denmark, he worked with physician Hans Christian Hagedorn and pharmacist August Kongsted. The first Danish patient was treated with insulin in March 1923, and Nordisk Insulinlaboratorium was established that year.
Scientific legacy
Krogh continued studying physiology after receiving the Nobel Prize. His work on respiration, gas exchange and the microcirculation demonstrated how physical principles and quantitative measurements could be used to understand biological processes.
The Krogh cylinder remains a useful conceptual model for studying oxygen diffusion, although modern research has refined the model using more detailed knowledge of blood flow, oxygen gradients and the three-dimensional structure of capillary networks.
Krogh retired from the University of Copenhagen in 1945 but continued his research. He died in Copenhagen on September 13, 1949, aged 74.
More than a century later, oxygen delivery to tissues is understood to involve cardiac output, blood flow, arteriolar regulation, capillary perfusion, blood oxygen content, diffusion and tissue metabolism.
Krogh’s original explanation has evolved, but his decision to study circulation at the microscopic level changed the understanding of how blood supplies individual tissues. His work established the capillary network and oxygen diffusion as central to the study of tissue oxygenation and microcirculation.

Hawaii bracing for ‘enormous’ storm as Lala strengthens into a hurricane
The Big Island has not experienced a direct hurricane landfall in 155 years
Hurricane Lala gathered strength on Saturday as it moved along a track that could result in a rare direct landfall on Hawaii’s Big Island.
The National Hurricane Center upgraded Lala to a Category 1 hurricane after maximum sustained winds reached 75 mph (120 kph). The storm’s eyewall was projected to pass over or near the southern end of the island by Saturday evening, bringing its strongest winds to high-altitude volcanic slopes.
The Big Island has not experienced a direct hurricane landfall in 155 years. Regardless of whether the eye makes landfall, meteorologists warned that higher elevations near the Mauna Kea volcano could receive up to 25 inches (63.5 centimeters) of rain.
The rainfall creates a risk of life-threatening mudslides in mountainous areas where residents live off the grid in improvised housing. Officials urged individuals in vulnerable locations to seek safe shelter immediately.
Even if the system drops slightly below hurricane strength, the NHC noted that wind speeds across mountain peaks and both windward and leeward slopes "are often up to 30% stronger than the near-surface winds" cited in its advisories.
"This is an enormous storm," Gov. Josh Green said. Tropical storm-force winds stretched outward up to 220 miles (350 km), with effects expected to reach Oahu and Kauai by Sunday morning.
Heavy flooding and wind-driven wildfires are potential hazards across the island chain.
Mike Caputo, a 50-year-old local fire captain living in Keaau on the east side of the Big Island, said the principal threats are flash flooding and falling trees, particularly the albizia species.
"They’re not very sturdy but they grow extremely large," Caputo said. "They can make roads impassable. I made sure my trees were trimmed a few days ago."
Tropical storm warnings have been declared for Maui, Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Oahu, Kauai, and Niihau.
Historical research into newspaper records by a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist indicates that a Category 3 hurricane struck the northeastern shore of the Big Island in 1871. Current models show Lala tracking "very close to the southern tip of the Big Island," according to Vanessa Almanza, a National Weather Service meteorologist in Honolulu.
Authorities and residents took precautions across the region. Public shelters were opened, community events were canceled, and ranchers were advised to leave cattle in open pastures rather than structures susceptible to collapse. "It doesn’t take landfall to create destruction," Almanza said.
Forecasters expect total rainfall of 8 to 12 inches (20.3 to 30.5 centimeters) across Maui and lower areas of the Big Island, with 4 to 6 inches (10.2 to 15.2 centimeters) predicted across the remainder of the island chain.
The hurricane center also warned that the storm could cause "life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," alongside hazardous storm surges and ocean swells "likely to cause life-threatening surf and rip current conditions."
As of 8 a.m. local time, Tropical Storm Lala was positioned approximately 90 miles (145 kilometers) southeast of South Point and about 300 miles (485 kilometers) southeast of Honolulu, carrying maximum sustained winds of 70 mph (110 kph) while moving west-northwest at 12 mph (19 kph).
Authorities urge vigilance
State Representative Jeanné Kapela urged residents to remain cautious. The southern portion of the island is rural and remote, featuring coffee farms and cattle ranches, but has seen recent population growth due to lower living costs. Kapela expressed concern for residents living off the grid in unpermitted homes.
"If you feel now that your house doesn’t have a great roof or might not be able to withstand hurricane force winds, then first things first you go to a family or friend’s house and you kind of hunker down there," she told The Associated Press. "We're hopeful the storm moves through quickly, but we're preparing for whatever comes."
The impending storm follows severe flooding that affected many residents in March. Agricultural producers are concerned about experiencing further crop damage, according to Hawaii Farm Bureau director Brian Miyamoto.
Wind increases fire concerns
As wind speeds increase across the archipelago, dry and breezy conditions outside the primary storm zone will elevate wildfire risks, Almanza noted.
In 2023, the town of Lahaina on Maui was destroyed by a severe fire driven by powerful winds from a hurricane passing far to the south.
"Since the fire, everybody is way more aware of weather in general and our environment and things that are happening," said Archie Kalepa, a Lahaina resident known for his ocean skills who has been closely monitoring the storm.
To the northwest, Kauai was hit by Hurricane Iniki as a Category 4 storm in 1992—an El Nino year similar to current climate patterns, where warming waters in the equatorial Pacific enhance hurricane activity.
"It did $3 billion worth of damage. It destroyed thousands of homes, and it did kill six people," said Steven Businger, the professor who conducted the historical research on the 1871 storm. "We just can never know if a storm is going to turn."
