Days after the Bar Council of India (BCI) tried to prevent NALSAR students from enrolling with State Bar Councils before a backlash forced it to recant, BCI chairman Manan Kumar Mishra on Saturday (August 15, 2026) apologised to law students for any hurt caused by his words or communications.
In a three-page letter issued on Independence Day, Mr. Mishra — who is also a senior advocate and BJP MP — said he regretted and apologised for any of his statements or directives that may have hurt students.
“If anything connected with the present controversy, any of my words, or letter, has hurt the feelings of our law students, I sincerely regret and apologise for the same. There should be no hesitation in saying so. An expression of regret is not a matter of prestige or ego. It is simply an acknowledgment that the feelings and concerns of our students matter,” he said.
Freedom of expression
The BCI chairman did not name any particular institution or directly identify the controversy in his letter. Instead, he focused on the concerns raised by students and stressed that their views should be heard with patience, sensitivity, and respect.
He emphasised that law students, particularly those studying at national law universities and other leading institutions, are capable of forming their own views and should not be subjected to pressure or influence. He said students should be allowed to independently assess the facts and reach their own conclusions.
Acknowledging that protests are an important part of democracy, Mr. Mishra said that students must always remain free to express their views.
‘Keep an open mind’
“At the same time, the legal tradition teaches us something equally important, namely that when further facts or clarifications emerge, every issue should be reconsidered objectively and with an open mind. There is no inconsistency between expressing a genuine grievance and thereafter fairly considering a clarification,” he added.
Describing convocation ceremonies as important milestones in the lives of graduating students and their families, Mr. Mishra said the choice of whether to attend must rest entirely with the students, adding that no student should be forced either to participate or to stay away.
The latest controversy was triggered by NALSAR students who did not want the Chief Justice of India to be the chief guest at the convocation because of his comments about student protests. The BCI had then sought to penalise students for their “campaign” against the CJI, who later slammed the BCI’s actions as well.
Seeking dialogue and mutual respect
The BCI chairman emphasised that differences between the judiciary, the Bar, universities, and law students should not be allowed to damage their relationship in the long term. Disagreements should ultimately be addressed through dialogue, clarification, and mutual respect, he said.
Mr. Mishra appealed for the issue to be approached with an attitude of fairness and reconciliation. “The issue should not be allowed to acquire a political or extraneous colour through outside influence. Our law students are mature and discerning enough to examine the facts, consider the clarification offered, and take their own independent decision,” he added.

5 people shot at US university as police probe multiple suspects

A shooting involving multiple suspects and five people shot at Virginia State University prompted a campus lockdown early on Saturday.

For “Sacred Creatures” director Frieda Luk, belief can be comforting, ridiculous, exhilarating and hard to explain.
“I’m really fascinated by when people believe in something,” she tells Variety. “One person believes in something, and then a group of people, and then it slowly becomes this massive phenomenon. It goes viral.”
That fascination drives Luk’s debut feature, which world premieres in competition at the Edinburgh International Film Festival. Starring Olivia Luccardi, James Cusati-Moyer and Romina D’Ugo, the Canada-Italy production follows three estranged siblings reuniting in rural Italy after middle sister Miriam (Olivia Luccardi) is released from psychiatric treatment following an experience she understands as a spiritual awakening rather than a breakdown.
“This movie is my exploration of believing in something and belief,” says Luk. “Miriam has agency. She knows herself and she makes choices. However, when she becomes a figure that people rally around, people are imbuing her with meaning. When she becomes abstract, she no longer controls the message.”
Popular on Variety
That uncertainty extends to the film itself, which slips between psychological drama, comedy and magical realism without settling comfortably into any of them. For Luk, the tonal slipperiness developed naturally from writing. “I set up the situation and these characters, and as I’m writing, I’m following what they’re doing. What I’m waiting for is how they surprise me,” she says.
	One influence was Marco Ferreri’s “La Grande Bouffe,” the grotesque story of four men attempting to eat themselves to death. “The comedy is following through that premise in a serious way, because if you actually are going to eat yourself to death, you’re going to have gastrointestinal problems,” Luk says. “It’s also very silly. It never takes itself too seriously.” Italian cinema was integral to “Sacred Creatures” from the start. Luk points to films of the 1970s, admiring their willingness to move between modes contemporary cinema can sometimes keep separate. “A lot of the ’70s movies, especially European ones, are completely in between genres.” 
Luccardi was similarly keen to avoid reducing Miriam to a diagnosis. “She is healing from the lack of belief from people and everyone thinking that something was wrong with her,” Luccardi explains, adding that Miriam feels “meant for something greater.”
There was another, less metaphysical piece of direction that unlocked the character: Luk told her Miriam was like a cat.
	
“She’s very much like: ‘I’m letting you in on my terms. No, I actually don’t want you to touch me. I want to be a pet, but not like that,’” laughs Luccardi.
“I did a lot of cat direction,” Luk dryly admits.
As Miriam grows more secure in herself, Luccardi subtly changed the physical quality of the performance.
“There was more of a calmness in my breath,” she says. “She was more relaxed and calm and just flowed. Before, she may have been a little more stressed and tightly wound.”
That growing self-possession becomes visual in the film’s party scene, where Miriam arrives in a voluminous yellow-green dress that immediately separates her from the room around her. There is something of Bette Davis’ party entrance in “All About Eve” to the moment: costume becomes a declaration of presence, allowing Miriam to suddenly occupy a different plane from everyone watching her.
Luk wanted the dress to be “kind of ridiculous looking, but also kind of chic,” something that would “take up some space” without seeming entirely out of place. “Miriam is new and a little ridiculous,” she says, with its uncontained “fluffiness” signalling “an irreverence to what has come before.”
Luccardi’s relationship with it was rather less reverential by the end of the shoot. “At the beginning, it was great. At the end… I wore it a long time,” she jokes. “As with every costume, you love it at the beginning and then you’re like: ‘Can we burn it, please?’”
The surrounding family remain skeptical of their sister’s burgeoning allure to those around her. Luk, an only child who grew up surrounded by cousins, was amused by the way relatives can inhabit incompatible versions of the same history.
“They’re always competing,” she says.
	The instinct of creating a story that makes life easier to comprehend ultimately expands beyond the siblings.
Luk grew up without religion, but many childhood friends were religious and invited her to churches and youth groups. Watching from the outside, she was intrigued by their ability to surrender themselves to faith.
	“I would watch them read a text and believe in that text and treat it like this holy thing,” she recalls. “It was really hard for me to give myself over to something like that.”
At Catholic services, she found herself captivated by the incense, clothing and ceremony.
	“I was like: ‘This is so fun and theatrical.’ I can see how it could be really comforting,” she says. “There’s a community-oriented spirit to it. Being a fan of a big sport is kind of fun. Yelling at a team is fun.”
The director began thinking about fandoms, sports and social media with much the same curiosity. What separates a few people who regularly gather from a movement?
	
“What if people hung out, and then that becomes a movement?” she says. “A few people hang out, and then more people hang out. Then you do it regularly, and what happens?”
The film is shot in Piedmont and Italy provided a fertile landscape for those questions. Luk recalls seeing reports about a teenage protester and wondering why there couldn’t be a patron saint for protest, and what the origin story of a new saint might look like.
But after all that construction of a film, a family history, a faith and perhaps even a saint, the director isn’t interested in providing audiences with a final answer about Miriam.
“I want people to come away examining why they believe in something and how,” she says, “and that there is a pleasure in believing something.”
“You never know if you are right or you are wrong. You might be wrong.”
Or, as Luccardi puts it: “You never know if someone’s crazy or if someone’s enlightened. Who knows?”
“It’s a fine line.”

Firefighters battle wildfire tearing through Belgian nature reserve
- Published
Firefighters battled a wildfire tearing through Belgium's largest nature reserve on Saturday, with the blaze described as the country's worst in recent history.
Residents were ordered to evacuate two nearby villages as the flames consumed a third of the High Fens, with local officials warning the fire - which had been burning since Friday - could reach homes.
Water-bombing aircraft and helicopters were sent from across Europe to aid the firefighters working in the park near its eastern border with Germany.
It was among a number of wildfires burning across Europe on Saturday, including a forest fire which caused hundreds of residents to leave their home in south-western France.
Local officials in Belgium said the blaze remained out of control as of Saturday afternoon.
Nicolas Yernaux, a spokesperson for the regional authorities in Wallonia, said the fire was the country's "largest in recent history".
"There is a risk that the fire could reach homes, but we are deploying all available resources to protect them," he said, with a nearby gymnasium opened to accommodate those evacuating their homes.
Authorities said they had been hampered by weather conditions as well as the park's terrain - which consists of bog-like territory, moorland and forests.
Firefighters had "allowed parts of the heathland to burn because the area is very difficult to access," Yernaux said.
Gregory Melotte, one of those working to extinguish the blaze, told Belgian broadcaster RTBF: "We managed to calm the fire coming from the plain, to prevent it from spreading into the fir forest. We still succeeded in our mission, but it's not over yet.
"The flames are coming towards us, the wind has shifted twice, once in our favour, once against us."
The country activated the European Union's civil protection mechanism to trigger reinforcements from other countries.
European Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said two Swedish water-bombing aircraft and two helicopters, one from the Czech Republic and one from the Netherlands, were on their way.
Meanwhile, local officials said 650 residents evacuated their homes as a wildfire burned in Landes, south-western France.
The fire began on Thursday and, according to authorities, reignited on Saturday - with more than 500 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze.
Forest fires have also been reported in Croatia, Spain and Serbia since Friday, after a summer of extreme heat which has seen swathes of land across Europe either going up in flames or scorched brown.
The EU's climate monitoring service, Copernicus, has confirmed that western Europe experienced its hottest June-to-July period on record.

When the leaders of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey got together last week to forge a new defense agreement, they emphasized that their pact wasn’t aimed at any particular country. But one country was surely on everybody’s mind: the Islamic Republic of Iran.
Iran has positioned itself as the most overtly anti-Western state in the region, and the coming together of three prominent Muslim-majority countries aligned with the West, two of which have land borders with Iran, signals its isolation. Iran has endured months of war with Israel and the United States without losing, but it has done so in part by repeatedly attacking neighboring countries that house U.S. military bases. Now these countries are among those closing ranks against Iran in an agreement signed in and named for Mecca, Islam’s holiest city.
The symbolism can’t be lost on Tehran. The parties to the Mecca pact include some of the world’s most powerful Muslim-majority countries: the two with the biggest economies in the region (Turkey and Saudi Arabia, which also spend the most on their militaries), and the Muslim world’s sole nuclear power (Pakistan).
Iran has traditionally maintained good relations with Turkey and Pakistan; its cultural bonds with these two countries are strong and go back centuries. More recently, the Islamic Republic has worked to improve its relations with Saudi Arabia, particularly since reestablishing diplomatic ties with Riyadh in 2023.
Even so, Iran’s regional policies have put the country at odds with these and other neighbors. Tehran gave its full support to the regime of Bashar al-Assad in Syria, which rebels who were backed by Ankara and Riyadh overthrew in 2024. The Iranian military exchanged strikes with Pakistan in 2024 and attacked Saudi Arabia in recent weeks. Iranian missiles were intercepted over Turkish airspace earlier this year. Tehran-backed militias in Yemen and Iraq have attacked Saudi interests. More broadly, Iran’s anti-American stance clashes with the official orientations of all three signatories of the Mecca agreement.
Skeptics will point out that the new defense pact might not mean much in practice. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a similar deal last year but did not invoke it when Saudi Arabia came under attack during the current conflict. But the language of the Mecca accord is stark: “Any armed attack against any of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” The arrangement includes a new organization, to be overseen by a secretariat in Saudi Arabia, and regular meetings among the foreign and defense ministers of the three countries, along with their military chiefs. Turkey’s foreign minister, Hakan Fidan, has compared the new organization to NATO and suggested that Egypt, the most populous Arab state, is likely to join. Altogether, the pact suggests a significant improvement in relations between Turkey and the Arab states—a development that could help stabilize the entire region.
Iranian officialdom has mostly greeted the news of the Mecca pact with studied nonchalance. A spokesperson claimed to welcome the arrangement as evidence that the member countries would no longer rely on the United States. A reformist civil-society activist suggested to me that the Mecca agreement could be “an opportunity, not a threat,” insinuating that Iran could one day join it. But some hard-line politicians are less sanguine. Ebrahim Azizi, the head of the Parliament’s foreign-policy committee, posted on Saturday that the Mecca three “haven’t found the right path yet. We warn them about miscalculations. No mistake will go unanswered.”
Washington has long encouraged its allies in the Middle East to work together. Throughout much of the Cold War, regional alliances held off both Soviet communism and Arab radicalism, which meant that the United States felt the need to intervene only rarely and briefly. Iran was a crucial part of this architecture—intervening, together with Saudi Arabia, in civil wars in Oman and Yemen to help defeat Communist-backed rebels, and helping to found the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in 1969. President Richard Nixon so relied on Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi to help keep the U.S. out of Middle Eastern affairs that in 1972 he told Pahlavi, “Protect me.” Then came the Iranian Revolution of 1979, and with it, a new era of chaos and discord.
Iran is not the only Middle Eastern country excluded from the emerging security arrangement that Mecca portends. Israel, too, is absent. The 2020 Abraham Accords normalized Israel’s relations with the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan, but the big prize was always Saudi Arabia, which has conditioned recognition of Israel on progress toward the formation of a Palestinian state. Israel is currently moving away from this prospect rather than toward it. Pakistan doesn’t recognize Israel either. Turkey has diplomatic and military relations with Israel, but the two countries have drifted apart in recent years.
If Israel still wants to work toward regional recognition, it may find that its best course is to patch things up with Turkey and try to meet the Saudis halfway. At least these two countries don’t share the depth of Iran’s animus against Israel.
Iran, too, will be faced with a choice. It can go on supporting militias and destabilizing the region, which will further isolate it. Or it can embrace the regional consensus on economic development, diplomatic reconciliation, and a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine conflict. The Islamic Republic can either militate against Mecca, in other words, or give up its revolutionary ambitions at last.

I'm not corrupt: TMC's Asish Banerjee found hanging at party office, note found
He was a five-time MLA from Rampurhat, having represented the constituency for 25 consecutive years starting from 2001. Banerjee, however, lost the seat to Bharatiya Janata Party's Dhruba Saha in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly polls.
Trinamool Congress leader and former West Bengal Assembly Deputy Speaker Asish Banerjee was found hanging inside a party office in the state's Birbhum district on Sunday morning.
He was an ex-minister and also a five-time MLA from Rampurhat, having represented the constituency for 25 consecutive years from 2001 to 2026. Banerjee, however, lost the seat to Bharatiya Janata Party's Dhruba Saha in the 2026 West Bengal Assembly polls.
His body was recovered from a TMC office adjacent to his Rampurhat residence. This came a day after the former TMC MLA participated in a local Independence Day celebration and hoisted the Tricolour there.
A purported suicide note has also been recovered. In the purported letter, Banerjee vehemently denied any wrongdoing, stating he was never involved in corruption throughout his political career.
He apparently referred to supposed allegations of wrongdoings related to the Tarapith Rampurhat Development Authority (TRDA), where he had served as the chairperson.
Banerjee claimed that he had no role in the planning and development agency's tender-related decisions, cheque issuance, plan approvals or no-objection certificates. He alleged that attempts had been made to "malign" and humiliate him, and said he felt that entering politics had been a mistake.
The veteran TMC leader also wrote that he could not always protest "wrongdoings" within the party. After his electoral defeat, Banerjee was not seen to be particularly active in politics, party sources, cited by news agency PTI, said.
His death comes months after the TMC lost power in West Bengal following its 15-year rule, with the BJP forming the government after the 2026 Assembly polls.
The change in political fortunes has also seen several former TMC leaders and legislators face corruption-related investigations and arrests.
The exact circumstances leading to Banerjee's death were not immediately clear. Police have launched an investigation and the body has been sent for postmortem.

On 31 July, “Umit” – which means hope in Kazakh – was released into a nature reserve on the edge of Lake Balkhash after more than a decade of careful planning to return the caspian tiger to the region. With this release, Kazakhstan became the first country to restore its tiger range after they had been thought extinct, with the last reliable sighting in the country recorded more than 70 years ago.
Umit – a wild-caught female tiger transported from the Russian far east – will be joined by more big cats in the coming years, with plans to establish a self-sustaining population of about 50. A wild-caught male flown from Russia is still being monitored by authorities and will be released when he is judged fit to survive alone. Two wild tiger cubs are also being reared on the reserve in special enclosures, with as little human contact as possible, and are likely to be released into the marshlands next year, to feast on boar, deer and kulans, a type of wild donkey.
“Today, we became witnesses of a truly historic event,” declared Yerlan Nysanbayev, Kazakhstan’s environment minister, after the release. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken.”
The caspian tiger was considered extinct in the 1970s after decades of fur hunting, habitat destruction and eradication campaigns. Its range once spanned from eastern Turkey to north-west China, including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Iran and swathes of central Asia, mostly in forest highlands and along the edges of lakes and rivers, particularly in Tugai forests that were widely destroyed for agriculture.
It was officially declared extinct in 2003, but a scientific breakthrough just six years later laid the foundation for the recent release. DNA analysis of the tiger’s genetic history revealed that the caspian tiger and the amur tiger found in eastern Siberia were almost identical, with populations probably intermingling until the early 1900s before they were isolated by hunting. What became known as the caspian tiger spread west from Siberia and were separated from the amur tiger by a single letter of genetic code.
“For all intents and purposes, this is the return of the caspian tiger, only this time they flew instead of walking,” said Dale Miquelle, an authority on Siberian tigers who formerly headed the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Russia programme. “The idea of bringing back a subspecies of tigers that has disappeared is very exciting. This is as close as we’re going to get to that process.”
Today, it would be practically impossible for the caspian tiger to re-establish its former range. A 2017 feasibility study identified two places in the region with enough suitable habitat to re-establish populations, both in Kazakhstan. The most promising was thought to be Ile-Balkhash, where Umit was released, which the Kazakh government made a nature reserve in 2018.
While this summer’s release is the first example of a cross-border tiger translocation, there have been several successful releases in the Russian far east as part of efforts to restore the amur tiger’s former range. One scheme involved rescuing orphaned cubs whose mothers had been shot by hunters in Siberia, and then releasing them into former ranges when they were strong enough. The project, which Miquelle worked on, was a huge success – especially because there was no human contact with the young big cats.
“The success rate was pretty close to 100% after the release. These animals adapt amazingly quickly. One young female killed a Himalayan black bear within 24 hours of being released and others have learned to hunt on their own in the wild really quickly,” he says.
But it is not all good news. Wild tigers have suffered a catastrophic century, with numbers falling from about 100,000 at the beginning of the 20th century to about 5,500 today. In many parts of Asia, they are still declining – and facing new threats from climate breakdown and disease. In recent years in Russia, African swine fever wiped out enormous numbers of wild boar, a tiger’s favourite prey, causing many to target human settlements. Ensuring there is enough food for the returning caspian tigers is key to their survival, says Miquelle.
“I am very hopeful this can work. In Russia, a number of translocations resulted in the recolonisation of tiger habitat. So there’s a blueprint that suggests that this can work as long as there is suitable habitat and sufficient prey,” he says.

AI can't be managed by any existing department, so EY is creating a new one.
The Big Four firm is setting up a new function called the "AI Value Realization Office" to centralize its AI spending and ensure the technology delivers measurable impact.
Dan Diasio, EY's global consulting AI leader, told Business Insider the firm expects the office to be fully operational within a couple of months.
Its job is to govern AI spending, drive returns, monitor usage, decide which AI initiatives to scale, and oversee how AI reshapes jobs.
Most companies allocate corporate budgets along departmental lines. However, AI spending and its potential payoff can cut across IT, finance, sales, HR, and operations, said Diasio.
"If you fund by department, you end up addressing a bunch of use cases inside of each of the functions. And what that often means is that you're leaving a lot of value on the table," he said.
EY-Parthenon research found that 75% of the potential enterprise value from AI comes from horizontal value streams — meaning across multiple functions — compared with 25% from projects contained within individual functions, Diasio said.
The AI office will govern the value strategy, looking not just at the dollar-for-dollar calculation but at a broader assessment of whether AI initiatives are changing business performance, Diasio said.
It "will help make sure that funding flows where the biggest opportunities are," he said.
Creating a corporate function to manage a growing cost or risk isn't a new idea. Modern-day HR departments emerged during the Great Depression as companies sought more systematic ways to hire and fire workers, while treasury teams took shape in the 1970s, when floating exchange rates made currency movements a bigger risk for multinational companies.
The AI value realization office is the modern-day equivalent, reallocating a set of responsibilities scattered across finance, technology, and other teams to a strategic function in its own right.
'Client zero'
The Big Four professional services pitch themselves as "client zero" for the AI future. By testing the technology on their own employees and operations, they can show clients what works — and sell them advice on doing the same.
The firms have also committed billions to the new technology. In 2023, EY said $1.4 billion went toward building the foundation for the EY.ai platform.
Like all businesses, AI providers' move to change pricing models has put pressure on professional services firms to use the technology effectively and limit costs.
EY has implemented an "invisible" AI router behind some of its specialized AI tools. The router directs employees to the best model for the task at hand, and has helped reduce token consumption by 60% since its implementation in April, alongside other governance strategies.
Saving measures are also becoming more important to clients as they get a clearer idea of what AI actually costs, said Diasio. Many started by experimenting while AI providers subsidized some of the expenses. Now they are confronting the real price tag and asking EY how to organize themselves as they scale AI.
In an EY US AI Pulse survey released in July, 98% of 534 senior decision-makers said token spending had made them reconsider their approach. The survey was conducted between April and May.
So far, companies have generally paid for AI by tightening budgets across the board and reallocating money, said Diasio. Giving AI governance more clout — through a function like the AI value realization office — will be a "critical part" of how EY's clients move forward, said Diasio.
Most clients aren't setting up dedicated AI offices yet, Diasio added.
"It's something that I imagine over time will become a function," he said. "The focus is beginning to shift more toward what the organization looks like on the other side of this."

'I lost $14,000 in a month': Investors hit by Korean stock market's wild swings
- Published
Bank worker Yongjoon Kim lost 20 million Korean won ($14,000; £10,500) on the South Korean stock market last month.
Kim's money was meant to help buy a home, as he is getting married later this year.
Instead the value of his tech investments slumped by around 25% in July.
"It's going to sting and I'm going to have to work really hard to make up for this," Kim says. "But for others who have taken more risk, they're going to feel the pain."
Many of his friends are worse off, and now in a "desperate" situation after "going all in" with their savings, he says.
While plenty of investors are piling into technology stocks, sharp market swings mean the bets don't always pay off, with prices often moving on every major headline.
Nowhere is that instability more pronounced than in South Korea's tech-heavy Kospi, widely regarded as the world's most volatile stock index.
A global frenzy around artificial intelligence has driven wild swings in the value of the country's biggest chipmakers.
The Kospi faced "one of the sharpest corrections" in its history between June and August, comparable to the drops seen during Covid-19 and the 1997 Asian financial crisis, says Wee Khoon Chong from financial services company BNY.
The index more than doubled its value since the start of the year to rise above 9,000 points in mid-June, before plunging to 5,500 within a few weeks. It has now recovered some ground to about 6,800 points.
A key reason for the sell-off in recent weeks has been concerns over the huge amounts of money being spent on AI, Wee adds.
The slump has had a big impact on many of the country's personal investors who bought tech stocks over the past year.
For Woongsa Kim, a look at his shares trading app is a painful reminder of what he had made then lost by investing in the South Korean stock market.
At the start of the year, he used about half of a bonus from work to buy shares in tech giant SK Hynix.
The stock quadrupled in value before most of those gains were wiped out, leaving his investment, now worth about 300 million won, at roughly half the value of its peak.
"Thinking about it just brings tears to my eyes," Kim told the BBC.
The sell-off came after tech shares had soared for months, "generating the extreme euphoria" that has moved some personal investors to take out loans to invest, says investment analyst Tobias Reger.
It has been most acutely felt by people who used leverage - a form of borrowing in the financial markets.
Leveraging lets an investor control a larger number of stocks than their own cash would otherwise allow, which delivers a bigger profit if the shares rise.
However, if the stocks fall past an agreed level it can trigger what is known as a margin call - when a broker demands payment of the debt.
By the end of July an estimated 1.2 million South Korean personal investor accounts had faced margin calls, equivalent to about one in every 30 working-age adults in the country.
Leveraged trading is a growing trend among personal investors that has also picked up in markets like Taiwan and the US, says Frank Benzimra, the head of Asia equity strategy at financial services group Societe Generale.
That has raised the risks around AI-related stocks, he adds.
'Gut-wrenching' slump
After his US-listed Nvidia shares soared by more than 1,000%, Chanyong Park, who works in marketing, says he put most of the profits into SK Hynix shares. But that bet went sour as their value has fallen by around $10,000.
"This was money I'd invested to save before planning to leave my job around October to start my own business. But now I'm seriously wondering whether I'll have enough."
Park plans to hold on to his SK Hynix shares in hopes of a rebound, although recent swings have made him hesitant to invest more.
"It doesn't always feel like movements are driven by rational reasons - sometimes it still feels a lot like gambling," he says.
Another investor Youngji Park says he went "all in", putting the majority of his available cash into Samsung shares that peaked at a total value of 45 million Korean won.
But his investment has suffered a "gut-wrenching" slump, Park says.
- The 20-somethings betting big on tech stocks 
  - Published20 July
- Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m? 
  - Published27 July
He too plans to keep hold of his shares in the hope that they will rise again.
"I feel like a fool for trusting the Korean stock market," he says. "It's a long-term game now. I'll just have to wait it out."
College student Soomin Yi says she pooled money with a friend to invest in SK Hynix after experiencing "fomo" (fear of missing out).
But she now wishes she had sold her shares in the company when they peaked at three million won each in June, instead of buying into speculation that they would rise to five million won.
"We didn't really have anyone around us who is experienced in investing, and we did not study investing seriously before buying the stock," Yi says.
What this means for the rest of the world
The huge swings in Korean shares are also raising concerns about some other markets around the world.
Tech-heavy indexes like Japan's Nikkei 225 seem to be moving in tandem with the Kospi's wild swings, Societe Generale's Benzimra says.
But the majority of the world's stock markets are unlikely to see that level of violent moves as they include a wider mix of companies, he adds.
"I don't think we can see the same kind of volatility in large diversified markets such as the [Tokyo Stock Price Index] or the US equity markets," Benzimra says.
And traders who diversified their portfolios say it has helped cushion the blow from the stock market rout.
"I think this whole episode is a warning to Korean investors, especially young investors, not to put everything in one basket and hope for the best," says Yongjoon Kim, who also has shares in overseas markets.
He adds that he should have taken a more cautious approach to investing in tech stocks.
His fiancée, Gaeon Lee, is optimistic that the market will recover despite losing part of the savings they had set aside for a new home.
But she worries about Kim, saying the constant need to monitor their investments has taken a toll on him.
"Seeing our home savings take a hit in the stock market was definitely a wake-up call," she says.

Won't live much longer: Fasting Jharkhand student slams govt ahead of stir 2.0
A Ranchi student protestor said he may not survive much longer as the JPSC-JSSC agitation entered its 23rd day, with the hunger strike continuing for 13 days. Protesters have announced an August 20 gherao of CM Hemant Soren's residence and demanding his resignation.
A student protestor in Ranchi has said he does not think he will survive much longer as the agitation by JPSC-JSSC aspirants entered its 23rd day, with the hunger strike continuing for 13 days.
“The government is not serious at all. I don’t think I will survive much longer; the situation is critical,” protestor Prem Nayak said.
Nayak said he developed a fever on Friday and that authorities tried to take him away for treatment, but he refused. He also said that the authorities took Devendra Nath Mahato away and were not allowing him to return, claiming that their intention was to break the movement.
PROTESTERS PLAN AUGUST 20 GHERAO OF CM'S RESIDENCE
Nayak said discussions were ongoing among protesters about laying siege to Chief Minister Hemant Soren’s residence, although nothing had been finalised. He said a ‘Jail Bharo Andolan’ would be a better option than laying siege to the CM’s residence and suggested shutting down all schools and colleges as another measure.
The protesters have announced that they will burn effigies of Chief Minister Hemant Soren and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi at district headquarters across all 24 districts of Jharkhand on Sunday. They have also announced a gherao of Soren’s residence on August 20 and said they would remain there until their demands are met.
For the first time, the protesters have also demanded Soren’s resignation over alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations.
The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has demanded cancellation of the JSSC-CGL examination and the 11th-13th JPSC examination, along with a CBI probe into the irregularities. It has also sought an inquiry by a panel of retired judges from outside Jharkhand.
The protesters accused the ruling JMM and Congress of playing politics over their issues and said that the JMM-Congress alliance had failed to take concrete action on their demands. They also demanded that Rahul Gandhi withdraw support from the JMM-led coalition if Soren was not listening to him.
“We will gherao the chief minister's residence on August 20. We seek his resignation as both the JMM and the Congress are playing politics with us. We also demand that Rahul Gandhi withdraw support from the JMM-led coalition if the CM is not listening to him,” JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch leader Ravindra Paswan said.
The students also criticised Gandhi, saying he had expressed support for them but that no concrete action had followed. They demanded that Congress withdraw support from the JMM-led government if it was unwilling to act on their concerns.
STUDENTS HOLD TIRANGA YATRA IN RANCHI
The agitation entered its 22nd day on Saturday as thousands of students and job aspirants took out a ‘Tiranga Yatra’ in Ranchi to mark the country’s 80th Independence Day and press for transparency and reforms in the recruitment examination system.
The protesters marched from Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium, the site of the ongoing agitation, to Albert Ekka Chowk. They carried national flags and raised slogans such as “Bharat Mata Ki Jai” and “Vande Mataram”. Two wheelchair-borne demonstrators who were on fast also participated in the march.
Many students said their larger goal was to restore trust in Jharkhand’s recruitment system.
“Independence doesn’t just mean freedom from the British, but also freedom from inequality of opportunities, corruption and injustice,” the JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch said.
MAHTO SAYS POLICE STOPPED HIM FROM JOINING MARCH
The protest also drew attention to JLKM leader Devendra Nath Mahto, who had been on a hunger strike for 14 days. Mahto alleged that police prevented him from leaving Sadar Hospital to participate in the Tiranga Yatra.
A video of the incident showed a security official blocking Mahto’s path as he tried to leave the hospital. Several workers of the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha (JKLM) urged the official to allow him to join the yatra, while the official appeared to ask them to let the fasting activist rest.
Mahto questioned why he was being prevented from attending the march at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium.
“After 80 years, we have realised that we have got only nominal freedom. Under which provision of the Constitution am I being stopped?” he said.
Mahto also alleged that attempts were being made to divert the students’ movement and claimed that some people were trying to dismantle the agitation nearly a month after it began.
SOREN PROMISES ACTION ON RECRUITMENT IRREGULARITIES
The escalation came despite assurances from Chief Minister Hemant Soren that the alleged recruitment irregularities would be investigated impartially.
In his Independence Day address, Soren acknowledged that questions surrounding recruitment examinations had shaken the confidence of an entire generation of job aspirants. He said anyone found guilty of paper leaks, corruption or other irregularities would face strict action irrespective of their influence or position.
Soren also cautioned against declaring anyone guilty without evidence and said justice must be based on facts. He said merely apprehending those responsible for irregularities would not be enough and called for systemic changes to prevent manipulation of examinations.
The measures outlined by the government include a time-bound annual examination calendar, technology-secured examinations, timely publication of answer keys and OMR sheets, and multi-level accountability in the recruitment process.

While the allegations were loosely based on actual complaints about conditions at Detroit Animal Control, El-Sayed wasn’t in charge of the shelter when they first surfaced.
In August 2026, after Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic Party primary election, a rumor spread online questioning his record as the head of Detroit's health department, which took over supervision of Detroit Animal Control a few months after El-Sayed took office. According to social media posts, he ran a "dog slaughterhouse" there and oversaw the euthanasia of 74% of the city's shelter dogs.
For instance, a widely posted meme (archived) stated:
Abdulrahman El-Sayed got EXPOSED for the dog slaughterhouse he ran as Detroit's Director Health where they killed 74% of all dogs in their 'care'. MAGA Mike Rogers odds of winning are SURGING!
(Snopes reader)
Snopes readers emailed us asking if this was true.
Public evidence shows that while these allegations were loosely based on actual complaints about conditions at the shelter, El-Sayed wasn't yet in charge of Detroit Animal Control when the complaints first surfaced. Rather, he inherited the shelter's problems when animal control was moved from the police department's control to the health department's in late 2015.
As such, we rate this claim as false.
We'll start by breaking down the timeline of events. El-Sayed was an assistant professor of epidemiology at Columbia University from 2014 to 2015. In August 2015, he was appointed executive director of the Detroit Health Department. In the fall of 2015, El-Sayed's health department took over supervision of animal control from the police department.
The accusations about the center and its poor treatment of dogs went public well before El-Sayed was appointed to run the health department, much less oversee animal control. For example, thousands of people signed a petition launched on June 18, 2015, to shut down animal control, claiming it euthanized 95% of the animals it collected.
Brittany Roberts, a former animal control employee filed (archived) a whistleblower 
Roberts worked at the department from March 2015 and was fired in September 2015, shortly after El-Sayed became head of the health department, which was still transitioning to officially take over animal control. Two days after she filed the lawsuit, then-Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan announced the health department would take over animal control.
Detroit's police department was in charge of Detroit Animal Control from 2012 to fall 2015 according to news reports at the time. In October 2015, El-Sayed announced that the city's health department would take over:
This move to the health department is an opportunity for us to focus on two important and interrelated aspects of animal welfare in the city: decreasing the harmful public health consequences of stray animals – including dog bites, zoonotic diseases like rabies, and traffic accidents caused by stray animals – while also facilitating the transfer of dogs from our shelter to eventually get into caring homes.
In December 2015, El-Sayed replaced the former animal control director Harry Ward with Melissa Miller. Miller began her tenure as director on Dec. 21, 2015. El-Sayed prevented local news outlet 7 Action News from interviewing her, citing the outlet's past negative coverage of Detroit's animal control department.
In a 2024 podcast interview, El-Sayed described part of his role at the health department was managing animal control, which he said "was a mess at the time":
When I was the new director of the Detroit Health Department, I inherited a part of the job that I never trained for and never thought I would do, which is Detroit Animal Control. And it was a mess at the time, and I needed somebody who I could trust, who could come in and do right by the animals and right by the people of the city of Detroit. And Mel Miller was that person.
The Detroit News reported that the city animal shelters had a 74% euthanasia rate in 2015. El-Sayed took over in the fall of that year. After the health department began its oversight, animal control's budget doubled from around $1.2 million to $2.3 million, according to Detroit News. The department also increased hiring, volunteer programming and dog bite prevention efforts.
Further, a 2018 Detroit News report said the city's animal shelters' euthanasia rate fell from 74% in 2015 to about 35% in 2017, according to annual shelter reports submitted to the Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development. In 2016, the Michigan Humane Society gave its former building to Detroit Animal Control.
El-Sayed resigned from the health department in 2017 to run for governor.
For further reading, Snopes has previously reported on the false claim that El-Sayed said he believed the U.S. deserved the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

The Taliban has taken a terrible toll on the education of girls — and boys as well
By Grade 11, Hashmat Mubariz had stopped attending school regularly. He was still officially enrolled. The Taliban had not barred him from the classroom, as they had barred his two sisters. But Mubariz, who later taught himself English, became an English instructor and now hosts a podcast and helps run a nongovernmental organization, said the school he once attended no longer felt like a place of learning.
"I felt I was wasting my time at school rather than learning," he said.
Before the Taliban returned to power five years ago — on August 15, 2021 — Mubariz remembered his public school as friendly and relatively open. Students studied English, science, mathematics, biology and literature alongside religious subjects. They could speak in class, share their opinions and ask questions. The school was not perfect, he said, but it felt safe and focused on learning.
Mubariz, 19, says after the Taliban takeover, that atmosphere slowly disappeared.
"Many people believe that only girls' education is affected," Mubariz said. "But boys are also facing a serious education crisis."
The Taliban's restrictions on girls and women have been sweeping and severe, barring girls from secondary schools and women from universities and robbing millions of any formal path to education. But interviews with boys and young men show another, less visible part of Afghanistan's education crisis: Boys are still allowed to attend school, but many say the education being offered inside the classroom has changed so sharply that it no longer prepares them for the future.
NPR spoke to 15 middle and high school students in Kabul, Herat, Helmand, Ghazni, Ghor, Mazar-e-Sharif and Bamiyan. They described similar experiences: less attention to science, languages such as English and Persian, and civic subjects; more pressure to study religion; stricter rules around appearance; and a growing belief that secular education may no longer lead TO a future career. Students and families said the shift has been especially severe in parts of the south, including Helmand and Kandahar, where families already placed a stronger emphasis on religious studies and Taliban rule has deepened that pressure.
The remaking of boys education
The first changes were visible. Male teachers were ordered to grow longer beards and wear turbans and traditional clothing. Students, too, were expected to follow new rules governing their clothing and appearance.
But the most serious changes happened inside the classroom.
English, science and biology received less attention, Mubariz said, while the Quran and other religious subjects became more prominent. Religious instruction was no longer confined to Islamic studies. Teachers of science, mathematics and English were expected to include Quranic verses, sayings and traditions attributed to the Prophet Muhammad or other religious messages in their lessons.
"Religion became part of almost every class," he said.
For many Afghan children, particularly in areas where access to public schools is limited, madrasas are among the only educational institutions available to them.
Religious education has become a central priority under The Taliban rule, while modern schools have received far less attention. The Taliban ministry of education says it now oversees 22,972 religious education centers, compared to about 5,000 that were registered under the previous government.
That does not mean all of those centers are newly built. The Afghanistan Human Rights Center says only 316 centers were newly created; many others were existing centers that have since been added to The Taliban education systems. Over the same period, the ministry says only 269 new modern schools were established.
The Taliban's Ministry of Education did not respond to messages from NPR seeking comment.
A woman educator's perspective
Shabana Basij-Rasikh, an Afghan educator and co-founder of the School of Leadership Afghanistan"SOLAx", said the damage to boys' education cannot be measured only by what has disappeared from the curriculum. Boys are also learning from a society in which girls vanish from classrooms after sixth grade and women are increasingly pushed out of public life. Her greatest concern is for younger boys who have no memory of Afghanistan before the Taliban returned. "Their only normal is not seeing girls in school. Their only normal is not seeing women in the public sphere," she said. "It's a matter of time before those young boys are going to become young men who will be making decisions in our society."
Basij-Rasikh said she sees echoes of the Taliban's first period in power, when religious texts increasingly displaced science and other subjects and restrictions on dress eventually extended to younger boys. She remembers her own brother struggling with the traditional clothing the Taliban required him to wear to school. "The same thing is playing out again," she said. "And this is not a surprise to people in Afghanistan."
The restrictions imposed on women are also affecting whether boys remain in school, Basij-Rasikh said. With women increasingly prevented from working, more of the responsibility for supporting families falls on men and boys. "Today we have an authority in Afghanistan that has made it a matter of national policy to restrict space for women and then place a lot of that burden on men and boys," she said. "Naturally you see boys dropping out of school to shoulder that responsibility of providing for their families."
A different kind of classroom
Even before 2021, Mubariz said, students sometimes hesitated to raise sensitive questions about politics, war, religion or powerful figures. Afghanistan was still a conservative society shaped by years of conflict, and students knew that certain questions could be misunderstood, draw unwanted attention or upset teachers and classmates. But after the Taliban returned, he said, that caution turned into fear. Students avoided asking questions that could be considered controversial, and teachers no longer encouraged open discussion.
"I could not express even one percent of my real opinions or ideas," he said. "I always felt that I had to stay silent because speaking openly could have serious consequences."
Mubariz and other students interviewed by NPR described a deeper loss inside schools: students losing interest in learning, while some teachers seemed discouraged, absent or unable to teach their subjects as they had before. During the first months after the Taliban takeover, many teachers were not paid, Mubariz said. Some stopped coming to school regularly. Experienced teachers left and were replaced, in some cases, by people who lacked the knowledge or training to teach their subjects properly.
Mubariz eventually decided he could learn more on his own.
Although he stayed in school to take the graduation exam last year, he also studied independently, read books and searched for other educational resources. He also chose not to sit for the Kankor, Afghanistan's national university entrance exam, because he believed that attending university in Afghanistan would not offer him a solid education.
"I achieved these things because I educated myself, not because of the school system," he said.
An 18-year-old Grade 12 student from Ghazni Province described the Taliban takeover as the moment when everything changed "overnight." He asked not to be identified because he feared that speaking openly could endanger him and his family.
He was in Kabul as rumors spread that the Taliban would enter the city. That night, his family received a call telling them to go to the airport. They joined the enormous crowds trying to get inside but turned back after seeing people injured in the chaos.
"It happened like a dream," he said.
For several months afterward, his school remained closed. When boys were eventually allowed to return, the changes were not immediately dramatic. His teachers were still there, and classes resumed.
But the girls did not return.
"Months and years passed," he said. "Not even for one day were the girls' secondary schools reopened."
At the beginning of the current school year, he said, boys in grades 7 through 12 at government schools were told to wear white clothing and a turban.
He did not object to the clothes themselves. Traditional clothing is part of Afghan culture, he said. What he opposed was being forced to wear it at school. He obtained his transfer papers and moved from a government school to one of the country's 3,000-plus private schools, largely to avoid the requirement.
But even at the private school, he said, the curriculum also changed. Lessons related to Afghanistan's civic and national life received less attention, including discussions of Parliament, the Loya Jirga, or grand assembly, the previous government's constitution and other political institutions.
But what troubles him most is not only what has disappeared from textbooks. It is the growing belief among young Afghans that education may no longer lead anywhere.
He sees graduates of engineering programs selling vegetables or working as day laborers. He remembered one poor young man who had spent much of his life studying but ended up selling potatoes because he lacked money and powerful connections.
"I don't understand what has happened to Afghanistan," he said. "You see people sitting in important positions who cannot even write their own names."
He also believes that students from wealthy or influential families can gain access to opportunities that remain closed to better-qualified students from poor families. For young people watching this happen, studying can begin to feel pointless.
Giving up
Mubariz has seen that loss of hope among his own classmates.
Some dropped out of school. Some went to Iran, while others tried to reach Europe. One of his closest friends struggled to continue his education while trying to support his family after his father, who had worked for the former government, lost his livelihood.
The family fell into severe financial hardship. Mubariz said his friend eventually lost hope and died by suicide.
"It was one of the most painful experiences I have ever witnessed," he said.
For Mubariz, his friend's death was part of a wider crisis. Many young Afghans see people with bachelor's, master's and doctoral degrees unable to find work while graduates of religious schools may have better prospects under the Taliban government.
He worries that more families will eventually conclude that conventional education has no value.
"If this continues, more young people may choose religious schools over regular education," he said. "That will have serious consequences for Afghanistan's future."
Inside Mubariz's own family, the consequences are already visible.
His two sisters were students before the Taliban prohibited girls from continuing beyond primary school. Their family does not have access to high-quality online education, so Mubariz tries to teach them himself. They study languages, read books and use whatever materials they can find.
Some girls have managed to continue their education online, but even that option remains uncertain.
Zainab, a grade 9 student, said she considers herself fortunate to be able to attend online classes. She asked to be identified only by her first name Many girls her age have no access to secondary education at all. She asked to be identified only by her first name for fear that her comments would cause the Taliban to target her family.
But her family can barely afford the cost of the internet she needs for school. The connection is also slow and unreliable much of the time, making it difficult for her to hear her teachers or follow an entire lesson.
"Classes sometimes freeze or disconnect before the teacher has finished explaining the material," she said. "When the connection fails, I miss part of the lesson and must try to catch up on my own."
Her education now depends on whether her family can continue paying for internet data and whether the connection is strong enough when class begins. She has no classroom, laboratory or library, and no guarantee that she will be able to connect the next day.
Still, Zainab said she knows she is among the relatively small number of Afghan girls who have found a way to keep studying.
"I am lucky to have the opportunity to study," she said, "but the lack of reliable internet service makes learning more stressful than it needs to be."
Mubariz still hopes to study abroad. He said he received admissions and scholarship opportunities in 2025 and 2026 from universities including Cornell University, the University of Connecticut and the University of St Andrews. But he was unable to secure student visas and lost those opportunities.
He continues searching for another way to leave Afghanistan and continue his education.
What frightens him most is not simply what he and his sisters have lost. It is what the country will become after another generation grows up without qualified teachers, meaningful academic instruction or the freedom to question what it is being taught.
His parents grew up during decades of conflict and had limited access to education. Their family still feels the consequences. Now Mubariz fears the same deprivation will shape the next two or three generations.
The school doors remain open to boys like Mubariz and the 18-year-old student from Ghazni, but both question what remains of the education offered inside. Girls such as Zainab have been pushed out of the classroom entirely and left to depend on costly, unreliable alternatives.
For a generation of Afghan students, education has become something they must struggle to preserve largely on their own.
Fatima Faizi is a journalist based in New York. She previously reported for The New York Times in Afghanistan, and her work focuses on human rights, women, education and the impact of Taliban rule on daily life.

A reverse image search of keyframes from the video revealed the footage was posted on July 22 on Instagram with “#cjpprotest”. Hindi text superimposed over the video translates to: ‘This student was brutally beaten up; India’s daughter is pleading by holding the feet of the police.”
View this post on Instagram
One policewoman visible in the video has a shoulder strap which mentions ‘Bihar’.
Notably, Patna witnessed the first CJP solidarity rally on July 22. Another video from the same Instagram page shows the distressed woman trying to show her bag and her books to prove that she is a student and reason with the police.
View this post on Instagram
We also found another video uploaded by Darsh News on July 22, where the same woman could be seen being roughed up by police.
In the video, the reporter says that the visuals were from around the Hartali More flyover in Patna. Taking a cue, we were able to geolocate the place of the incident.
Thus, it can be conclusively stated that the viral video is being falsely circulated with claims that they are visuals of protesers in Jharkhand being roughed up. In reality, the video was filmed during a CJP solidarity rally in Patna.

Indian National Racing Challenge 2W: Close win for Sarthak Chavan, Ann Jennifer tops
Pune’s Sarthak Chavan, 19, snatched a dramatic victory with a last-lap move as he led a 1-2 finish for the Petronas TVS Racing team in the Super Sport 301-400cc race to launch his campaign on a bright note in the MRF Indian National Racing Challenge 2W at the Madras International Circuit on Saturday.
For the best part of the six-lap race that saw a huge crash involving Rakshith Dave and Savion Sabu (both riders unhurt) at Turn-2, Sarthak was tucked in behind pole-sitter and teammate Chiranth Vishwanath from Bengaluru and Hyderabad’s Rahil Pillarisetty (RACR Castrol Power1). In the last lap, Sarthak passed both while surviving a contact with Chiranth at Turn 11 for a close win. Chiranth finished second, ahead of Rahil, last year’s Pro-Stock National champion.
Meanwhile, Chennai’s Ann Jennifer (Motul Sparks Racing) dominated the Super Stock 165cc Intermediate field for a fine win, while Alwin Xavier (RACR Castrol Power1) from Thrissur took the honours in the Super Stock 301-400cc Open class. Both categories were run concurrently.
Bengaluru’s Savion Sabu (Madrabbit Racing) rode a very mature race for a fine win in the Pro-Stock 200cc class, moving up from P6, while Coimbatore’s Hari Haran (RACR Castrol Power1) emerged triumphant in the Stock 165cc (Novice) category. Another Bengalurean, Ashwin R, a private entrant, topped the Stock 301-400cc (Novice) race that went down to the wire.
Alwin Xavier benefited when teammate and race leader, 16-year-old Kabilesh Rajini Krishnan, retired as the throttle body came off in the fifth and penultimate lap. Xavier made the best of the situation to win the race ahead of Bengaluru’s Seshadri (Motul Gusto Racing) and local challenger Kamal Navas (Rockers Racing).
Former National women’s champion Ann Jennifer, the only female rider on the Super Stock 165cc Intermediate grid, did as she pleased to win without any serious challenge. Ipone Yakuza Racing India’s Ajai Xavier and Anand Kumar came in second and third, respectively.
The RACR Castrol Power1 team started the day with a win in the Stock 165cc (Novice) category through Hari Haran, who survived a close battle in the lead bunch. Completing the podium were Motul Sparks Racing teammates Yashwant Varma from Visakhapatnam and Meghalaya’s Faruk Ali Sohtun.
Poojita Anil Kumar, the 18-year-old from Bengaluru, notched her maiden win at the National level as she fought her way to a brilliant victory in the Women’s (Apache RTR 200) category at the Petronas TVS Racing One-Make Championship.
Starting from pole position, Poojita, in her third competitive season, had a poor start and dropped to sixth. However, she kept her nerves to fight back into contention and then took the lead, which she maintained to the checkered flag for a well-deserved win. Fellow-Bengalurean Dhrishya Nair finished second, ahead of Vadodara’s Kinjal Raj.
Hyderabad’s Rajender Beedani and Vignesh Pothu from Mancherial won the Open (Expert, RR 310) and Rookie (Apache RTR 200) races, respectively.

Mumbai’s Praful Jhaveri appointed coach and captain of St. Kitts and Nevis chess team
Mumbai-based FIDE trainer and arbiter Praful Jhaveri has been appointed coach and team captain by the St. Kitts and Nevis Chess Federation for the 46th Chess Olympiad.
The Chess Olympiad will be held in Uzbekistan from September 15 to 28.
Jhaveri’s appointment came after a recommendation from IM Abhilash Kelkar, who coached the same team in the 2024 Olympiad. Kelkar recommended Jhaveri’s books to the association, which promoted the appointment.
“I have already started training the young and passionate team. We are realistic about the challenge ahead and will strive for a respectable performance. It would be especially fulfilling if the team’s unrated players are able to earn their first FIDE ratings,” Jhaveri said in a statement.

Story so far:
The Kerala government is considering a multi-agency probe into the previous LDF government’s failed bid to bring the Argentina football team and its legendary captain Lionel Messi to Kochi for an international friendly. A Sports Department inquiry has now flagged alleged financial irregularities, serious procedural lapses and possible violations of foreign exchange and money laundering laws.
Also read | How Kerala’s Messi dream faded amid stadium row | Explained
What is the controversy about?
The controversy centres on the previous LDF government’s efforts to bring the Argentina national football team, the 2022 FIFA World Cup champions led by Lionel Messi, to Kochi for an international friendly. Then, Sports Minister V. Abdurahiman announced in July 2023 that the Latin American giants would probably play two exhibition matches in Kochi in 2025, triggering widespread excitement in the football-crazy State.
The proposed visit was repeatedly postponed before hopes were finally dashed when the itinerary released by the Argentina Football Association (AFA) in May 2025 did not feature a stop in Kerala or anywhere else in India. Following the Congress-led United Democratic Front’s rise to power, Sports Department Special Secretary N. Prasanth investigated the matter and submitted his report earlier this month. At a press briefing on August 14, Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan revealed that the report contained “very serious allegations” and that the government was considering a multi-agency investigation.
What does the inquiry report say?
The report has flagged alleged financial irregularities running into crores of rupees and several violations of rules and procedures. It has recommended a probe by competent investigative agencies to uncover possible criminal, financial and regulatory violations and fix responsibility. One of the key issues is a claim by the sponsor of the now-botched visit, Reporter Broadcasting Company (RBC), that it had paid $15 million (₹126 crore at the time) to the AFA. The inquiry, however, found no documentary evidence to establish that the money was actually remitted. There is also no record of a formal agreement between the Kerala government and the AFA, or between the government and the sponsor.
How was the sponsor selected?
Gold and Global, a Kalamassery-based firm, wrote to the government in July 2023 offering to bring the Argentina team to Kerala and meet the entire cost of the visit. Reportedly, the company had been registered just days before it sent the letter and had a capital of only ₹1 lakh. It also allegedly had the same address as RBC, which later emerged as the sponsor. The inquiry report found “serious procedural lapses” in selecting the private company as organiser and sponsor. Mandatory procedures such as inviting expressions of interest and conducting a public tender were allegedly bypassed. The relevant government order on the selection was also not found in the files.
Did the sponsor sign the AFA deal before government approval?
RBC signed an agreement with the AFA on December 20, 2024 — four days before the Sports Department issued an order stating that steps had been initiated to bring the Argentina team to Kerala. The Sports Kerala Foundation, a not-for-profit company under the Department of Sports and Youth Affairs, was subsequently appointed to oversee the project, while the sponsor was permitted to organise two exhibition matches. But there was a crucial missing link; neither RBC nor the State government had signed an agreement or memorandum of understanding for the proposed visit. Yet the agreement between RBC and the AFA described the project as being undertaken with the cooperation of the State government. The Sports Department also committed to providing security for the Argentina team, raising questions over who had given such an assurance before formal government approval.
What is missing from the official files?
The inquiry has found significant gaps in the documentary trail. Copies of emails purportedly exchanged from Abdurahiman’s official account with AFA officials Leandro Petersen and Pablo J Diaz have surfaced, but several of them are missing from government files. The report has also flagged the minister’s private secretary for allegedly bypassing senior officials while conveying instructions relating to the proposed visit.
What happened to the match and stadium?
The controversy was not confined to the proposed match. The stadium itself became part of the deal, with the sponsor being allowed to carry out renovation work ahead of the proposed fixture. Argentina was scheduled to play an international friendly at the Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium in Kochi on November 25, 2025. The match, however, was called off. RBC later claimed that the team would visit during the March 2026 international window, but went silent thereafter. The Greater Cochin Development Authority (GCDA) also came under fire for handing over the stadium to the sponsor for renovation allegedly in violation of prescribed procedures, including the need for an agreement.
RBC returned the stadium on November 28, 2025, initially claiming to have carried out renovations worth ₹70 crore, which was later brought down to around ₹25 crore. The claim later came under scrutiny, with then GCDA chairman K. Chandran Pillai describing the investment as “amorphous” and “subjective”.
What’s sponsor’s version of the allegations?
RBC shot down allegations of financial irregularities as baseless and that they have only improved the stadium at its investment. RBC managing director Anto Augustine claims to have the agreement and proof of payment but declined to disclose them ostensibly due to their ‘non-disclosure’ nature and the ongoing litigation in international court of arbitration. He also challenged to prove that a company called Gold and Global operated from its address. He also shot down the allegation that the GST department has issued a summons to the sponsor seeking ₹22.68 crore in tax in connection with the claimed ₹126-crore transaction.
What happens next?
The Sports Department inquiry has recommended further investigation by the Vigilance and central agencies. Chief Minister V D Satheesan has indicated that the government is considering a multi-agency probe. Such an investigation could examine how the sponsor was selected, the claims surrounding the ₹126-crore payment, whether any funds were actually transferred, the official correspondence, the AFA agreement and the handing over of the stadium.

A formulation manufacturing facility of Aurobindo Pharma subsidiary near Hyderabad has been issued a warning letter by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (U.S. FDA).
The action on the facility of Eugia Pharma Specialities, the subsidiary, follows the four observations the regulator had issued in February after an inspection and in May, an Official Action Indicated (OAI) status.
Subsequent to OAI, the unit has received a warning letter, Aurobindo Pharma said on Firday (August 14, 2026) even as the parent company shares were in the spotlight. Around noon, the shares on BSE were around 1.25% down at ₹1,636.20 each recovering from a sharper decline when the market opened.
Aurobindo Pharma, in a filing, said it did not anticipate any impact on the existing supplies to the U.S. markets. The said facility, Unit I of Eugia Pharma Specialities, is contributing to around 2% to the company’s overall group revenue, it said.
For the quarter ended on June, this fiscal, the parent company had reported ₹9,150 crore revenue from operations, while for FY26 it had logged ₹33,653 crore revenue from operations.
The company remains committed to working closely with the U.S. FDA and continues to enhance its compliance on an ongoing basis, Aurobindo Pharma said.
Post-inspection, the U.S. FDA classifies facilities into three categories:Official Action Indicated (OAI) means regulatory and/or administrative actions are recommended; No Action Indicated (NAI) meaning no objectionable conditions or practices were found during inspection; and Voluntary Action Indicated (VAI) which means objectionable conditions or practices were found, but it is not for any administrative or regulatory action as the other two categorisations issued by the U.S. FDA.
Aurobindo forms new arm
On August 13, Aurobindo Pharma announced the incorporation of a new wholly owned subsidiary company Auropharm Overseas in India. The new entity had been set up with the objective of undertaking manufacturing and marketing operations in India and foreign countries, it said in a filing.

Real Madrid sign Diomande in deal worth up to £120m
- Published
Real Madrid have signed Ivory Coast international Yan Diomande from RB Leipzig for a fee worth up to £120m (140m euros).
The 19-year-old winger has signed a seven-year contract and his price tag could surpass the £115m (133.9m euros) Real agreed to pay Borussia Dortmund for Jude Bellingham in June 2023.
Paris St-Germain had been frontrunners for the teenager but the Champions League winners pulled out of a potential move on Sunday after a £102.5m bid was rejected.
If Real end up paying the full £120m for Diomande he would become the fourth most expensive player in history, behind PSG's Neymar and Kylian Mbappe, and Liverpool's former Newcastle striker Alexander Isak.
Diomande is also the most expensive African player, surpassing the £72m Arsenal paid Lille for fellow Ivory Coast international Nicolas Pepe in 2019.
Diomande was previously a target for Liverpool, who had an initial bid of £69m rejected in June, as they search for a replacement for Mohamed Salah, who joined Turkish club Trabzonspor on Thursday.
- Diomande's rapid and remarkable rise to Real Madrid 
  - Published29 July
Diomande is Real's sixth summer signing under new head coach Jose Mourinho, joining Bernardo Silva, Ibrahima Konate, Denzel Dumfries, Marc Cucurella and Carlos Espi.
In a statement, the teenager thanked Leipzig fans for their "incredible support", and said: "Who knows? Maybe we'll meet again one day in the Champions League."
But he said the move to Madrid "is a childhood dream come true", adding: "I am all the more grateful to the management at RB Leipzig for making this move possible despite my current contract."
He was named the Bundesliga's Young Player of the Season for 2025-26, having scored 12 goals and registered eight assists in the competition.
He appeared in all four of Ivory Coast's World Cup games as they were eliminated in the round of 32 by Norway.
Diomande moved from his native Ivory Coast to an academy in the United States before joining Spanish side Leganes in 2025 and then Leipzig later that year.
Why have Real Madrid signed the teenager?
Real Madrid's move for Diomande reflects the club's commitment to signing elite young talents before they reach their peak.
At just 19 years old, the Ivorian winger has become one of the game's most exciting prospects thanks to his explosive pace, dribbling, creativity and attacking impact.
After scoring 13 goals and providing 10 assists across all competitions in his first full season in Europe with Leipzig, Diomande attracted interest from several major clubs.
One of Diomande's biggest strengths is his versatility. Comfortable on either wing, he can create chances, beat defenders one-on-one, is a skillful dribbler and can contribute goals.
From the left, he can cut inside on to his right foot and threaten goal, while from the right he can use his pace and crossing ability to create opportunities for team-mates.
This flexibility makes him a strong fit for Real Madrid, who have been searching for greater consistency in the right-wing position.
The 120m euros fee shows how highly Real Madrid rate Diomande's potential, and they believe he has the ability to become a key player for the future.
Diomande formed a strong partnership with right-back Ridle Baku at Leipzig, and his attacking threat could be enhanced further by linking up with creative and experienced full-backs Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cucurella at Real.
