The Truths That Failed Jason Arday
Systemic, ritualized dishonesty undid the Cambridge professor.
Yesterday in London, Jason Arday, the controversy-plagued British academic and author, was found dead. Made famous as the youngest Black professor in Cambridge’s more than 800-year history, Arday had been dogged by weeks of scrutiny amid accusations of plagiarism, fake qualifications, and a fabricated backstory filled with hard-to-believe details.
He claimed to have been mute until age 11 and illiterate until 18, disadvantages that did not deter him from getting a Ph.D., which he earned by age 30. He claimed, too, that he had suffered from various medical conditions throughout his life, including autism, epilepsy, locked-in syndrome, testicular cancer, and a brain tumor. He was, by his account, a world-class endurance athlete who had racked up a variety of impressive feats, including running 600 miles in six days. Then there were his academic accomplishments: Arday was billed as a once-in-a-generation talent, whose research in his field—the sociology of education—was “the best in the world,” according to Hilary Cremin, the head of Cambridge’s faculty of education. He claimed to have received a book advance of 1.4 million in unspecified currency for his memoir, released this week by Simon & Schuster. It was a meteoric rise, until it wasn’t.
Last month, Nathan Cofnas—a former Cambridge researcher who may politely be described as a philosopher with a special interest in race and IQ, and who may impolitely be described as a professional racist—published in his newsletter what appeared to be significant evidence of Arday’s plagiarism. This month, as it became apparent that much of the Arday legend was most likely just that, the academic became an object of international obsession, especially in British media and on X. He resigned from Cambridge last week, though this did not stem the flood of attention.
The online hive mind, in particular, was brutal until the moment of Arday’s death, at which point the collective swarm did an about-face. The same platform that loosed an algorithmically accelerated torrent of abuse is now dominated by kind remembrances and mawkishness. I find the whole pageantry grotesque.
What I propose is that the public give Arday a courtesy in death that he was often denied in life: Let’s treat him like a person. Not like Cambridge’s magical negro, or like Simon & Schuster’s golden goose, or like the fetish object of internet racists, but like a flawed human being who should still be alive but is not. That requires being honest about who Arday was, not despite his tragic death but because of it. After all, it was systemic, ritualized dishonesty—his own and others’—that undid him.
Here is the truth about Jason Arday: A preponderance of evidence suggests that he was a serial fabulist and unrepentant plagiarist who successfully conned a British academic aristocracy so blinded by do-gooder racial neurosis that it was unable to spot lies that would have been obvious to any Joe Schmo. (Arday denied intentional misconduct and suggested that his apparent plagiarism was a result of his autism, which he said meant that he tended to learn through imitation.) As evidence of those seeming lies mounted, the powerful institutions that had made him continued to back him, doubling down and raising the stakes. Simon & Schuster stood by its author—or perhaps more accurately, stood by its product. Even as the evidence of fraud became all but undeniable, the publisher did not merely declare that it would press forward with Arday’s book; it had the audacity to tout “the professionalism and integrity he has brought to every stage of the publication.”
Then those on the racist right—frothing with glee that they took no trouble to conceal—pressed their advantage, punch-drunk on the double intoxicant of incandescent liberal hypocrisy and a Black man’s failure. The mob swelled, online and in the media. Some people joined out of perfectly legitimate indignation at the apparent obliteration of academic standards that the ordeal attested to. Some joined out of ghoulish pleasure at seeing a beneficiary of DEI, as they cast him, cut down to size.
Everyone following this story would do well to engage in some reflection. I will confess that, until yesterday, I had watched the Arday saga unfold with some combination of amusement and distress. Amusement because of the undeniable comic absurdity to the revelation that the best and brightest minds at Cambridge had been so easily deceived by a man who claimed to have run nine marathons in about as many days on a fractured fibula, and who maintained that his future had been predicted by a Brazilian shaman. Distress because I could relate to some of the things that Arday might have experienced.
I have written, in this magazine and elsewhere, about what it is like to be the beneficiary of affirmative action in elite spaces. I have seen, firsthand, the way a specific kind of white progressive treats Black men who have overcome obstacles. They cannot conceal a certain blend of of pity and glee when they learn, for example, that my biological father left before I was old enough to walk, or that I was raised for a time by a single mother. It is a look that says, How far you’ve come, and how kind I am for helping you go further. I have always found such encounters stomach-churning. But I can also imagine—if you came up hard and are unaccustomed to kindness—how good it might feel, and how tempting it might be, to do and say things that make people give you that look again and again, whether or not the things you’re saying are strictly true.
Two images have rattled around in my head since the news of Arday’s death. The first is from a 2023 BBC clip celebrating his hiring at Cambridge. Cremin, Arday’s Cambridge colleague, clasps both of his hands in the manner of a cherished loved one as they stare into each other’s eyes. The camera zooms in on their white and Black hands interlocked and lingers there. The second image was posted on X last night: a screenshot of a list of article headlines about the Arday scandal, stretching to several pages, published by one British outlet alone. It represents but a few watts of the international spotlight that had been trained on the academic.
I have been dwelling on these two images—the theatrical interracial handclasp; the pages and pages of monomaniacal media coverage of what was ultimately a niche academic scandal—because together they speak to a terrible reality. Arday was fetishized in his ascendancy by white liberals, for whom he served as a mirror in which they could see their own goodness. And he was fetishized in his downfall by white conservatives who saw him as a test case for their own obsessions with an academic apparatus that they believe is not meritocratic enough—which is to say, not white enough.
The right would have us believe that the Arday scandal is a story of affirmative action taken to its most caricaturish conclusion. Many progressives see it as something else: a racist witch hunt in which self-righteous zealots with suspect motives hounded a man to death. The problem with these narratives—and it is a sticky problem—is that they are both right.
To be a Black person in elite institutions, and particularly in elite academia, is to have the standards simultaneously set too low and too high: too low because only a Black person with Arday’s dubious qualifications and seemingly invented biography could have been elevated to the top of the mountain in academia and publishing; and too high because only a Black person could have been pushed off that mountain with such nakedly racist enthusiasm, his tumbling fall so ruthlessly documented, analyzed, and cheered. When a famous white man errs, people tend to rightly understand his mistakes or transgressions as an individual’s missteps. When a famous Black man does, the errors are typically turned into spectacle, characterized as proof of the inferiority, suspected all along, of his race.
Around the same time yesterday afternoon that I learned of Arday’s fate, I came across another piece of news: an announcement that Ross Barkan, a white novelist and journalist, had just been dropped by New York magazine after the publication—having investigated allegations regarding dozens of instances of plagiarism in Barkan’s writing—concluded that his work “did not live up to our editorial standards.” Swiftly afterward, Barkan announced that he would now focus on writing a new column at The Nation, another venerable outlet, where he will get a very public second chance.
It is impossible to know what is in someone’s head or heart in their final moments. I have to imagine, though, that Arday understood well enough the world he had entered and how its rules tend to work: When you are Black, some people will open the door for you far wider than they should. And when that door abruptly comes swinging shut, you will be offered no second chances.

There’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner. If you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, there's no wrong time of year to get a new planner. After testing dozens of planners myself, my favorite ones are often either customizable or undated, making it easy to pick them up whenever you want.
The world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.
After trying dozens of planners over the last year, I think these standout favorite planner styles could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts digitally.
Updated August 2026: The Erin Condren Academic Planner is my new academic planner pick, and I've added a new section on planner accessories.
The Best Planners
If you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.
The undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size, since it's finally enough space for me (almost too much, which is a rare find), but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.
The covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.
If you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6. The 2026 Cousins are out of stock at most retailers, but you can still find them on Hobonichi's website.
There are tons of colors, covers, and other accessories you can get for it, too. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to distracting English words on the corners of each page. There's no academic year version of the Hobonichi, but there are July starts for both the Techo and the Techo Cousin that will cover the rest of 2026, or buy an on-sale January version and skip the first half of it. The Hobonichi planners for 2027 will be released September 1; details for launch day are on Hobonichi's website.
I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there's other variations of planners you can find from Erin Condren. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.
I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, and it's a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most important to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”
You can find a similar academic planner on Erin Condren's website, but it costs more since you'll have customization options, and you get many more cover options; Target only has one.
I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.
I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely new planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.
I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and important things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the plan for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.
You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner. The A5 fits up to four notebooks that you can purchase individually, or get the Travel Notebook Set ($63) that includes three notebooks and a clear cover for $10 off buying them individually.
Honorable Mentions
Like I said, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.
More Planners I’ve Tried
Agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.
Ban.do 17-Month Planner for $35: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) This 17-month version is made to start for the school year and go through the end of 2027, but you can also find 12-month planners if you prefer.
Happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $24: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.
Laurel Denise Academic Planner for $59: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, because the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did.
Leuchtturm1917 18-Month Planner for $33: This is a solid, minimalist planner that as a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.
Muji Undated Weekly Planner for $9: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.
Papier Hardcover Academic Year Planner for $29: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style) but the academic one has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid year and academic layout options.
Passion Planner Mid-Year Planner for $45: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to plan out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.
Some Planner Accessories
Looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.
Passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your plans by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.
Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson
Plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!
Planner Alternatives
Not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.
Former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey opts for a plain, lined notebook. After trying dozens, her favorite is the Midori MD Notebook with paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!). It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid. Grey says there's just something meditative about turning over a blank page at the beginning of each week and carefully jotting down her schedule, plans, and workload. Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.
WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson says he doesn't use a planner, but each day he writes down the handful of things he's going to do on a single 3-by-5 index card. The index card with this to-do list lives in his pocket, along with a small notebook in which he jots down notes throughout the day—often the source of the following day's to-do list. The notebook and index cards fit inside this very cool waxed canvas notebook cover. Gilbertson says he copied this system from one of the most successful people he has known, and after nearly 20 years, it's still better for him than any other system he's tried. It's cheap, lightweight, and easy to manage. —Medea Giordano
FAQs
Why Choose a Paper Planner?
Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.
What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?
Paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to plan out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.
What Sizes Do Planners Come In?
Here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.
- A5 (5.8 by 8.3 inches)
- Regular/Medium / B5 (7 by 9 inches)
- Large/Letter (8.5 by 11 inches)
- Personal/Pocket (3.5 by 5.5 inches)

Five injured, one critically, in shooting at Virginia State University
- Published
Five people have been injured, one critically, in a shooting at Virginia State University which involved multiple suspects, the university has said.
Officers responded to the incident outside a residence halls at about 01:28 local time (05:28 GMT) on Saturday.
Five individuals, who were all found with gunshot wounds, were taken to local hospitals. Four had injuries which were not deemed to be life-threatening, the university said.
It was not immediately clear if any suspects have been arrested. The BBC has approached local police for comment.
A temporary lockdown on the campus has since been lifted but a "significant" law enforcement presence is still on site, the university confirmed in a statement.
It added that Chesterfield County Police are leading the investigation with help from other local law enforcement and campus police.
Virginia State University (VSU) has about 5,000 students and is just over 20 miles south of Richmond, the capital of the US state of Virginia.
It is also one of the country's historically black colleges and universities.
Such institutions were created to provide higher education to disenfranchised African Americans, who were otherwise prohibited from attending most colleges.
According to the university's website, classes for the new term were set to begin on Monday and campus dormitories opened for returning students on Friday.

As part of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s newly expanded DCU, a more grounded take on the “Green Lantern” comics may surprise audiences who associate the character with the Ryan Reynolds film that received poor reviews back in 2011.
But for co-creators Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King, “Lanterns” is all about going back to the original iteration of the character when he was “an entirely different kind of superhero.”
“We’re talking about almost a century’s worth of storytelling, and now we get to carry that baton,” Lindelof told Variety. “But then at the same time, the audience is hungry for something original and relevant, and they want storytellers to take risks. Those risks can’t feel like they’re gimmicks; they have to feel like they have real emotional stakes.”
Popular on Variety
The show follows Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) as he is forced to take John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) under his wing as a backup. As the Green Lantern, Hal has the power to create material items through his ring and acts as an intergalactic space officer. Things take a dark turn after a series of unexplainable deaths draw Hal and John to a small town in Nebraska.
As creators, King brings a wealth of experience as a comic book writer, while Lindelof created the “Watchmen” TV series. Mundy, who served as showrunner on “Ozark,” is new to the comic book world.
“I know that if Damon didn’t work on this show, I would have used — and I think Tom would say the same — ‘Watchmen’ as a real touchstone of how you do a show and have it be emotional and about real people, while also honoring the comic book part of it,” Mundy said.
In addition to the grounded approach that “Watchmen” takes, “Lanterns” also shares similarities in how the show explores race, colonization and justice. King explained how “there’s a wonderful coincidental parallel with comics that ‘Watchmen,’ in the ’80s, set the standard for a generation of comic book writers who were like, ‘Oh, we can talk about those themes using superheroes!'”
Poorna Jagannathan, who plays the conniving and mysterious Zoe, hopes that shows like “Lanterns” invite more actors into the DCU who don’t read comic books.
“I thought I’d be with a green screen wearing a suit, talking to no one at all, just into the abyss,” she told Variety at Thursday’s premiere on the Paramount lot. “I hesitated because I didn’t know this world at all. I felt like I didn’t belong, actually. I felt bad that I was so ignorant about it.”
“I don’t think that only this universe will be affected by it; I think every show in the genre will be affected by what happened on ‘Lanterns,'” she added. “It’ll be a blueprint on how to take something big and keep it with a beating heart.”
As the DCU continues to expand and test the waters of audiences, both with the success of films like “Superman” and the underwhelming reception to “Supergirl,” how audiences react to “Lanterns” could determine if early conversations about Season 2 turn into an official renewal.
“The one thing that fans hate more than being listened to is fan service and that sort of idea of doing something just to placate them. And so I do think that fandom is not a monolith,” Lindelof said of navigating fandom expectations. “There are some fans who want more risky, edgy sort of revisionist storytelling inside of these adaptations, and some fans who are just basically like, ‘Give me what I love.'”
There are certain canonical elements that the “Lanterns” team had to carefully maneuver, such as how the show ties into John Stewart’s involvement in “Man of Tomorrow,” and the return of Guy Gardner (Nathan Fillion), who also appears in “Superman” and “Peacemaker.”
But when it comes to what “Lanterns” might signal for the future of the newly revamped DCU, it’s all about creative voices being at the forefront.
“You can’t go out of bounds in terms of storylines that James and Peter want to do,” Lindelof said. “But artistically, they’re giving us a lot of freedom to tell the story how we want.”
“Lanterns” premieres Sunday, Aug. 16 on HBO Max.

Bead Street’s fraying legacy: craft hub faces uncertain future as shops bow out
‘Storefronts have changed a lot these few years. More than half of these accessory shops are now eateries,’ one business owner says
In a cramped handicraft shop in Hong Kong’s Sham Shui Po neighbourhood, 70-year-old Jen Kwong was sifting through reels of embroidered and sequinned ribbons while other shoppers around her were hunched over containers of tiny beads and trinkets.
Kwong, who had worked for four decades during the golden age of Hong Kong’s textile manufacturing industry, still tailors and alters clothing for her grandchildren with her sewing machine at home.
But she feared Yu Chau Street, also known as “Bead Street” for its enclave of fabric and accessory shops, would soon become a thing of the past.
The streetscape, now dominated by eateries, is due to change even more as four accessory retailers on the block around Yu Chau Street, Ki Lung Street and Nam Cheong Street announced that they would be shutting their doors by the end of the month.
“This entire street used to be full of these types of crafting shops, but now, only a few are left,” Kwong said.
Reminiscing about the heyday of the manufacturing enclave, she recalled the long queues around the block just to shop at Japanese zip maker YKK Corporation, which shut its Sham Shui Po storefront in 2008.

Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets of a Welsh village as her coffin is brought home
Fans have gathered in a Welsh village to bid farewell to singer Bonnie Tyler
LONDON -- Hundreds of fans lined the streets of a seaside Welsh village on Saturday to bid farewell to late singer Bonnie Tyler as her coffin was brought home.
The Grammy-nominated Welsh pop star, beloved worldwide for her 1983 chart-topping power ballad “Total Eclipse of the Heart," died last month in a hospital in Portugal. She was 75.
Tyler was hospitalized in May in Faro, where she had a home, for emergency intestinal surgery.
Locals and fans from around the United Kingdom and beyond took to the streets of Mumbles, near the city of Swansea, to see the hearse, which carried her coffin, draped in a Welsh flag. Dozens waited outside the singer's former home or left floral tributes there.
“She was always coming home and making sure that she came back to her fans in Wales," said Carys Edwards, 18. “Her songs really did touch a lot of people here in Wales; we loved her a lot."
Tyler was born Gaynor Hopkins, a coal miner’s daughter in public housing with an outside toilet in Skewen, Wales, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) outside Swansea. She grew up with three sisters and two brothers.
The singer earned three Grammy nods and in 2013 represented Britain at the Eurovision Song Contest, where she came in 19th. She was honored as a Member of the Order of the British Empire in 2022 for her services to music by Queen Elizabeth II, thanks mainly to “Total Eclipse of the Heart."
The ballad shot to the top of the charts in Britain and the United States and has had more than 1 billion streams, boosted by real eclipses in 2017, 2024 — and most recently during this week's solar eclipse.
She was also known for other hits including “It's a Heartache” and “Holding Out For a Hero," from the soundtrack of the film “Footloose.”
A celebration of Tyler’s life for family and friends will take place at a church in Swansea on Monday, before the singer makes a final journey through her hometown of Skewen.

In August 2026, people alleged a video authentically showed popular Twitch streamer Hasan Piker making derogatory remarks about Black people and saying he wished the U.S. would return to a time of lynchings. The video, comprising three separate clips, circulated at a time when Piker — a left-leaning political voice who streams live for many hours almost daily — was campaigning for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Party's U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan.
For example, on Aug 11, conservative political commentator Scott Jennings — who often appears on "CNN NewsNight with Abby Phillip" — reposted (archived) the 41-second video, in which Piker appears to make several offensive statements targeting Black people, such as, "I don't give a f*** what Black people care about," and mentions going "back to a better time when lynchings were happening." Other people shared the video, as well.
After showing it, Jennings asked his audience, "Might these Black voters find a home in the Republican Party this fall? Well, if Democratic campaigns are adopting the Piker plan of returning our country to lynchings, that just might happen."
In sum, the video consists of genuine sentence fragments uttered by Piker — that is, they weren't fabricated using AI or other digital fakery — but the fragments were stitched together out of context and out of order to twist their original import. Piker's full, unedited thoughts, delivered forcefully with vulgarities and verbal attacks that some readers might question, appeared to reflect a desire to prioritize winning elections over dwelling on issues that, in his mind, have resulted in electoral losses.
A full review of Piker's unedited remarks confirms Jennings falsely claimed Piker said he was in favor of bringing back lynchings. In the original stream, Piker's remarks on lynchings were sarcastic reactions to a user's chat comment and opinions expressed by someone else in a separate video.

Snopes located all three past streams and has presented those videos with transcripts later in this article.

Online travel aggregator EaseMyTrip (EMT) slipped into the red in the June quarter of the financial year 2026-27 (Q1 FY27), posting a consolidated net loss of ₹11.7 Cr compared to a net profit of ₹44 Lakh in the year-ago period. On a quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) basis, the company managed to narrow its loss by 24.2% on a sequential basis from ₹15.4 Cr loss incurred in the March quarter. The loss comes despite the online travel aggregator’s (OTA’s) operating revenue climbing 18.4% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹134.7 Cr during the quarter under review from ₹113.8 Cr in Q1 FY26. However, sequentially, operating revenue declined 11.3% from ₹151.9 Cr. Including other income of ₹6.6 Cr, EaseMyTrip’s total income increased 18% YoY to ₹141.3 Cr from ₹119.7 Cr. Despite the revenue growth, the company slipped into the red as its total expenses jumped 29.8% to ₹152.7 Cr from ₹117.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Service costs more than doubled to ₹39.2 Cr from ₹18 Cr in Q1 FY26. Meanwhile, employee benefit expenses increased 4.2% to ₹32.8 Cr from ₹31.4 Cr. Its advertising and sales promotion expenses rose 10.7% YoY to ₹18.5 Cr, while payment gateway charges increased 19.4% to ₹16.4 Cr. Other expenses surged 20.7% to ₹38.1 Cr during the quarter. A Deeper Look At EMT’s Q1 Performance The uptick in the company's top line was driven by its hotel packages services. The segment's revenue during the quarter more than doubled YoY to ₹67.6 Cr Meanwhile, revenues from its air passage and other services, trains, buses, and other offerings, dipped. While air revenue declined 4% YoY to ₹54.8 Cr, other services' revenue contribution halved to ₹12.3 Cr. Segment wise, EMT’s quarterly hotel night bookings almost doubled to 6.47 Lakh. The company’s trains, buses, and others segment recorded a 45.8% YoY decline in Q1 FY27, with bookings decreasing from 4.3 Lakhs to 2.4 Lakhs. Overall, the OTA claimed that its gross booking revenue (GBR) grew 14.8% to ₹2,371 Cr in Q1 FY27 from ₹2,065.8 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year. Despite the decline in revenue, flights still brought in the highest gross bookings for EMT, accounting for 74.1% of Q1 FY27 GBR. Hotels and holiday packages brought in 24.9% GBR and trains, buses and other services made up the remaining 1%. EMT said that it had worked on its “strategic priorities” in the quarter, including Dubai operations expansion, AI-led travel innovations and strengthening Hotels & Holidays business. EMT’s Dubai operations recorded gross booking revenue (GBR) of ₹461.8 Cr in Q1 FY27, up 45.2% YoY from ₹318.1 Cr in Q1 FY26. “Q1 FY27 marks an important phase in EaseMyTrip’s Vision 2030 journey, as we continue to translate our strategic priorities into tangible business momentum... Alongside this business momentum, we are continuing to invest in initiatives that strengthen the value we deliver across the travel journey...We are also building greater depth across our integrated travel ecosystem, with continued expansion across Hotels, Holidays, domestic tourism, Airport Services, Duty Free, Meet & Greet and other emerging travel categories," chairman Nishant Pitti said. Shares of EMT ended Friday’s training session 3.55% higher at ₹6.41 apiece on the BSE.

A Perfect Album for a Frustrating Decade
Phoebe Bridgers’s new record is heavy with post-pandemic disappointment.
One of the coronavirus pandemic’s many terrible legacies is the slow smothering of ambition in popular culture. In the depths of the crisis, media—music, movies, and all the rest—were widely hailed as a “balm” for anxieties and a “lifeline” to the shared society we could look forward to someday returning to. Yet at the same time, that pre-pandemic sense of cohesion was being destabilized. Entertainers emerged from lockdown to find their fans wild-eyed with obsession and everyone else utterly unreachable. The ensuing years in the arts have felt strange and stilted—defined by stalled dreams, a shattered common stage, and a nervous relationship between artists and audiences.
The Southern California folk singer Phoebe Bridgers is one artist who experienced the unique intensity of a pandemic breakthrough. In June of 2020, her hushed and biting second album, Punisher, was received with the sort of acclaim suggesting the arrival of the next great American songwriter. She was funny and thoughtful on social media, and fans came to regard her with all the intimacy of a best friend—despite her requests for them to step back and respect boundaries. Now, after more than half a decade, she’s released her third full-length album, Lost Weekend—a beautiful but frustrating document of post-pandemic disappointment.
From her early days drawing buzz as a teenage disciple of pillow-voiced balladeers such as John Lennon and Elliott Smith, Bridgers’s appeal has lain in her ambivalence. She is an adventurer with a reclusive streak; she wants to see the world outside of her phone and then get back to bed. Many of her songs play like travelogues through a corrupted civilization—its skies littered with chemtrails and satellites, its bars patrolled by users and abusers. Her sighing style of singing and the downward lilt of her melodies suggest that the world’s fallen nature simply tires her out. “There’s no place like my room,” she sings on Punisher’s closing track, “I Know the End.”
In the years after that album, Bridgers didn’t actually disappear. She collaborated with the likes of Paul McCartney, SZA, and Taylor Swift, who proclaimed “she is the reference now” for modern songwriters. She released a splashy album with the supergroup boygenius. But none of this work had the sheer density of insight—the line-after-line sense of surprise—that has defined Bridgers’s solo music. (Her 2017 single “Motion Sickness” begins “I hate you for what you did / And I miss you like a little kid / I faked it every time, but that’s alright.”) Earlier this year, she embarked on a tour at which audience members were banned from using their phones—a sign that she was coming back to her main project on her own, self-protective terms.
On paper, Lost Weekend is everything that the follow-up to a breakthrough should be: epic-scale, richly orchestrated, musically evolutionary. A glittering cast of collaborators includes the hitmaking producer Jack Antonoff, the Pulitzer-winning composer Caroline Shaw, the indie multi-instrumentalist Alex G, the mandolin-wielding MacArthur fellow Chris Thile, and—suspectedly, under a pseudonym—the It Boy vocalist of 2020s rock, Geese’s Cameron Winter. They’ve created a moody, varied soundscape featuring drum machines, hard guitars, and oases of country plucking.
The first three songs are stunning. “The Outside” opens with Bridgers alternating between Laurie Anderson–style vocoder confessions and swirling piano paired with clean vocals. As she moves from the inorganic to the organic and back again, she also slips between tempos for an effect as mesmerizing as a shadow flickering in a stream. Then comes “Lost Boys,” a should-be smash single in which layers of chiming instruments coalesce into one swinging, shaggy mass. On “Kill Me,” rustling guitars convey cold unease until the chorus offers a hint of warmth. “This is gonna kill me,” sings Bridgers. Then she pauses to add, offbeat, “wait.”
These early tracks portray Bridgers at the height of her success—crowd-surfing at concerts and surrounded by friends—yet feeling alienated. “I pretended it was make believe,” goes a great line from “Lost Boys,” capturing the psychological trickery that results from disassociating from one’s own life. When “Kill Me” crescendos in gang-sung cries of “Let’s go missing,” it’s an exciting cliff-hanger: Bridgers sounds poised to take the listener down a rabbit hole to somewhere fantastical and fresh.
Instead, reality persists, murky and enervating. “The Governor’s Waltz” finds her at a famous music festival, feeling—yet again—disconnected and on edge. Fingerpicked guitars and toybox melodies are creepy yet obvious, like a Tim Burton movie. The lyrics bait gossip blogs by seeming to refer to an ex and the girl he replaced her with. These blind items should be interesting: Bridgers once knew how to make inside jokes land for everyone. But many of her descriptions, across the album, are naggingly opaque or inert. “You had a nosebleed, you were in my way / And you didn’t remind me of anything,” she sings, a line that’s intriguing only because it hints at her own creative blockage.
For much of the rest of the album, she seems to want to let her musicians do the talking. A number of songs are structurally fragmentary, featuring sudden cuts into silence or lengthy digressions into “folktronica” (a term for banjos-and-beats music of the sort that was last trendy in the 2000s). These seemingly avant-garde touches unfortunately scan more like boho-café fare. In May, Bridgers was seen wearing a T-shirt for Kid A—the numbed-out, synth-driven curveball that Radiohead released in 2000 after achieving alternative-rock dominance. But Bridgers isn’t leading a cutting-edge band that’s built up internal chemistry over years for unpredictable results. She’s enlisted a prestigious mishmash of stars to whip up variations on two moods: looming dread and wistful uplift.
The story she’s telling should have been strong enough to land without so much filigree. On “Still Standing,” she seems to refer to abuse of her mother by her father, who died in late 2022. Rather than just condemning him, Bridgers spends part of the album examining the traits he passed on to her, for good and ill. At the same time, she’s wrestling with a fatalistic view of fame. “Surviving my gift until I get shot,” she sings on the title track—a chilling line on an album with a Lennon-inspired name. Her personal demons and public pressures really do sound suffocating. Can she possibly escape them?
The twist of Lost Weekend is that it suggests a happy answer to that question. On the roaring and catchy “Bobby,” she sings about a blissful home life with a lover, who also shows up as a savior figure in other songs. Their meet-cute seems to be described in the first line: “I saw you slow dancing alone in your room.” Bobby is almost certainly her real boyfriend, the comedian Bo Burnham, and she’s implying that she fell for him while watching his acclaimed 2021 Netflix special, Bo Burnham: Inside, a document of stir-crazed social isolation.
It’s quite the revelation: Back in the pandemic, Bridgers was in the exact same position as her audience—stuck at home and having her life changed by something on a screen. Burnham, himself an object of overwhelming public fascination, has mostly stayed out of the spotlight since Inside, though he has seven writing credits on this album. Virtual desire becoming real, isolation giving way to communion, a life built outside the digital panopticon—these are powerful themes for the 2020s. But too often, the album meets its moment in a sad way: with strained, distant songwriting that suggests its creator’s hesitation about reconnecting with the crowd.

The Infra.Market IPO was never easy to follow. It all started with RDC Concrete. In 2021, Infra.market acquired RDC Concrete from True North for around ₹730 Cr, and for a while, the talk was about taking this ready-mix concrete business public. Then the picture changed. One reason could be that RDC was only one part of Infra.Market’s larger building materials business. Over the next few years, the company expanded into steel, tiles, aggregates, construction chemicals, paints and other categories through acquisitions and manufacturing businesses. The question then shifted from whether RDC should go public to whether Infra.Market itself should be listed, given the spread-out operations and business interests. As if in response to that, Infra.Market confidentially filed draft IPO papers with the market regulator SEBI in October 2025. The plan was to raise roughly around ₹5,000 Cr through IPO. The proposed IPO plan consisted of equal split of fresh issue and offer for sale. This listing was supposed to bring fresh capital into the business. Now, there is another twist. Infra.Market is looking to use its listed subsidiary Shalimar Paints as the route to tap public money. Shalimar Paints has proposed to acquire shares and compulsory convertible preference shares (CCPS) of Infra.Market through a swap. The transaction involves securities worth around ₹10,545 Cr, while Shalimar has also proposed a ₹1,000 Cr qualified institutional placement (QIP). In simple terms, InfraMarket is using the reverse-listing route through a company that it already controls. Among Indian startups, it would become one of the first to list through such a strategy. But for a startup that has spent a few years preparing for an IPO, the question is obvious: why take this route now? Especially after getting the SEBI nod for a separate listing. Questions sent to Infra.Market didn’t elicit any response at the time of publishing this story. Has The IPO Market Got Harder? People close to Infra.market told Inc42 that the current market conditions are not considered favourable for a standalone IPO. According to sources, the Shalimar Paints transaction offers a quicker route to the public markets and could also help the startup repay a portion of its debt. An industry insider tracking the startup said Infra.Market could otherwise have had to wait another six to eight months for an independent IPO. “From what it seems, the company may not be getting the investor traction or valuation it had expected from a standalone listing,” the person added. One person familiar with Infra.Market’s plans told Inc42 that the company will withdraw its confidential IPO papers, effectively putting its standalone listing plan on hold. Infra.Market had raised ₹732 Cr in a Series G round in 2025 at a valuation of around ₹24,600 Cr. It then filed confidential IPO papers to raise ₹5,000 Cr. Even after filing the IPO papers, the startup continued to raise debt as it expanded its business. The Shalimar Paints transaction now offers a different route. The basis structure is straightforward. Once the transaction is completed, Infra.Market could become an unlisted material subsidiary of Shalimar Paints. The two companies have also discussed the possibility of unifying the businesses at a later stage. The above quoted industry executive compared the approach to a SPAC, although the structures are different. The comparison is useful because it captures the basic idea: a listed company is being used as the route for a private business to reach public markets. Does this make financial sense though? Inside The ₹24,620 Cr Valuation And ₹6,057 Cr Debt On the financial front, Infra.Market’s consolidated net profit rose to around ₹300 Cr-₹325 Cr in FY26, from ₹220 Cr in FY25, sources told Inc42 earlier. Revenue grew 7% YoY to nearly ₹20,000 Cr during the year. EBITDA stood at ₹1,750 Cr-₹1,800 Cr, while EBITDA margin expanded by 100 basis points to 9%, according to the sources. However, it is the latest valuation report of Infra.Market, reviewed by Inc42, which gives a better picture of where the company stands financially. A valuation report dated April 10, 2026, values Infra.Market at an equity value of roughly ₹24,620 Cr, using a discounted cash flow method, as of February 28, 2026. The report puts Infra.Market’s enterprise value at around ₹28,124 Cr. It then adds ₹1,028 Cr of cash and cash equivalents, deducts ₹6,057 Cr of debt, adds ₹2,303 Cr of non-current assets, and deducts ₹778 Cr of non-controlling interest to arrive at ₹24,620 Cr equity value. It is worth noting that Infra.Market’s cash and cash equivalents declined from around ₹1,557 Cr in FY25 to ₹1,028 Cr as of February 28, 2026, a drop of roughly 34%. This leaves the company with around ₹5,029 Cr of net debt. Its credit profile has also weakened. India Ratings in March this year moved Infra.Market’s rated debt to IND BB+/Negative. The agency also clarified the “issuer not cooperating”, saying it did not receive key information on areas including operational performance, liquidity, cash generation consolidated net debt and repayment schedules. Against this backdrop, Shalimar’s proposed ₹1,000 Cr QIP assumes greater importance. Shalimar said the fundraise will provide capital to the enlarged business and improve its access to public markets. People with knowledge of Infra.Markets’s plan said some of the money could also be used to repay a portion of its debt. It must be noted that in February this year, Infra.Market also wanted to raise an additional debt of ₹1,250 Cr from Singapore-based private credit platform Ascertis Credit. While Shalimar hasn’t explicitly said the ₹1,000 Cr would be for loan repayment, a ₹1,000 Cr equity raise would give the group fresh capital equal to around 16.5% of Infra.Market’s current gross debt. The Share Swap May Only Be The First Step The size of the proposed swap makes it clear that this is not a small investment by Shalimar Paints into its parent entity. Shalimar plans to issue around 417.02 Mn equity shares worth approximately ₹3,544.7 Cr and 811.20 Mn CCPS worth around ₹ 6,895.2 Cr. It has also proposed a separate preferential issue of around ₹105.9 Cr. Combined, this becomes ₹10,545 Cr transaction. But it is pertinent to mention that the bulk of this transaction is a non-cash transaction as it will be a share swap, through which Infra.Market investors will receive securities in the listed entity Shalimar Paints. This is a crucial distinction. For Infra.Market’s investors, the transaction changes the nature of what they own. Instead of holding shares in an unlisted building materials company, now they would own a stake in a listed entity. That gives them access to a public market without waiting for Infra.Market to complete a conventional IPO. Then, there is the second part of this transaction that is equally important. People familiar with the matter said the current share swap arrangement does not cover some of Infra.Market’s foreign investors, including Tiger Global, Accel and Nexus. According to an investor who has closely tracked the company, there is some procedural work around these investors and a second swap deal is expected. “The idea is to have a unified cap table,” the investor said. If that happens, the current ₹10,654 Cr transaction would only be one stage in moving Infra.Market’s entire shareholder base into a listed structure. The biggest difference between the two listing routes may come down to timing. A standalone IPO would require Infra.Market to return to the market, complete the process with SEBI, conduct investor marketing, and settle on a valuation at a time when public market appetite for new-age businesses can change quickly. The Shalimar Paints transaction gives it a different option. One investor who has closely monitored Infra.Market said the company may have felt that an independent listing would be difficult at this point. The Shalimar route, the person said, gives Infra.Market time to build the business and deliver. There is also the matter of the promoters and existing investors. A conventional IPO comes with restrictions on promoter holdings and a long preparation cycle. The Shalimar swap changes the route through which Infra.Market’s shareholders get listed securities, although that exact lock-in treatment will depend on the final transaction structure and regulatory approvals. The bigger questions now are what the final listed entity will look like; where Infra. Market’s debt will sit, how much of the QIP goes towards reducing it, and at what valuation the remaining private investors are bought into the listed cap table. The answers to these will determine whether the Shalimar transaction is simply an alternate route to an IPO or the start of a much larger restructuring of Infra.Market’s ownership and capital structure. US-based WeWork Inc yesterday offloaded WeWork India shares worth ₹244.1 Cr via multiple open-market transactions. As per BSE data, WeWork Inc sold 35 Lakh shares, or 2.53% stake, of the India-based coworking giant at ₹697.55 apiece to rake in the amount. The stake sale was executed by the US-based coworking giant, via its affiliate 1 Ariel Way Tenant Limited, at a discount of 1.4% to the stock’s last closing price on Friday. The shares that flooded the market were lapped up by Motilal Oswal Asset Management Company, Citigroup, HDFC Standard Life Insurance Company, Motilal Oswal Mutual Fund and ICICI Prudential Mutual Fund (MF). While Motilal Oswal, via the two entities, lapped up 13.6 Lakh shares for a total sum of ₹94.9 Cr, ICICI Prudential MF bought 14.2 Lakh shares worth ₹99.2 Cr. Meanwhile, Citigroup Global Markets Mauritius and HDFC also cornered stakes worth ₹25 Cr each. WeWork Inc owned 14.82% stake, or 2.05 Cr shares, in the listed coworking giant at the end of June 2026. Post the latest bulk deals, the US-based coworking giant has diluted its shareholding in the company by more than 17%. The bulk deals come as the investor looks to book profits amid a sharp uptick in WeWork India’s share prices. The stock has zoomed more than 43.3% in the past three months and is up 16.8% on a year-to-date (YTD) basis. However, the stock has declined 6.08% in the past week as a weak Q1 FY27 continued to weigh on WeWork India’s share price. The coworking giant reported a loss of ₹4.1 Cr during the quarter, down 71% from ₹14.2 Cr incurred in Q1 FY26. However, operating revenue rose 28% to ₹683.8 Cr in Q1 FY27 as against ₹535.3 Cr in the year ago period. On the operational front, WeWork added nearly 7,000 desks in Q1 FY27, expanding its operational desk capacity to over 1.3 Lakh desks. During the quarter, it also expanded its footprint to 79 centres across eight cities, hosting 9.1 Mn sq ft of operational area. Shares of WeWork India closed Friday’s trading session 1.57% lower at ₹707.8 on the BSE.

The crowd gathered at Mahabalipuram Beach just stared into the water. Some were taking their kids to the beach on a cloudy Saturday morning, while a few others were out for a run. Regardless of what brought them there, their eyes were glued to the waves as Japan’s Ikko Watanabe went on to win the men’s QS title and complete an all-Japan sweep on the final day of the World Surf League Shore Temple Classic QS 2000 and Pro Junior (JQS).
After five days together at Mahabalipuram, the camaraderie among the surfers was evident. Competition aside, the Japanese contingent cheered for Thailand’s Isabel Higgs throughout the Women’s Qualifying Series final, even though she was up against Mirai Ikeda, one of their own.
Spectators were scattered across the beach, some perched on fishing boats parked on the wet sand, everyone watching as the surfers rode the Bay of Bengal waves one last time before the WSL wrapped up.
The day’s events included the men’s semifinal heats, where Ikko Watanabe and Tenshi Iwami secured their spots in the final, set to take place later the same day. The Pro Junior men’s semifinals ended with Ren Okano, Taro Takai, Yuma Nagasawa and Sentaro Sakai scoring the highest, inching closer to winning the title.
ALSO READ | From Mahabalipuram to Asian Games in Tahara, Ikko Watanabe sees stronger Asian swell
The semifinals of the Pro Junior women’s event set up an interesting final: Mirai Ikeda and Isabel Higgs, who would also battle it out for the Women’s Qualifying Series (QS) title, along with Hinano Shimizu and Hinata Shimizu, twin sisters who would be competing against each other in a final for the first time.
For a beach as vast as Mahabalipuram, the blare of the horn seemed to pull the scattered crowd towards the best viewing points. No one wanted to miss who would take the title home, and even the 11.00 am sun was not enough to send spectators looking for shade.
Whispers as the Pro Junior women’s finalists paddled out suggested that Mirai Ikeda could leave Mahabalipuram with two titles. But once the heat began, it was twin sisters Hinano and Hinata Shimizu, along with Isabel Higgs, who climbed the scoreboard. Mirai struggled to break into the top spots, while Hinata took control with smooth turns and composed landings. When the horn sounded twice, Hinata’s 14.23 remained unmatched. Hinano followed with 12.23 to finish second, completing a one-two finish for the sisters.
The Pro Junior men’s final kept the crowd watching. Ren Okano’s 13.00 pushed leader Yuma Nagasawa, but the latter held on with 14.17. When the horn sounded, the Japanese contingent rushed towards Nagasawa, showering him with hugs before lifting him onto their shoulders.
For Mirai, there was little time to dwell on her fourth-place finish in the junior final. Between that result and the call for the Women’s QS final, she sat with her back against a fishing boat, listening to her coach, with little trace of the smile she had carried through the competition.
The next heat changed the mood. Mirai moved into the lead in the Women’s QS final and, when the horn sounded, her 1.60-point advantage still stood at the top of the scoreboard. After missing out in the junior event, she responded with victory in the senior category, keeping alive a possible Japanese sweep across all four titles.
That sweep was completed in the men’s QS final between Ikko Watanabe and Tenshi Iwami. The Indian surfing team watched from the shore, trading predictions, while phones were held up waiting for the two surfers to produce an ‘Instagrammable’ manoeuvre. They delivered one of the closest battles of the Shore Temple Classic. Watanabe took the title, with Iwami finishing just 0.33 points behind. Watanabe’s 17.10 was the highest heat total recorded at the competition.
At the prize distribution ceremony, Arun Vasu, President of the Asian Surfing Federation and Surfing Federation of India, turned attention to what came next. He hinted that India will host two WSL events in 2027, one in the Andaman Islands, as announced during the opening ceremony. After five days at Mahabalipuram, it was a closing note that pointed beyond the beach and towards India’s growing place on the international surfing calendar.

EXCLUSIVE: Cue the “Nobody cares, Sean” memes — Scott Foley is coming back to Scrubs. He will reprise his fan-favorite character Sean Kelly on the upcoming second season of the ABC revival.
Foley’s return is being announced today at D23’s “Scrubs: Scrubbing Back” panel moderated by Foley and featuring series stars/executive producers Zach Braff (John “J.D.” Dorian), Donald Faison (Christopher Turk) and Sarah Chalke (Elliot Reid), along with showrunner/executive producer Aseem Batra.
Deadline can reveal that Foley will be recurring and, in a full-circle moment, Sean will go back to where his journey on the show started, dating Elliot (Chalke).
The duo will be rekindling their romance just as J.D. is embarking on a relationship with Charlie (Rachel Bilson), who was introduced in the Season 1 finale.
Watch on Deadline
“Scott Foley’s back to be love interest for Sarah, and Rachel has been mine; the dynamic with us all together is just hilarious, and we’re having so much fun,” Braff told Deadline.
Added Chalke, “The writers were like, how do we bring back Elliot’s neurosis, and they thought that Scott would be a good way to do that.”
Foley made his Scrubs debut at the end of Season 1, when Sean, a marine biologist and animal trainer at SeaWorld, was admitted to Sacred Heart with Elliot as his doctor. The two had a brief fling before she dumped him.
Sean and Elliot reconnected again in Season 3 and dated for awhile, taking their relationship long-distance when Sean went to New Zealand. Elliot broke things off shortly after Sean returned as her romance with J.D. started to heat up, news Sean did not take well. He eventually moved on with J.D.’s baby mama Kim Briggs (Elizabeth Banks).
Foley had been on Scrubs creator Bill Lawrence’s wish list for the revival for awhile.
“I really want to have Scott Foley back, I want to have him back on the show just so Zach can say ‘Nobody cares, Sean,'” Lawrence said at PaleyFest in April, referring to the famous dismissive line J.D. uses in conversations with Sean on the original show. The catchphrase took on a life of its own and, two decades later, it continues to haunt Foley, with fans using it to respond to any post he puts up on social media.
Foley brought up the infamous line when he came out on stage at D23.
‘This is personal for me. For those of your who don’t know, I played a character names Sean Kelly. Nobody cares, I heard that,” he said.
In a January interview, Foley revealed that Braff had asked him to return in Season 1 of the new Scrubs and that he had been scheduled for an episode but the schedule could not be worked out.
“I’m sure we’ll find the time,” Foley said at the time as he was promoting his Prime Video series It’s Not Like That. The streamer ended up canceling the well received family drama after one season, and Foley’s two-season arc on Will Trent came to an end in May, rendering the Felicity and Scandal alum available.
In Season 2 of Scrubs, J.D., Turk and Elliot have leveled up from interns to icons at Sacred Heart. Now, the respected doctors inspire the next generation while balancing the ups and downs of working in a hospital. Together with characters new and old, they are navigating this next chapter with laughter, heart and some surprises along the way. Foley’s return certainly qualifies as one of the surprises.
	In addition to Braff, Faison and Chalke, the Season 2 series regular cast includes Ava Bunn as intern Sam Tosh.
The original series’ creator Bill Lawrence serves as executive producer on the revival via his Doozer Productions alongside the company’s Jeff Ingold and Liza Katzer as well as showrunner Aseem Batra and stars Braff, Faison and Chalke. Scrubs is produced by 20th Television, a part of Disney Television Studios. The series will return to ABC Sept. 30 with a two-episode premiere, airing Wednesday and streaming next day on Hulu.
In addition to Scrubs, Foley has done three other Bill Lawrence series, Cougar Town, Undateable and Whiskey Cavalier. His upcoming movies include Keep Coming Back and August. He is repped by Gersh and Atlas Artists.

Don’t Expect Russians to Protest the War
Ukraine may have hoped that deeper drone attacks would cause Russians to rise up, but mass demonstrations don’t look likely.
This summer, Ukraine began one of the most ambitious campaigns of its war with Russia. It launched drones deep into Russian territory, hitting some of the country’s biggest oil refineries and causing a nationwide fuel shortage. In some areas, Russians have waited for gas for as long as 69 hours, in lines stretching miles. Impatient drivers have beaten and stabbed one another. Even state-controlled media have acknowledged the problem.
Ukraine and its allies seemed to hope that frustrated Russians would rise up in protest. After more than four years, the war had finally “come home.” Now that more citizens were feeling its effects, one might assume, they would demand its end and apply pressure to President Vladimir Putin ahead of parliamentary elections in the fall. But so far, no mass uprising appears likely, now or anytime soon.
Russians are used to inconveniences. Under Soviet rule, they lived with shortages of just about everything. Lines were so ubiquitous that academics theorized about Russian identity being shaped by waiting. Books were published with chapter titles such as “The Queue as a Form of Soviet Life.” The newspaper Socialist Industry estimated that Soviet citizens spent 30 billion working hours a year waiting in line for essential goods.
In the late 1980s, at the peak of Soviet scarcity, my family lived on the outskirts of Gorky, a city east of Moscow. Sometimes my mother would send me shopping. I hated it. At a small, gray store called Vegetables, I would wait in line to pick through boxes of rotting produce, hoping to find an acceptable carrot or beetroot for borscht. Then I went to Bread, where I waited some more. Shelves were half empty. The only item that never seemed to run out was margarine; enterprising salespeople tried to make it more appealing by sculpting it into hedgehogs, which they put in display cases. Lines got even longer on the rare days when cheese or butter were delivered. Meat hardly ever came.
Still, nobody protested. We waved away the deprivation and delays. Everyone lives this way, we told ourselves. After all, Soviets knew the cost of complaining. In 1962, thousands of demonstrators gathered to protest wage cuts and government-imposed price increases. In response, Premier Nikita Khrushchev’s government deployed thousands of troops, who killed roughly two dozen demonstrators in what became known as the Novocherkassk massacre.
Russians continue to fear their government. I recently called my former neighbor in St. Petersburg, an art teacher and activist whom I’ll call Svetlana. When I asked whether she had witnessed any street protests, she laughed. “Are you guys living on the moon out there?” she asked me. “Don’t you get how dangerous it is here?”
“It’s even worse than in the Soviet days,” Svetlana continued. “One guy bragged to me the other day that he’d reported his neighbor to the FSB”—the successor of the KGB—simply for listening to anti-war music. She also told me about an acquaintance who had spent two years in prison for leaving a poem and flowers at a monument to a Ukrainian poet. In most households, gripes about the regime don’t leave the kitchen.
At the start of the war, demonstrations were more common. In 2022, police arrested nearly 19,000 anti-war activists, according to OVD-Info, an independent human-rights group. Since then, protests have all but disappeared. This year, one of the most notable critics of the regime was a veteran named Alexander Lunin. In June, Lunin put on his military uniform and recorded a speech denouncing Putin and the war. He posted it on social media, where it received more than 12 million views in 24 hours. The police jailed him, and Lunin publicly apologized for “giving in to emotions due to fatigue.”
Earlier this week, the only anti-war party was banned from parliamentary elections. Far-right politicians had sued the party, named Yabloko, alleging that it had received foreign funding, violated copyright law, and promoted “extremism.” The supreme court ruled in the far right’s favor, removing Yabloko from the ballot. Only a few hundred Russians protested outside the court.
Most Russians seem to have inherited the long-suffering mentality of the generations who grew up under Soviet rule. Rather than tiring of the war, “Russians realize that they are under attack, and that it’s time to stand together and tighten their belts,” Irina Borogan, a journalist who has studied Russian dissidents, told me. When the BBC asked a middle-aged man living in Crimea about the fuel shortages, he shrugged them off: “We are humans. We’ll adapt.”
Last month, I called Konstantin Sonin, an economist and a professor at the University of Chicago who left Russia in 2015. He told me that his friends in Moscow have made only the barest wartime accommodations—such as sending their kids to summer camp in Gelendzhik, a town on the Black Sea coast, instead of one in the heavily shelled Crimea, even though both areas are well within range of Ukrainian drones. He sounded astonished by his friends’ comfort with risk. “We’ve seen what Ukrainians have been capable of coping with,” Sonin told me. “Russians can endlessly adapt to this crisis too.”
I heard a similar message from Vladislav Inozemtsev, a Russian economist and political scientist who lives in the United States. Inozemtsev told me that his friends in Moscow have used their contacts to circumvent the fuel shortage and get gas delivered to their door. “It’s twice the normal price, but they can afford it; the middle class quickly adapts to difficulties,” he said, while acknowledging that Russians in rural areas will likely have a harder time.
By some accounts, Moscow hardly looks like the capital of a country fighting a war of attrition. Denis Volkov, the director of the Levada Center, an independent polling organization, described his walk to work to me. The city center, he told me, is filled with decorations that the government has put up: an oversized samovar, an inflatable elephant, sprawling flower beds. Volkov said that he sees no sign of a public revolt. “I would say that the expectations of a revolution in Russia are not based on any real facts,” he said. “All our data proves the opposite.”
A few months before the war, Levada found that Putin’s approval rating was 63 percent. In June, it was 74 percent, although it has been dropping since the start of the year. A majority of Russians—52 percent—said that their country was moving in the right direction. “People blame mainly the West and Washington for all their troubles” instead of Putin, Volkov said. These findings undoubtedly reflect the reluctance of citizens in an authoritarian country to complain to pollsters about their government. Nonetheless, according to Volkov, Levada found that 16 percent of Russians said that they would participate in street protests, up from 11 percent in 2024. Last year, 16 percent of respondents said they felt fear or sadness. This summer, that figure was 29 percent.
Even though there have been no signs of mass protest, Putin is preparing. This year, the Kremlin increased the budget for the national guard and other law-enforcement agencies to a record high of more than $47 billion. Just like Russians who fear the reprise of Soviet-era government violence, Putin also has a precedent to worry about. In 1991, after years of keeping Russians off the streets, the Soviet regime was unable to stop a rally of hundreds of thousands in Moscow, which accelerated its end. Putin may not have much reason to fear such a protest in the near future, but he can’t be too careful.

Novak Djokovic suffered in the second set from punishing heat and humidity on Saturday but made a match of it before falling 2-6, 6-4, 6-4 to Argentine Thiago Tirante in what could be the Serb’s last appearance at the ATP-WTA Cincinnati Masters.
The second-round battle lasting for more than two and a half hours was the first match for the 39-year-old with 24 Grand Slam singles titles since he lost to Jannik Sinner in the Wimbledon semifinals more than a month ago.
Djokovic, who claimed the last of his three Cincinnati titles in 2023, claimed the opening set with little fuss.
He won a brutal 18-minute third game of the second, saving four break points over nine deuces but bending over in distress between points and even dropping to his hands and knees after one particularly grueling exchange.
Djokovic took a medical timeout after that game, with the physio and then a doctor coming on court to assist with assessments and ice towels.
After Tirante took the second set both players cooled off in the locker room.
Slightly revived, Djokovic set the pace again in the deciding set. But it all went wrong in the ninth game, when Djokovic saved three break points before getting it wrong on a drop shot to bring up a fourth break chance that his opponent converted.
Tirante clinched the biggest win of his career in the next game as Djokovic again failed to land a drop shot on match point.
The Serb, who must now try to regroup before the US Open starts on August 30, admitted he might have played his last match in Cincy.
“It looks like I won’t be back, unfortunately to play here,” he said, confirming that the sweltering weather got the better of him.
“It was a combination of the heat and humidity, all those things,” he said. “Everything involved makes it worse.”
Seventh seed Flavio Cobolli, runner-up at the French Open, defeated Miomir Kecmanovic 6-1, 4-6, 6-3.
Martin Landaluce beat Matteo Arnaldi 6-4, 4-6, 6-4 to reach a third-round clash against Tirante.
Zverev wins all-nighter
