- Reports circulated that, in May 2025, a Texas sheriff's deputy searched a data pool of more than 83,000 license plate-scanning cameras made by surveillance tech company Flock Safety to find a woman whose partner alleged she performed a self-administered abortion. Public records confirm the officer did conduct such a search.
- We left this claim unrated because evidence for what motivated the search is mixed. While the deputy reportedly said they were attempting to locate the woman and her children to "check their welfare" (as they believed she may have been hurt by her partner), the investigation was, at that time, characterized as a "death investigation of a non-viable fetus" and the listed reason for the search was "had an abortion, search for female."
- Officers who arrived at the residence treated it as a potential crime scene, placing what the woman's partner told them was the frozen fetus in a "small body bag" and contacting the district attorney's office to ask whether the woman could be charged and "a civil lawsuit against the pharmaceutical company that supplied the pill" could be filed.
- It wasn't until five days after the death investigation was opened that the woman told authorities her side of the story and an aggravated assault case was opened against her partner. She told officers she ran from home, taking her child with her, after he threatened to kill her.
- Even if the woman performed an abortion on herself, Texas' anti-abortion penalties rarely apply to the person receiving the abortion.
- Flock has faced increasing scrutiny over its broad-reaching surveillance, which critics say infringes on personal privacy.
As public awareness of the spread of cameras made by surveillance company Flock Safety grew in August 2026, a claim resurfaced online that in May 2025, a Texas deputy pulled data from a network of 83,000 license plate identification cameras to track a woman who allegedly performed an abortion on herself.
The claim spread across several social media platforms, including Instagram and X. Another example of the claim had previously been posted on Facebook (archived) on July 8:
(Facebook user Feminist News)
After the U.S. Supreme Court overturned landmark abortion ruling Roe v. Wade in 2022, it became almost entirely illegal to have an abortion in Texas, though penalties rarely apply to the person receiving the abortion. The story above emerged amid growing concerns over police misuse of surveillance systems — including, reportedly, to stalk romantic interests.
We looked into the claim and found publicly available records confirm a Texas sheriff's deputy searched data across thousands of camera networks comprising more than 83,000 cameras made by Flock Safety, a company that uses automated license plate readers to identify cars.
According to an internal sheriff's office incident report obtained by Snopes, the deputy who made the search reported being concerned for the woman's welfare. "I began to believe the victim may have been hurt by [her partner] due to the call and it not making sense," the deputy wrote. "I wanted to use resources available to help find where the victim and her children could be to make sure they were okay."
Below, we analyze available evidence to understand how an officer used Flock data to track down a woman who went through a violent experience — and why.
Timeline of events
Incident reports and other documents reviewed by Snopes laid out a timeline of what occurred:
- April 23, 2025: The woman left her residence after her partner allegedly assaulted her. The man later told authorities he confronted her after finding what he thought was evidence of an abortion, saying an argument led to her leaving with their son and not coming back. The evidence included packaging for an abortion pill and what he thought was an aborted fetus, which he then stored in his freezer.
- May 8, 2025: According to the man, he made contact with his lawyer, who advised him to report the incident.
- May 9, 2025: The man contacted the Johnson County Sheriff's Office, reporting an "abortion incident involving his girlfriend." Deputies arrived and put up crime-scene tape, took photographs, collected the "fetus" for evidence and sent officers to attempt to contact the woman for a welfare check. They opened a "death investigation of a non-viable fetus" and reportedly contacted the district attorney's office to ask whether the woman could be charged. At this time, a deputy submitted the Flock search for her license plate number, reportedly out of concern her partner may have hurt her, as the man's story was not making sense.
- May 14, 2025: The woman arrived at the sheriff's office to report the alleged assault. Authorities opened an assault case against her partner, who public records show had previously been convicted of aggravated robbery.
- May 22, 2025: The lead detective signed a warrant for the man's arrest.
- June 11, 2025: A medical examiner determined the "fetus" was a blood clot. A few hours later, the lead detective officially recommended the case be changed to "cleared by exception" for that reason.
Officer searched data from more than 83K cameras
According to data Snopes reviewed from MuckRock — a nonprofit, collaborative tool that allows users to share records acquired through the Freedom of Information Act — the Flock search log indicated that on May 9, 2025, a Johnson County deputy named "J. Smith" searched 6,809 camera networks, totaling 83,345 cameras, between April 9, 2025, and May 9, 2025, for "Case #2500002320." The deputy listed the reason as: "had an abortion, search for female."
(MuckRock.com)
In an internal incident report from January 2026, the officers involved gave their accounts of the situation. The officer who submitted the Flock search, J. Smith, used a "TLO" (most likely "TransUnion Locator Services" — a massive investigative data platform law enforcement officers often use to find background information on people) to find the color and make of the woman's car as well as the license plate number.
"I entered the vehicle into FLOCK to see if we could see where the victim and her children might be at due to multiple different locations being given for the victim and her children," the deputy wrote in the report. "Deputies had attempted to try and contact the female, but were unsuccessful. The FLOCK hit showed the victim had been in Dallas prior but nothing recent."
What motivated the Flock data search?
News media outlet 404 Media originally reported on the search data, which digital rights organization Electronic Frontier Foundation characterized as an "abortion investigation."
It's important to note that the internal report was dated Jan. 30, 2026 — more than eight months after the incident. Until the internal report emerged, there was no documented, primary evidence the officers were concerned for the woman's safety.
According to the internal report, the deputy who submitted the search was not present at the home but rather "just was assisting with trying to locate the victim and her children to check their welfare." The deputy wrote:
I began to believe the victim may have been hurt by the RP [reporting person] due to the call and it not making sense.
The RP who was in a relationship with the victim didn't know anything about the victim which also wasn't making sense of where she could have been with the children.
I wanted to use resources available to help find where the victim and her children could be to make sure they were okay.
A detective at the home also reportedly told the man he "did not understand why it took him over two weeks to process what happened or contact his family attorney," then sent officers in nearby cities to look for the woman at various addresses "for a welfare check."
Johnson County Sheriff Adam King told 404 Media that "her family was worried that she was going to bleed to death, and we were trying to find her to get her to a hospital." The incident had occurred more than two weeks before the sheriff's office got involved.
As part of the death investigation, officers photographed and placed a stainless steel tumbler containing what the woman's partner told them was the fetus in "a small body bag." While at the home on May 9, they treated the area as a potential crime scene, including filling out a crime-scene log and putting up crime-scene tape.
Deputies at the home also discussed options for criminal charges related to the alleged abortion, according to the report. It read:
Deputies discussed the legal implications of the situation, noting that while the girlfriend self-administered the abortion pill, there were no criminal charges applicable under current Texas law.
CSI and CID collected all relevant evidence, including photographs and printed materials provided by [the woman's partner].
Deputies also considered the possibility of a civil lawsuit against the pharmaceutical company that supplied the pill.
According to the arrest warrant affidavit for the man, as well as the internal police report, deputies contacted the district attorney's office on May 9 to ask whether the woman could be charged. They were informed that the state "could not statutorily charge the abortion or miscarriage of the non-viable fetus."
When the woman arrived at the station on May 14, the lead detective "was initially under the impression [she] came to the Sheriffs Office to tell her side of the story about the non-viable fetus," according to the arrest warrant affidavit. The internal report read:
Detective Miller started out the interview with [the woman] by explaining the State would not be statutorily charging her with anything at this time so if she came to report [her partner] assaulting her because she learned he called the Sheriff's Office about the non-viable fetus trying to get her in trouble, there was no need.
What were the legal implications?
After a medical examiner determined the blood tissue deputies originally thought was a fetus was, in fact, a blood clot, according to the internal report, the lead detective on the death investigation wrote on June 11:
Disposition recommend case be changed to cleared by exception due to the tissue collected on May 9th, 2025, from [the woman's partner], being that of a blood clot and not a viable fetus.
This death investigation is linked to JCSO case number 25-00002423.
Please refer to that case for further information.
According to the FBI, "cleared by exception" means that "elements beyond law enforcement's control prevent the agency from arresting and formally charging the offender."
It's unclear how the investigation would have proceeded had the blood clot been a fetus. The initial case opened by the sheriff's office did not name abortion as a criminal offense; rather, it was a death investigation — a routine action following deaths that take place outside of hospitals and similar settings.
Investigating why a pregnancy loss occurred is medical in nature — an investigation to determine what caused fetal death. However, in many states, law enforcement has investigated pregnancy loss as a criminal case. In April 2025, for example, a Georgia woman was arrested after a miscarriage when a witness claimed she placed the fetal remains in a dumpster.
According to the nonprofit Pregnancy Justice, Texas has fetal personhood language applicable to criminal law.
Flock's inconsistent messaging
A spokesperson for Flock told Snopes via email that "the woman was reportedly being searched for as a missing person in what appears to have been a domestic violence case, not as a suspect."
This is not entirely correct. When the officer conducted the Flock search on May 9, the investigation was, at that point, officially characterized as a "death investigation of a non-viable fetus" — not a domestic violence case — even though the investigators' reports compiled later did express concern for the woman's well-being. We also found no evidence a missing person report had been filed.
Flock has also been inconsistent in its messaging. On June 19, 2025, the company released a statement (archived) ostensibly correcting what it called a "Women's Healthcare Falsehood" that did not mention domestic violence.
The company claimed a "family called to ask for help" because they "feared she was hurt." There is no evidence of this in the documents reviewed by Snopes; the official record indicates the woman's partner — who later was charged with assaulting the woman — called authorities to report "an abortion incident involving his girlfriend" that occurred weeks earlier.
Although it's true no charges were filed against the woman, the search was performed as part of a death investigation and authorities listed both the woman and her partner as subjects in the investigation.
Access to Flock data raises privacy concerns
A Texas deputy did use Flock data from a network of more than 83,000 cameras to find a woman her partner told authorities had performed an abortion on herself.
While an internal report says the deputy claimed to have performed the Flock search out of concern for the woman's welfare, this does not detract from the fact that, regardless of an individual officer's intentions, law enforcement officials have unprecedented ability to track civilians without a warrant because of Flock's vast network of surveillance cameras.
DeFlock, a site used to track such cameras with a crowdsourced map, estimates that, as of this writing, there are 130,235 cameras in view across the U.S. — approximately 107,000 of which are Flock cameras.
Flock has marketed itself to local law enforcement agencies as a modern solution to fight crime across jurisdictional lines with 24/7 coverage, providing police departments with "indiscriminate evidence from fixed locations."
"When people ask whether police officers can misuse Flock systems, the honest answer is simple: Yes. And when they do, they should be held accountable," a Flock blog post from May 2025 read.
In the case of this police officer scanning a data pool of more than 83,000 cameras to find one woman, many details remain difficult to review and were made transparent only through the findings of records requests made by civilians and journalists.
The data pool the Texas officer searched also tapped into networks in states where abortion is not illegal, such as Washington and Illinois. Though in January 2026 Flock said it does not share data with federal agencies such as Immigration and Customs Enforcement, in August 2025 the company said it had "engaged in limited pilots with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), to assist those agencies in combatting human trafficking and fentanyl distribution" before it said it had paused its operations with federal agencies.
The University of Washington's Center for Human Rights has documented multiple instances of federal collaboration with local Flock client agencies, leaving much unknown when it comes to how civilians could be tracked across the state lines for the purpose of criminalizing women who receive abortions or otherwise.
On Aug. 13, 2026, Flock announced several changes to its access policies in response to the backlash, including recommending cutting default data retention from 30 days to seven. We reached out to Flock seeking more information regarding what is meant by Flock would "recommend" cutting the retention period — including whether it was possible to bypass this recommendation. We will update this story if we receive a response.
Although the woman in Texas wasn't charged for anything related to an abortion, she was the subject of a death investigation and the case was "cleared by exception" only after a medical examiner determined the alleged fetus was a blood clot. Court records show her partner, as of this writing, awaits trial on one count of aggravated assault and one count of family-violence assault.

Quick Answer
Round Sync is a free, open-source Android app that brings Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, and dozens of other cloud services into one place. It lets you browse, move, sync, stream, and encrypt files without ads, paid tiers, or separate apps.
These days, no amount of storage is sufficient, as everything, right from images and videos to apps, has become quite hefty in size. I have lost count of the different cloud storage apps I have installed on my phone right now. I use Google Drive for work, OneDrive for my personal media, Dropbox for something I used years ago, etc. Every single one of them wants its own app, its own login screen, its own little corner on my phone’s home screen. The worst part is that none of them talk to each other.
That is exactly what Round Sync does, and it fills the gap. This free Android app lets you connect pretty much every cloud storage app and manage all of them from a single app. Let us know more about it.
What is Round Sync?
Round Sync is a free, open-source Android app that lets you manage all of your cloud storage in one place. It is a unified file browser that requires no premium tier, shows you no ads, and no “upgrade to unlock more” nonsense. It is built on top of Rclone, which is a widely respected open-source command-line tool that has been the backbone of cloud management on Linux and other platforms for years. What Round Sync does is take that Rclone command-line tool and wrap it in an actual Android interface that a regular person can tap through without ever touching a terminal.
Enough of the technical aspect of the app (which a normal user wouldn’t even care for); let us talk about the main reason you would want to keep this app installed on your phone. Since it is built on Rclone, it inherits support for dozens of cloud storage backends, be it Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, Box, pCloud, Mega, Amazon S3, Backblaze B2, and self-hosted options like Nextcloud and WebDAV servers, among many others.
While most of them require an easy guided setup screen inside the app, for others, you need to import the Rclone configuration file. All in all, Round Sync eliminates the need to switch between multiple apps to check whether the file synced correctly. You open Round Sync once and see everything organized into folders side by side.
Round Sync treats cloud storage as local storage
For different cloud storage services, you need their separate apps on your phone. This not only eats up your phone’s storage but also makes it hard to make sure that everything is working perfectly fine. Moving files between two different cloud accounts means downloading them first locally and then re-uploading them manually. Round Sync ensures that you can list, view, download, upload, move, rename, and even delete files/folders directly. You can move things between remotes without that awkward double download-then-reupload dance.
It also plugs into the Android Storage Access Framework, so your cloud storage can show up inside other apps’ file pickers. Your gallery app, a document editor, whatever needs to browse or save a file. That is a small detail, but it is the kind of integration that separates an app that merely displays your cloud files from one that actually behaves like a part of the OS.
Here are some of the best features of Round Sync:
- Automated syncing: This is one feature that makes Round Sync genuinely useful. You can set up sync tasks that run automatically on a schedule. For instance, backing up your camera roll to Google Drive every night or mirror a work folder to OneDrive whenever you are on Wi-Fi. Once configured, you don’t have to think again.
- Stream, don’t just store: Round Sync isn’t just about copying and moving files around; you can also use it to stream media directly from your cloud storage. It can also serve your files and folders over FTP, HTTP, WebDAV, or DLNA. In simple terms, your phone can act as a media server, and you can point your phone to your smart TV or other device connected to the same network, and it will pull files straight from your phone.
- Privacy gets taken seriously here: If you are curious about how your files are handled by Round Sync, you should know that it supports 256-bit encryption through Rclone’s crypt remotes. This means that you can layer client-side encryption on top of any provider, including in the free tier on the provider’s servers.
- Works on almost all Android phones: Round Sync works on Android 7 or above, and ships builds for ARM, ARM64, x86, and x86_64 architectures. This means that it is not only available for flagship phones, but also for older phones as well. The UI follows the Material 3 design language, and there is proper dark theme support as well.
Getting Round Sync is super easy
Do note that, like most open-source Android apps, Round Sync isn’t available on the Google Play Store. But if you know, there are several Play Store alternatives like F-Droid, from where you can download this app. You can also download it from IzzyOnDroid, along with its GitHub release page.
Additionally, you need to sideload this app on your phone. If you don’t know a thing about sideloading apps on Android, this Samsung guide has everything you need to know about sideloading on Android. Setting up the app itself is quite straightforward. You get the app, install it, add a “remote” for each cloud storage you want to connect, and browse your files within a couple of minutes.
Should you use it?
If you’re the kind of person who only checks their cloud storage once a week, then Round Sync may not feel beneficial to you. The UI may not feel as polished as the one you get with Google Drive, and setting it up is a bit more manual compared to dedicated apps. However, if you manage multiple cloud storage accounts and want a one-stop shop for them, along with all the features you get on top, then Round Sync makes perfect sense. This also frees up your RAM since 5 different apps are not running in the background and eating up your RAM.

After doing three loops around the parking lot, you finally see a free spot. You step on the gas to claim it, but an SUV cuts in front of you and steals the space. You stomp on the brakes, jerking to a halt. You might forgive the other driver, but your Toyota remembers.
Later, as you drive home, your eyes wander to the restaurant that just opened on the corner. Your car loudly beeps you back to attention, the dashboard scolding, “keep eyes on the road.” Your car is watching you, and that hard stop and brief glance to the side are data sent directly to your car insurer, churning into an algorithm that decides your future premiums.
This surveillance model, called telematics, has become standard in auto insurance, as companies promise to save policyholders money if they agree to share their minute-to-minute driving data. They don’t actually save you money — a report by the Maryland Insurance Administration showed a mixed bag of premium changes with no real overall savings — but that hasn’t dissuaded companies.
As telematics grows in auto insurance, the human body is next. White House health officials and health insurance executives are pushing to bring a telematics model to mainstream medicine. “My vision is that every American is wearing a wearable in the next four years,” health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told House members in 2025. Kennedy claims devices that track your sleep, heart rate, glucose levels, and other metrics will help Americans “take control” of their health. And indeed, there are now countless wearables to track your vital bodily data — from your heart rate and daily steps to your ovulation and hormone levels.
But if the short history of telematics in the auto insurance taught us anything, it’s to be skeptical of any promises attached to shareable surveillance data, especially if corporations are involved.
Several key ethical questions for consumers remain unanswered.
First, there is not much evidence that wearables will lower any overall costs. If anything, wearables provide an ulterior profit motive for insurance companies.
Second, there are major privacy concerns embedded into the free sharing of minute-by-minute bodily data to corporations. How exactly will the data be used and how securely stored?
More broadly, the wearables endeavor promotes a highly individualized view of health that fails to acknowledge how social structures and inequalities shape our lifetime risk to disease. These risks could be attenuated with thoughtful health policy. Instead, the Department of Health and Human Services wants to slap an Apple Watch on your wrist.
Despite these unanswered questions, health and life insurance industries have already begun introducing telematics-style tracking. Programs like John Hancock’s Vitality (developed by the South African third-party company Discovery Limited), UnitedHealthcare’s Wellness Rewards, and others offer discounts, gift cards, and points for “good” behaviors.
In tandem, MAHA has been gearing up to use federal resources to promote a mass adoption of wearables. The White House strategy report to “make children healthy again,” for one, proposes linking wearable data to electronic health records. The FDA also reclassified AI-enabled wearables in January, claiming that they will not be treated as heavily regulated medical devices as long as they do not claim to diagnose or treat diseases.
Wearables do have some potential to have a positive change. In the best-case scenario, health insurance premiums would go down and Americans would live longer and more ailment-free lives. One NYC-based family medicine physician we spoke with said the people who bring wearable data to their appointments do tend to be the most health-conscious patients. But do the health conscious seek out wearables, or do wearables make users more health conscious? It’s unclear. Furthermore, the data generated are not very useful or actionable for doctors or wearers — and they are often inaccurate.
More pressingly, there is a major incentive to use consumer data to expand their profit margins. In the car industry, catchily named plans like Drivewise (Allstate), DriveEasy (Geico), and Snapshot (Progressive) extract as much data as possible from you and your car, including braking, time of day, and phone usage. Ideally, the data would be used to improve driver behavior and reduce accidents. There are some studies that point to improvement, but these are mostly for trucking fleets, and the data need to be combined with coaching and other strategies. Instead, drivers agree to opt in for lower premiums, and insurers line their pockets selling the data to third parties. The same may happen with wearable data and health insurance.
Dump five sugars in your morning coffee, skip the afternoon workout, and somewhere in a server farm in Nebraska, a spreadsheet decides you are the kind of person who dies young. Your data could be weaponized by your insurer to increase your premium and label you risky. When we are at risk, we need help, yet insurance companies and MAHA want to make the person at constant “risk” also responsible for managing that increased risk themselves.
When a hurricane hits, when cancer strikes, when a drunk driver runs a red light, no amount of personal optimization saves you. The telematics model, whether applied to your Camry or your cardiovascular system, is not a health strategy and it is not sound policy. The insurance industry has spent decades figuring out how to avoid paying for your health. Now, with an app and a MAHA press release, we may be handing the keys to the people who were already driving us into a ditch.
Andréa Becker, Ph.D., is an assistant professor of sociology at Hunter College and the author of “Get It Out: On the Politics of Hysterectomy.” Previously, she was a postdoctoral fellow at the University of California, San Francisco for the ANSIRH research group. Paul Kamuf is an ex-creative director turned sociologist. His graduate research centers on the impact of new technologies on workers, the workplace, and human relationships.

BJP Rajya Sabha member and former Indian cricketer Harbhajan Singh recently re-shared a video on his official X account. Originally posted by an X user, Arshdeep Singh Saini, the clip shows two young men standing by the roadside in a seemingly disoriented state with their bodies appearing limp and their movements unusual. Sharing the video in the context of Punjab’s drug abuse problem, Singh expressed anguish, and wrote, “Very sad to see the situation of Punjab…”
Very sad to see the situation of Punjab 💔💔 . Punjab and its youth deserve better. This issue needs honesty, accountability, and urgent action—not denial. https://t.co/Vb6si8eAaj
— Harbhajan Turbanator (@harbhajan_singh) August 10, 2026
The post, published on August 10, has been viewed over 100,000 times, and shared more than a 1,000 times. (Archive)
Drug abuse remains a major issue in Punjab, which is slated to go to assembly polls in 2027. Harbhajan Singh, who switched from the AAP to the BJP in April 2026, shared the video while raising questions about accountability and the incumbent AAP government’s handling of the crisis.
Several other social media users also posted the same video with similar captions, pointing to the growing drug abuse problem in Punjab.
Fact Check
To begin with, we noticed that Punjab Police had reshared Singh’s post mentioning that the viral video was from Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan, and not from Punjab. The post from Punjab Police’s official handle urged users to verify facts before posting things online. (Archive)
The video being circulated is from Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan—not Punjab—and has no connection with Punjab Police.
A Punjabi audio track does not make an incident a Punjab incident.
We urge users and social media accounts to verify the facts and location before posting… https://t.co/bNHwjXVXsC
— Punjab Police India (@PunjabPoliceInd) August 10, 2026
Mainstream news media outlets such as Times of India and India Today also fact-checked Singh’s viral claim. All the reports echoed the claim of Punjab Police and mentioned that the video was from Sri Ganganagar, Rajasthan, although no detail of the actual incident or the original video was shared.
To verify whether the video was indeed from Sri Ganganagar, we continued our investigation.
On August 13, around midnight, the Times of India published a story on its digital portal on the Sri Ganganagar zombie drug case. According to the article, Sri Ganganagar district police detained two persons who staged a scene pretending to be under the influence of the so-called “zombie drug.”
Quoting district police superintendent Hari Shankar, the Times of India article mentioned that the detained youths were Yogesh and Yoginder, who had filmed the video for Instagram.
Armed with this piece of evidence, we carried out another round of investigation and came across a Facebook post by SBT News or Sandhya Border Times News. According to this platform, the two youths were detained from Bhambhu Colony area of Sri Ganganagar city after they had filmed the video on August 7.
We then geolocated the spot to make sure the scene was indeed from Bhambhu Colony.
The viral video had three important markers which helped us to geolocate the exact spot where the 41-second-long clip was filmed.
In the video, the two youths are seen standing in front of an iron pillar with orange and black markings at its base. Such markings are commonly seen at Indian Oil petrol pumps, and the tiled flooring in the video is also typical of petrol pump premises. Tall iron pillars bearing the pump’s branding are also commonly found outside petrol stations.
The road in front of the petrol pump appears to be a two-way road, with a divider in the middle. Cars can be seen travelling on both sides of the divider, while two flags mounted on tall poles are visible on the divider. On the opposite side of the road, a vacant plot overgrown with vegetation can also be seen.
To geolocate the spot, we searched for Indian Oil petrol pumps near Bhambhu Colony in Sri Ganganagar, looking for one beside a two-way road and opposite a vacant plot with dense vegetation. We found a petrol pump that matched these features exactly.
Thus from these above findings, it is clear that the video which BJP MP Harbhajan Singh shared was not from Punjab. It is from Sri Ganganagar in Rajasthan. Besides, according to police, the two men in the video were enacting being under the influence of drugs for an Instagram reel.

Donald Trump has threatened to declare the strait of Hormuz as “a territory of the United States” as his administration struggles to conclude the war with Iran.
During a speech at a police academy on Long Island, New York, on Friday, the US president said he would “pretty soon” designate the waterway – a crucial chokepoint for global trade, through which about a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies typically pass – a US territory.
The comment came as peace talks with Iran remain at an impasse following failed negotiations, with Tehran refusing to reopen the strait, which has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.
Almost six months into the war, there is little indication that negotiations will soon yield peace, as Iranian officials continue to defy Trump’s demands. The US has been blockading Iranian shipping and ports in recent months in an effort to pile economic pressure on Tehran.
“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said on Friday. “Essentially, that’s what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.”
The seriousness of Trump’s remark, and whether it signaled a new policy position for his administration, was not immediately clear.
Responding on X, formerly Twitter, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, said Tehran would not be intimidated by threats, or a show of force, by the US – and added that the strait of Hormuz would only be opened, or closed, under Iran’s authority.
Earlier this week, the president claimed that the US had “total control” over the strait and said “I think we will keep it” on Truth Social, despite the waterway being an internationally navigable strait bordered by Iran and Oman.
Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the war, forcing working Americans to pay significantly more at the pump.
Nevertheless, on Friday, Trump said that Americans who have had to “pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” should remember that they are “doing it so that a very evil country cannot have a – really, it’s the No 1 state sponsor of terror in the world – we don’t want them to have a nuclear weapon.
“When you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK, I mean, it’s not. I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing,” he added.
Over the past six months, the Trump administration has repeatedly claimed victory in the war, saying Iran’s regime has been pleading for a deal.
Tehran has remained steadfast in its demands, saying as recently as last Saturday that it will not reopen the strait of Hormuz unless the US “corrects its behavior”, “completely compensate[s]” Iran for war damage, lifts sanctions and “unconditionally” releases frozen assets.

Why Chinese youth are turning to an 84-year-old Cambridge professor for support
To some of his 2.4 million followers, he is Grandpa Cute. Meet Alan Macfarlane, the gentle academic soothing China’s anxious generation
Wearing a black mariner’s cap and with a wall-to-wall bookshelf as a backdrop, Cambridge University professor Alan Macfarlane greets his social media audience with a soft ni hao – “Hello” in Chinese.
In his latest video, Macfarlane follows this signature opening by thoughtfully answering a question pulled from the comments: why has making genuine friends become so difficult?
Few would have expected an 84-year-old British anthropologist and historian from Cambridge University to become a social media heartthrob in China – yet Macfarlane has done exactly that.
Young Chinese affectionately call him “Grandpa Cute” or “Dumbledore”, after the beloved Harry Potter character, while his gentle, jargon-free reflections on education, purpose, anxiety, relationships, artificial intelligence (AI) and cultural understanding resonate deeply in a fast-paced, high-pressure society.
Through an intimate Q&A format, Macfarlane has amassed more than 2.4 million followers in roughly one year since launching on the Chinese social media platform RedNote in 2025, with videos often gaining millions of views.
His channels on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – and Bilibili, another major video-sharing platform, have also attracted about 170,000 and 540,000 followers, respectively.

Google began offering third-party app store downloads in the Play Store earlier this week, but US District Judge James Donato says the company isn’t doing enough. After reviewing the process for accessing the first non-Google store, Donato ruled that Google has added unnecessary “anticompetitive friction,” ordering the company to rectify the issues.
While Epic and Google are patching things up with a global partnership agreement, the two are still on opposite sides of the antitrust case in the US. Google lost the case in 2023, and the intervening years have been about determining how to implement remedies to address Google’s anticompetitive behavior. One of the court’s key elements is the requirement that Google include third-party app stores in the Play Store, giving users an easy way to get apps from non-Google sources. Aptoide Games became the first such app store recently.
However, Google worked hard to avoid this outcome, attempting to settle with Epic to keep third-party app stores out. When it was forced to admit the Aptoide store under the terms of the ruling, Google didn’t exactly put up a banner welcoming third-party app stores. In fact, Judge Donato found in a Thursday hearing that Google’s implementation was not good enough, according to The Verge.
While there is a link to the Play Store’s alternative app store page, it’s buried several levels deep in its confusing menus. Epic lawyer Yonatan Even showed the court that even searching for “app store” and “aptoide” didn’t show the intended results like any other search. Instead, the Play Store shows an “are you looking for” banner that links to the third-party app store page.

BP has answered Donald Trump’s call for oil companies to help rebuild Venezuela’s fossil fuel industry with new plans to develop a large offshore gasfield.
BP will partner with two oil firms with close links to the Trump administration to develop the second phase of the Loran gasfield, in one of the first large-scale foreign investments in Venezuela since the US ousted its leader Nicolás Maduro in January.
The London-listed oil company holds a licence to develop the field alongside a Qatari company owned by the Al-Khayyat brothers, the Syrian-born billionaires working with Ivanka Trump, the president’s daughter, and her husband, Jared Kushner, to build a controversial multibillion-dollar resort in Albania.
BP will also work alongside the overseas investment arm of UAE’s national oil company run by the industry minister, Sultan Al Jaber, who in 2025 promised Trump that the Gulf state would grow its investments in the US energy sector more than sixfold to $440bn (£325bn) within a decade.
The deal makes BP one of the first large-scale international oil firms to return to Venezuela after the rival Shell secured a licence to develop the first phase of the Loran field earlier this summer. Caracas is also in talks over oil projects with the Italian oil company Eni.
Meg O’Neill, BP’s chief executive, described the licence as “an important step forward” in the company’s collaboration with Caracas, which “reflects the progress we have made together”.
BP is one of a handful of European oil firms that have returned to the basin since Trump called for foreign oil companies to invest “at least $100bn” to help rebuild and tap Venezuela’s oil resources after capturing the country’s former president.
The US oil companies ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips have begun scouting opportunities in Venezuela, but have been slower to play a role in its fossil fuel revival after the Latin American country nationalised the industry in 2007. Chevron remained in the country as a minority partner to Venezuela’s state oil company and has continued to produce crude.
BP’s licence was awarded almost four months after it agreed to work with the Venezuelan government to explore potential gas development. It was also one of the first big agreements struck by O’Neill, a US-born former ExxonMobil executive, in her first month at the helm.
O’Neill said: “BP has a longstanding presence in the region and deep experience developing major gas resources. Together, these agreements provide a strong foundation to progress Venezuela’s offshore gas potential and unlock the next phase of development.”
Venezuela is believed to have the largest oil reserves of any country in the world, and in the late 1990s produced more than 3.5m barrels of a oil a day as one of the top 10 crude producers in the world. However, a quarter of a century of neglect, underinvestment and corruption have erodedits oil industry and caused output to fall to roughly 1m barrels a day.
In the months since the Trump administration seized control of Venezuela’s oil industry, oil output has climbed to 1.2m barrels a day, allowing exports to US refineries to reach their highest level since 2019.

Kenya bids to host 2029 World Athletics Championships
- Published
Kenya has submitted an official bid to host the 2029 World Athletics Championships as it seeks to become the first African nation to stage the sport's flagship event.
Nairobi faces rival bids from London, Rome and Munich, with a decision by World Athletics expected next month.
Athletics Kenya said its "robust" bid is backed by the country's government and presents a "compelling case" to bring the championships to the continent.
"The government has committed its full support to the bid, ensuring the necessary organisational framework, security measures and modern infrastructure required to host a world-class global showpiece," a statement added.
BBC Sport Africa understands that Kasarani Stadium, which has a capacity of 48,000, would be the intended venue.
Kenya has a long and decorated history in athletics, especially middle- and long-distance running, and boasts 72 World Championship and 38 Olympic gold medals.
Seventeen current world records are held by Kenyans across track and road events, including both men's and women's marathons.
The Kenyan team finished second in the overall medal table at last year's World Championships in Tokyo, with seven golds among their 11 podium finishes.
Kenya has previously hosted the 2007 World Cross Country Championships in Mombasa, the World Under-18 Championships in Nairobi in 2017 and the World U20 Championships in the capital in 2021.
Nairobi also staged the 2010 African Athletics Championships at Nyayo National Stadium.
Kenya failed with a bid for the 2025 World Championships, but winning the rights to stage the 2029 edition would be another big step for the East African country on the international sporting scene.
It is set to co-host next year's Africa Cup of Nations football tournament alongside neighbours Tanzania and Uganda.
In May, Botswana became the first African nation to host the World Athletics Relays when they took place in Gaborone.

O'Connor secures European gold in heptathlon
- Published
Kate O'Connor said her late grandmother "would have been jumping for joy" as the Ireland athlete won gold in the heptathlon at the European Championships in Birmingham.
The Newry-born 25-year-old entered the final event, the 800m, with a 51-point lead on nearest challenger Emma Oosterwegel of the Netherlands.
O'Connor needed to finish within 3.4 seconds of Oosterwegel to seal overall victory and did just that, with the Dutchwoman winning the race in 2:10.87 as O'Connor - in third behind Sveva Gerevini of Italy - clocked 2:11.74.
It meant that O'Connor came top with 6,751 points - a national record - with Oosterwegel taking silver on 6,713 and Netherlands' Sofie Dokter claiming bronze on 6,664.
This success builds on the gold O'Connor won at the Commonwealth Games for Northern Ireland in July and silver at last year's World Championships.
"A couple of years ago, I probably wouldn't have thought this would happen to me," O'Connor told RTE Sport.
"It's been a long two years. I know there's been medals [won], but there is an increase in pressure with every competition, so each has been different to try and navigate that and this competition has been no different. It's been difficult from start to finish and I didn't have it easy for a second.
"This year has been really tough from outside - my granny dies earlier this year and I don't think I give my dad enough credit, but it hit home for him and the way he turned up to training day-in and day-out...
"This is my dream, but it's his dream too and I have to dedicate this medal to my granny because she was both of our biggest fans and would have been jumping for joy if she was here."
'The most nerve-racking 800m of my life'
O'Connor entered day two in third place after four events, 42 points behind overnight leader Adrianna Sulek-Schubert, after personal bests in the 100m hurdles (13.30secs) and 200m (23.79) on Friday. She also matched her best of 1.86m in the high jump and threw 13.96m in the shot put.
Her personal best form continued in the long jump on Saturday morning with a leap of 6.55m, and a throw of 50.16m in the javelin took her overall total to 5,812 points.
That was 51 ahead of Oosterwegel who had moved into second with Dokter third as Poland's Sulek-Schubert dropped to seventh after a disappointing start to the day.
It all came down to the 800m on Saturday evening and O'Connor raced into an early lead before Oosterwegel took the initiative, but the Dundalk St Gerard's AC athlete remained on her shoulder as Gerevini then mounted a charge.
While Oosterwegel passed the Italian to win the race, O'Connor was within a second which was enough to claim a second gold medal in a matter of weeks.
"That was the most nerve-racking 800 of my life," O'Connor said.
"I had a job to do and I know I've had quite a few jobs to do over these last few days - some I've executed and some I haven't.
"I was so nervous before that run, but when I hear cheers like that for me [from the Irish support] going around those two laps, there was no way I was going to let that gold medal slip through my fingers.
"I did want to win the race, but with 50 metres to go I knew I had enough in me to stay within the three seconds and I just wanted to leave here injury-free and with a gold medal around my neck."
'Important I finished' - Johnson-Thompson
Great Britain's Katarina Johnson-Thompson finished last in the first 800m heat to be 21st overall.
The 33-year-old Olympic silver medallist came into the competition after competing just once - at a shot put event in Loughborough in May - since claiming bronze at last year's World Championships in Tokyo.
Johnson-Thompson, the world champion in 2019 and 2023, entered Saturday 324 points off the pace in 16th and continued to struggle.
"It is obviously far from my best," Johnson-Thompson told BBC Sport.
"Not the competition I would have wanted, but in a way it is. I finished.
"As a heptathlete it is not easy to come into a competition not in shape. You can't get knocked out in a heat and go home. It was important to me that I finished. I wanted to do it for them [coaching team and physiotherapist] as we worked so hard to be here.
"I have been coming here since English schools. I have been coming here a long time and I have been an athlete for a long time. It has been great to experience the stadium."
Her GB team-mate Jade O'Dowda finished 13th with 6,191 points after a fifth-place finish in heat one of the 800m.
Coscoran claims 1500m bronze
Andrew Coscoran secured a fourth medal for Ireland in Birmingham with bronze in the 1500m.
The Dubliner dropped to seventh at one stage in a thrilling race, but managed to find another kick to surge into third with a time of 3:36.24 for his first major outdoor medal, edging GB's Jake Heyward into fourth.
Stefan Nillessen of the Netherlands took gold with Sweden's Samuel Pihlstrom claiming silver.
"That's a product of a lot of work over the years," Coscoran told RTE Sport.
"A lot of strength work, a lot of speed work - it eventually paid off. I've been working so hard for this for so long."

Thomas's phone alarm buzzes at 9:30 pm -- it's time for the aspiring bodybuilder to start injecting himself in the stomach with several banned peptides.
He takes vials from his refrigerator of GHK-Cu, which he tells AFP will give him "beautiful skin", and Retatrutide, which will help him "feel less hungry".
After adding a liquid to reconstitute the synthetic peptides, he disinfects the syringes and shoots both into his lower abdomen.
Thomas, whose name has been changed, takes GHK-Cu daily and Retatrutide three times a week.
"It takes a little organisation, but it's become a routine," said Thomas, who goes to the gym almost every day.
He is one of a growing number of people attempting to "optimise" themselves by using peptides, a class of substances being widely promoted online by influencers, celebrities and the wellness industry.
Viral social media posts claim peptides can offer a range of seemingly miraculous benefits including glowing skin, stronger muscles, deeper sleep, a more alert mind -- and even provide an avenue to prevent ageing.
However experts warn there is little evidence to support these claims, and that because these peptides have not been studied properly, they can pose serious health risks.
That is why these peptides remain banned in many countries, including in France where Thomas lives.
In the United States, however, a panel recommended loosening restrictions on a range of peptides last month.
The decision outraged many medical experts, who accused Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. -- an avowed fan and user of peptides -- of packing the panel with people who have strong ties to the peptide industry.
Very real health risks
Peptides are short chains of amino acids that assemble to form proteins, which are the body's building blocks.
They occur naturally in the body, helping dictate processes such as repairing tissue.
Peptides reproduced in a lab are the active ingredients in many common medications including insulin and GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.
However unauthorised forms of synthetic peptides sold online have increasingly been promoted by influencers and gyms promising a more effective workout.
Thomas was already using steroids when he was introduced to peptides six months ago.
Along with GHK-Cu and Retatrutide, he sometimes injects himself with Selank for help with anxiety and BPC-157, which promises to more quickly repair soft tissue such as ligaments.
Because these peptides are not authorised for sale in France, there are no official guidelines for how to use them.
In online discussion forums such as Reddit and Discord, communities of mostly men exchange advice on how much and how often they should inject themselves.
"You read the studies, you look at the lab tests, and you see all the positive effects," said Thomas, who believes that the risks are "rare and not serious".
Self-experimentation 'worthless'
However neuroscientist Armelle Rancillac at French research institute INSERM warned that knowledge on how to use these peptides remains limited because they "have often not been tested on humans".
Earlier this year, INSERM said that "no large-scale, randomised controlled clinical trial has confirmed" the promised benefits of peptides, warning that some pose "very real health risks".
"We are not giving research enough time to prove its worth," Rancillac emphasised, adding that" scientifically worthless" accounts of self-experimentation were being given too much credence.
Numerous nations have reported people being hospitalised after using peptides. In June, Australia's government reported six cases of acute liver injury linked to products labelled Retatrutide.
It is difficult to determine how many people are using peptides, but the recent increase to exposure is enough to "raise alarm", Fabien Ohl, a sports sociologist at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland, told AFP.
Ohl criticised the "biological view" being pushed online that the human body is "capital" to be exploited by taking chemical substances to improve one's physical appearance.
For example, one website selling peptides promised to provide "the chemical architecture for those seeking absolute biological optimisation".
Self-proclaimed experts online also sell advice vowing to help men "optimise" their physique.
Ohl criticised this view of masculinity as problematic, warning it normalised an idea of "the biological male who is potentially more violent and aggressive".

Students protesting against alleged job and exam irregularities have demanded Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren's resignation, accusing Congress and JMM of playing politics.
According to a report by news agency PTI, the students have also demanded that Congress withdraw support from the JMM-led coalition if the Jharkhand CM does not listen to them.
The protesters announced on Saturday that they will burn effigies of Soren and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on August 16. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch also said that it will gherao the CM's residence on August 20.
Deep Dive
The students have been protesting over alleged irregularities in examinations conducted by the JPSC and JSSC. They were demanding cancellation of the JSSC-CGL examination.
Hemant Soren's assurance
Hemant Soren, on Saturday, assured that the state government was working to ensure transparency in examinations, especially those conducted by bodies such as the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) and the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC).
"For me, the youth of the state are very important to me and their faith in us. We have decided to bring changes in the system. Transparent examination will be ensured," Soren said while addressing the gathering at a state-level Independence Day celebration.
He said that the state government has initiated "Chhatron Ki Baat - Chhatron Ke Sath" and sought their suggestions to improve the education system. He said that students' contributions remain crucial to establishing a "good education system".
The Jharkhand CM told the youth to have faith in the state government and assured that "talent will not be allowed to go to waste due to mafia". He also said that transparent examinations will be ensured in the future.
"I want to urge the youth that their dreams will be protected. I want to assure that talent will not be allowed to go to waste due to the mafia. This is a serious challenge before the nation. For me, the youth of the state are very important to me and their faith on us. We have decided to bring changes in the system. Transparent examination will be ensured," Soren said.
Congress leader backs Soren
Congress leader Rajesh Thakur Hemant Soren's remarks on alleged irregularities in the JPSC-JSSC recruitment process, saying the Chief Minister had acknowledged the issue and assured students that steps would be taken to address it.

The display is gorgeous. Excellent touchpad and backlit keyboard. Decent battery life and performance. Charges from both sides. 16-GB model available, unlike MacBook Neo.
TIRED
8 GB of RAM in base model is just not enough. No headphone jack.
It’s hard to talk about the new Dell XPS 13 without mentioning the MacBook Neo. To say it takes inspiration from the choices of its rival would be an understatement—whether that’s the type of processor, the quality of the display, or the amount of memory.
But don’t think that’s a bad thing. The Dell XPS 13 feels different from other Windows laptops you can buy for $700 (or $900 for the better configuration), and a lot of that is for the better. I have some beef with this laptop's starting configuration, but I also can’t deny what makes it so compelling and unique, even among the very best laptops you can buy.
Incredible Value
The MacBook Neo did one thing very well: translate what people love about MacBooks into a $700 package (or $600 at the time it was announced). In terms of the things you can touch and feel, the MacBook Neo is every bit as premium-feeling as a MacBook Air. The materials used in the chassis, the quality of the keyboard and trackpad, and the caliber of the display—none of it has the “budget device” stink. There's more to the story of the MacBook Neo than that, but you can tell it’s how Apple made decisions on which features to cut or compromise on.
Unlike nearly every Windows laptop selling for under $1,000, the Dell XPS 13 takes that same approach. Even the base configuration comes with a 2560 x 1600-resolution touch display with a 120-Hz refresh rate, up to 427 nits, and excellent color reproduction. The touchpad is glass and feels excellent to use. In terms of build quality, it’s top-tier. It’s made out of aluminum, and there’s no flexing to be heard of in the chassis. It opens with one finger, and the hinge doesn’t wobble. The bezels around the display are tiny, giving it a very modern look. It’s also incredibly thin at just half an inch thick, matching the MacBook Neo. That’s all very attractive stuff that makes a strong first impression when handling the device for the first time.
Here are some things the new Dell XPS 13 has that the Neo doesn’t:
A touchscreen display
A 120-Hz refresh rate
A backlit keyboard
Two up-to-date, 10-Gbps USB ports (one on each side!)
Support for two 4K monitors (or three if the lid is closed)
Fast storage speed
The one thing it’s missing is a headphone jack. The MacBook Neo includes one, and I do think that’s an unfortunate miss. But I really appreciate that Dell didn’t skimp on port quality. There’s one USB-C port on each side of the device, both of which can support a 4K display simultaneously at 60 Hz, charge the device, or transfer files at 10 Gbps.
While the speakers aren’t what I’d call good, Dell did throw in two tweeters for 8 watts of output. They’re at least on par with the Neo. It's the same story with the 1080p webcam. The addition of an IR camera for Windows Hello login is appreciated.
So, with all that, you might be wondering how Dell is getting away with selling the XPS 13 for a starting price of $700. There's a catch, as always.
More Memory Please
Dell made two significant compromises to reduce the price of the XPS 13. First, it uses a lower-powered Intel processor, the Core 5 320. Dell is surely saving money on this six-core chip, but to my surprise, I was impressed by this modest little piece of silicon. The XPS 13 is one of the first laptops to use this chip, which is part of the new Intel Wildcat Lake line. There are some other laptops coming out with this chip, meant to compete with the Apple A18 Pro used in the MacBook Neo and the Qualcomm Snapdragon X. The Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i is one such option, which uses the Intel Core 7 350, but as a 16-inch laptop, it's hardly a competitor to the highly compact XPS 13.
But really, there’s plenty of performance here for what the device is intended to be used for. The Core 5 320's raw single-core performance and graphics aren’t as strong as the A18 Pro, but in terms of multicore performance, it’s much more powerful. Then, there's the battery life. You're not getting quite as much as the MacBook Neo, but I was satisfied being able to stay away from the outlet all day and still last 15 hours in local video playback.
Memory is the other major area of compromise, and it’s where my concerns lie. The $700 model starts with only 8 GB of RAM, which is what I tested. This is rare these days. You’d have to be shopping in the sub-$500 category to find an 8-GB Windows laptop, which puts the $700 Dell XPS 13 in perspective. It’s a more premium laptop than you could ever find at that price in terms of build quality, display, trackpad, and keyboard. But it’s actually quite expensive for the amount of memory you get. Fortunately, Dell includes 512 GB of storage in all the models, which is also an important consideration when evaluating the price. While it was originally stated that the device would be configurable up to 1 TB of storage, right now you're maxed out at 512 GB.
But maybe you’re wondering whether you really need 16 GB of RAM. After all, five years ago, it was the default on laptops at this price. I was curious how well an 8-GB model could handle multitasking. Outside of the MacBook Neo, I haven’t used an 8-GB laptop in a long time, as even budget-level Windows machines have come with 16 GB of RAM over the past few years.
The RAM limitation was much worse than I even expected. Performance generally starts to slow when you’re using 80 percent of the available memory. At idle, with no open applications, Windows 11 was using well over 80 percent of memory due to background processes. Ending the background tasks that Microsoft Edge is always running brought that down to 70 to 75 percent, but Search alone was taking somewhere between 150 and 190 megabytes of memory at all times. That’s not Dell’s fault, but there’s a reason Microsoft has been pushing for broader acceptance of 16 GB of RAM as a base. More AI functionality means more background tasks running at all times, which drastically eats up your available memory.
Ten tabs in Chrome put this dangerously close to maxing out the memory. You get spikes up to over 95 percent at times. As you can imagine, getting the Dell XPS 13 to use up nearly 100 percent of the available memory took almost no effort at all. Just play one YouTube video in the background while keeping a handful of browser tabs open. A laptop that feels sluggish with just a few browser tabs open is acceptable for a laptop that costs $300. But it’s questionable, given that Dell is selling this device for $700. Regardless of how pretty and portable the design is, I would only recommend this version of the laptop for those with fairly minor computing needs. You don't want this if you're using it for most of your day.
That wasn’t quite my verdict, however, about the MacBook Neo. And I promise: That’s not because I’m biased against Windows. Apple has taken a lot of flak over the years for suggesting that 8 GB of RAM on a Mac is equivalent to 16 GB on Windows. That’s an exaggeration, but it is true that it takes a bit more to slow down the MacBook Neo. I pulled up the same exact series of tabs in Google Chrome, and the Neo experienced less lag and choppiness. Neither is meant for professionals, but it's worth mentioning since Dell is trying to position the XPS 13 directly against the MacBook Neo.
There's Good News
Here’s the upside: Unlike Apple, Dell does sell a 16-GB model. It’s a $200 increase, but it takes the XPS 13 from being disappointing to something incredibly solid. I can’t, in good faith, recommend that most people buy the $699 model that comes with only 8 GB of RAM. But as a $900 laptop with 16 GB of RAM, the Dell XPS 13 is excellent. In fact, it just might be the best laptop you can buy under $1,000. It’s $100 more than the MacBook Neo with 512 GB of storage, but it’s the superior laptop in nearly every aspect you can measure.
None of my favorite Windows laptops under $1,000 can really compete. That includes the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x, HP OmniBook 5 14, Asus Zenbook A14, and the Dell 14 Plus. Some of those are cheaper or more powerful than the base Dell XPS 13, but none are more compelling than the 16-GB variant. So, yes, the XPS 13 is fantastic, and you should absolutely buy it—just not the 8-GB version.

There is a lot of excitement and some trepidation among The X-Files fans about Ryan Coogler’s reboot for Hulu, currently in production. While we’re waiting, Hulu just released Chris Carter’s revamped (and R-rated) director’s cut of the 2008 standalone spinoff film The X-Files: I Want to Believe, distinguishable from its predecessor with a slightly different title: The X-Files: I Want to Believe–Vrach Frankenshteyn.
(Minor spoilers below but no major reveals.)
I Want to Believe received mixed reviews at its release and didn’t exactly light up the box office, but it still grossed $68 million against its $30 million budget. By 2015, the project led to the return of The X-Files as a limited-run TV series, with the six-episode season 10 debuting in 2016. Mulder and Scully were reunited 14 years after the events of season 9 as the FBI reopened the X-Files under Assistant Director Walter Skinner (Mitch Pileggi). The response was strong enough to warrant a follow-up ten-episode season in 2018, focusing on Mulder and Scully’s search for their missing son, William.
So one could hardly call I Want to Believe a failure. I quite enjoyed the film, but I always had a niggling sense that something was missing. That suspicion was confirmed when Carter made an appearance on David Duchovny’s podcast last summer and revealed that the studio had insisted he cut numerous scenes to get the desired PG-13 rating. Carter also hinted that a director’s cut was in the offing. “I made it too scary,” Carter told Duchovny of his original vision. “Now I have a chance to go back and make the scary movie that I always intended.”
Originally slated for a June release on Disney+, I Want to Believe–Vrach Frankenshteyn eventually moved to Hulu with an August 14 release. It’s largely the same film as in 2008, just rejiggered to emphasize the stronger horror aspects that Carter originally envisioned. Per the official premise:
When a group of women is mysteriously abducted, it becomes a case right out of The X-Files. Years after walking away from the FBI, Fox Mulder and Dana Scully are pulled back from the shadows when a federal agent vanishes without a trace. In a case you’d never see on TV, their only lead is a disgraced, defrocked priest claiming to have horrific psychic visions of the crime. Forced to confront the ghosts of their past, the partners must navigate a chilling winter landscape and an even darker human monstrosity. The truth of these crimes is out there somewhere… and it will take Mulder and Scully to find it.
Ars Technica caught up with Carter to learn more.

Ars Technica: The original series always had some elements of horror. I’m curious about why you wanted to make a feature film that was more overtly horror with I Want to Believe.
Chris Carter: We certainly mined the horror genre over and over. The show always works at the intersection of science and science fiction. The original inspiration for this movie was that I read about a doctor who had done a head transplant from one monkey to another monkey’s body, and he’d done it successfully. Immediately I said, “That’s an X-File. I’ve got to tell that story.”
Of course, I wanted to tell it with human beings. So I flew to Cleveland, Ohio, where this doctor was, and he told me how he did it. It was successful, but ultimately the monkey died. But then I started thinking, “Well, maybe this is a way to live forever.” If you could transplant your head onto a younger person’s body, you could possibly keep doing that until something went wrong.
There’s this tech-bro fascination with living forever right now. So this story is as relevant now as it was back then. It’s a great time to tell this story. And I got to go back and revisit something that I was unable to make the way I wanted to make it, due to studio executives who really didn’t know the show. I had promised them I’d make a PG-13 movie because I thought, “That’s what I make on TV every week.” But it turns out that both the executives and the MPA, the people who do the ratings, are less permissive with a PG-13 movie than network television was with horror.
Ars Technica: There’s more to your director’s cut than just restoring a few deleted scenes. You’ve done a full re-edit.
Chris Carter: I worked with two different editors, people I respect and I’ve worked with before who weren’t involved with it all originally. I asked them to watch the movie and help me to refine the cut and make it the scary movie that I originally intended to make. It was heroic on their part. The movie was originally edited by an Academy Award winner, and so coming in and basically re-editing his vision took some courage.
That said, I think the editors alone, just in the way they re-approached the movie, really helped it. I gave them the reins early on, and then when they gave those cuts back to me, that’s when I started to work on it. They added material, they took out material, they restructured material. I wanted to make a good, scary movie. The [2008] movie was a relationship movie for Mulder and Scully that happened to have an X-Files case. The weighting was wrong, and I wanted to remaster that.

Ars Technica: Vrach Frankenshteyn is Russian for Victor Frankenstein. You dabbled with that theme in the series occasionally as well. What keeps drawing you back to that particular well?
Chris Carter: Creating life anew, breathing life into something that is inert, is fascinating to me. That story just fascinates me. The Mary Shelley story is much different than the original Frankenstein movie. They didn’t use lightning bolts to bring the creature to life. It was much more like an X-Files story. I’ve always drawn on my love of that story. Even if it’s not as pointedly like The Postmodern Prometheus, that science lives and breathes in several places in The X-Files.
Ars Technica: For many fans, Mulder and Scully will always be the beating heart of The X-Files. What makes them such an enduring couple, even if they are not always technically “together”?
Chris Carter: Scully being a scientist and Mulder being a believer in the paranormal, and that they agree to disagree wonderfully—it’s part of the nature of their relationship. I think it’s their mutual respect for one another. That, for me, is the ideal man-woman relationship. It feels inevitable. It feels destined. I have that relationship with my wife. I believe in those connections, and I believe that everyone has a path. It’s just figuring out what path to take. Sometimes the path presents itself and you can’t see it. But with Mulder and Scully, they found their paths, and they’re traveling them together for better or worse.
Ars Technica: Back in 2008, you said that if I Want to Believe did well, there was a third X-Files film you were eager to make. Is that still ticking away in the back of your mind?
Chris Carter: It is ticking away in the back of my mind. If you watch the two reboots, there are four episodes [collectively] called “My Struggle.” They are the bookends for each of those series. They ended up in a place where people either loved me or hated me—when Scully revealed that she was pregnant. That is part of a bigger story, and I want to tell that story sometime. Right now, I think everyone’s focus is more on the Ryan Coogler reboot, and I don’t want to do anything to get in the way of that. I respect him, admire him, and want to see his vision. The story that I want to tell, if it is told—and I sure hope it will be—will be apart from that, but we certainly can’t ignore it.
Ars Technica: Did you envision when you created The X-Files that the series would become such a cultural touchstone for so many people?
Chris Carter: No, I didn’t. I was sitting alone in my mid-30s. I’m working in Hollywood. I’ve been hired to create TV shows. I love movies like the Sherlock Holmes movie Murder by Decree. I love Kolchak: The Night Stalker. I have all these things that are inspiring me. I put them all together into a—call it a kiln. And I fired the kiln, and I opened it up and it’s The X-Files. I had never in my wildest dreams believed that I’d be sitting here talking to you today about The X-Files, that there’d be a Lego set coming out, that it would’ve changed people’s lives.
At the 30th reunion anniversary in Minneapolis, I had 12-year-old, 10-year-old kids come up and say they love the show. And I have to think to myself, “Your parents probably didn’t even know each other when the show first aired.”
I’ll tell you another story that is near and dear to me. My wife and I were running on the beach not long ago; we run for 10 minutes, and we walk for a minute. When we started walking in that minute, I look up and I see an image that I recognize immediately. I start walking toward this young woman in her early 20s who’s wearing a graduation gown and holding her mortarboard in her hand. On the top of the cap, it’s got an image of Mulder and Scully. And it says, “The future is out there.” I say, “I know that image.” She said, “Oh yeah, it’s Mulder and Scully from The X-Files.” And I said, “I know, I know. I wrote that show.”
It was a wonderful moment. She didn’t grow up with the show, she found the show. That’s the mind-blowing thing to me: it inspired her enough to put it on her graduation gown and cap. That kind of thing you can never imagine when you sit down to create something.
The X-Files: I Want to Believe–Vrach Frankenshteyn is now streaming on Disney+ and Hulu.
