What I Saw in Sinaloa
The U.S. is trying to destroy Mexican cartels. But so far, a turf war has only deepened.
Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.
Last Tuesday night, I was eating sushi with a Mexican police chief in downtown Culiacán, a city that had momentarily flickered back to life amid a bloody cartel turf war. At the table next to us was a birthday party. The police chief ordered a salmon roll. Through the window, I could see groups of families and friends walking on the sidewalk, past car dealerships and strip malls, after months of self-imposed lockdown.
Among them were three influencers who pulled up to a KFC down the street. They were dressed as food-delivery workers, carrying insulated bags on their backs, joking with one another and livestreaming everything with their phones. César Gastélum, the group’s front man, had become famous for such innocuous pranks. Even as thousands were murdered by the cartels, Gastélum, a stocky, bearded 24-year-old, posted videos of himself dancing in pajamas, dressing as a priest, sipping iced coffee. He had more than 700,000 followers on TikTok.
It was this kind of incongruity that had drawn me to Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa. The city is the center of the fiercest and most consequential battle between armed groups in Mexico, and I wanted to untangle what was behind the surge of violence. From afar, it was difficult to tell whether someone like Gastélum was proof that the mundane and the horrific could coexist here, as they have for decades across Mexico, or whether he was a symbol of something else—the way drug cartels had quietly co-opted even the city’s least likely protagonists.
At about 8 o’clock, Gastélum and his friends were recording themselves waiting for their fried-chicken orders when two men on a motorcycle drove past. “Those guys scare me,” Gastélum said. He then seemed to regain his calm, joking about his skinny jeans in front of the camera when the motorcycle returned. It stopped momentarily in front of the three young men. The driver, wearing a black helmet with a face shield, raised a gun about two feet from Gastélum’s head and fired. The livestream captured the moment of the bullet’s impact and then went dark.
Someone on the city’s ambulance team texted me when the 911 call came in, and I ran across the street to the KFC. I got to the scene as police were arriving. Gastélum’s body lay at the drive-through’s exit, a ribbon of blood streaming toward the sidewalk. A cluster of soldiers gathered nearby, some of them scrolling through Gastélum’s TikTok feed. A small group of crime photographers were taking photos and uploading videos.
“As you can see, they have killed another influencer here in Culiacán,” José Ángel Beltrán of Luz Noticias said, narrating on Facebook Live.
Culiacán, for years the axis of Mexico’s drug wars, is now the focus of a U.S. effort to demolish drug cartels—something President Trump has said he’s willing to use military force to achieve. It is in many ways an understandable target: The Sinaloa cartel, which has administered the state for decades, is responsible for trafficking millions of kilos of fentanyl, meth, and cocaine into the United States. The Justice Department has indicted both the Sinaloa governor and the Culiacán mayor for cooperating with the cartel. Several of its leaders are serving life sentences in the U.S., and others have been targeted by Mexican security forces using intelligence from the United States.
And yet, so far, these actions have only deepened the civil war between two Sinaloa-cartel factions, one run by the children and supporters of Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán (the Chapitos), and the other run by allies of Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada García (the Mayos). In 2022, there were 476 homicides in Sinaloa. In 2025, it had 1,657. Government action against organized-crime groups in Mexico has almost always had such an effect—increasing violence without significantly altering the flow of drugs into the United States. But the current Sinaloa turf war—la narcopandemia, locals call it—has created new categories of victims, far from the foot soldiers and hit men targeted in previous spasms of violence. Now influencers and content creators are recruited by cartels to distribute their messages online. And university and vocational students have been kidnapped, presumably because their skills are needed by criminal groups. Each time a young person here is killed or vanishes, there are immediate questions about whom he or she might have been working for. When drug traffickers allegedly subsidize TikTok dances, a victim’s innocence can be almost impossible to discern.
As forensic police arrived at the KFC, Beltrán told me that another TikToker had been killed a few blocks away months earlier. A fitness influencer, El Tata, was murdered while leaving a shopping center. The body of a YouTuber, El Pinky, was found showing signs that he had been gagged and bound. About a dozen other influencers in Sinaloa have been killed, kidnapped, or attacked. Each time, the Mexican government investigated whether the influencers had somehow been linked to one group and targeted by the other. Last year, an unidentified plane dropped thousands of flyers over Culiacán that accused a number of influencers and musicians of having ties to the Chapitos (Gastélum was not on the list).
Standing in front of the crime scene as the forensic police hovered around Gastélum’s body with flashlights, I asked Beltrán why he thought a goofy livestreamer would be a target in a cartel turf war.
“Did you see that he was wearing a cowboy hat?” Beltrán asked me.
Cowboy hats have become a symbol of the Mayos faction of the cartel. The implication was that Gastélum, while performing juvenile pranks, had been making a subtle nod to one group’s power. Online commenters rushed to make the same point.
Beltrán filmed one last video of Gastélum’s body as it was taken away, and then he tapped me on the shoulder. Another victim had been found half a mile away: a man shot in the city’s botanical garden after a screening of a Lady Gaga documentary. I went with him to cover it. When we got there, it was dark, and the body was lit by a streetlight. Beltrán took his phone out again and started streaming.
“Hello again, everyone,” he said. “It’s another rough night in Culiacán.”
The next day, I drove 30 minutes from downtown Culiacán to a neighborhood called Costa Rica, on the outskirts of the city. I passed several motorcyclists who had their face covered by a ski mask. These punteros, as they’re called, have for years worked as low-level informants for the cartel. Even before the fracture of Sinaloa, the cartel was famous for its capacity to monitor every inch of Culiacán. In addition to deploying the punteros, it placed hundreds of cameras across the city and set up surveillance teams in residential neighborhoods.
The Mexican government has surged hundreds of soldiers and national guardsmen across the city, ostensibly to disrupt the criminal groups who have terrorized it. But the military presence is overwhelmingly performative. On the road to Costa Rica, I watched as punteros and soldiers nonchalantly drove past one another.
I pulled up to the squat house of Marta Pérez Guzman, whose son, David Antonio Ruelas Pérez, had been kidnapped by armed men along with his classmate José Isaías Ibarra Duarte. There were 2,154 disappearances in Sinaloa last year, but the kidnapping of Ruelas, 22, and Ibarra, 23, had received more attention than most. The men were students at an aviation school in Culiacán, and many here suspected that they had been abducted to work on cartel aircraft. There was another notable fact: Ibarra is a U.S. citizen, born in Los Angeles.
His mother, Graciela Duarte Valdez, had wondered whether that would be enough to nudge the U.S. government to act. After all, Trump had articulated in Truth Social posts and Fox News interviews his desire to intervene in Mexico. She had traveled to the closest U.S. consulate, in the neighboring state of Sonora, and made her case. Not only was her son still missing, but the Mexican attorney general’s office had obtained surveillance footage of the kidnapping and showed it to her. Through tears, Duarte described seeing footage of four men who wore ski masks and carried rifles getting out of a minivan and forcing her son and Ruelas into a second car. It all took only a few seconds.
She felt abandoned by the Mexican government’s investigators, who asked questions suggesting that the boys had been working for a cartel faction before the kidnapping. When she went to the U.S. consulate, officials took notes and thanked her for coming (when I asked the State Department about the case, a spokesperson told me in a statement that it was “aware of reports of the kidnapping of a U.S. citizen in Mexico” but did not elaborate). Duarte was despairing; she knew that just a small fraction of disappeared people were later found alive in Sinaloa. One day last year, she heard that Governor Rubén Rocha Moya was visiting her neighborhood. She ran to meet him.
“Please help,” she told the governor, as she held a missing-person poster with her son’s photo and name on it. Rocha told her he would try.
A few months later, Duarte was skimming her Facebook feed for information about missing people and recovered bodies when she saw a news story that said Rocha had been indicted by the United States for colluding with the cartel. The U.S. government had acted, but she could not bring herself to see the move as productive or helpful. Rocha temporarily resigned and fled Culiacán. The Mexican government announced that it would support him until the U.S. showed more evidence of his collusion.
“All I could think was that I had begged that man for help,” Duarte said. “But of course, he did nothing. He had been working for the cartel the whole time.”
About a third of Mexico is controlled by organized criminal groups, according to a U.S.-government analysis. Culiacán—even during its most peaceful stretches—has been a prime example. The cartel presence here has never been subtle. One man in his early 20s told me that his childhood friends had been recruited to work in fentanyl labs and would return smelling like chemicals for weeks. The children of cartel kingpins enrolled in the city’s top prep schools. In one cemetery, families of deceased cartel operatives erected graves the size of suburban homes. Each time the cartel’s fractures sent the city into spirals of violence—in 2010 and 2017—they ended the same way: not with the disintegration of organized crime but with one faction emerging as the victor.
The Trump administration believes that it can avoid repeating this pattern, partially by going after Mexican politicians who support the cartel—“all the government officials that are part of the ‘Culiacán clan,’” Sara Carter, the director of the White House’s Office of National Drug Control Policy, told a journalist earlier this year. The U.S. has also continued its decades-long strategy of targeting top cartel operatives, largely by funneling intelligence to elite Mexican-military units who have conducted a number of successful operations. That partnership is deeper than it has been in years. But I didn’t meet anyone in Culiacán who believes that the strategy will reduce violence here. So far, it hasn’t reduced drug flows, either. Even officials in the Mexican government who are in favor of attacking criminal groups privately dismiss the Trump administration’s absolutist goal of eliminating cartels, given the enormous demand for drugs in the United States.
“On Day one, President Trump designated major cartels—including Sinaloa—as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, unlocking powerful sanctions, asset seizures, and enhanced prosecutorial tools to crush their operations. We will not allow cartels to profit off of poisoning our children and grandchildren,” Lauren Bis, a White House spokesperson, told me in a statement.
As César Gastélum’s body was buried last week, some of the city’s influencers posted tributes to him, as if describing a fallen comrade. “We need to take care of ourselves,” one wrote to his 2.3 million followers. Even Mexico’s president weighed in, promising to find the assailants. Duarte had followed the news. Gastélum was just a year older than her son.
But she was following another story more closely. The government had detained a dozen young alleged cartel operatives in a rural area outside Culiacán. It published photos of the boys and men, their faces blurred. Many of their T-shirts were off, revealing skinny frames. Duarte zoomed in on one of them. It was hard to tell, but he looked at least a little bit like her son.

Amid a torrent of fan-friendly news about Disney projects across the media spectrum, Disney leadership took time on the first day of the three-day D23 fan fest weekend in Anaheim for panels that offered a behind the scenes look at the Mouse House’s business strategies and vision for driving growth in the streaming era.
One of the topics tackled was how to reach next-generation Disney fans with next-generation content formats to keep the company’s many franchises relevant to Gen Alpha and beyond. Disney’s push into the booming vertical media space — aka microdramas and other shortform clips designed to be viewed on mobile phones — was discussed in detail during a session with Eric Schrier, Disney’s president of Direct-to-Consumer International Originals, Strategic Programming and Emerging Media, and Erin Teague, who is executive VP of Product Management for Disney Entertainment and ESPN.
The conversation was moderated by Jon YouShaei, a YouTube and Instagram executive turned creator and podcaster, and it also featured the perspective of Disney-centric creator Blake Silva as a panelist.
Popular on Variety
Schrier emphasized that the “Verts” push on Disney+ is a significant investment for the Mouse. The company last week unveiled a pact with TikTok designed to encourage more fans to create clips with authorized Disney IP. This is a big change for the company that has historically vigorously enforced its copyright and trademark rights.
	“We’ve always looked at making film and television in very finite formats. Half hours, hours, feature
length films. And now you can tell any story. Creators are just storytellers,” Schrier said. “We’ve always talked about our creators before there were actually creators. The creator of ‘Paradise,’ Dan Fogelman, he’s a creator. We talk about them as creators. And so they’re just different types of storytellers. So how do we bring those stories to Disney+? How do we complement what we already have on platform? And it’s early days, but we’re really excited about this next generation of storytellers that are out there that are into Disney+.”
	
Teague pointed to examples that demonstrate how smart promotion and word-of-mouth via social media helps drive viewership to Disney’s biggest investments in TV and film.
“There will never be a replacement for that long-form original content but what is interesting is the way that it is now being supplemented by the shorter form analysis, the clips,” Teague said. As with live game coverage for sports, she said, “the additional commentary and analysis around the game is just as interesting. And so the ways that we can merge those experiences to give people exactly what they want, when they want it in a split second, I think, is the challenge.”
Silva asserted that most experienced creators who hone their focus on key brands and franchises know how to plug themselves in to the company’s priorities. He said the TikTok deal and Disney+’s embrace of creator content has been invigorating for the Disney-verse.
	“We look at social media and clips going viral, about movies or scenes from movies all the time,” Silva said. “So imagine how that would translate and convert when they’re already in the app, to watch
it immediately. I really believe in the creator to talent pipeline. It’s really exciting to think how could this create the next Mister Rogers, my idol.”
Teague underscored that fans expect to be part of the action in ways that were unimaginable to their parents and grandparents.
“Next generations of fans are expecting more from their entertainment experience. They want to be a part of the story. They want to put themselves in the story. They want interactivity. They want to have more agency in the storytelling experience with the democratization of creativity,” Teague said.
Teague also took part in a session on how ESPN’s increasingly global sports profile is helping Disney find subscribers and fans.
“ESPN is effectively synonymous with sports as a brand. So diehard sports fans know and love ESPN and have forever, that will never change. We will never stop serving the diehard, loyal sports fan because that’s our base,” Teague said during the session moderated by Joe Earley, Co-President of Direct to Consumer for Disney Entertainment.
“But two trends are happening. One, the internet and native generations. Gen Alpha, Gen Z, etc. They are now expecting more from their sports fandom and their sports experience,” Teague said. “The technology is evolving and we’re thinking about how to also superserve the casual sports fan, because that fandom is equally as real. And it turns out it looks very similar to Disney fandom. And so we’re thinking about this consistently across our product experiences.”
Freddy Rolón, ESPN’s head of global sports and talent office, reeled off the latest stats for ESPN’s reach with 43 linear networks in more than 130 countries and territories, and it is available on Disney+ in more than 100 markets. For the month of June, ESPN reached 640 million digital and social users.
	“We reach more casual fans, we reach more female fans on Disney+ and then on the flip side, ESPN
brings to Disney+ a credibility about sports, authenticity about sports, and then really a recurring reason for fans to come back to the platform. Not just for the games, but for the game around the game,” Rolón said. “When we think about all those platforms, they work in concert. They’re not necessarily individual. We think about the game on Disney+, the coverage, and the social media platforms all working together to reach fans with information when they want it.”
Jo Fox, senior VP of marketing for ESPN, said the tighter connection to Disney+ as the platform has expanded significantly across Europe, Middle East, Asia and Latin America has been hugely beneficial. ESPN has made the strategic decision to make key programs available via Disney+ even for subscribers who don’t get the bundle.
“We use the Disney+ platform and their audience, who might be different to our ESPN core audience, and we can talk to them more directly and get them more enthused about sports and ultimately engaging with Disney+ and ESPN as well,” Fox said. “So as an example of that, we will have select college football games and ‘College GameDay’ unlocked on Disney+ coming up. Because the mascots, the pageantry, the tribal nature of it, the excitement around it. It seems like an amazing sport to be able to unlock some of these select games on Disney+ and talk to this new fan base.”
Earley also moderated a session on Disney+’s international content strategy for local-language production with Schrier and Carol Choi, Disney Asia Pacific’s executive VP of Integrated Marketing & APAC Original Strategy.
It’s a balancing act of leveraging the platform’s worldwide reach with the need to keep subscribers engaged on a consistent basis. Local-language content has long been seen as key to reducing subscriber churn rates.
“What we’re really looking to do is tell stories for local audiences and be hyper-local. We call it local for local. So we make French shows for France, Spanish shows for Spain, or Brazilian shows for Brazil. And we do that all over the world,” Schrier said. “We’re going to be increasing that significantly to have local audiences have something that expresses their culture and their sensibility. And what’s happened organically out of that local for local strategy is that those stories are now traveling back to other parts of the world.”
Korea and Japan are prime areas of focus for Disney+ and local-language production.
“Our local creators and storytellers really appreciate the ability for them to tell stories that are authentic to the local cultures with the support of people who’ve been telling stories like their whole career, like Eric and his team,” Choi said. “With that guidance, we’ve been very fortunate to have produced a number of hits, as well as having audiences outside of APAC discover these stories and content.”
Choi pointed to recent buzzy Disney+ series including “Tempest,” “Perfect Crown” and “A Shop For Killers.” Earley added, “Some of those Korean dramas put up numbers that rival or even exceed some of the global originals as well.”
(Pictured top: Disney’s Eric Schrier, Carol Choi and Joe Earley speak at D23 in Anaheim on Aug. 14.)

Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha (JLKM) leader Devendra Nath Mahto, who has been undergoing treatment at Ranchi Sadar Hospital, has slammed the police for stopping him when he tried to take part in the Tiranga Yatra organised by the protesting students on the occasion of 80th Independence Day on August 15, 2026.
Mr. Mahto, who is leading the faction of JPSC-JSSC Nyay Manch, has been on a hunger strike for the past 14 days in support of the demands raised by the students over alleged irregularities in the recruitment examination in Jharkhand.
Also Read :Independence Day LIVE updates
When the police did not allow him to leave the room where he was admitted, an altercation took place between police personnel and Mr. Mahto. The JLKM leader alleged that he sustained an injury to his chest while being stopped and jostled by the police. Mr. Mahto also alleged that the police assaulted and beat up his associates who came to rescue him.
He also shared the footage of the altercation on his official social media account.
“For 14 days, I have been on a hunger strike, and today the police tried to push and forcefully stop me along with my companions. The police also assaulted my people who were with me. Despite being hungry for several days, I stand firm for my rights and the voice of the people. They cannot silence our voice by stopping us in this manner,” Mr. Mahto wrote on X.
Police action ‘raises serious questions’
He further said, “Despite being on a hunger strike for 14 days, the way the entire police force came down aggressively just for expressing a desire to hoist the national flag and participate in the Tiranga Yatra raises several serious questions on this day of Independence. During this time, my people were also brutally beaten and thrashed to the ground. Is this the free India we gained from the sacrifices of Lord Birsa Munda and Bhagat Singh? Is this the form of India that Subhas Chandra Bose, Khudiram Bose, Chandrashekhar Azad, Mahatma Gandhi, and Baba Saheb Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar dreamed of?”
After the alleged assault, Mr. Mahto, along with his people, sat down on dharna right outside his room.
“Until I am allowed to leave from here, I will keep sitting right here. I will not even get my treatment done, and I will stay here to raise my concern. My fight is for the rights of the people and for justice. They (Police) cannot silence my voice by stopping me,”Mr. Mahto said.
Later, he spoke to his party supremo and MLA Tiger Jairam Mahto over a video call and narrated his ordeal, how he was stopped by the police and allegedly assaulted.
“The answer will be sought from the government on the floor of the House. On the 80th Independence Day in free India, why was a protester, who has been on a hunger strike for 14 days, prevented from hoisting the flag? Why was he stopped from joining the Tiranga Yatra? And why is he not being given the freedom to seek treatment as per his own wish? The answer to all these questions will be sought from the government on the floor of the house,” Mr. Mahto said in the post later in the day.
Mr. Mahto was highlighted earlier when educationist Sonam Wangchuk spoke to him over a video call and urged him to end his fast on August 5, 2026. Also, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke had spoken to him over a video call, inquiring about the protest.
Repeated attempts to contact Ranchi Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) Rakesh Ranjan and Ranchi City SP Paras Rana proved futile.

The final Wish Orb in Anime Expeditions works a little differently from the others. There is no physical orb to hunt down on a map, as you instead need to complete a set of quests to unlock it. Here is everything you need to do to get Wish Orb 7 in Anime Expeditions and finish the Dragon’s Wish event.
How to Get Wish Orb 7 in Anime Expeditions
Unlike the previous Wish Orbs in Anime Expeditions, Wish Orb 7 does not have a location. You will not find it sitting somewhere in East Town or any other map. Instead, you need to complete all seven quests listed in the event menu.
- Spend 5,000 Gems
- Complete Floor 50 of Tower
- Obtain 5 Dragon equipment
- Own 3 Level 3 buildings at the Expedition Hub
- Complete any regular Challenge 6 times
- Obtain Prodigy from the East Town questline
- Obtain Prodigy (Rage) by evolving Prodigy
Some of these quests are straightforward, while others can take a little more preparation. You can use Anime Expeditions codes to get useful resources for summoning units and upgrading your loadout, which can help you finish several of these requirements faster.
If you are unsure which units are worth investing in, check our Anime Expeditions tier list before spending your resources.
How to Get Prodigy for Wish Orb 7
The Prodigy quest requires you to progress through the East Town questline. You will eventually obtain Prodigy as part of this questline, so focus on clearing the required objectives instead of trying to find the unit elsewhere.

Extreme heat, humidity, cold weather and changes in routine can make periods harder to manage. But persistent changes in cycle length, bleeding or pain should not simply be blamed on the weather; medical attention should be sought
A period arriving a few days earlier or later than expected can be unsettling, particularly during a heatwave, a spell of heavy rain or a sudden change in routine. The menstrual cycle is primarily regulated by hormonal signals between the brain and ovaries. Weather does not directly control menstruation, but extreme conditions can place physical stress on the body and affect sleep, hydration, physical activity, appetite and stress levels. These changes may, in turn, affect ovulation and the symptoms experienced around a period.
How it works
Sandhya Vasan, director and senior consultant, gynecology, SIMS Hospital, Chennai, says extreme weather can act as a physiological stressor. The body’s stress response involves hormones such as cortisol, which can affect the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian (HPO) axis that regulates ovulation and menstruation. If this hormonal signalling is disrupted, ovulation may be delayed, occur earlier or, in some cases, be skipped, resulting in a longer, shorter or irregular cycle.
The evidence linking weather directly to menstrual changes, however, remains limited. Much of the effect may come from the changes that extreme weather brings to everyday life rather than from temperature itself.
Heat can amplify symptoms
Extreme heat can make an already uncomfortable period harder to manage. Dehydration, fatigue and poor sleep can add to the physical stress of menstruation and may make cramps, headaches, dizziness and premenstrual symptoms more noticeable.
P.M. Gopinath, director of reproductive medicine, Kauvery Hospital, Vadapalani, Chennai, says heat causes blood vessels to dilate as the body attempts to lose heat. At the same time, sweating leads to fluid and electrolyte loss. Together with heat-related fatigue and disturbed sleep, these changes can make menstrual symptoms feel more intense.
Pavithra Ramakrishnan, consultant, obstetrics, gynecology and reproductive medicine, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, OMR, Chennai, says some women may notice heavier or lighter bleeding, fatigue and headaches during extreme heat. Dehydration and physical stress can also affect the timing of ovulation, potentially shifting the next period.
However, a change in bleeding should not automatically be considered a response to temperature. Persistent or significant changes require assessment for other causes.
Some women may be more vulnerable to the effects of extreme weather. These include adolescents whose cycles are still becoming regular, women with PMOS (previously PCOS) or thyroid disorders, athletes, outdoor workers and those with limited access to water and rest. Women approaching perimenopause, or those prone to migraines or low blood pressure, may also find symptoms more difficult to manage.
Cold weather effects
The relationship between cold weather and menstruation is less clear. Cold can cause blood vessels to constrict and muscles to tighten, which may make cramps feel worse for some women. Reduced physical activity during colder weather can also contribute to discomfort.
Heavy rain and flooding create a different menstrual health concern. When transport is disrupted or access to toilets, clean water and menstrual products is limited, maintaining menstrual hygiene becomes more difficult. The problem is therefore not only physical discomfort but also access to basic facilities needed to manage menstruation safely.
Humidity and hygiene
Hot and humid conditions can also increase sweat and moisture around the genital area. This can contribute to irritation, chafing and skin infections, particularly when tight synthetic clothing or damp clothes are worn for long periods.
Dr. Gopinath recommends changing menstrual products regularly, wearing breathable cotton underwear and keeping the area clean and dry. Scented products that can irritate sensitive skin should be avoided. Cloth pads should be washed thoroughly and dried completely before reuse.
Managing periods
Managing the effects of extreme weather largely involves reducing the additional physical stress on the body.
Adequate fluid intake is important, particularly during hot and humid weather. There is no single amount of water that everyone needs each day; requirements vary with temperature, physical activity and individual health. Water-rich foods such as cucumber, watermelon and citrus fruits can also contribute to fluid intake.
A balanced diet, including iron-rich foods, can help maintain energy levels, particularly for women who have heavy menstrual bleeding. Light physical activity such as walking, stretching or yoga may help with cramps. During extreme heat, strenuous exercise can be shifted to cooler parts of the day, with adequate rest and fluids.
Keeping a menstrual calendar can help distinguish an occasional change from a persistent pattern. Recording the dates of periods, duration of bleeding, flow and associated symptoms can also provide useful information during a medical consultation.
When to seek help
The most important distinction is between a temporary change during extreme weather and a persistent menstrual problem.
A period that is slightly early or late after a period of heat, poor sleep or disrupted routine may not indicate an underlying disorder. But repeated irregularity should not be explained away as a weather-related effect.
Doctors recommend medical evaluation if cycles remain irregular for about three cycles, bleeding becomes unusually heavy or pain is severe. Periods lasting more than seven days, fainting, significant dehydration, fever or foul-smelling discharge also warrant medical attention. Severe pain that does not improve with usual measures should not be ignored.
Conditions such as PMOS (previously PCOS) and thyroid disorders can cause irregular periods and abnormal ovulation independently of weather. If such conditions are suspected, appropriate evaluation and treatment may be needed.
Weather can therefore influence menstrual health, particularly by adding physical stress or worsening existing symptoms. But it should not become an easy explanation for persistent changes that warrant medical attention.

The Iran war’s mental toll on US sailors
Sailors are sounding the alarm about conditions on the USS Lincoln.
Welcome to The Logoff: The cracks are starting to show in President Donald Trump’s Iran campaign.
What’s happening? Conditions on a US warship deployed in the Middle East have grown so dire, multiple sailors have reportedly tried to go overboard (at least one did so but was rescued safely, according to CNN).
The attempts to jump overboard comes as family members of sailors are raising concerns with Democratic lawmakers about deteriorating mental health on the ship amid sanitation issues and shortages of food and basic supplies.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier has been deployed for more than 250 days, starting last November, including a stretch of more than 200 days at sea — a modern record. Its deployment was supposed to end months ago, in May, but has continued as Trump’s Iran war stretches on.
How is the administration responding? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday that reports about conditions on the Lincoln are “completely misrepresented.” Help is on the way for the Lincoln, though, with another US aircraft carrier en route to the area to replace it (according to the Wall Street Journal, the replacement was already planned, and not in response to deteriorating conditions on the Lincoln).
Why does this matter? Conditions on the Lincoln are not the only recent stumbling block for the US war with Iran. Earlier this month, we learned more about the US’s increasingly serious shortages of key offensive and defensive missiles, including THAAD and Patriot interceptors used to protect US troops and allies. On top of that, the Washington Post reported Thursday that the US has run through around a quarter of its Reaper drones, which cost tens of millions of dollars apiece.
It’s the latest example of how the math of the war is starting to slant against the US: Reaper drones and Patriot missiles are incredibly expensive, while Iran has figured out how to mass-produce attack drones on the cheap. And with no end in sight, shortages and situations like the Lincoln will only become a larger problem.
And with that, it’s time to log off…
Here’s some good news from my colleague Adam Clark Estes: As wrecked as your attention span may feel, it’s not permanently degraded. He talked with attention experts to figure out how to repair his, and how we can all do the same. You can read his full story here with a gift link — and then, for all of our brains’ sake, let’s log off. We’ll see you back here tomorrow.

Keeper Bihina stars as Cameroon upset Morocco to make Wafcon final
- Published
Michaely Bihina was the heroine as the Cameroon goalkeeper saved an extra-time penalty and three more spot-kicks in a shootout to send her side though to the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations final at the expense of host nation Morocco.
The 22-year-old pushed away Fatima Tagnaout's attempt from 12 yards in the 118th minute to ensure the game in Rabat finished 0-0 after 120 minutes.
Bihina then brilliantly kept out efforts from Kenza Chapelle, Maryame Atiq and Sakina Ouzraoui to leave the Moulay Hassan Stadium in stunned silence.
Teenage Cameroon defender Myriam Nyadjou held her nerve to secure a 3-1 win on penalties for the Central Africans.
The Indomitable Lionesses will face Malawi in Sunday's final (19:00 GMT) after the southern Africans beat Algeria 3-1 earlier on Wednesday.
Cameroon's run to the final is all the more remarkable given they were knocked out in qualifying and only progressed to the finals on the strength of their world ranking after the Confederation of African Football decided to expand the tournament to 16 teams midway through the preliminary process.
Morocco suffer heartbreak again
While the first Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) semi-final was littered with chances and incident, the late game in the capital was a far tighter affair.
Morocco created little to reflect their dominance of the ball against an organised and disciplined Cameroon side who grew in confidence in the latter stages of the second half.
The Atlas Lionesses came close to an opener in the 14th minute when Sanaa Mssoudy diverted Hanane Ait El Haj's right-wing cross against the right-hand upright, and the forward also thrashed into the side-netting on the hour mark.
A flurry of late chances came at the end of regulation time, with Imane Saoud shooting straight at Bihina, Mssoudy heading wide and Michaela Abam firing over the Morocco bar.
Abam then had a shot blocked towards the end of the first period of extra time and Morocco defender Atiq headed over in the second half.
The match's key incident came right at the end of extra time when Morocco were presented with a glorious chance to win the tie following a video assistant referee (VAR) review, with Togolese official Vincentia Amedome deciding Nyadjou had caught Ouzraoui in the face with her arm.
Ait El Haj had converted from the spot in the quarter-final win over South Africa but substitute Tagnaout assumed responsibilities and the winger's tame left-footed effort was palmed away by Bihina.
There was more to come from the Cameroon keeper, who joined Portuguese giants Benfica in February and had previously made a remarkable nine stops in her side's quarter-final upset against 10-time champions Nigeria.
Chapelle put her effort too close to Bihina but two stunning stops followed to deny Atiq and Ouzraoui.
Khadija Er-Rmichi had kept her side in the shootout by saving an effort from Grace Mendoua, but the Morocco keeper had little answer to Bihina's heroics.
A semi-final defeat comes as a big blow to Morocco, who have invested heavily in football in recent years and hired Spain's Women's World Cup winning manager Jorge Vilda in an attempt to claim a maiden continental crown.
The Atlas Lionesses were runners-up in 2022 and reached the final of the delayed 2024 Wafcon last July, but threw away a 2-0 half-time lead against Nigeria and were forced to settle for second place again.
Cameroon, meanwhile, return to the final for the first time since losing to Nigeria as tournament hosts in 2016.
The Indomitable Lionesses have lost three previous finals and coach Valentine Nguele, who only took charge in June, will need to nullify the threat of the Chawinga sisters Tabitha and Temwa when her side come up against Malawi on Sunday.
Whoever comes out on top, it will be a new name on the trophy.
On Thursday Ivory Coast take on Ghana (17:00 GMT) and Nigeria meet South Africa (20:00 GMT) in African play-offs for the chance to go into an inter-continental qualifier for the 2027 Fifa Women's World Cup.

Ukraine ramps up long-range strikes, attacks Russia's Samara industrial site
Kyiv is trying to make Russians feel the consequences of the invasion.
A large-scale Ukrainian attack struck industrial infrastructure in Russia’s southwestern Samara region Saturday, a Russian official said.
Ivan Noskov, head of the region's capital, Samara, said air defense forces had repelled a “massive” missile attack, with “localized damage” to the city’s industrial sites. He also said that medical assistance has been provided to those injured in the attack, but did not give further details.
Ukraine has stepped up its long-range aerial attacks on Russian military industries and energy facilities, aiming to cut Moscow’s revenue for the war and make Russians feel the consequences of the invasion, now in its fifth year.
Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Kyiv’s forces had carried out a strike against Samara’s Progress Center, which operates under Russian space agency Roscosmos and is involved in producing rocket technology and electronics.
He said that the strike used Ukraine’s domestically produced Flamingo missiles to hit the site, which is approximately 900 kilometers (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Zelenskyy also said Russia's Savasleyka air base, some 700 kilometers (430 miles) from the front line, had also been hit.
“Peace is needed, and this must be evident in Russia — through concrete damage to specific facilities,” Zelenskyy wrote.
While most of Ukraine’s strikes have a range of less than 200 kilometers (125 miles), its longer-range attacks have increased dramatically this year. It launched three times as many of those strikes in July as it did in January, according to data from ACLED, an independent conflict monitor. Repeatedly hitting deep into Russia has forced its military to stretch air defenses over a larger area.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Saturday that it had shot down 598 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions, as well as the Black and Azov Seas and the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.
Separately, two people, including a nine-year-old child, were wounded when a Ukrainian drone attack hit a private home in the town of Shatura in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said.
Elsewhere, a Russian strike on an apartment block in southeastern Ukraine Saturday killed a three-month-old baby and wounded 11 people, local officials said.
Drones hit the building in the town of Marhanets, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration.
Popular Reads
Meanwhile, hundreds of mourners gathered in Kyiv at a memorial ceremony dedicated to 3-year-old Dmytro Kucher and his grandparents, Halyna and Petro Kucher, who were killed by a Russian drone strike on August 8.
Multiple Russian drones destroyed the family’s home in the Brovary district, northeast of Kyiv.
An initial ceremony was held at Kyiv’s Spaskyi Lyceum, where Halyna had served as school principal for more than 20 years, before moving to a churchyard in the suburb of Zazymia, close to the former family home.
The couple’s son, Oleksandr Kucher, said that his parents had been together since the fifth grade. “They died together,” he said. “The Shahed (drone) completely tore my mother apart. We recovered only about two kilograms (about 4.4 pounds) of her remains.”
He described his 3-year-old son, Dmytro, as “our little miracle” and “the soul of our family.”
“He kept my parents, me and our entire family going,” Kucher said.
Russia's Ministry of Defense also said Saturday that it had targeted warehouses and infrastructure at the Ukrainian ports of Odesa, Izmail and Yuzhnyi.
Ukraine’s Air Force said that Russia launched 152 drones over the country Saturday, of which 124 were destroyed.

New Delhi, Aug 16: The National Testing Agency (NTA) on Sunday released the provisional answer keys for 84 subjects of the UGC-NET June 2026 examination.
In a post on X, the NTA said the challenge window is open and it will remain open from August 16 to 18 till 11:59 PM.
Candidates will have to pay a processing fee of Rs 200 per question challenged, with the last date for fee payment being August 18 till 11:59 PM, it said.
For the three remaining subjects -- English, Commerce and Sociology -- a committee was constituted to examine complaints received regarding various types of errors in the question papers, it said.
Based on the recommendations of the committee, a separate public notice concerning these three subjects will be issued later on Sunday, the NTA said.
The agency said candidates have been advised to rely only on information published on the official NTA website and its verified social media handles.
UGC-NET is conducted to determine the eligibility of candidates for the posts of Assistant Professor and admission to PhD programmes. The examination comprises two papers: Paper I, which includes 50 questions on teaching aptitude, reasoning ability, and general awareness, and Paper II, which contains 100 subject-related multiple-choice questions.
The NTA also said that the joint CSIR UGC NET June 2026 candidates can also access the provisional answer key and challenge window.
"Please review the details carefully and use the official portal to submit challenges from 16 to 18 August 2026, up to 11:00 PM," it said.
The Joint CSIR-UGC NET June 2026 examination were held on July 17 and 18 in Computer-Based Test (CBT) mode to determine the eligibility for the award of Junior Research Fellowship (JRF), appointment as Assistant Professor, and admission to Ph.D. programmes in institutions across India.

Several Palestinians injured as settlers continue attacks in West Bank
Israeli settlers continued their assaults on Palestinians and their property in the occupied West Bank, injuring several people. Here are the details of some of these attacks, reported by Wafa.
• Israeli settlers beat up three Palestinians and sprayed them with pepper spray in the al-Masoudiya area, on the outskirts of the village of Burqa, northwest of Nablus. The settlers also damaged the front of their vehicle.

• Local sources told Wafa the settlers stormed the northern outskirts of Sinjil and released their livestock among residents' homes.

Operation Toofan: Anti-narcotics drive to be intensified during Onam, warns Chennithala
Thiruvananthapuram, Kerala Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala has said the anti-narcotics drive, Operation Toofan, will be intensified during the Onam festive season and warned drug peddlers against indulging in illegal activities.
"The second wave of Operation Toofan will be launched after Onam, striking back with ten times the force," he further said.
In a video message posted on social media, Chennithala said Operation Toofan has emerged as a massive success and credited the public and police for the campaign's achievements.
"Operation Toofan is rushing towards a massive victory. I extend my heartfelt greetings to the people and police personnel leading this effort. Operation Toofan stands as the greatest example that if the police and the public stand together, no drug mafia can survive on this land," he said.
He said the courage shown by the public in passing secret information to the police had been the primary reason behind the success of the drive.
"If the public was once afraid of the drug mafia, today the drug mafia is afraid of the public. Look at the tremendous change Kerala has witnessed over the past 74 days and nights-just imagine the transformation that can happen in a year," he said.
"When we unite and fight together, we can completely wipe out the drug mafia," he added.
As the Onam festival approaches, the public should maintain high vigilance and inform the police if they come across the use of deadly drugs under the cover of celebrations, he said.
"We are maintaining strict vigilance at the borders against drug products that may attempt to enter Kerala targeting the Onam season. Shocking details of numerous drug cases have come to light in recent days. Through ongoing arrests, the entire network of drugs in Kerala has come under complete police surveillance," Chennithala said.
He said "Toofan 2" would soon begin with a special focus on educational institutions.
"This surveillance system set up around schools will free our children from the trap of drugs. Operation Toofan has become a model for the entire country, and we can be proud of it. People across the nation are now embracing a campaign modelled after Toofan," he said.
Chennithala also warned political and other organisations against protecting those involved in drug offences.
"Whether it is someone from my party or another party, coming with excuses like 'he is my nephew' or 'she is my niece, please save them' will be of no use when it comes to Operation Toofan. I remind you that offenders will end up in jail and face severe consequences," he said.
He said some people had initially believed that Operation Toofan would "come and blow over quietly", but the campaign would continue until drugs were wiped out.
"On average, six people are being arrested under Operation Toofan every hour in Kerala. Total arrests are reaching 10,000. Operation Toofan is the largest narco-hunt ever conducted in the country," he said.
He said major hospitals across Kerala were prepared to provide "Toofan Care" to those willing to come out of drug addiction, while the Indian Medical Association was preparing a dedicated rehabilitation protocol for the programme.

Brain injuries are among the military's most pressing health problems, making advancements in treatment critical. To that end, the Pentagon's research arm is exploring ways to help an injured brain rebuild damaged connections and heal itself.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, says it wants to develop noninvasive tools that can "enhance the brain's ability to adapt and rewire itself" after an injury, DARPA's page on the effort says.
"Though the key to the brain's remarkable adaptivity is neuroplasticity, we lack the tools to stimulate plasticity in specific functional circuits to avoid global change, and/or unwanted side effects," the agency says.
To solve those problems, DARPA has launched a new program called SHINE, which is short for "Selective Harnessing of Intrinsic Neuroplasticity Engineering." The effort is in its earliest stages, but could have important implications for people recovering from traumatic brain injuries.
The US military has faced rising rates of TBI recently, as troops fighting the war against Iran have come under drone and missile fire, explosions from which cause "blast overpressure," a common cause of TBIs. Beyond enemy attacks, the repeated use of certain weapons, such as artillery, mortars, and shoulder-launched rockets, by US troops can also cause traumatic brain injuries.
The military's attention to brain health has grown as researchers have learned more about the effects of repeated exposure, and as news stories have highlighted previously overlooked mild and frequent injuries, said Vik Bebarta, a former military emergency physician who now serves as the strategic lead for the Marcus Institute for Brain Health at the University of Colorado Anschutz.
While certain jobs involving proximity to explosions are historically more closely associated with TBIs, there are other, less obviously risky military and national security jobs in which personnel are vulnerable to such injuries. Recent reporting from The New York Times highlighted the potential for injury among Coast Guard personnel tasked with navigating rough waves, which can repeatedly jar the brain and cause lasting harm.
After 20 years of war in the Middle East during the Global War on Terror, military medicine has become a finely honed tool for treating wartime trauma wounds, Bebarta said. "The next thing we need to look at is protecting the brain from damage and measuring exposure, detecting it earlier, developing treatments, both medications and non-invasive, to improve cognitive performance over careers."
The challenge is moving beyond what Bebarta called a "light switch concept of 'were you exposed or not exposed."
"It's a continuum," he said.
TBI assessments require regular evaluations and monitoring, and while some symptoms may be treatable, other effects may not be. Diagnosing such injuries is difficult, too, Bebarta said. Brain injuries are not easily detected, though the Pentagon is fielding blood-based tests to help and aims to screen more troops for brain health.
Existing approaches intended to promote neuroplasticity, including medication, brain stimulation, and behavioral therapies, generally don't isolate the circuits affected by an injury, DARPA says. The agency is seeking to direct treatment at those specific pathways, leaving other parts of the brain untouched.
Brain injuries don't just affect military personnel. Many Americans with TBIs, for instance, sustained injuries during falls, vehicle crashes, or physical assaults, according to the US Centers for Disease Control. Combative and contact sports can also contribute to brain injuries. Patients who've experienced a TBI may struggle with persistent memory, concentration, mood, and movement problems.

Families with teenagers in education know the private, hidden pain of exam season. But this year, what might have been a summer of quiet family anxiety has erupted in several countries into public unrest.
Exam-related turmoil has led to mass student protests in Mexico after nearly 60,000 university applicants were forced to resit tests amid suspected cheating, while Portugal’s disastrous attempt to digitise school exam marking sparked the country’s worst education crisis in decades.
By far the largest and most ground-shaking incident was in India, however, where an exam paper leak affected millions of students and was linked to more than a dozen students taking their own lives. The scandal forced the education minister to resign, and challenged the government’s hold over its 1.4 billion citizens.
Why does this exam season seem to be particularly tense and volatile? Experts say the growth of AI cheating and attempts by academic institutions to digitise examinations are at the heart of the issue. When coupled with the high stakes of good grades in an increasingly precarious global economy, the result can be explosive.
“It would seem that exams are getting more fraught on a global scale,” said Dr Sarah Eaton of the Werklund School of Education at the University of Calgary. “The pressure on young people has absolutely changed.
“We’ve seen the economic situation change around the world in the last decade. And the results of one examination determining a person’s entire future really creates untenable pressure on young people,” said Eaton, a leading expert on academic ethics. “This is a tragedy when young people are dying by suicide because of an examination outcome.”
When a single test can determine a young person’s entire future, cheating is no longer just about individuals but becomes a systematic issue, said Eaton. This is compounded when illicit commercial industries, known as the “education mafia”, exploit student desperation by stealing and then selling exam papers, something that has become widespread in India and elsewhere.
Students from across India joined the mass demonstrations led by the Cockroach Janta party, a youth-led protest campaign that began as an online satirical joke and grew into a nationwide outcry that poses an unprecedented challenge to Narendra Modi’s government.
“When you get large-scale fraud combined with systemic failure, there’s almost a guarantee of a breakdown of public trust,” said Eaton. “And once that trust is broken, it’s almost impossible to regain. I can’t imagine how India is going to deal with this, just given the levels of corruption and fraud that we’ve seen.”
In Portugal, the national fallout from a failed push by its education minister, Fernando Alexandre, to fully digitise the exam marking process has landed the government in a crisis. Parents, teachers, and students have been protesting, demanding Alexandre’s resignation after his policy resulted in serious marking errors.
Similar demonstrations took place in Mexico. The National Autonomous University of Mexico (Unam), the country’s most prestigious university, announced that due to abnormally high marks in entrance exam results, which raised suspicions of widespread cheating, approximately 58,000 students would have to retake the exam.
Schools worldwide are rushing to deal with AI use by students, either through bans or teaching AI literacy and ethics to pupils. Denmark announced this month that from the new term, teenagers would have to make a verbal defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating.
Eaton has implemented similar reforms in her class. “AI can generate a perfect essay in seconds. So an essay is no longer a viable way to demonstrate students’ learning,” she said. “We should let it die with dignity and find other ways to assess student learning.”
In Eaton’s view, cheating is a “human problem” and so grading and assessing student learning has historically also been a human responsibility, which she said cannot easily be off-loaded to the latest tech.
But what institutions around the world have been doing instead, she said, is hoping technology can be easily and cheaply used to prevent cheating en masse.
Dr Thomas Lancaster, a computer scientist at Imperial College London who researches the educational use of generative AI, has studied how cheating has gone hi-tech. It is no longer about sneaking notes written on a sleeve, he said, but sophisticated communication.
Lancaster says students have always cheated but it has become far easier, with pupils using earpieces or miniature cameras, and increasingly, communicating with friends or family with access to internet searches.
“I think the number of notes you sneak in, they’re only useful if they’re the right notes and if you can interpret them very quickly,” he said.
“But with any kind of communication technology, you can have that expertise waiting outside for you in a human form. They either know the answers; they’ve got the expertise; or they can look them up online. You can go further than that now and have access to AI to communicate directly during the exam as well,” he added. “It’s spy technology, really.”
Rather than individual student misconduct, Eaton said the failure to properly train educators was forcing students to spend valuable time trying to navigate through these “broken” systems rather than focusing on learning.
“This idea of these mass examinations happening at scale, it sort of dehumanises the learning process and the assessment process,” she said.
This, she said, “sort of perpetuates this idea that examinations are the most important thing for students. I think we’ve lost the thread. Learning should be the most important thing for students.”

Protest, enrolment ‘freeze’, CJI’s rap, then apology: Blow-by-blow of NALSAR row
BCI chairman Manan Kumar Mishra on Saturday apologised to the law students and said he sincerely regretted if their feelings had been hurt.
The Bar Council of India (BCI) has been embroiled in a controversy recently over its order to freeze the enrolment of the entire 2026 graduating batch of NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad. While the a move that was later rolled back amid backlash, the row continues to simmer.
In a fresh, BCI chairman Manan Kumar Mishra on Saturday apologised to the law students and said he sincerely regretted if anything connected with the controversy, including his words or letter, had hurt their feelings. This was preceded by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant rapping the BCI for its intervention in the NALSAR University of Law enrolment controversy.
The National Academy for Legal Studies and Research University, or NALSAR, is a public law school in Hyderabad, Telangana. NALSAR is also among the various national law Universities across India.
Here is a look back at how the NALSAR-BCI-CJI row unfolded over the past few weeks:
Opposition to CJI's presence as chief guest at convocation
A group of NALSAR students opposed the proposed participation of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant as the chief guest at the university’s convocation. They wrote to the vice-chancellor, registrar, and professors voicing their objection.
The first representation was submitted on July 23 by 70 members of the outgoing LLB batch. Students from several later batches subsequently expressed their support for the representation, HT reported earlier.
In an email sent to the university officials, students raised their objection as they cited the refusal of the Supreme Court bench, led by CJI Kant, to hear a plea regarding the alleged police brutality against students during the July 20 ‘Chalo Sansad’ march in New Delhi's Jantar Mantar.
"As students of law, our concern is narrower and more specific to us as a graduating batch. A convocation is meant to be a moment where the University's own values, including a commitment to constitutional rights, access to justice, and reasoned engagement with grievances, are visibly reflected in the choices it makes," the students wrote in their email, as per news agency PTI.
BCI halts NALSAR enrollment, then withdraws move
BCI's Mishra directed all State Bar Councils not to enroll any 2026 law graduate from NALSAR University as advocates until further orders.
NALSAR was also asked to provide an authenticated report naming those who had started, organised, coordinated or mobilised the campaign against the CJI’s proposed participation in the convocation. It also sought information on any faculty members, research scholars, alumni, student organisations or outsiders being involved in the boycott.
It also sought details of the representations, signatories, meetings, social media groups, media interactions, and any calls for a boycott or disruption.
The first communication said the temporary freeze was required, as allowing enrolment while the inquiry was underway could interfere with the process.
But the order was rolled back within hours after backlash with Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke also threatening a protest.
The revised notification reversed the earlier order and stated that the "vast majority" of the students were innocent and should not be held responsible for the alleged misconduct of a few.
CJI raps Bar Council
On Friday, CJI Surya Kant slammed the BCI amid the NALSAR row and said the Council had “no business” interfering with students’ right to protest. He said the court would not allow students to be stopped from raising their voice through lawful and peaceful protests as he restrained the BCI and all state bar councils from pursuing any punitive or criminal action against students and faculty university in connection with the controversy.
“The BCI is unnecessarily taking action in this matter. If students have a cause or a reason to protest, they have a right to protest. Nobody can stop them, and we will not allow this,” said the CJI after senior advocate K Parameshwar mentioned the matter before the bench, HT reported earlier.
Bar Council's apology
After CJI's strong remarks, Bar Council's Mishra apologised to the law students on Saturday and said he sincerely regretted if anything connected with the controversy, including his words or letter, had hurt their feelings.
Addressing a letter to his ‘dear young friends’, Mishra said the developments of the past few days had caused “concern and anguish” among a section of the student community and acknowledged that whenever students felt hurt or aggrieved, their concerns deserved to be heard “with patience, sensitivity and respect”.
“If anything connected with the present controversy, any of my words, or letter, has hurt the feelings of our law students, I sincerely regret and apologise for the same,” Mishra said.
“There should be no hesitation in saying so. An expression of regret is not a matter of prestige or ego. It is simply an acknowledgment that the feelings and concerns of our students matter,” he added.

Fun, retro style that appeals to both teens and adults. Well-priced. UL-2271 and 2849 certified. Frame triangle is big enough to attach a folding lock.
TIRED
Seat is cheap-feeling and very hard. No suspension and no way to carry cargo. Range takes a huge hit on hills. No battery IP rating for water resistance. Not a “real” BMX.
Though I’ve since gotten used to it, every time I ride the electric blue Joe Rev 2 electric BMX, people stare. Their heads turn as they drive past, eyes narrowed. “Is that an adult riding a BMX bike?” I imagine the thought process going. “Why is it so fast? Why is it so big?” These are valid questions, and they all have the same answer: Because it’s fun.
In fact, my entire family has taken turns riding this bike all over town for the past four weeks, testing it up and down hills, taking it on grocery runs, and even staying out riding until the battery drained. The verdict? The Joe Rev 2 may not be the smoothest ride, but for the price, it’s a unique and worthwhile option for basic cruising and casual riding.
All Eyes on Me
Photograph: Kat Merck
California-based Retrospec specializes in affordable outdoor toys; primarily paddleboards, longboards, bikes, and no-frills ebikes like the foldable Judd Rev 2, which WIRED contributing reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani wrote “captures the vibe of being a 12-year-old kid and riding your bike more than anything I’ve ridden in some time.”
The entry-level Joe Rev was created in this same spirit—a full-sized, BMX-inspired frame with fun color options (electric blue, matte gray), 3-inch tan wall balloon tires, and those unmistakable handlebars. There are no apps or fancy readouts, no lights, and no shocks. Just five levels of pedal assist and a throttle attached to a single-speed drivetrain and 750-watt rear-hub motor.
Photograph: Kat Merck
“No cream, no sugar” is even printed on the chain stays, lest one forget the minimalist doctrine. On the plus side, this lack of bones allows the Joe Rev 2 to weigh in on the lighter side at 56 pounds.
This is the second iteration of the original Joe Rev, which is still available (for now) at the sale price of $1,200. The Rev 2 sports a bigger 500 Wh battery with a listed 60-mile range (up from 48 miles) and an updated display. Namely, a 2-by-2.5-inch LCD screen on the left handlebar displaying power level, battery life, and speed, as opposed to the original’s bare-basic hub with buttons.
The battery can be quickly locked and unlocked from the bottom of the frame with a key and charges from red to full green in several hours; it weighs about 7 pounds, so it’s easy enough to carry in a backpack, though at 18 inches long, it could be a tight fit if your bag is already packed.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
Teen Spirit
At one point during the testing period, my almost-14-year-old son, who is 5’ 10” and 145 pounds, took the Joe Rev 2 out on a full battery to see how long he could ride in our town of hills. We were all surprised to find he hit the red “recharge” light in about 20 miles. It shouldn't have been too much of a shock, given that the hills were steep, and he was using the throttle primarily. But it is a good reminder that, like all ebikes, the Joe Rev 2’s range will vary dramatically depending on rider weight, speed, and conditions.
Interestingly, there’s an ominous warning sticker on the Joe Rev’s frame that states no one under 16 is to ride this bike. It does have pedals and a maximum speed of 20 mph, making it a Class 2 ebike—legal in many, if not, most states for kids under 16.
When I asked Retrospec if there was anything specific about the Joe Rev 2 that would preclude younger teens from riding it, their rep told me the company “follows the most stringent regulations across the markets where their ebikes are sold. As a result, their minimum recommended rider age is 16. If local laws permit younger riders, such as a 12-year-old, it is ultimately up to parents or guardians to determine whether their child has the maturity, experience, and ability to safely operate an ebike.”
However, an adult-sized, mature 14- or 15-year-old could be a gray area. My son is allowed to ride the Joe Rev 2 occasionally, but not regularly. If you decide to go this route, know this bike was deemed acceptable by several teens in my orbit, though stylistically a couple notches below the e-moto-style frames popularized by brands like MacFox.
How It Rides
As is typical with ebikes, some assembly of the Joe Rev 2 is required upon arrival. Chiefly, attaching the wheels, pedals, and handlebars, for which it comes with a generously sized set of hex wrenches. The first night, it took a couple of tries to get the front wheel seated properly—there was a slight wobble during my husband’s inaugural ride around the block, but after further tightening, it has not resurfaced. The brakes are mechanical disc with 180 mm rotors, which also occasionally needed tightening, but otherwise caused no issues during the testing period.
My own first ride was on a flat surface, around the parking lot of my son’s former elementary school. I found that the five levels of pedal assist kick in quickly and almost forcefully; the throttle is an easy-to-use thumb switch located on the left handlebar. The frame feels like a good size for my height (5’ 6”), and the whole setup was easy to parse in just a couple of minutes.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Aside from the lack of suspension—you will feel every bump—my only major complaint is the seat. In fact, my butt still hurts as I write this from even a short ride yesterday. The Joe Rev 2's seat is hard, plasticky, and small—definitely worth swapping out if you’re going to be commuting on this or otherwise riding it daily.
My 5’ 8” husband rides the Joe Rev 2 to the grocery store several times a week, an activity he greatly enjoys, and over time we’ve found ourselves wishing there were an easy way to carry cargo, such as the ability to bolt on a basket or saddlebags. To be fair, though, I’m not sure it would ultimately be worth the reduction in range, though the bike does have a payload capacity of 350 pounds. We do, however, greatly appreciate the open space in the frame to attach a folding lock. (We went with the Seatlylock FoldyLock for $90).
One thing I have not yet been able to test is the water resistance. I live in western Washington state, where it rains nine months out of the year, and the Joe Rev 2's battery is mounted at the bottom of the down tube, where it could easily be splashed. There's no given IP rating for water resistance, so while I'm sure the battery housing can handle a light, occasional spray, riding the bike on a super-rainy day would make me nervous.
It also bears mentioning that if you're hoping for a real BMX bike with which you can do tricks, the Joe Rev 2 is not that. Insofar as being a BMX, the only quality seems to be the handlebars. Nothing about it feels nimble, and at this weight, you’re not taking it to the skate park—the only jumps and rail hops happening are in your imagination.
However, if you do happen to lose control of yourself and break something, the Joe Rev 2 is UL 2849 Certified for the electrical system and UL 2271 Certified for the battery, meaning that, unlike with many other internet-purchased direct-to-consumer bikes, your local bike shop may be able to repair it. Though this depends heavily on the type of repair needed; it’s worth calling to be sure.

Jharkhand student protesters intensified their agitation in Ranchi on Saturday, with leaders giving the Hemant Soren government until August 18 to address alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations or face a mass march towards the Chief Minister’s residence on August 20.
The protest by JPSC-JSSC aspirants has now entered its 22nd day, with students demanding the cancellation of the JSSC-CGL and JPSC 11th–13th examinations and an independent investigation into alleged irregularities.
Student leader Ravindra Paswan said the movement would enter a more aggressive phase if the government failed to respond to the demands. Invoking revolutionary figure Bhagat Singh, he said protesters were no longer willing to rely solely on peaceful demonstrations.
“Today, we are changing the course of our movement. We have had enough of Gandhian methods and peaceful protests. They simply aren't listening. We are now going to adopt the path of Bhagat Singh. We are prepared to face bullets, even if the government shoots us in the chest, for this cause. We will continue our agitation until our demands are met.”
Paswan said the protesters had issued an ultimatum to the government, demanding action by August 18.
“We are issuing an ultimatum to the government: meet our demands by the 18th. Cancel the JSSC results, scrap all exams conducted by the TDPL agency, and order a CBI inquiry into all of them.”
He warned that failure to meet the demands would trigger a larger mobilisation on August 20.
“If this is not done, lakhs of students and youths from Jharkhand will lay siege to the Chief Minister's residence on the 20th...”
The protesters are seeking cancellation of the JSSC-CGL and JPSC 11th–13th examinations. They have also called for a probe by the Central Bureau of Investigation or a panel of retired judges from outside Jharkhand.
Another student leader, Piyush Kumar, said protesters would begin burning effigies at district headquarters from Sunday.
“We are going to burn the effigies of the Hemant Soren-led Jharkhand government, Chief Minister Hemant Soren himself, Rahul Gandhi, and all the parties supporting them.”
Kumar also referred to the proposed August 20 Assembly gherao, describing the earlier protest outside the Vidhan Sabha as only a “preview” of the next phase of the agitation.
The protests have centred on allegations of irregularities in recruitment examinations and demands for greater transparency in Jharkhand's government recruitment system.
The agitation has also drawn attention to the condition of JLKM leader Devendra Mahto, who has reportedly been on hunger strike for 14 days.
Mahto has alleged that police prevented him from leaving Sadar Hospital to participate in the protest march. Videos circulating on social media purportedly show Mahto in a scuffle with security personnel while attempting to leave the hospital. The circumstances of the incident could not be independently verified.
Protesters say their demands extend beyond the disputed examinations and concern wider issues of equal opportunities and public confidence in the state's recruitment system.
The Jharkhand government has acknowledged concerns over the recruitment process.
In his Independence Day address, Chief Minister Hemant Soren said allegations surrounding recruitment examinations had shaken the trust of an entire generation. He assured students that claims of irregularities would be investigated impartially and that those found guilty would face legal action.
At the same time, Soren cautioned against declaring anyone guilty without evidence, saying any action must be based on facts.
“Merely apprehending the guilty is not the solution,” Soren said, stressing the need for systemic changes to prevent manipulation of examinations.
Soren outlined measures including a time-bound annual examination calendar, technology-secured examinations, timely publication of answer keys and OMR sheets, and multiple levels of accountability in the recruitment process.
With the August 18 deadline approaching, the Jharkhand government now faces the prospect of a significantly larger student mobilisation in Ranchi if the protesters' demands remain unresolved.
