Police report lodged after elderly man shoved to ground in dispute over patting girl's head
The incident, which was captured on CCTV, took place at a food court in Roxy Square mall along East Coast Road.
SINGAPORE: A police report has been lodged over an incident at a food court involving an elderly man who was shoved to the ground following an interaction in which he patted a young girl on the head.
The police confirmed on Sunday (Aug 16) that a report had been made and investigations are ongoing.
The incident came to public attention after social media posts by Bei-Ing Wanton Noodle appealing for information to identify a man involved in the confrontation.
The business operates two stalls, one at Roxy Square mall along East Road and the other in a coffee shop near Telok Kurau Road.
According to the posts, the incident happened on Saturday and involved the father of the person who wrote the posts.
CCTV footage posted by the business showed the incident taking place at the Roxy Square outlet.
The family said the man, who is in his 70s and has difficulty walking, had been walking past a table and using tables for support when he briefly reached out and patted a young girl on the head.
The child's father then became upset and confronted the elderly man, the family alleged.
CCTV footage showed the elderly man being shoved and falling to the ground.
The family said relatives who were present helped him up. It added that the elderly man initially did not want to pursue the matter further.
The other man later sat down with him, apologised and offered him a drink, according to the posts.
In a subsequent Facebook post, the family said the elderly man was suffering from back pain following the incident and appealed for information that could help identify the people involved.
It also urged those with information to contact the relevant authorities.
Another post, which was later removed, contained footage showing the two men seated across from each other at a table. According to the accompanying text, the girl's father apologised and said he had been "overprotective" of his daughter.
In a third post, Bei-Ing Wanton Noodle reiterated its appeal for information and said the matter remained unresolved.

Barely 200 kilometres from Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, where students and youth of the country came together in thousands to demand educational reform in India, a notice was served on a university, declaring that most of its built structures were illegal and would soon be demolished.
The institute, Mohammad Ali Jauhar University (MAJU), located in Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, was established in 2006 by the Mohammad Ali Jauhar Trust, founded by Azam Khan, one of the founding members of the Samajwadi Party. Khan, a former MP and 10-time MLA from Rampur, was one of the most powerful politicians in the region until the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) came to power in 2017.
MAJU is recognised by the University Grants Commission (UGC) and holds minority institution status. However, its staff and student body comprise people from varied backgrounds and religious communities, vice-chancellor (VC) Prof Zaheeruddin and students themselves told Alt News.
On July 15, the Rampur Development Authority (RDA) issued a notice to the university declaring that 38 of its 40 buildings were illegal and would be demolished within 20 days. The university was told to carry out the demolition itself, failing which, the RDA would carry out the demolition while charging the university expenses. However, the demolition order was stayed on July 28 by the chairman of RDA and the Moradabad divisional commissioner, Aunjaney Kumar Singh, till August 10.
Only a day after the notice, on July 16, a ‘counselling camp’ was set up outside the university’s main gate, the VC said. On the same day, the UP Public Works Department (PWD) declared an internal road belonging to the campus as a public road while installing signage, he alleged.
On July 27, Alt News visited the 475-acre campus on the first day of the semester. The buildings — designed, according to the VC, in the image of the White House and Turkish mosques — looked grand but lifeless as several structures stood half-built with construction abandoned mid-way. An air of uncertainty loomed over the campus and on the faces of the very few students who were present.
Some students, who were protesting the demolition, told Alt News that a student delegation had met the DM and sought written assurance that the buildings would not be demolished until the matter was decided by the Supreme Court. The DM gave only a verbal assurance and declined to put it in writing, they said.
‘All Buildings Constructed Before RDA’s Jurisdiction’
Zaheeruddin, who served as pro-VC and chairman of the department of law at Aligarh Muslim University (AMU) before joining MAJU in April 2025, said that a prior show-cause notice had been issued on June 28 seeking a response from the university on the demolitions.
The university’s response was deemed unsatisfactory by the RDA, which called for a physical meeting on July 14, attended by registrar SN Salam and the institute’s legal counsel. The authority only heard their arguments for five minutes, and the next day, the demolition order arrived, said Zaheeruddin, adding: “This was completely unexpected for us. Our classes were running, admissions were fully underway. Compared to the past two years, more admissions were happening this year.”
The VC told Alt News the 38 buildings were constructed before 2016, when the university grounds fell under the gram panchayat, not the RDA. The RDA’s jurisdiction was extended to cover the land only through a notification in September 2024, he said, asserting that the authority is retrospectively taking action against buildings. “All buildings they have mentioned were constructed by 2016, when RDA had no presence in this area at all,” he said.
He further highlighted that multiple regulatory bodies — UGC, Bar Council of India, paramedical and nursing councils — have inspected and approved the university’s infrastructure over the years as part of their accreditation process.
Missing Paperwork & The 2019 Raid
The VC, however, did not want to show the approved maps to prove the buildings’ legality citing legal proceedings. “The matter is before both the divisional commissioner and the Allahabad high court. The university’s lawyers have advised against discussing legal specifics,” he said.
On the other hand, Salam, the registrar, offered a different explanation for the missing paperwork. He claimed that during a state-ordered raid in 2019, when police forces were deployed on campus, large quantities
of documents were seized. “They took so many documents, and we don’t know where they took them or find out which documents they took,” he said.
Salam recounted the 2019 raid, “As police and district officials raided the campus, the VC was confined to one floor, the registrar to another, the accounts staff locked elsewhere. There were media reports that around 8,000 books stolen from a 200-year-old madrassa had been recovered from the university. But when the matter reached court, only 26 books were produced.”
Both the VC and registrar claimed that during the raid, several books were destroyed, many of which were hand-written manuscripts. They also claimed that 42 large cupboards, purchased from Kolkata, with receipts and transport documents, were shown as stolen property. Alt News could not independently verify the claims made by the VC and the registrar on the 2019 raid.
The Sudden ‘Counselling Camp’
Exacerbating the adminstration’s and students’ worries after the notice was served, was the sudden counselling camp, allegedly set up the very next day to encourage students to enroll in other universities.
Among those at the camp were officials from Guru Jambheshwar University, Moradabad — a state university whose campus construction began in March 2024, currently operating from a temporary campus with just two rooms built, and teachers from Raza Degree College, Rampur. Their task, the VC said, was to inform prospective students that MAJU would soon be demolished and that they should apply for admission at Guru Jambheshwar University.
“I felt terrible, they were maligning us right in front of us, sitting outside our campus. I was shocked that government teachers were doing this and the district magistrate had set up the camp while we are still a functioning university,” Zaheeruddin lamented.
Arguing that the counselling camp amounted to contempt of court, he mentioned that the administration wrote to the Rampur DM citing a 2019 high court stay order that specifically ordered that students and staff of the university must not be harassed. The camp was removed after two days, on July 18 evening.
The Students’ Plight
When Alt News visited the campus, the students, now thrust into indefinite anxiety over their futures, were sitting in protest in front of the main gate, demanding that the RDA withdraws the demolition. “We are protesting since July 18 because RDA should withdraw this order. There are 3,000-4,000 students studying here, don’t snatch the pen from their hands,” said a 5th-year student from Panipat, Haryana.
Students echoed the administration’s account on the ‘pattern’ of state action which haunted their campus. Every year during admissions, they said, new action or rumours would surface, discouraging parents and prospective students. “Every year, fear is planted in children’s hearts that the university will be shut down,” said another student.
A student from Bareilly said his brother studied at MAJU between 2014 and 2017. After that, the perception in his area was that the university had already shut down. When he arrived for admission in 2015, he was urged not to enrol by several people in and around the area, with claims that the fees were too high and the university could collapse at any time.
The students further claimed that district officials attempted to curb their protest as the SDM arrived at the protest site on July 18 around 10 PM with policemen and asked the students to move their protest inside the campus, away from the main gate. District-level intelligence wing officials also called several parents, urging them to get their children to stop protesting, students alleged.
The students said they raised the issue with the district administration, which assured them that such pressure tactics would not be applied. Another protesting student mentioned that he had written twice to Saurav Das, the chief spokesperson of the Cockroach Janta Party, but had received no response at the time writing this report.
Alt News is withholding the names of the students who spoke to us in order to protect their identity.
RDA Officials Evade Queries
When we reached out to the RDA, we were re-routed through four different officials. We contacted RDA’s vice-chairman Ajay Kumar Dwivedi, also the district magistrate of Rampur, under whose name the July 15 notice was issued. His personal assistant, Ankush, directed us to the RDA secretary, Nitin Madan. The secretary, after answering some of our questions, directed us to the tehsildar, Ranveer Singh, who spoke briefly and redirected us to RDA assistant engineer Manoj Sisodia.
According to every official, only two of the 40 buildings had approved maps, obtained from the panchayat before RDA’s jurisdiction was extended to the area. The remaining 38, they said, had no approval from any authority — the Zila Panchayat, gram panchayat, or RDA. This formed the basis of the demolition notice, they said.
Upon being asked whether the matter could be resolved through compounding, a process where illegal construction is regularised by paying a fine and obtaining retrospective approval, Singh said it had been considered but rejected because the land use at the university site is not permissible under RDA’s current master plan. Sisodia, on the other hand, said that the university had never submitted a compounding proposal to RDA. However, the VC told Alt News that the institute believed that compounding was something RDA would initiate.
Further, we asked whether RDA had issued demolition notices to any other structures in the 62 villages that came under its jurisdiction since September 2024. Madan said “many have happened” without naming a single case. Ranveer Singh added “it keeps happening from time to time”, also offering no specifics. Sisodia eventually admitted that notices issued to other parties are “confidential and that the university’s case attracted attention only because it is a larger structure”.
“The university is in the wrong, but considering everything, the government, higher authorities, the courts, have taken their decision,” Sisodia said while acknowledging the dire condition of the students if the demolition is carried out.
The Azam Khan-Aunjaney Singh Connection
Parellel to all this runs another storied controversy between Azam Khan and Aunjaney Kumar Singh. During the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, complaints were filed by the then assistant development officer (panchayat), Anil Kumar Chauhan, and local BJP leader Akash Saxena against Khan for alleged hateful and provocative remarks against the then DM of Rampur, Aunjaney Kumar Singh, and other BJP leaders.
This led to Khan’s conviction in October 2022 with three years of imprisonment and his subsequent disqualification from the UP state assembly. His conviction was later overturned and he was acquitted by a higher court in Rampur.
Formerly an IAS officer of Sikkim cadre, Singh, hailing from Mau district in UP, notably has been serving as a government official in the state for 11 consecutive years now, and is presently on his sixth extension, which is set to end on August 14. Interestingly, in April last year, Singh accepted Khan’s plea against the imposition of Rs 20 crore fine in another case related to construction of MAJU.
According to Zaheeruddin, the demolition hearing, which was supposed to take place on August 3 at the court of divisional commissioner, has been postponed to August 10, bringing under scrutiny the apparent pendulum swing in the official relationship between Singh and Khan — from the district administration’s actions during Singh’s tenure as Rampur DM that culminated in Khan’s conviction, to subsequent administrative decisions that provided relief in matters concerning Khan’s university, and now the stay on the demolition proceedings.
The Unanswered Question
Beyond the missing approvals and the land use dispute, there is a deeper contradiction that neither the university nor the RDA addressed. During the April 2025 hearing concerning the Rs 20 crore labour cess fine, Khan had argued before the divisional commissioner that 10 of MAJU’s buildings were constructed by the UP PWD and UP Nirman Nigam using MP/MLA development funds.
Khan had then received relief after the divisional commissioner’s court nullified the cess fine imposed by the assistant labour commissioner (ALC) of Rampur. The same court, under the same authority of Singh, has now served a demolition notice to the institute. A pertinent question emerges: If state agencies built these structures with public funds, how did construction proceed without the approved maps?
Four government offices, multiple courts, contradictory bureaucratic positions and years of litigation have turned MAJU into a case study in administrative uncertainty. Whether the buildings ultimately stand or fall will be decided in court. Until then, it is not politicians or officials who bear the immediate cost of this prolonged impasse, but thousands of students who continue to attend classes while wondering if the campus they study in will still exist by the time they graduate.

Amit Malviya gets Congress notice over 'Rahul insulted National Anthem' allegation
Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit has sent a legal notice to Amit Malviya over a BJP post alleging Rahul Gandhi insulted the National Anthem. The notice says a technical glitch replayed the anthem and seeks removal of the post and an unconditional apology.
Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit on Saturday sent a legal notice to the BJP’s IT cell chief Amit Malviya, after the party’s official X account shared a video clip, accusing the Leader of the Opposition, Rahul Gandhi, of ‘insulting’ the National Anthem during the National Convention of the Rachnatmak Congress on August 13.
In the clip, Rahul Gandhi appeared on the dais, shaking hands with several other leaders and walking on the stage while the National Anthem was being played in the background. Sharing the clip, BJP4India, the official account of the party, wrote, “Look, Rahul Gandhi has once again insulted the national anthem. The national anthem that every Indian takes pride in, which embodies the honour, prestige, and glory of the nation, must be respected as the duty of every citizen. But Rahul Gandhi has disgraced it, once again exposing his anti-national attitude.”
Following the incident, lawyer politicians Amrish Ranjan Pandey and Ambuj Dixit served the notice on behalf of Dikshit to Malviya, as he is the national in-charge of the party’s information and technology cell and also the social media department. The notice asked for the ‘immediate removal of the content and also an unconditional apology’ for the post.
“The purpose of this Notice is not to object to political criticism or to enter into a political debate with you. Political disagreement, criticism and even strong political expression are an ordinary and necessary part of democratic life. What cannot be accepted, however, is the deliberate presentation of an accidental technical error at an event as a deliberate act of disrespect towards the National Anthem, particularly when the complete audio-visual record shows otherwise,” the notice read.
It also clarified that the National Anthem was ‘duly played’ during the event and the Congress leaders did pay their respects to the song. However, due to a technical glitch in the audio box, the song was accidentally played another time, when the leaders were busy interacting with each other.
“It was only thereafter, due to an inadvertent error in the operation of the audio system, the National Anthem was accidentally played once again. Neither my client nor any other person on the dais had any prior knowledge that the audio track would be replayed inadvertently. The moment the error became apparent, the audio operator immediately stopped the playback. It is entirely possible that, like other audios generally played in such venues, the National Anthem had been put on repeat in the system and was therefore inadvertently played again,” it further added.
Malviya has not immediately responded to the allegations.
The legal notice came amid a separate political standoff between the Congress and the BJP over the rendition of India's National Song, Vande Mataram.
The face-off between the two parties erupted after the Independence Day celebration at the Congress party headquarters in New Delhi. A video from the programme appeared to show that Sonia Gandhi, the party’s Parliamentary Chairperson and the National President, Mallikarjun Kharge, were making hand gestures that seemed to ask workers to stop playing the rendition of the National Song. Moments later, Rahul Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition, was also seen following the same gesture.
It soon snowballed into a major bipartisan friction, with the BJP taking jibes against the Gandhis and Kharge. Amit Malviya added fuel to the fire as he said that Sonia Gandhi became ‘agitated’ after hearing the full version of Vande Mataram.
“For the first time, the entire ‘Vande Mataram’ was sung at the Congress headquarters on Independence Day. After the initial stanzas of Vande Mataram were sung, Sonia Gandhi became agitated and asked for the rendition to be stopped rather than played in full. Rahul Gandhi too appeared to signal that it should end,” he wrote on X.
“They were told to let it continue. The message was clear: the complete National Song is now to be respected under the new legal framework, and intentional obstruction or disturbance can invite serious consequences,” he further added.

They say to be cringe is to be free. And on LinkedIn, I needed a taste of freedom. Which is why I fully embraced using Cringebot 3000, a website that creates purposely grating AI-generated slop for you to post to LinkedIn.
Why on Earth would you want that? That's the wrong question. The better one is: How did we get to this point?
Cringebot 3000 is the unholy creation of Peter Epstein, who runs a Los Angeles-based PR firm for advertising industry clients. After the website blew up on Reddit and the influential Hacker News site this week, I caught up with him over the phone to find out what kind of twisted mind would aspire to be the Oppenheimer of LinkedIn slop.
"The goal is to make it a little less serious and try to take what's become its own sort of form, like poetry — LinkedIn 'thought leadership' is its own form — and try to take that form and make it a little more fun and a little more silly," he explained.
He wanted to try vibecoding something with Claude, and first created the site at the beginning of this year, but only more recently fine-tuned it to be reliable at mass-producing this kind of slop at scale.
LinkedIn has an AI slop problem and I'm not helping
LinkedIn has long had a problem with cheesiness and people posting purposely engagement-baiting posts. It's been almost a decade since we witnessed the terrifying birth of a new posting form known as "broetry" — posts where:
They use line breaks for every sentence. And the content is something like What potty training my toddler taught me about 2b2 SaaS sales. 
The ability to use AI to write this kind of stuff has turned LinkedIn into a real slophouse. LinkedIn is well aware and trying to fight it: it recently added a feature where you can report a post for "AI slop" the same way you might for harassment or spam.
"People complain about LinkedIn AI slop, but was LinkedIn that great before AI slop?" Epstein pointed out.
Partly because of this kind of content, I haven't found LinkedIn to be a "fun" place to post. But the tantalizing idea of becoming a LinkedInfluencer now dangled before me, warm and weightless. I needed to shake the shackles of caring about "good" posts or "seeming human" and plunge into the deep end of the slop pool.
Now sure, I could use any LLM to come up with some quasi-inspirational business wisdom pablum to post on LinkedIn. But Cringebot 3000 makes it even easier. Just type in a topic — could be a single word, and then select from eight separate flavors, such as "The Vulnerability Post (oversharing with a motivational twist)", "The Inspiring Story (finding life lessons everywhere)"or "The Corporate Dropout (quit the 9-5 to follow my passion)".
I typed in "AI in journalism" as my topic and chose "You Go Girl! (empowerment culture and smashing glass ceilings)" for the style.
The output was perfect LinkedIn slop: a meandering story with a grippy opening sentence and a corny kernel of truth at the end. It was loaded with hashtags (and a disclaimer at the very bottom that it was written by Cringebot 3000).
Here's the text (you can skim it):
Okay so I need to tell you all something that happened to me last Tuesday that I am still not fully recovered from. 
I was pitching a story to my editor about AI writing tools replacing journalists, and I accidentally sent the draft that my AI assistant had written ABOUT ME to the entire newsroom listserv.
The AI had described me as "a mid-level content facilitator with moderate narrative instincts."
Moderate. Narrative. Instincts.
I cried in the bathroom for eleven minutes.
But here is what happened next, and this is the part that matters.
Every woman in that newsroom replied-all within twenty minutes. Not to laugh. To share their own AI horror stories. The investigative reporter whose AI fact-checker confidently cited a country that no longer exists. The foreign correspondent whose translation bot rendered her entire interview in the subjunctive mood. The editor whose AI headline generator called a piece about the Supreme Court "a fun romp."
We built something that afternoon in that reply-all thread that no algorithm could have generated.
We built a coalition of women who refuse to let machines define our narrative instincts, moderate or otherwise.
The AI didn't replace us. It accidentally introduced us to each other.
Now we have a weekly meeting. We are rewriting the rules of how women in journalism engage with these tools, on our terms, with our voices, telling our stories.
The AI called me moderate.
The sisterhood said: absolutely not.
#WomenInJournalism #AIInJournalism #MediaInnovation #WomenSupportingWomen #JournalismTwitter #TechAndMedia #GlassCeilingSmashed #SisterhoodIsPowerful #OwnYourNarrative #cringebot3000
This post was generated with tongue firmly in cheek by LinkedIn CringeBot 3000. (link in comments)
Awful, right? I immediately copy and pasted it to my LinkedIn and let that sweet, sweet engagement roll in.
The reaction was mixed. People who knew me well recognized it was an AI-generated joke.
But according to LinkedIn's analytics of the reach of my post, 96% of viewers were people not in my network — strangers who didn't know this is would be highly out of character for me to write. I started seeing some comments from strangers as if this was a genuine anecdote about the workplace.
Oh no, what have I done
"I love this so much! Way to hold each other up and take control of the literal narrative!" commented someone I didn't know.
To make things worse, the post itself was a rousing success by LinkedIn standards. I got far more engagement and comments on this than I have for any of my other recent posts with links to articles I wrote or other career news.
Basically, the Cringebot3000 is way better at LinkedIn than I am.
Like a true LinkedIn Thought Leader, I am choosing to learn from my failures. Whatever shriveled shred of humanity that still flickers inside me that normally prevents me from posting garbage on LinkedIn is something I should treasure, not be ashamed of. No more AI slop for me. Well, unless Cringebot4000 comes out.

Expensive earbuds: When and why it's worth paying more
Will you notice the difference if you buy an expensive pair?
By the mid-2000s, earbuds were tangled in pockets across the globe. The iPod and other portable media players had revolutionized the music business. Digital music distribution quickly relegated the local record shop to a relic, while downloaded MP3s from iTunes (or other, less-than-legal sources) allowed listeners to cram more music into their pockets than most people had in their homebound physical collections. Music had become truly mobile, and easily pocketable earbuds symbolized that freedom.
But while music became more accessible than ever, the same cannot be said for sound quality. Each iPod came with a pair of plastic white earbuds, so ubiquitous that the stark lengths of cord swung wildly from dancing silhouettes in one of Apple's most memorable ad campaigns. The only problem? Those earbuds were absolute garbage. Audio enthusiasts would ditch Apple's free earbuds without even wearing them, but most people didn't understand what a poor listening experience Steve Jobs had subjected them to.
Today, even as wired earbuds come back into vogue, things are much different. For one, new devices don't have a headphone jack to begin with, let alone earbuds in the box (or a charger, for that matter). But the average pair of cheap earbuds in the 2020s delivers a much better experience than those old, tangly iPod earbuds.
The word 'earbud' technically refers to a bud that rests on the outer ear. Old iPod earbuds or today's basic AirPods are the quintessential examples. On the other hand, buds that protrude into the ears with silicone or foam tips are known as in-ear monitors, or IEMs. But since most people use the word 'earbud' to refer interchangeably to both fits, and since high-end buds are almost invariably in-ears, that's the style on which this article is focused.
Whether wired or wireless, it's hard to find a pair of modern earbuds that don't sound at least somewhat decent, and if you're not an audiophile, you don't need to shell out too much cash for a pair that'll have you shaking your hips while you do the dishes. While the high-end market continues to flourish, offering premium sound and smart features, here's what you need to know before you shop.
Which kinds of earbuds are the most expensive?
The most expensive earbuds nowadays tend to be in one of two categories. The first are the in-ear variety. These are usually wired earbuds meant for audiophiles, musicians and audio engineers, and they are designed to deliver unparalleled sound quality with no other frills. By contrast, other expensive earbuds are high-end, true wireless stereo (TWS). These are your AirPods Pro 3, your Sony WF-1000XM6, and so on. These buds market themselves as high-tech lifestyle accessories, and they are often packed with smart features like active noise cancellation (ANC), ambient audio passthrough and spatial audio. While premium true wireless buds are often designed with more emphasis on their sound quality than you'll find on cheaper earbuds, sound quality is not their primary selling point. Technically, any buds that seal inside the ear with silicone or foam tips are a subset of IEMs, including TWS buds, but most people do not use the term IEM to refer to them.
For most listeners looking to drop a Benjamin or two on a pair of buds, the adaptive functionality of premium wireless models makes them an attractive choice. Even the best wireless earbuds won't be turning many audiophile heads, but they still sound great for blocking out the ruckus of a train, airplane or coffee shop. Even audio-forward models like the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) and the aforementioned Sony WF-1000XM6 are geared toward sound profiles tuned for recreational listening, at least out of the box, with their real claim to fame being that both are contenders for best-in-class ANC performance and their ability to pack a lot of tech into a pocketable package. Again, these earbuds often sound excellent, but they're made for a wider range of uses.
IEMs, meanwhile, are for transparent or analytical listening. They are designed to fit deeper into the ear canal, creating superior passive noise canceling as opposed to ANC. This means they won't be a good choice for the noisy environments in which premium true wireless earbuds thrive. Most of their cost stems from the use of high-end audio components and acoustic tuning, with prices increasing the more complex that craftsmanship becomes. You might find an audio engineer making use of them while mixing music from a hotel room, a player tracking instruments in a studio or a stage artist monitoring their band while singing in a packed arena. IEMs are also the province of audiophiles, who are likely to pair them with a portable music player packed with lossless music files, the better to enjoy a more precise listening experience.
Affordable earbuds are better than ever
Although more expensive earbuds can be justifiably pricey, that doesn't mean they're automatically a good choice for everyone. If you're the sort of person who's never even thought about adjusting the sound quality settings in Spotify, you won't benefit much from the subtle sound quality of top-shelf earbuds. And if it's ANC you're after, it can be had for far less.
On our roundup of the best wireless earbuds for 2026, Engadget chose the Anker Soundcore Space A40 as our budget pick. For just about $55, they pack in most of the marquee features of their more expensive and well-known competitors, including very serviceable ANC and a highly adjustable EQ. There's a vast middle ground between the Anker buds and the most expensive options, with true wireless buds that bring something to the table at every price point.
As for IEMs, while they can soar into the mid-four-figures, most audiophiles and musicians tend to stick below $500 when selecting a pair. And for budget-conscious shoppers, Headphones.com has recommendations reaching as low as $20. If you're really feeling strapped for cash, my personal recommendation has long been the JVC Gumy in-ear earbuds, which provide the best sound I've found for under $10.
Long gone are the days where cheap earbuds are a death sentence for audio quality. Today, decent audio can be had for less than a chicken sandwich, and the gains you'll make as you climb the price ladder are diminishing. At the top end, you pay for true wireless convenience or IEM precision and craftsmanship, but the vast majority of people will find their best buds by browsing with a strict budget.

What the world's oldest telecommunications company looks like today
It's nearly two hundred years old.
BT Group is best known today for broadband, mobile service and the infrastructure running underneath much of the UK's communications network. Its history, however, starts long before the telephone was a household fixture. BT's lineage reaches back to the Electric Telegraph Company, founded by William Fothergill Cooke and businessman John Lewis Ricardo in 1846 to commercialize electric telegraph technology developed by Cooke and Charles Wheatstone.
The Electric Telegraph Company merged with the International Telegraph Company in 1855, forming the Electric and International Telegraph Company, before being taken over by the General Post Office in 1870. So BT's claim to 1846 comes through its family tree, rather than one company somehow surviving intact for nearly two centuries.
BT isn't the only telecom company with an impressive pedigree, either. Sweden's Telia traces its roots to a state telegraph agency founded in 1853, Telecom Egypt points to its first telegraph line in 1854 and Norway's Telenor dates its beginnings to the Norwegian Telegraph Administration in 1855.
France can go further still, with a state-run optical telegraph network dating to 1794. The catch is that none of these are perfect apples-to-apples comparisons. Like BT, their histories run through government agencies, reorganizations and later commercial companies, which makes crowning a single "world's oldest" telecom company considerably messier than comparing birthdays.
BT's 1846 roots took a few detours
The early British telecommunications business had the sort of structure you might expect from a brand-new technology in Victorian Britain. Private companies built competing networks, struck agreements with railways and fought for customers while lawmakers figured out what exactly to do with all these wires suddenly appearing around the country. By the late 1860s, Parliament was debating whether the government should simply buy the telegraph companies and put the network under the Post Office, but not everyone was sold on this idea.
During debate in 1868, MP George Goschen called it "most absurd" to think the Post Office could create a "hunger and thirst ... for telegrams" among rural customers who could send much cheaper letters instead. Parliament went ahead anyway. Private telegraph systems were bought and consolidated under state control, with the Electric and International Telegraph Company joining the Post Office network in 1870.
Telephone infrastructure eventually took a similar route. The National Telephone Company was absorbed into the Post Office system in 1912, then Post Office Telecommunications became British Telecom in 1980. British Telecommunications formally took over the Post Office's telecoms and data-processing operations in 1981, before privatization began in 1984 with the government selling a majority stake in the newly formed BT plc.
So much for a straight line from 1846.
What BT looks like today
The telegraph machines are long gone, but moving information around Britain is still very much the business. Modern BT operates several familiar consumer brands, including BT itself, EE and Plusnet, alongside its business services operation. It also owns Openreach, the infrastructure company responsible for maintaining and expanding the UK's main fixed telecom network.
If anything inside modern BT resembles that original telegraph business in spirit, it is probably Openreach. It looks after the copper wires and fiber cables connecting homes and businesses, then provides access to hundreds of communications companies that sell broadband and phone services directly to the people using those lines, rather than serving most households itself.
Openreach has been legally separate from BT since reforms proposed by Ofcom, with its own board, employees, management and strategy. However, BT Group still owns it since Ofcom did not require a full ownership split. Mobile is another major part of what BT became. BT completed its acquisition of EE in 2016, giving the group control of what was then the UK's largest mobile network, and EE's 5G+ network now reaches 77 percent of the UK population. BT has also brought BT Mobile back in 2026 for its broadband customers.
William Cooke probably would not recognize much of that, but the cables might look reassuringly familiar. As of June 30, Openreach's full-fiber footprint covered 23.4 million premises, with 9.4 million connected.

WHO welcomed Mr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Spain’s Secretary of State for Health and his delegation on 23 and 24 April 2024 to discuss joint global health priorities. Amongst others, Spain's focus is on universal health coverage and health systems strengthening; pandemic response and emergency medical teams; organ and tissue transplantation; malaria and other tropical diseases; and polio.
During the visit, participants focused on plans and on-going work across a number of areas, including WHO’s Transplantation Program to increase availability; ethical access and oversight of transplantation of human cells; tissues and organs. They also discussed social determinants of health; tobacco and alcohol control; primary health care; access to medicines; universal health coverage; ensuring healthy lives at all ages; nutrition and food safety; health workforce; and emergencies.
Mr Javier Padilla was accompanied by Ms Paola Cannata Molero, Director of the Cabinet of the Secretary of State for Health, Mr Jacobo Fernández Álvarez, Technical Secretary General, Mr Héctor Tejero Franco, Advisor in the Cabinet of the Minister of Health and Responsible for Health and Climate Change, and Mr Roberto Carro Vázquez, Senior Technician of the Office of the Secretary of State for Health. The delegation also had representatives of Spain’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations Office and Other International Organizations in Geneva, including H.E. Ambassador Ms A. Díaz-Rato Revuelta, H.E. Ambassador Ms Clara Cabrera Brasero, and Counsellor Ms María del Carmen Martínez de la Peña.
The Spanish delegation met with Dr Ailan Li, Assistant Director General (ADG) for Universal Health Coverage, Healthier Populations, Dr Catharina Boehme, ADG for External Relations and Governance, Dr Yukiko Nakatani, ADG for Access to Medicines and Health products and ADG for Antimicrobial Resistance ad interim, Dr Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director for WHO Health Health Emergencies Programme.
Left to right: Dr Maria Neira, Director, Environment, Climate Change and Health, H.E. Ambassador Aurora Díaz-Rato Revuelta, Dr Javier Padilla Bernáldez, Secretary of State for Health, Michael Ryan, Deputy Director-General and Executive Director, WHO Health Emergencies Programme. Credit: WHO/Chris Black
WHO’s Management and their teams thanked Spain for their financial and technical support over the years. Spain’s support was instrumental in the last biennium in improving access to quality essential health services and medicines; addressing climate change and healthier environments; and strengthening country capacity in both data and innovation. Spain continues to be a champion of the Global Polio Eradication Initiative.
Spain also contributes to WHO’s work in tackling malaria and neglected and other tropical diseases, and has helped the Organization strengthen countries’ preparedness, readiness, prevention and response for health emergencies, epidemics and pandemics. Spain’s contribution to WHO’s Health Emergency Appeal has helped to protect health in humanitarian emergencies to break the cycles of poverty.
As a world leader in the field of organ and tissue transplantation, Spain plays a key role in WHO’s efforts through its Ministry of Health to improve the safety, quality, efficacy and access to transplants. WHO appreciates and acknowledges Spain as a partner who is not only leading and sharing expertise in support of countries’ development of sustainable, self-sufficient organ transplant systems, but also more generally, a key partner to WHO in health for all.

Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Saturday (August 15, 2026) seconded Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s “intellectual Naxals” comment made during his Independence Day address in New Delhi.
Mr. Fadnavis said that while “armed Naxalism had been defeated, an ideological form of Naxalism prevails”. Addressing the nation on the 80th Independence Day, Mr. Modi said “intellectual Naxals” (dimagi Naxals) have become part of the system and continue to pose a threat to society. The Prime Minister urged citizens to “identify and isolate” them.
Backing Mr. Modi’s statement, Mr. Fadnavis said: “I think the Prime Minister has made a very appropriate reference. Naxalism with a gun has ended. But, we are seeing a more dangerous kind of ‘dimagi Naxalism’.”
Proud to be ‘dimagi Naxal’: Congress’ P. Chidambaram hits back at PM
“Unfortunately, we saw one such example even at today’s Congress programme. The decision to play the complete Vande Mataram on August 15 was taken within the constitutional powers of the country. If reports that Sonia Gandhi was unhappy because the full Vande Mataram was played are true, then what else can this be but ‘dimagi Naxalism’ among people whose minds are filled with anarchy,” he said.
Women’s reservation bill
On the Prime Minister’s pitch to move a Bill to reserve seats for women in Parliament, Mr. Fadnavis said parties opposing the proposal should understand the constitutional conditions attached to the 2023 legislation.
“Those who are selectively reacting to the PM’s appeal on women’s reservation should remember that when the women’s reservation legislation was approved through a constitutional amendment in 2023, two conditions were put in it. The first was completion of the Census and the second was delimitation after the Census. Only after these two processes can the women’s reservation be implemented,” Mr. Fadnavis said.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah had previously introduced the Bill to increase the number of seats in both Houses of Parliament alongside the women’s reservation Bill. The move was opposed by Opposition MPs, especially from southern states, as it could potentially reduce their representation. That Bill was defeated in a session four months ago.
“Today, the situation is the same as it was under the 2023 legislation. If women’s reservation is to be implemented under that law, the Census has to be completed and then delimitation has to be carried out. If you want another option, the only way is to support the new constitutional amendment that has been proposed,” he said.
He accused the Opposition of taking contradictory positions.
“In 2023, you supported the Bill with your vote. Therefore, you also know that women’s reservation cannot be given under that legislation without these two pre-conditions. If you genuinely want women’s reservation, then support the constitutional amendment and pass it with a two-thirds majority. Only then can women get reservation in 2029,” Mr. Fadnavis said.
Mr. Fadnavis also criticised Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge for their absence from the Independence Day function, saying opposition to the BJP should not be equated with opposition to the country.
